translations.an10.13:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these ten fetters. Which ten? Five lower fetters and five higher fetters. And which are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, grasping at precepts and observances, sensual desire, and ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: “Bhikkhus, to the extent that there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; with form or formless; percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared the foremost among them. In the same way, whatever wholesome qualities there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness, converge in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:2: Just as, bhikkhus, the footprints of all living beings that walk on the ground fit into the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant's footprint is declared the foremost among them because of its great size; in the same way, whatever wholesome qualities there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness, converge in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:3: Just as, bhikkhus, in a peaked house, whatever rafters there are all lead to the peak, slope toward the peak, and converge at the peak, and the peak is declared the foremost among them; in the same way, whatever wholesome qualities there are, all of them are rooted in heedfulness, converge in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:7: Just as, bhikkhus, whatever petty kings there are, all of them are followers of a wheel-turning monarch, and the wheel-turning monarch is declared the foremost among them; in the same way, bhikkhus … etc. …
translations.an10.15:8: Just as, bhikkhus, whatever light there is from the stars, all of it does not equal a sixteenth part of the light of the moon, and the moonlight is declared the foremost among them; in the same way, bhikkhus … etc. …
translations.an10.15:9: Just as, bhikkhus, in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and the clouds have vanished, the sun, rising into the sky, dispels all darkness from space and shines, blazes, and radiates; in the same way, bhikkhus … etc. …
translations.an10.17:1: “Bhikkhus, live with a protector, not without a protector. One who lives without a protector lives in suffering. There are these ten qualities that make for a protector. Which ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous, living restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and training by undertaking the training rules. Since a bhikkhu is virtuous … etc. … and trains by undertaking the training rules, this is a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.17:2: Furthermore, a bhikkhu is learned, a sustainer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has heard much of, retained, recited, mentally pondered, and well penetrated by view. Since a bhikkhu is learned … etc. … well penetrated by view, this is also a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.17:3: Furthermore, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, good associates. Since a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, good associates, this is also a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:10: Furthermore, a bhikkhu is mindful, possessing the highest mindfulness and alertness, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago. Thinking, ‘This bhikkhu is mindful, possessing the highest mindfulness and alertness, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago,’ the elder bhikkhus think he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle-ranking bhikkhus … the new bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and instructed. Being sympathized with by the elders, the middle-ranking, and the new bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected for him, not decline. This is also a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:11: Furthermore, a bhikkhu is wise, possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. Thinking, ‘This bhikkhu is wise, possessing the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering,’ the elder bhikkhus think he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle-ranking bhikkhus … the new bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and instructed. Being sympathized with by the elders … etc. … not decline. This is also a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:2: “Bhikkhus, live with a protector, not without a protector. One who lives without a protector lives in suffering. There are these ten qualities that make for a protector. Which ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous … etc. … training by undertaking the training rules. Thinking, ‘This bhikkhu is virtuous, living restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and training by undertaking the training rules,’ the elder bhikkhus think he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle-ranking bhikkhus … the new bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and instructed. Being sympathized with by the elders, the middle-ranking, and the new bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected for him, not decline. This is also a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:4: Furthermore, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, good associates. Thinking, ‘This bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, good associates,’ the elder bhikkhus think he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle-ranking bhikkhus … the new bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and instructed. Being sympathized with by the elders, the middle-ranking, and the new bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected for him, not decline. This is also a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:5: Furthermore, a bhikkhu is easy to speak to, possessing qualities that make him easy to speak to, patient, and receiving instruction respectfully. Thinking, ‘This bhikkhu is easy to speak to, possessing qualities that make him easy to speak to, patient, and receiving instruction respectfully,’ the elder bhikkhus think he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle-ranking bhikkhus … the new bhikkhus also think he should be spoken to and instructed. Being sympathized with by the elders, the middle-ranking, and the new bhikkhus, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected for him, not decline. This is also a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, a mendicant is skilled and tireless in the various duties for their fellow practitioners, possessing the ability to investigate the proper means, and is capable of acting and organizing. The senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think that such a mendicant should be spoken to and exhorted. For one who is pitied by the seniors, the middle ones, and the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, a mendicant loves the teaching and is pleasant in conversation, finding great joy in the higher teaching and the higher discipline. The senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think that such a mendicant should be spoken to and exhorted. For one who is pitied by the seniors, the middle ones, and the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the undertaking of wholesome qualities, being steadfast, firm in effort, and not shirking the responsibility regarding wholesome qualities. The senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think that such a mendicant should be spoken to and exhorted. For one who is pitied by the seniors, the middle ones, and the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. The senior mendicants, the middle mendicants, and the junior mendicants think that such a mendicant should be spoken to and exhorted. For one who is pitied by the seniors, the middle ones, and the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that makes for a protector.
translations.an10.20:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, at a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants...
translations.an10.20:10: And how is a mendicant one whose bodily activity is stilled? Here, a mendicant, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and remains in the fourth absorption, which is purified by equanimity and mindfulness, neither-painful-nor-pleasant. That is how a mendicant is one whose bodily activity is stilled.
translations.an10.20:11: And how is a mendicant one whose mind is well-liberated? Here, a mendicant's mind is liberated from greed, liberated from hate, and liberated from delusion. That is how a mendicant is one whose mind is well-liberated.
translations.an10.20:2: “Mendicants, there are these ten abodes of the noble ones, in which the noble ones have dwelt, are dwelling, or will dwell. What ten? Here, a mendicant has given up five factors, possesses six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has discarded individual truths, has completely given up searching, has unsullied intentions, has stilled bodily activity, is well-liberated in mind, and is well-liberated in wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how is a mendicant one who has given up five factors? Here, a mendicant has given up sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. That is how a mendicant is one who has given up five factors.
translations.an10.20:4: And how is a mendicant one who possesses six factors? Here, a mendicant, seeing a sight with the eye, is neither overjoyed nor dejected, but remains equanimous, mindful, and aware. Hearing a sound with the ear... smelling an odor with the nose... tasting a flavor with the tongue... touching a tangible with the body... cognizing a phenomenon with the mind, they are neither overjoyed nor dejected, but remain equanimous, mindful, and aware. That is how a mendicant is one who possesses six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how is a mendicant one who has a single guard? Here, a mendicant is endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness. That is how a mendicant is one who has a single guard.
translations.an10.20:6: And how is a mendicant one who has four supports? Here, a mendicant uses some things after reflection, endures some things after reflection, avoids some things after reflection, and removes some things after reflection. That is how a mendicant is one who has four supports.
translations.an10.20:7: And how is a mendicant one who has discarded individual truths? Here, whatever individual truths are held by various ascetics and brahmins—such as ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’; ‘the world is finite’ or ‘the world is infinite’; ‘the soul and the body are the same’ or ‘the soul and the body are different’; ‘a Realized One exists after death’, ‘a Realized One does not exist after death’, ‘a Realized One both exists and does not exist after death’, or ‘a Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all these have been struck down, discarded, thrown away, vomited up, let go, abandoned, and relinquished. That is how a mendicant is one who has discarded individual truths.
translations.an10.20:8: And how is a mendicant one who has completely given up searching? Here, a mendicant has given up the search for sensual pleasures, given up the search for existence, and the search for a spiritual life has been stilled. That is how a mendicant is one who has completely given up searching.
translations.an10.20:9: And how is a mendicant one who has unsullied intentions? Here, a mendicant has given up the intention of sensuality, the intention of ill will, and the intention of cruelty. That is how a mendicant is one who has unsullied intentions.
translations.an10.24:1: At one time the venerable Mahācunda was staying among the Cetis at Sahajāti. There the venerable Mahācunda addressed the mendicants: “Friends, mendicants!” “Friend,” those mendicants replied to the venerable Mahācunda. The venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: Suppose, friends, a man who is actually rich claims to be rich, a man who is wealthy claims to be wealthy, a man who is affluent claims to be affluent. When some business requiring money arises, he is able to provide money, grain, silver, or gold. Then they would know of him: ‘This venerable one, being rich, claims to be rich; being wealthy, claims to be wealthy; being affluent, claims to be affluent. Why is that? Because when some business requiring money arises, this venerable one is able to provide money, grain, silver, or gold.’
translations.an10.24:2: “Friends, a bhikkhu might make a claim to knowledge, saying: ‘I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma.’ If greed remains overcoming that bhikkhu, or hatred … or delusion … or anger … or hostility … or contempt … or insolence … or stinginess … or evil envy … or evil desire remains overcoming him, then he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, greed does not exist, for greed remains overcoming this venerable one; this venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, hatred does not exist … delusion … anger … hostility … contempt … insolence … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire does not exist, for evil desire remains overcoming this venerable one.’
translations.an10.24:3: Friends, a bhikkhu might make a claim to development, saying: ‘I am developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.’ If greed remains overcoming that bhikkhu, or hatred … or delusion … or anger … or hostility … or contempt … or insolence … or stinginess … or evil envy … or evil desire remains overcoming him, then he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, greed does not exist, for greed remains overcoming this venerable one; this venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, hatred does not exist … delusion … anger … hostility … contempt … insolence … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire does not exist, for evil desire remains overcoming this venerable one.’
translations.an10.24:5: Suppose, friends, a man who is actually poor claims to be rich, a man who is not wealthy claims to be wealthy, a man who is not affluent claims to be affluent. When some business requiring money arises, he is not able to provide money, grain, silver, or gold. Then they would know of him: ‘This venerable one, being poor, claims to be rich; being not wealthy, claims to be wealthy; being not affluent, claims to be affluent. Why is that? Because when some business requiring money arises, this venerable one is not able to provide money, grain, silver, or gold.’
translations.an10.24:9: Friends, a bhikkhu might make a claim to knowledge and a claim to development, saying: ‘I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; I am developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.’ If greed does not remain overcoming that bhikkhu, or hatred … or delusion … or anger … or hostility … or contempt … or insolence … or stinginess … or evil envy … or evil desire does not remain overcoming him, then he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable one understands in such a way that, for one who understands, greed does not exist, for greed does not remain overcoming this venerable one; this venerable one understands in such a way that, for one who understands, hatred does not exist … delusion … anger … hostility … contempt … insolence … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire does not exist, for evil desire does not remain overcoming this venerable one.’
translations.an10.29:1: “Bhikkhus, as far as the Kasis and Kosalans extend, as far as the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala extends, King Pasenadi of Kosala is reckoned the foremost. Yet even for King Pasenadi of Kosala there is change and alteration. Seeing this, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple becomes disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned, he becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, let alone toward the inferior.
translations.an10.29:10: Perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster. Just as a flax flower is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster, or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster; even so, perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in luster. One is percipient thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the fifth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: Perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster. Just as a kaṇikāra flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster, or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster; even so, perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in luster. One is percipient thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the sixth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and with a red glow. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, red in color, red in appearance, and with a red glow; or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is red, red in color, red in appearance, and with a red glow; even so, not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and with a red glow. They are conscious: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the seventh dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:13: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and with a white glow. Just as the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, and with a white glow; or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, and with a white glow; even so, not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and with a white glow. They are conscious: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the eighth dimension of mastery. These, bhikkhus, are the eight dimensions of mastery.
translations.an10.29:14: The best of these eight dimensions of mastery is when, not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and with a white glow, and is conscious: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ There are beings who are conscious in this way. But even for beings who are conscious in this way, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate toward the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: There are these four ways of practice. Which four? Painful practice with slow intuition, painful practice with swift intuition, pleasant practice with slow intuition, and pleasant practice with swift intuition—these, bhikkhus, are the four ways of practice.
translations.an10.29:16: The best of these four ways of practice is pleasant practice with swift intuition. There are beings who have practiced in this way. But even for beings who have practiced in this way, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate toward the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: There are these four perceptions. Which four? One perceives the limited; one perceives the exalted; one perceives the immeasurable; one perceives the dimension of nothingness, thinking ‘there is nothing’—these, bhikkhus, are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The best of these four perceptions is when one perceives the dimension of nothingness, thinking ‘there is nothing.’ There are beings who are conscious in this way. But even for beings who are conscious in this way, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate toward the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: Bhikkhus, as far as the sun and moon revolve and the quarters shine and beam, so far does the thousandfold world system extend. In that thousandfold world system, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sinerus, kings of mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand Great Kings, a thousand heavens of the Four Great Kings, a thousand heavens of the Thirty-three, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tusita heavens, a thousand heavens of the Gods who Delight in Creation, a thousand heavens of the Gods who Wield Power over Others' Creations, and a thousand Brahma worlds. As far as the thousandfold world system extends, Mahābrahmā is reckoned as the foremost there. But even for Mahābrahmā, bhikkhus, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate toward the best, let alone the inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, bhikkhus, when this world contracts. When the world is contracting, beings for the most part pass away to the Abhassara realm. There they exist, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, glorious, and they remain for a very long time. When the world is contracting, the Abhassara gods are considered the foremost. Yet even for the Abhassara gods there is change and transformation. Seeing this, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple becomes disillusioned with that. Being disillusioned with that, they lose passion for the foremost, let alone for what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: There are these ten bases for kasina meditation. Which ten? One perceives the earth kasina—above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable; one perceives the water kasina … the fire kasina … the air kasina … the blue kasina … the yellow kasina … the red kasina … the white kasina … the space kasina … one perceives the consciousness kasina—above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. These, bhikkhus, are the ten bases for kasina meditation.
translations.an10.29:5: The best of these ten universal bases is when one perceives the consciousness universal, above, below, across, undivided, and limitless. There are beings who have such a perception. But even for beings who have such a perception, there is alteration and change. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it. Being disillusioned, they become detached from the highest, let alone the low.
translations.an10.29:6: There are these eight bases of overcoming. What eight? Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly; overcoming them, one thinks, ‘I know, I see.’ This is the first base of overcoming.
translations.an10.29:7: Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are limitless, beautiful or ugly; overcoming them, one thinks, ‘I know, I see.’ This is the second base of overcoming.
translations.an10.29:8: Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly; overcoming them, one thinks, ‘I know, I see.’ This is the third base of overcoming.
translations.an10.29:9: Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are limitless, beautiful or ugly; overcoming them, one thinks, ‘I know, I see.’ This is the fourth base of overcoming.
translations.an10.51:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an10.51:3: And how is a mendicant skilled in the ways of their own mind? Suppose a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, would examine their own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or a bowl of clear water. If they see any dust or blemish there, they try to remove it. But if they don’t see any dust or blemish there, they are happy and satisfied: ‘How fortunate that I am clean!’ In the same way, a mendicant’s self-examination is very helpful for skillful qualities: ‘Do I usually live full of covetousness or without covetousness? Do I usually live with a mind of ill will or without ill will? Do I usually live overcome by dullness and drowsiness or free from dullness and drowsiness? Do I usually live restless or not restless? Do I usually live with doubt or have I crossed over doubt? Do I usually live angry or not angry? Do I usually live with a defiled mind or an undefiled mind? Do I usually live with a stressed body or an unstressed body? Do I usually live lazy or with energy aroused? Do I usually live unconcentrated or concentrated?’
translations.an10.51:4: If, while examining themselves, a mendicant knows: ‘I usually live full of covetousness, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness, doubt, anger, a defiled mind, a stressed body, laziness, and I am unconcentrated,’ then that mendicant should apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to give up those bad, unskillful qualities. Suppose their clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, they would apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness. In the same way, that mendicant should apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to give up those bad, unskillful qualities.
translations.an10.54:2: And how is a mendicant skilled in the ways of their own mind? Suppose a woman or a man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, would examine their own facial reflection in a clean, bright mirror or a bowl of clear water. If they see any dust or blemish there, they try to remove it. But if they don’t see any dust or blemish there, they are happy and satisfied: ‘How fortunate that I am clean!’ In the same way, a mendicant’s self-examination is very helpful for skillful qualities: ‘Am I someone who gains internal serenity of heart, or am I not? Am I someone who gains insight into principles through higher wisdom, or am I not?’
translations.an10.54:5: But if, while examining themselves, a mendicant knows: ‘I am not someone who gains internal serenity of heart, and I am not someone who gains insight into principles through higher wisdom,’ then that mendicant should apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to gain those skillful qualities. Suppose their clothes or head were on fire. In order to extinguish it, they would apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness. In the same way, that mendicant should apply extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to gain those skillful qualities. After some time, they gain both internal serenity of heart and insight into principles through higher wisdom.
translations.an10.54:6: But if, while examining themselves, a mendicant knows: ‘I am someone who gains internal serenity of heart, and I am someone who gains insight into principles through higher wisdom,’ then that mendicant, standing on those skillful qualities, should apply themselves further to the ending of the defilements.
translations.an10.58:1: “Mendicants, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you: ‘In what are all things rooted? How do they come into being? What is their origin? Where do they converge? What is their head? What is their authority? What is their supreme? What is their core? Where do they merge? What is their final goal?’ Being asked this, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, bhante, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, bhante, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the mendicants will remember it.”
translations.an10.58:2: “Then listen, mendicants, and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those mendicants replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.59:1: “Therefore, mendicants, you should train like this: ‘Our minds will be well-acquainted with our going forth, and arisen evil unskillful qualities will not remain obsessing the mind; our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of impermanence, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of non-self, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of unattractiveness, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of danger, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of the world’s evenness and unevenness, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of the world’s being and non-being, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of the world’s origin and passing away, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of giving up, our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of dispassion, and our minds will be well-acquainted with the perception of cessation.’ That is how you should train, mendicants.”
translations.an10.60:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. At 그 time the venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and reflects: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all activities, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, cessation, nibbāna.’ This is called the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant lives giving up and not clinging to any attachments, fixations, mental prejudices, or underlying tendencies in the world. This is called the perception of non-delight in the whole world.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of dissatisfaction with all activities? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant is horrified, humiliated, and disgusted by all activities. This is called the perception of dissatisfaction with all activities.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and sits down, having folded their legs crosswise, set their body erect, and established mindfulness in front of them. Ever mindful they breathe in, mindful they breathe out. Breathing in long, they know: ‘I breathe in long.’ Breathing out long, they know: ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, they know: ‘I breathe in short.’ Breathing out short, they know: ‘I breathe out short.’ They train: ‘I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.’ They train: ‘I will breathe in calming the bodily activity.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out calming the bodily activity.’ They train: ‘I will breathe in experiencing rapture.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out experiencing rapture.’ They train: ‘I will breathe in experiencing pleasure.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out experiencing pleasure.’ They train: ‘I will breathe in experiencing the mental activity.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out experiencing the mental activity.’ They train: ‘I will breathe in calming the mental activity.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out calming the mental activity.’ They train: ‘I will breathe in experiencing the mind.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out experiencing the mind.’ Gladdening the mind … concentrating the mind … freeing the mind … contemplating impermanence … contemplating dispassion … contemplating cessation … They train: ‘I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment.’ They train: ‘I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment.’ This is called mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If you, Ānanda, were to speak these ten perceptions to the mendicant Girimānanda, it is possible that having heard these ten perceptions, his illness would be stilled on the spot.”
translations.an10.60:2: “Bhante, the venerable Girimānanda is sick, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, bhante, if the Blessed One would visit the venerable Girimānanda out of compassion.” “If you, Ānanda, were to speak ten perceptions to the mendicant Girimānanda, it is possible that having heard these ten perceptions, his illness would be stilled on the spot.
translations.an10.60:3: What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of unattractiveness, the perception of danger, the perception of giving up, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of dissatisfaction with all activities, and mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut and reflects: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, activities are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.’ Thus they live contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates of clinging. This is called the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-self? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘The eye is non-self, forms are non-self; the ear is non-self, sounds are non-self; the nose is non-self, odors are non-self; the tongue is non-self, tastes are non-self; the body is non-self, tactile objects are non-self; the mind is non-self, mental phenomena are non-self.’ Thus he dwells contemplating non-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of unattractiveness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the tips of the hairs, enclosed by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, contents of the stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine.’ Thus he dwells contemplating unattractiveness in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of unattractiveness.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘This body is full of suffering, full of danger. For various diseases arise in this body, such as: eye-disease, ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, headache, earache, mouth-disease, tooth-disease, lip-disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, stomach-ache, fainting, dysentery, piercing pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, nail-scratch, psoriasis, bloody bile, diabetes, hemorrhoids, pustules, fistulas; diseases arising from bile, from phlegm, from wind, from a conflict of the humors, produced by change of season, produced by careless conduct, produced by assault, produced by the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination.’ Thus he dwells contemplating danger in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of giving up? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, and obliterates it. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will... He does not tolerate an arisen thought of harmfulness... He does not tolerate any arisen evil unwholesome states; he abandons them, dispels them, terminates them, and obliterates them. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of giving up.
translations.an10.61:1: “Bhikkhus, a first point of ignorance is not seen, such that one could say: ‘Before this, ignorance did not exist; then it came to be.’ But even though this is said, bhikkhus, it is seen: ‘Ignorance has this as its condition.’
translations.an10.61:2: I say, bhikkhus, that ignorance has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? ‘The five hindrances,’ it should be said. I say, bhikkhus, that the five hindrances have a nutriment... ‘The three kinds of misconduct’... ‘Lack of restraint of the sense faculties’... ‘Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension’... ‘Improper attention’... ‘Lack of faith’... ‘Hearing the untrue Dhamma’... ‘Association with bad persons,’ it should be said.
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, bhikkhus, association with bad persons, being fulfilled, fulfills the hearing of the untrue Dhamma; hearing the untrue Dhamma, being fulfilled, fulfills lack of faith; lack of faith, being fulfilled, fulfills improper attention; improper attention, being fulfilled, fulfills lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension; lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension, being fulfilled, fulfills lack of restraint of the sense faculties; lack of restraint of the sense faculties, being fulfilled, fulfills the three kinds of misconduct; the three kinds of misconduct, being fulfilled, fulfill the five hindrances; the five hindrances, being fulfilled, fulfill ignorance. Such is the nutriment for this ignorance, and such is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:4: Just as, bhikkhus, when it rains in thick droplets on a mountaintop (...) that water, flowing down according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies; the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies, being filled, fill the small ponds; the small ponds, being filled, fill the large lakes; the large lakes, being filled, fill the rivulets; the rivulets, being filled, fill the great rivers; the great rivers, being filled, fill the great ocean; such is the nutriment for that great ocean, and such is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, bhikkhus, association with good persons, being fulfilled, fulfills the hearing of the true Dhamma; hearing the true Dhamma, being fulfilled, fulfills faith; faith, being fulfilled, fulfills proper attention; proper attention, being fulfilled, fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension; mindfulness and clear comprehension, being fulfilled, fulfills restraint of the sense faculties; restraint of the sense faculties, being fulfilled, fulfills the three kinds of good conduct; the three kinds of good conduct, being fulfilled, fulfill the four establishments of mindfulness; the four establishments of mindfulness, being fulfilled, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment, being fulfilled, fulfill true knowledge and liberation. Such is the nutriment for this true knowledge and liberation, and such is its fulfillment.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an10.7:2: “Reverend Sāriputta, could a mendicant gain a state of immersion such that they would not be percipient of earth in earth, nor of water in water, nor of fire in fire, nor of air in air, nor of the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, nor of the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, nor of the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, nor of the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor of this world in this world, nor of the next world in the next world; and yet they would still be percipient?”
translations.an10.7:4: “But how, Reverend Sāriputta, could a mendicant gain such a state of immersion?” “Once, Reverend Ānanda, I was staying right here in Sāvatthī in the Blind Men’s Grove. There I attained such a state of immersion that I was not percipient of earth in earth, nor of water in water, nor of fire in fire, nor of air in air, nor of the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, nor of the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, nor of the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, nor of the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor of this world in this world, nor of the next world in the next world; and yet I was still percipient.”
translations.an3.10:1: “Mendicants, a person who has three qualities and has not given up three stains is cast down into hell. What three? They are unethical, and have not given up the stain of unethical conduct; they are envious, and have not given up the stain of envy; they are stingy, and have not given up the stain of stinginess. A person who has these three qualities and has not given up these three stains is cast down into hell.”
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, in whatever place a mendicant understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ This is the second thing that a mendicant should remember for as long as they live.
translations.an3.15:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Benares, in the Gazelle Park at Isipatana. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an3.15:2: “Mendicants, once upon a time there was a king named Sacetana. Then King Sacetana addressed his chariot-maker: ‘My good chariot-maker, in six months’ time there will be a battle. Can you make me a new pair of wheels?’ ‘I can, your majesty,’ the chariot-maker replied. Then, in six months minus six days, the chariot-maker finished one wheel. Then King Sacetana addressed the chariot-maker: ‘My good chariot-maker, in six days’ time there will be a battle. Is the new pair of wheels finished?’ ‘Your majesty, in these six months minus six days, one wheel has been finished.’ ‘But can you finish the second wheel in these six days?’ ‘I can, your majesty.’ Having finished the second wheel in six days, the chariot-maker took the new pair of wheels to King Sacetana and said: ‘Your majesty, here is your new pair of wheels finished.’ ‘But my good chariot-maker, what is the difference between this wheel that took six months minus six days to finish and this wheel that took six days to finish? I don’t see any difference at all.’ ‘There is a difference, your majesty. Let your majesty see the difference.’
translations.an3.15:3: Then the chariot-maker set in motion the wheel that was finished in six days. When set in motion, it kept going as long as the impulse lasted, then it spun around and fell to the ground. But then he set in motion the wheel that was finished in six months minus six days. When set in motion, it kept going as long as the impulse lasted, then it stood still as if fixed to the axle.
translations.an3.15:5: Now, mendicants, you might think: ‘Surely that chariot-maker at that time was someone else?’ But you should not see it like that. I was that chariot-maker at that time. Then, mendicants, I was skilled in the crooks, flaws, and defects of wood. But now, mendicants, I am the Arahant, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, skilled in the crooks, flaws, and defects of the body; skilled in the crooks, flaws, and defects of speech; skilled in the crooks, flaws, and defects of the mind. For any mendicant or nun whose crooks, flaws, and defects of body, speech, and mind are not given up, they have fallen away from this Dhamma and Training, just like that wheel finished in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: For any mendicant or nun whose crooks, flaws, and defects of body, speech, and mind are given up, they are firmly established in this Dhamma and Training, just like that wheel finished in six months minus six days.
translations.an3.1:3: So, mendicants, the fool is a source of danger, the wise person is not. The fool is a source of calamity, the wise person is not. The fool is a source of misfortune, the wise person is not. There is no danger from a wise person, no calamity from a wise person, no misfortune from a wise person.
translations.an3.20:1: “Monks, a shopkeeper endowed with three factors before long reaches greatness and abundance in wealth. What three? Here, monks, a shopkeeper is shrewd, skilled, and resourceful. And how is a shopkeeper shrewd? Here, a shopkeeper knows his goods: ‘This product was bought for this much, it is being sold for this much; this will be the capital, and this the profit.’ That is how a shopkeeper is shrewd.
translations.an3.20:2: And how is a shopkeeper skilled? Here, a shopkeeper is skilled in buying and selling goods. That is how a shopkeeper is skilled.
translations.an3.20:3: And how is a shopkeeper resourceful? Here, those householders or householders' sons who are wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions, know the shopkeeper thus: ‘This shopkeeper is shrewd, skilled, and capable of supporting his wife and children, and of giving to us from time to time.’ They entrust him with wealth, saying: ‘Friend shopkeeper, take this wealth, support your wife and children, and give to us from time to time.’ That is how a shopkeeper is resourceful. Endowed with these three factors, a shopkeeper before long reaches greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu endowed with three qualities before long reaches greatness and abundance in wholesome qualities. What three? Here, a bhikkhu is shrewd, skilled, and resourceful. And how is a bhikkhu shrewd? Here, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ That is how a bhikkhu is shrewd.
translations.an3.20:5: And how is a bhikkhu skilled? Here, a bhikkhu lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and the undertaking of wholesome qualities, being steadfast, firm in effort, not shirking the responsibility regarding wholesome qualities. That is how a bhikkhu is skilled.
translations.an3.22:1: “Monks, there are these three types of sick people found existing in the world. What three? Here, some sick person, whether they get suitable food or do not get suitable food, whether they get suitable medicine or do not get suitable medicine, whether they get a proper attendant or do not get a proper attendant, does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: But here, some sick person, only if they get suitable food and not if they don't, only if they get suitable medicine and not if they don't, only if they get a proper attendant and not if they don't, recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: Therein, monks, because of that sick person who recovers only if they get suitable food... suitable medicine... and a proper attendant, therefore food for the sick is allowed, medicine for the sick is allowed, and an attendant for the sick is allowed. And because of this sick person, other sick people should also be attended to. These are the three types of sick people found existing in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: In the same way, monks, there are these three persons comparable to the sick found existing in the world. What three? Here, some person, whether they get to see the Tathāgata or do not get to see the Tathāgata, whether they get to hear the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata or do not get to hear it, does not enter the fixed course of rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.22:6: But here, some person, whether they get to see the Tathāgata or do not get to see the Tathāgata, whether they get to hear the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata or do not get to hear it, enters the fixed course of rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.24:1: “Monks, these three persons are very helpful to another person. What three? The person through whom another person has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; this person is very helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, the person through whom another person understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the origin of suffering’... ‘This is the cessation of suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’; this person is very helpful to that person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, the person through whom another person, with the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life; this person is very helpful to that person. These are the three persons who are very helpful to another person.
translations.an3.2:1: “Monks, a fool is characterized by his actions, a wise person is characterized by his actions; wisdom is brilliant in conduct. A fool is to be known by three qualities. What three? By bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. A fool is to be known by these three qualities.
translations.an3.2:2: A wise person is to be known by three qualities. What three? By good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind. A wise person is to be known by these three qualities.
translations.an3.30:4: A person of upside-down wisdom, unintelligent and undiscerning; even if he frequently goes into the presence of bhikkhus,
translations.an3.30:5: He is unable to grasp the beginning of the talk, the middle, or the end; for he lacks wisdom.
translations.an3.30:6: A person of lap-like wisdom is said to be better than him; even if he frequently goes into the presence of bhikkhus,
translations.an3.30:8: And a person of broad wisdom is said to be the best of them; even if he frequently goes into the presence of bhikkhus,
translations.an3.32:4: “Ananda, it is when a bhikkhu has the following thought: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nibbana.’ It is in this way, Ananda, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that there would be no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit in this body with its consciousness, nor any I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit regarding all external signs; and that he would enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit no longer exist.”
translations.an3.33:1: Then the venerable Sariputta went to the Blessed One, bowed, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Sariputta, I could teach the Dhamma in brief; I could teach the Dhamma in detail; I could teach the Dhamma both in brief and in detail; but those who understand are rare.” “Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma in brief, in detail, and both in brief and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
translations.an3.33:2: “Therefore, Sariputta, you should train yourselves like this: ‘There will be no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit in this body with its consciousness; there will be no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit regarding all external signs; and we will enter and dwell in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and underlying tendency to conceit no longer exist.’ That is how you should train yourselves, Sariputta.
translations.an3.33:3: When, Sariputta, a bhikkhu has no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit in this body with its consciousness, nor regarding all external signs, and when he enters and dwells in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom where these no longer exist, then he is called a bhikkhu who has cut off craving, discarded the fetter, and by the full breakthrough of conceit, has made an end of suffering. And it was with reference to this that I said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Udaya:
translations.an3.33:4: ‘The abandoning of sensual perceptions, and of both types of unhappiness; the dispelling of sloth, and the warding off of remorse.’
translations.an3.34:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma. Which three? Greed is a cause for the origination of kamma, hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma, delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma.
translations.an3.34:10: Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed without delusion, born of non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, originated from non-delusion: when delusion has vanished, that kamma is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising.
translations.an3.34:11: Suppose, bhikkhus, there were seeds that were intact, not rotten, not damaged by wind or sun, full of life, and well-preserved. A man would burn them with fire. Having burned them with fire, he would make them into ashes. Having made them into ashes, he would winnow them in a strong wind or let them be carried away by a swift-flowing river. Thus those seeds would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and no longer subject to future arising. In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed without greed, born of non-greed, caused by non-greed, originated from non-greed: when greed has vanished, that kamma is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising.
translations.an3.34:13: Born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion—the unwise one; whatever kamma is performed by him, whether a little or a lot; it is to be experienced right here, no other ground is found.
translations.an3.34:2: Whatever kamma, bhikkhus, is performed with greed, born of greed, caused by greed, originated from greed: wherever one’s selfhood is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there one experiences the result of that kamma, whether in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent life.
translations.an3.34:5: Suppose, bhikkhus, there were seeds that were intact, not rotten, not damaged by wind or sun, full of life, and well-preserved, sown in a good field, in well-prepared soil. And the sky would provide rain in due season. Thus those seeds would attain growth, increase, and abundance. In the same way, bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed with greed, born of greed, caused by greed, originated from greed: wherever one’s selfhood is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there one experiences the result of that kamma, whether in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent life.
translations.an3.34:6: Whatever kamma is performed with hatred … whatever kamma is performed with delusion, born of delusion, caused by delusion, originated from delusion: wherever one’s selfhood is reborn, there that kamma ripens. Wherever that kamma ripens, there one experiences the result of that kamma, whether in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent life. These, bhikkhus, are the three causes for the origination of kamma.
translations.an3.34:9: Bhikkhus, whatever kamma is performed without hatred, born of non-hatred, caused by non-hatred, originated from non-hatred: when hatred has vanished, that kamma is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising.
translations.an3.35:3: “Therefore, prince, I will ask you a question in return. Answer it as you see fit. What do you think, prince? Suppose there were a householder or a householder’s son with a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows shut. There he would have a couch spread with a long-fleeced woolen rug, a white woolen rug, a floral-embroidered rug, a rug of choice antelope hide, with a canopy above and red bolsters at both ends. An oil lamp would be burning there, and four wives would attend to him in all sorts of pleasing ways. What do you think, prince? Would he sleep happily or not? Or how does it seem to you?” “He would sleep happily, bhante. He would be one of those in the world who sleep happily.”
translations.an3.35:4: “What do you think, prince? Might there arise in that householder or householder’s son fevers born of passion, physical or mental, so that, burning with those fevers born of passion, he would sleep poorly?” “Yes, bhante.”
translations.an3.35:8: He always sleeps happily, the brahmin who is fully extinguished; who does not cling to sensual pleasures, cooled, without acquisitions.
translations.an3.39:10: Living thus, having known the state without acquisitions; the intoxications with health, youth, and life.
translations.an3.39:2: “Bhikkhus, I had three palaces—one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season. In the rainy season palace, for the four months of the rains, I was entertained by musicians—none of whom were men—and I did not descend from the palace. Whereas in other people’s homes the servants, workers, and staff are given broken rice with sour gruel to eat, in my father’s home the servants, workers, and staff were given fine rice with meat.”
translations.an3.39:3: “Bhikkhus, endowed with such prosperity and such refinement, this thought occurred to me: ‘An unlearned ordinary person, being himself subject to old age, not beyond old age, when he sees another who is old, is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted, forgetting his own situation. I too am subject to old age, not beyond old age. If I, being subject to old age, not beyond old age, were to be troubled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is old, that would not be fitting for me.’ As I reflected thus, bhikkhus, the intoxication with youth that I had was entirely abandoned.”
translations.an3.39:4: “An unlearned ordinary person, being himself subject to illness, not beyond illness, when he sees another who is ill, is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted, forgetting his own situation: ‘I too am subject to illness, not beyond illness. If I, being subject to illness, not beyond illness, were to be troubled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is ill, that would not be fitting for me.’ As I reflected thus, bhikkhus, the intoxication with health that I had was entirely abandoned.”
translations.an3.39:5: “An unlearned ordinary person, being himself subject to death, not beyond death, when he sees another who is dead, is troubled, ashamed, and disgusted, forgetting his own situation: ‘I too am subject to death, not beyond death. If I, being subject to death, not beyond death, were to be troubled, ashamed, and disgusted upon seeing another who is dead, that would not be fitting for me.’ As I reflected thus, bhikkhus, the intoxication with life that I had was entirely abandoned.”
translations.an3.39:7: “Bhikkhus, intoxicated with the intoxication of youth, a bhikkhu gives up the training and returns to the lower life. Intoxicated with the intoxication of health... Intoxicated with the intoxication of life, a bhikkhu gives up the training and returns to the lower life.”
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to old age, and also subject to death; though such is their nature, ordinary people are disgusted by them.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to be disgusted by those who have such a nature, it would not be fitting for me, living as I do.
translations.an3.40:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these three authorities. Which three? The authority of oneself, the authority of the world, and the authority of the Dhamma. And what, bhikkhus, is the authority of oneself? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut reflects thus: ‘I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of a robe. I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of almsfood, for the sake of a lodging, or for the sake of becoming this or that. But rather, I am beset by birth, old age, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; I am beset by suffering, overwhelmed by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known. If I were to seek the same kind of sensual pleasures that I left behind when I went forth from the home life into homelessness, or even worse ones, that would not be fitting for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be aroused and unsluggish, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and relaxed, my mind concentrated and one-pointed.’ Having made himself the authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless, and he maintains himself in purity. This, bhikkhus, is called the authority of oneself.”
translations.an3.40:3: “And what, bhikkhus, is the authority of the Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut reflects thus: ‘I did not go forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of a robe... Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known. The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. Now there are my fellow practitioners who live knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline, were to live lazy and negligent, that would not be fitting for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy shall be aroused and unsluggish... my mind concentrated and one-pointed.’ Having made the Dhamma itself the authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless, and he maintains himself in purity. This, bhikkhus, is called the authority of the Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the three authorities.”
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secret in the world for one who does an evil deed; your own self, O man, knows whether it is true or false.
translations.an3.40:5: Indeed, my friend, you despise your own self, a noble witness, you who hide the evil that is in yourself from yourself.
translations.an3.40:6: The gods and the Tathāgatas see the fool who lives crookedly in the world; therefore, with oneself as authority, with the world as authority, wise and meditative; with the Dhamma as authority, living according to the Dhamma, the sage who strives for the truth does not fall away.
translations.an3.48:1: “Mendicants, supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains, the great sal trees grow in three ways. In what three? They grow in branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow in bark and shoots; and they grow in softwood and heartwood. Supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains, the great sal trees grow in these three ways.
translations.an3.48:2: In the same way, mendicants, supported by a person of faith in a family, the people within grow in three ways. In what three? They grow in faith, they grow in ethical conduct, and they grow in wisdom. Supported by a person of faith in a family, the people within grow in these three ways.”
translations.an3.48:3: Just as a mountain made of rock, in the wild and great forest; supported by it, the trees, those lords of the forest, grow.
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins who were old, elderly, senior, advanced in years, and having reached the final stage of life—being one hundred and twenty years old—approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the polite and courteous talk was finished, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those brahmins said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, we are brahmins, old, elderly, senior, advanced in years, and having reached the final stage of life—being one hundred and twenty years old. But we have not done what is beautiful, we have not done what is skillful, we have not made a shelter from fear. Let Master Gotama exhort us, let Master Gotama instruct us, so that it may be for our lasting welfare and happiness.”
translations.an3.51:2: “Indeed, brahmins, you are old, elderly, senior, advanced in years, and having reached the final stage of life—being one hundred and twenty years old. And you have not done what is beautiful, you have not done what is skillful, you have not made a shelter from fear. This world, brahmins, is being swept away by old age, sickness, and death. When the world is thus being swept away by old age, sickness, and death, whatever restraint of body, restraint of speech, and restraint of mind one has here—that is one’s shelter, one’s cave, one’s island, one’s refuge, and one’s support after passing away.
translations.an3.51:3: Life is swept away, its span is short; for one swept away by old age, there are no shelters. Seeing this danger in death, one should perform merits that bring happiness.”
translations.an3.52:4: When the world is thus on fire, with old age and death; one should extract one's wealth by giving, for what is given is well-extracted.”
translations.an3.57:2: “Vaccha, those who say: ‘The ascetic Gotama says this: “Gifts should be given only to me... not to others' disciples is it of great fruit”’—they are not speaking what I have said. They misrepresent me with what is false and untrue. Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstacle for three people, a barrier for three. Which three? He creates an obstacle to the merit of the donor, he creates an obstacle to the gain of the recipients, and his own self is already undermined and injured. Vaccha, whoever prevents another from giving a gift creates an obstacle for these three, a barrier for these three.”
translations.an3.5:1: “Mendicants, a fool is to be known by three qualities. What three? They ask a question without reason, they answer a question without reason, and when another answers a question reasonably, with well-rounded, smooth, and appropriate words and phrases, they do not approve of it. A fool is to be known by these three qualities.”
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the polite and courteous talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, we are brahmins. We perform sacrifices and we get others to perform sacrifices. In this matter, Master Gotama, both the one who sacrifices and the one who gets others to sacrifice are practicing a path of merit involving many people, namely, the matter of sacrifice. But this one, Master Gotama, who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness from whatever family, who tames himself alone, calms himself alone, and extinguishes himself alone—thus he is practicing a path of merit involving only one person, namely, the matter of going forth.”
translations.an3.60:10: Furthermore, brahmin, someone does not reveal by means of a sign, but rather, having heard the sound of humans or non-humans or deities, they reveal: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is like this, your thought is such.’ Even if they reveal much, it is just so and not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:11: Furthermore, brahmin, someone does not reveal by means of a sign, nor by hearing the sound of humans or non-humans or deities, but rather, having heard the sound of the vibration of thought as one thinks and ponders, they reveal: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is like this, your thought is such.’ Even if they reveal much, it is just so and not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:12: Furthermore, brahmin, someone does not reveal by means of a sign, nor by hearing the sound of humans or non-humans or deities, nor by hearing the sound of the vibration of thought as one thinks and ponders, but rather, by encompassing with their own mind the mind of one who has attained a concentration without thought and pondering, they understand: ‘According to the way the mental formations of this good person are directed, immediately after this thought, he will think such and such a thought.’ Even if they reveal much, it is just so and not otherwise. This, brahmin, is called the miracle of telepathy.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, someone instructs thus: ‘Think thus, do not think thus; attend thus, do not attend thus; abandon this, enter and dwell in that.’ This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, brahmin, which miracle do you prefer as being more excellent and more sublime?”
translations.an3.60:14: “In this matter, Master Gotama, regarding the miracle where someone experiences various kinds of psychic power... even exercising mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world; this miracle, Master Gotama, only the one who does it experiences it, it belongs only to the one who does it. This miracle, Master Gotama, seems to me to be like a magic trick.”
translations.an3.60:16: “But, Master Gotama, as for the miracle of instruction: here someone gives instruction like this: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that; attend like this, don’t attend like that; give this up, enter and dwell in that.’ This, Master Gotama, is the miracle that I prefer among these three miracles, as it is more excellent and more sublime.”
translations.an3.60:17: “It’s incredible, Master Gotama, it’s amazing! How well-spoken this was by Master Gotama. And we regard Master Gotama as one who possesses these three miracles. For Master Gotama experiences many kinds of psychic power … even exercising power with the body as far as the Brahma-realm. For Master Gotama understands the minds of others by encompassing them with his own mind: ‘According to how this person’s mental formations are directed, immediately after this thought, he will think such-and-such a thought.’ For Master Gotama gives instruction like this: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that; attend like this, don’t attend like that; give this up, enter and dwell in that.’”
translations.an3.60:18: “Certainly, brahmin, your words are aggressive and intrusive; nevertheless, I will answer you. I do experience many kinds of psychic power … even exercising power with the body as far as the Brahma-realm. I do understand the minds of others by encompassing them with my own mind: ‘According to how this person’s mental formations are directed, immediately after this thought, he will think such-and-such a thought.’ And I do give instruction like this: ‘Think like this, don’t think like that; attend like this, don’t attend like that; give this up, enter and dwell in that.’”
translations.an3.60:19: “But, Master Gotama, is there even one other bhikkhu who possesses these three miracles, besides Master Gotama?” “Brahmin, it is not just one hundred, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred, but many more bhikkhus than that who possess these three miracles.” “But where, Master Gotama, are those bhikkhus staying now?” “In this very Saṅgha of bhikkhus, brahmin.”
translations.an3.60:2: “In that case, brahmin, I will ask you a question in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, brahmin? Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He says: ‘Come, this is the path, this is the way. Having realized it for myself with direct knowledge, I make known the unsurpassed goal of the spiritual life. Come, you too practice in such a way that you too will realize for yourselves with direct knowledge, enter, and dwell in the unsurpassed goal of the spiritual life.’ Thus this teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice accordingly for that purpose; and there are many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of them.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin? This being so, is this practice of merit involving many people or just one person, that is, the matter of going forth?” “This being so, Master Gotama, this practice of merit involves many people, that is, the matter of going forth.”
translations.an3.60:4: When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “Brahmin, of these two practices, which practice do you prefer as being less difficult, less involving of great effort, yet more fruitful and more beneficial?” When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are like this. These are the ones I honor, these are the ones I praise.”
translations.an3.60:5: A second time the Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “Brahmin, I am not asking you: ‘Who do you honor and who do you praise?’ I am asking you this: ‘Brahmin, of these two practices, which practice do you prefer as being less difficult, less involving of great effort, yet more fruitful and more beneficial?’” A second time the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are like this. These are the ones I honor, these are the ones I praise.”
translations.an3.60:7: Then the Blessed One thought: “Even for a third time, when asked a legitimate question by Ānanda, the brahmin Saṅgārava falters and does not answer. Let me release him.” Then the Blessed One said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “Brahmin, what was the topic of conversation today among the king’s officials as they sat assembled in the royal palace?” “Today, Master Gotama, this topic of conversation arose among the king’s officials as they sat assembled in the royal palace: ‘Formerly, it seems, there were fewer bhikkhus, but more of them displayed the miracle of psychic power transcending human capacity; but now there are more bhikkhus, but fewer of them display the miracle of psychic power transcending human capacity.’ This was the topic of conversation that arose today among the king’s officials as they sat assembled in the royal palace.”
translations.an3.60:8: “Brahmin, there are these three miracles. Which three? The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction. And what, brahmin, is the miracle of psychic power? Here, brahmin, someone experiences many kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through an enclosure, through a mountain as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though through water; he walks on water without sinking as though on earth; he travels through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he even exercises power with the body as far as the Brahma-realm. This is called the miracle of psychic power."
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of mind-reading? Here, brahmin, someone reads by means of a sign: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is like this, your thought is such.’ Even if he reads many times, it is just so and not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: ‘These are the four noble truths’ is the Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, untarnished, irreproachable, and not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins. Thus it was said. And with reference to what was this said? Dependent on the six elements, monks, there is the descent of the embryo; when there is descent, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling. For one who feels, monks, I declare: ‘This is suffering,’ I declare: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ I declare: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ I declare: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, (…) death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair are suffering, association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come to be.
