Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: For those who fall back on past deeds as the essential factor, monks, there is no desire or effort regarding ‘this should be done’ or ‘this should not be done.’ Since what should and should not be done are not truly and reliably found, they live unmindful and unguarded, and there is no legitimate ascetic discourse among them. This, monks, is my first legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view.
translations.an3.61:8: These, monks, are the three sectarian tenets which, when fully questioned, examined, and discussed by the wise, even if they go to the end, result in non-action.
translations.an3.61:9: But this, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, untarnished, irreproachable, and not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what, monks, is the Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, untarnished, irreproachable, and not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins? ‘These are the six elements’ is the Dhamma taught by me... ‘These are the six bases of contact’ is the Dhamma taught by me... ‘These are the eighteen mental explorations’ is the Dhamma taught by me... ‘These are the four noble truths’ is the Dhamma taught by me that is unrefuted, untarnished, irreproachable, and not censured by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an3.62:1: “Monks, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of these three dangers that separate mother and son. Which three? There is a time, monks, when a great fire breaks out. When a great fire breaks out, villages, towns, and cities are burned. When villages, towns, and cities are burning, there a mother cannot get to her son, nor can a son get to his mother. This, monks, is the first danger separating mother and son that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of.
translations.an3.62:2: Furthermore, monks, there is a time when a great storm breaks out. When a great storm breaks out, a great flood arises. When a great flood arises, villages, towns, and cities are swept away. When villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, there a mother cannot get to her son, nor can a son get to his mother. This, monks, is the second danger separating mother and son that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of.
translations.an3.62:3: Furthermore, monks, there is a time when there is danger from forest-dwelling rebels, and the country folk mount their wagons and flee. When there is danger from forest-dwelling rebels and the country folk are fleeing in their wagons, there a mother cannot get to her son, nor can a son get to his mother. This, monks, is the third danger separating mother and son that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of. These, monks, are the three dangers separating mother and son that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of.
translations.an3.62:4: “Monks, an unlearned ordinary person speaks of these three as ‘perils where a mother and son are separated,’ even though they are actually ‘perils where a mother and son are together.’ What three? There comes a time, monks, when a great fire breaks out. When the great fire breaks out, villages, towns, and cities are burned. While villages, towns, and cities are burning, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her son, and a son finds his mother. This, monks, is the first peril that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of as a ‘peril where a mother and son are separated,’ even though it is actually a ‘peril where a mother and son are together.’
translations.an3.62:5: Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when a great cloud rises. When the great cloud rises, a great flood occurs. When the great flood occurs, villages, towns, and cities are swept away. While villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her son, and a son finds his mother. This, monks, is the second peril that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of as a ‘peril where a mother and son are separated,’ even though it is actually a ‘peril where a mother and son are together.’
translations.an3.62:6: Furthermore, monks, there comes a time when there is the peril of a forest uprising, and the country folk mount their vehicles and flee. When there is the peril of a forest uprising and the country folk are fleeing in their vehicles, there comes a time when occasionally a mother finds her son, and a son finds his mother. This, monks, is the third peril that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of as a ‘peril where a mother and son are separated,’ even though it is actually a ‘peril where a mother and son are together.’ These, monks, are the three perils that an unlearned ordinary person speaks of as ‘perils where a mother and son are separated,’ even though they are actually ‘perils where a mother and son are together.’
translations.an3.62:7: There are these three perils where a mother and son are truly separated. What three? The peril of old age, the peril of sickness, and the peril of death. A mother cannot, by having her way, get this for her son who is growing old: ‘I am growing old, let my son not grow old.’ Nor can a son, by having his way, get this for his mother who is growing old: ‘I am growing old, let my mother not grow old.’
translations.an3.62:8: A mother cannot, by having her way, get this for her son who is falling sick: ‘I am falling sick, let my son not fall sick.’ Nor can a son, by having his way, get this for his mother who is falling sick: ‘I am falling sick, let my mother not fall sick.’
translations.an3.62:9: A mother cannot, by having her way, get this for her son who is dying: ‘I am dying, let my son not die.’ Nor can a son, by having his way, get this for his mother who is dying: ‘I am dying, let my mother not die.’ These, monks, are the three perils where a mother and son are truly separated.”
translations.an3.63:1: At one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of monks when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Venāgapura. The brahmin householders of Venāgapura heard: “It is said that the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan family, has arrived at Venāgapura. A good report of that Master Gotama has spread: ‘That Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, a knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ He makes known this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, having realized it through his own direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. It is good to see such Arahants.”
translations.an3.63:11: “It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is amazing! Who else but Master Gotama could be a gainer at will, a gainer without difficulty, a gainer without trouble, of such noble high and luxurious beds?”
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmin householders of Venāgapura went to the Blessed One. Some bowed to the Blessed One and sat to one side; some exchanged greetings with him and, after exchanging pleasant and polite conversation, sat to one side; some held up their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat to one side; some announced their name and clan and sat to one side; and some sat to one side in silence. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said to the Blessed One:
translations.an3.63:5: “Brahmin, there are these three high and luxurious beds that I now obtain at will, without difficulty, without trouble. What three? The celestial high and luxurious bed, the divine high and luxurious bed, and the noble high and luxurious bed. These, brahmin, are the three high and luxurious beds that I now obtain at will, without difficulty, without trouble.”
translations.an4.10:10: Beings go to saṃsāra, going to birth and death; but those who have fully understood sensual pleasures and the bond of existence in every way,
translations.an4.10:9: Bound by the bond of sensual pleasure and by the bond of existence, both; bound by the bond of views, preceded by ignorance.
translations.an4.18:1: “Monks, there are these four ways of not going to a bad destination. What four? One does not go to a bad destination through desire, one does not go to a bad destination through hatred, one does not go to a bad destination through delusion, one does not go to a bad destination through fear. These, monks, are the four ways of not going to a bad destination.”
translations.an4.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying among the Vajjis at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an4.1:4: “Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation; these things have been understood by the famous Gotama.
translations.an4.24:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāketa in the Kāḷaka monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an4.24:2: “Monks, whatever in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and examined by the mind—that I know.”
translations.an4.24:5: If I were to say of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized... 'I know it and I do not know it,' that would be the same for him.
translations.an4.24:7: Thus, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata, seeing what is to be seen, does not conceive of the seen, does not conceive of the unseen, does not conceive of what is to be seen, does not conceive of a seer. Hearing what is to be heard, he does not conceive of the heard, does not conceive of the unheard, does not conceive of what is to be heard, does not conceive of a hearer. Sensing what is to be sensed, he does not conceive of the sensed, does not conceive of the unsensed, does not conceive of what is to be sensed, does not conceive of a senser. Cognizing what is to be cognized, he does not conceive of the cognized, does not conceive of the uncognized, does not conceive of what is to be cognized, does not conceive of a cognizer. Thus, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is such among things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. And I say that there is no other 'Such' who is higher or more sublime than that 'Such.'
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed, held to be true by others; among those who are self-fettered, one who is 'Such' would not take as true or false what others say.
translations.an4.28:1: “Bhikkhus, these four noble lineages are original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, and never before adulterated; they are not being adulterated and will not be adulterated; they are not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe. He does not engage in an improper search for the sake of a robe. If he does not get a robe, he is not troubled; and if he gets a robe, he uses it without being tied to it, infatuated with it, or blindly attached to it, seeing the danger and understanding the escape. Yet he does not exalt himself or disparage others because of his contentment with any kind of robe. One who is skillful in this, not lazy, clearly comprehending and mindful, is called a bhikkhu standing in the ancient, original noble lineage.
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, a bhikkhu delights in development and finds joy in development; he delights in abandoning and finds joy in abandoning. Yet he does not exalt himself or disparage others because of his delight in development and abandoning. One who is skillful in this, not lazy, clearly comprehending and mindful, is called a bhikkhu standing in the ancient, original noble lineage. These, bhikkhus, are the four noble lineages... not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an4.28:5: A bhikkhu endowed with these four noble lineages, even if he dwells in the east, he overcomes discontent, and discontent does not overcome him. Even if he dwells in the west... the north... the south, he overcomes discontent, and discontent does not overcome him. Why is that? Because the wise one is a conqueror of both discontent and delight."
translations.an4.28:6: Discontent does not overcome the wise one, nor does delight overcome the wise one; the wise one overcomes discontent, for the wise one is a conqueror of discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels, by which the four-wheeled vehicle of gods and humans turns, and possessed of which gods and humans soon reach greatness and abundance in wealth. Which four? Living in a suitable locality, relying on superior persons, right self-direction, and having performed merit in the past. These are the four wheels..."
translations.an4.32:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of sympathy. Which four? Giving, endearing speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. These are the four bases of sympathy."
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and endearing speech, beneficial conduct here, and impartiality in things, each as is appropriate in each case; these sympathies in the world are like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: If these sympathies did not exist, a mother would not receive honor or respect because of her child, nor would a father because of his child.
translations.an4.33:1: “Bhikkhus, the lion, the king of beasts, comes out from his lair in the evening. Having come out, he stretches. Having stretched, he surveys the four quarters. Having surveyed the four quarters, he roars his lion’s roar three times. Having roared his lion’s roar three times, he sets out for food. Whatever animals hear the sound of the lion, the king of beasts, roaring, they for the most part are filled with fear, urgency, and terror. Those who live in holes enter their holes; those who live in water enter the water; those who live in the forest enter the forest; the birds take to the sky. Even those royal elephants, bound with strong leather thongs in the villages, towns, and capital cities, break and burst those bonds and, terrified, voiding excrement and urine, they flee here and there. So powerful, bhikkhus, is the lion, the king of beasts, among animals, so majestic and mighty.
translations.an4.33:2: In the same way, bhikkhus, when a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One... he teaches the Dhamma: ‘Such is identity, such is the origin of identity, such is the cessation of identity, such is the way leading to the cessation of identity.’ Then even those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, and full of happiness, dwelling for a long time in high celestial mansions, when they hear the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, they for the most part are filled with fear, urgency, and terror: ‘It seems, sirs, that we who were permanent are actually impermanent; we who were stable are actually unstable; we who were eternal are actually non-eternal. It seems, sirs, that we are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and included within identity.’ So powerful, bhikkhus, is the Tathāgata in the world with its gods, so majestic and mighty."
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, through direct knowledge, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, the Teacher, the peerless person in the world with its gods,
translations.an4.33:4: Taught identity and its cessation, the origin of identity, and the noble eightfold path that leads to the stilling of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: “Monks, there are these four supreme kinds of faith. What four? To the extent that there are beings—whether footless, with two feet, four feet, or many feet; with form or formless; percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared the supreme among them. Those who have faith in the Buddha have faith in the supreme. And for those with faith in the supreme, the result is supreme.
translations.an4.34:2: To the extent that there are conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the supreme among them. Those who have faith in the Noble Eightfold Path have faith in the supreme. And for those with faith in the supreme, the result is supreme.
translations.an4.34:3: To the extent that there are things conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the supreme among them, that is: the crushing of pride, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the round, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Those who have faith in the Dhamma of dispassion have faith in the supreme. And for those with faith in the supreme, the result is supreme.
translations.an4.34:4: To the extent that there are communities or groups, the Sangha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the supreme among them, that is: the four pairs of persons, the eight individual persons—this Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those who have faith in the Sangha have faith in the supreme. And for those with faith in the supreme, the result is supreme. These, monks, are the four supreme kinds of faith.
translations.an4.34:5: For those with faith in the supreme, knowing the supreme Dhamma; for those with faith in the supreme Buddha, the unsurpassed one worthy of offerings.
translations.an4.34:6: For those with faith in the supreme Dhamma, the peace of dispassion and happiness; for those with faith in the supreme Sangha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.34:7: Giving gifts to the supreme, supreme merit increases; supreme long life, beauty, status, fame, happiness, and strength.
translations.an4.35:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Then the Brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having exchanged polite and friendly greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: “Master Gotama, we designate a person as one of great wisdom, a great man, if they are endowed with four qualities. What four? Here, Master Gotama, he is very learned in various subjects; he understands the meaning of whatever is stated: ‘This is the meaning of this statement, that is the meaning of that statement.’ Furthermore, he is mindful, able to remember and recall what was done and said long ago. And in the various duties of a householder, he is skillful and tireless, endowed with the ability to investigate the proper means, capable of doing and organizing them. These are the four qualities, Master Gotama, by which we designate a person as one of great wisdom, a great man. If Master Gotama thinks I should be commended, let him commend me; if I should be criticized, let him criticize me.”
translations.an4.35:6: He who understood for all beings the release from the snare of death; for the welfare of gods and humans, he proclaimed the Way, the Dhamma; seeing and hearing which, many people find faith.
translations.an4.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was walking along the highway between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabya. The Brahmin Doṇa was also walking along the highway between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabya. The Brahmin Doṇa saw the wheels on the soles of the Blessed One’s feet, with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in every way; seeing them, he thought: ‘It is wonderful, indeed! It is amazing, indeed! These will not be the footprints of one who is a human being.’ Then the Blessed One stepped off the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree, crossing his legs, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then the Brahmin Doṇa, following the footprints, saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of the tree—graceful, inspiring faith, with peaceful faculties and a peaceful mind, attained to the highest self-control and serenity, tamed, guarded, with restrained faculties, a Great One. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One and said:
translations.an4.36:2: “Will you be a god, sir?” “Brahmin, I will not be a god.” “Will you be a gandhabba, sir?” “Brahmin, I will not be a gandhabba.” “Will you be a yakkha, sir?” “Brahmin, I will not be a yakkha.” “Will you be a human being, sir?” “Brahmin, I will not be a human being.”
translations.an4.36:4: “Brahmin, those taints by which I might have become a god, if they were not abandoned—those taints are abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Those taints by which I might have become a gandhabba... a yakkha... a human being... those taints are abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Just as, Brahmin, a blue, red, or white lotus, born in the water and growing in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsullied by the water; even so, Brahmin, born in the world and growing in the world, I have overcome the world and dwell unsullied by the world. Remember me, Brahmin, as a Buddha.”
translations.an4.37:1: “Monks, a monk endowed with four qualities is incapable of falling away and is right in the presence of Nibbāna. What four? Here, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue, guards the doors of his senses, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: And how, monks, is a monk accomplished in virtue? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, training himself by undertaking the training rules. This is how, monks, a monk is accomplished in virtue.”
translations.an4.37:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who guards the doors of the senses? Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye faculty; he achieves restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having felt a tactile object with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the mind faculty; he achieves restraint of the mind faculty. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who guards the doors of the senses.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu moderate in eating? Here, bhikkhus, reflecting wisely, a bhikkhu consumes food neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for fattening, nor for beautification; but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for keeping it unharmed, for supporting the spiritual life; thinking: ‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not arouse new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live in comfort.’ In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness? Here, bhikkhus, during the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, a bhikkhu purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion's posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, after noting in his mind the time for rising. After rising, during the last watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness. Possessing these four qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is incapable of falling away and is close to Nibbāna.
translations.an4.37:6: Established in virtue, a bhikkhu, / and restrained in the senses; / moderate in eating, / he is devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Living thus, ardent, / untiring day and night; / developing wholesome qualities, / for the sake of attaining security from bondage.
translations.an4.38:1: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has discarded individual truths is called ‘one who has completely given up searching, whose bodily activities are calmed, one who is withdrawn.’ And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has discarded individual truths? Here, bhikkhus, whatever individual truths are held by various recluses and brahmins—such as: ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’; ‘the world is finite’ or ‘the world is infinite’; ‘the soul and the body are the same’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body is another’; ‘the Tathāgata exists after death’ or ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death’ or ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all these he has shaken off, discarded, abandoned, vomited up, let go of, relinquished, and renounced. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has discarded individual truths.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu withdrawn? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is withdrawn. A bhikkhu who has discarded individual truths is called ‘one who has completely given up searching, whose bodily activities are calmed, one who is withdrawn.’
translations.an4.38:5: The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, / along with the search for a spiritual life; / thus the grasping at truth, / the accumulation of standpoints of views.
translations.an4.38:6: For one detached from all passion, / liberated by the destruction of craving; / searches have been relinquished, / and standpoints of views uprooted.
translations.an4.52:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which lead to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses experiential confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ This, bhikkhus, is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses experiential confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ This, bhikkhus, is the second stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses experiential confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ This, bhikkhus, is the third stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. These, bhikkhus, are the four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which lead to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.”
translations.an4.52:5: One whose faith in the Tathāgata / is unshakable and well-established; / and whose virtue is good, / dear to the noble ones and praised.
translations.an4.52:6: Whoever has confidence in the Saṅgha, and whose vision is upright; they say that person is not poor, their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: At one time the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Many householders, both men and women, were also traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Then the Blessed One left the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree. The householders saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of the tree. Having seen him, they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to them:
translations.an4.53:10: Both are faithful and generous, self-controlled, living according to the Dhamma; those husband and wife are affectionate toward each other.
translations.an4.53:11: They have many possessions, and comfort arises for them; their enemies are displeased with both who are equal in virtue.
translations.an4.53:2: “Householders, there are these four ways of living together. Which four? A wretch lives with a wretch, a wretch lives with a goddess, a god lives with a wretch, and a god lives with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a wretch live with a wretch? Here, householders, the husband is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, speaks lies, and is addicted to wine, liquor, and intoxicants; he is immoral, of evil character, living at home with a heart obsessed by the stain of stinginess, an abuser and reviler of ascetics and brahmins. And his wife is also one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, speaks lies, and is addicted to wine, liquor, and intoxicants; she is immoral, of evil character, living at home with a heart obsessed by the stain of stinginess, an abuser and reviler of ascetics and brahmins. This is how a wretch lives with a wretch.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is immoral, stingy, and abusive; but the wife is virtuous, generous, and free from stinginess; she is a goddess living with a wretched husband.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, generous, and free from stinginess; but the wife is immoral, stingy, and abusive; she is a wretch living with a godly husband.
translations.an4.5:1: “Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world. Which four? The person who goes with the flow, the person who goes against the flow, the person who is steady-minded, and the brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and stands on dry land. And what, bhikkhus, is the person who goes with the flow? Here, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and performs evil deeds. This is called the person who goes with the flow.
translations.an4.5:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who goes against the flow? Here, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not perform evil deeds; even with pain and even with sorrow, weeping with a tearful face, they live the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. This is called the person who goes against the flow.
translations.an4.5:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is steady-minded? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth, attaining Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. This is called the person who is steady-minded.
translations.an4.5:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and stands on dry land, a brahmin? Here, a certain person, with the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life. This is called the person who has crossed over, gone to the far shore, and stands on dry land, a brahmin. These, bhikkhus, are the four persons found existing in the world.”
translations.an4.5:5: Those people who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, not free from lust, enjoying pleasures here; they go again and again to birth and old age, overcome by craving, going with the flow.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore, the wise person here, with mindfulness established, not indulging in sensual pleasures or evil; even with pain, they should abandon sensual pleasures; they call that person one who goes against the flow.
translations.an4.5:7: One who has abandoned the five defilements, a trainee who is complete, not subject to decline; who has attained mastery over the mind and has concentrated faculties; that man is truly called steady-minded.
translations.an4.62:2: “Householder, there are these four kinds of happiness to be acquired by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures, from time to time and when the occasion arises. Which four? The happiness of ownership, the happiness of enjoyment, the happiness of freedom from debt, and the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of ownership? Here, a gentleman has wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous and righteously gained. He acquires happiness and joy, thinking: ‘I have wealth acquired by energetic striving... righteous and righteously gained.’ This is called the happiness of ownership.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of freedom from debt? Here, a gentleman owes nothing to anyone, whether little or much. He acquires happiness and joy, thinking: ‘I owe nothing to anyone, whether little or much.’ This is called the happiness of freedom from debt.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, a noble disciple is possessed of blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, and blameless mental action. He acquires happiness and joy, thinking: ‘I am possessed of blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, and blameless mental action.’ This is called the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness to be acquired by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures, from time to time and when the occasion arises.”
translations.an4.62:7: Knowing the happiness of freedom from debt, and then the happiness of ownership; a mortal enjoying the happiness of wealth, then sees clearly with wisdom.
translations.an5.23:1: “Mendicants, there are these five corruptions of gold. When gold is corrupted by these, it is not supple, malleable, or radiant; it is brittle and not fit for being worked. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, and silver. These are the five corruptions of gold. When gold is corrupted by these, it is not supple, malleable, or radiant; it is brittle and not fit for being worked. But when gold is free from these five corruptions, it is supple, malleable, and radiant; it is not brittle and is fit for being worked. Then it can be used for whatever kind of ornament one wishes—whether a ring, earrings, a necklace, or a golden garland—and it serves that purpose.
translations.an5.23:2: In the same way, mendicants, there are these five corruptions of the mind. When the mind is corrupted by these, it is not supple, malleable, or radiant; it is brittle and not rightly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. These are the five corruptions of the mind. When the mind is corrupted by these, it is not supple, malleable, or radiant; it is brittle and not rightly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. But when the mind is free from these five corruptions, it is supple, malleable, and radiant; it is not brittle and is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. Then, to whatever quality realizable by direct knowledge one inclines the mind for realization, one attains the ability to witness it there, provided the conditions are met.
translations.an5.23:3: If they wish: ‘May I experience the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; appear and vanish; go unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; dive in and out of the earth as if in water; walk on water without sinking as if on earth; travel through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird; touch and stroke with my hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; and exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world,’ they attain the ability to witness it there, provided the conditions are met.
translations.an5.23:4: If they wish: ‘With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, may I hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near,’ they attain the ability to witness it there, provided the conditions are met.
translations.an5.23:5: If they wish: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having encompassed them with my own mind. May I understand a mind with lust as “a mind with lust,” and a mind without lust as “a mind without lust.” May I understand a mind with hate as “a mind with hate,” and a mind without hate as “a mind without hate.” May I understand a mind with delusion as “a mind with delusion,” and a mind without delusion as “a mind without delusion.” May I understand a contracted mind as “a contracted mind,” and a scattered mind as “a scattered mind.” May I understand an exalted mind as “an exalted mind,” and an unexalted mind as “an unexalted mind.” May I understand a surpassable mind as “a surpassable mind,” and an unsurpassable mind as “an unsurpassable mind.” May I understand a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind,” and an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind.” May I understand a liberated mind as “a liberated mind,” and an unliberated mind as “an unliberated mind,”’ they attain the ability to witness it there, provided the conditions are met.
translations.an5.25:1: “Mendicants, when right view is supported by five factors, it has liberation of mind as its fruit and benefit, and it has liberation by wisdom as its fruit and benefit.
translations.an5.26:1: “Mendicants, there are these five bases of liberation where, for a mendicant who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind is liberated, the undestroyed defilements go to destruction, or the unreached supreme security from bondage is reached.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher teaches the Dhamma to a mendicant, but the mendicant teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as they have heard it and learned it. In whatever way the mendicant teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as they have heard it and learned it, in just that way they experience the meaning and experience the Dhamma in that Dhamma. When they experience the meaning and experience the Dhamma, joy arises. When they are joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body feels happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the second basis of liberation where... the unreached supreme security from bondage is reached.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a fellow practitioner... teaches the Dhamma... nor does the mendicant teach the Dhamma in detail to others... but the mendicant recites the Dhamma in detail as they have heard it and learned it. In whatever way the mendicant recites the Dhamma in detail... in just that way they experience the meaning and experience the Dhamma in that Dhamma. When they experience the meaning and experience the Dhamma, joy arises... the mind becomes concentrated. This is the third basis of liberation where... the unreached supreme security from bondage is reached.
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does he teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it, nor does he recite the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it, nor does he think about, examine, and mentally inspect the Dhamma as he has heard and learned it; but he has well grasped a certain object of concentration, well attended to it, well sustained it, and well penetrated it with wisdom. In whatever way a bhikkhu has well grasped a certain object of concentration, well attended to it, well sustained it, and well penetrated it with wisdom, in just that way he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in that Dhamma. When he experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness is born. When he is gladdened, rapture is born. When the mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth basis of liberation, whereby, while a bhikkhu dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his undestroyed taints come to destruction, and he reaches the unsurpassed security from bondage that he had not reached before.
translations.an5.27:1: “Bhikkhus, develop immeasurable concentration, being alert and mindful. When you develop immeasurable concentration, being alert and mindful, five knowledges arise personally within yourselves. Which five? The knowledge arises personally within oneself: ‘This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.’ The knowledge arises personally within oneself: ‘This concentration is noble and spiritual.’ The knowledge arises personally within oneself: ‘This concentration is not practiced by low people.’ The knowledge arises personally within oneself: ‘This concentration is peaceful, sublime, gained by tranquility, and attained to unification; it is not maintained by forceful suppression.’ The knowledge arises personally within oneself: ‘I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully.’
translations.an5.28:1: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the development of noble five-factored right concentration. Listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an5.28:10: Suppose, bhikkhus, on a piece of good ground at a crossroads, there was a chariot harnessed to thoroughbreds, standing with the whip lying ready. Then a skilled trainer, a driver of horses to be tamed, would mount it, take the reins in his left hand and the whip in his right hand, and drive it out and back wherever he liked, however he liked. In the same way, when the noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated, a bhikkhu extends his mind to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he wishes to realize, and he achieves the ability to witness it there and then, whatever the field may be.
translations.an5.28:15: If he wishes: ‘With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... may I understand how beings pass away according to their kamma,’ he achieves the ability to witness it there and then, whatever the field may be.
translations.an5.28:7: When the noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated, a bhikkhu extends his mind to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he wishes to realize, and he achieves the ability to witness it there and then, whatever the field may be.
translations.an5.28:8: Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a water jar placed on a stand, full of water, brimming over so that a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to tip it any which way, would the water come out?” “Yes, bhante.” “In the same way, when the noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated, a bhikkhu extends his mind to whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he wishes to realize, and he achieves the ability to witness it there and then, whatever the field may be.
translations.an5.28:9: Suppose, bhikkhus, on a level piece of ground there was a square lotus pond, bound by an embankment, full of water, brimming over so that a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to open the embankment any which way, would the water come out?” “Yes, bhante.” “In the same way, when the noble five-factored right concentration has been thus developed and cultivated, a bhikkhu extends his mind to whatever state... whatever the field may be.
translations.an5.2:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a trainee. Which five? The power of faith, the power of shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the power of faith? Here, a noble disciple is faithful; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ This is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the power of shame? Here, a noble disciple has shame; he is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he is ashamed of attaining evil, unwholesome states. This is called the power of shame.
translations.an5.2:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the power of moral dread? Here, a noble disciple has moral dread; he dreads bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he dreads attaining evil, unwholesome states. This is called the power of moral dread.
translations.an5.2:5: And what, bhikkhus, is the power of energy? Here, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, not casting off the duty regarding wholesome states. This is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what, bhikkhus, is the power of wisdom? Here, a noble disciple is wise; he possesses wisdom regarding arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers of a trainee.”
translations.an5.30:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Icchānaṅgala. There the Blessed One stayed in the Icchānaṅgala woodland thicket. The brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: “It is said that the ascetic Gotama, a Sakyan son who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is staying in the Icchānaṅgala woodland thicket. Concerning that Blessed Gotama, a good reputation has spread: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully enlightened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, unsurpassed guide for those who wish to be trained, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ He makes known this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, having realized it by his own direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. He reveals a spiritual life that is entirely full and pure. It is good to see such perfected ones.” Then, when the night had passed, the brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala took many kinds of food and went to the Icchānaṅgala woodland thicket; they stood outside the gatehouse making a loud noise, a great noise.
translations.an5.30:3: “May the Blessed One now accept, bhante; may the Holy One accept. It is now time for the Blessed One’s acceptance. Wherever the Blessed One goes now, the brahmin householders, the townspeople, and the countryfolk will incline in that same direction. Just as, bhante, when it rains in thick drops, the water flows according to the slope; even so, bhante, wherever the Blessed One goes now, the brahmin householders, the townspeople, and the countryfolk will incline in that same direction. Why is that? Because of the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.”
translations.an5.31:1: At one time … in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then Princess Sumanā, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, went to the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Princess Sumanā said to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: In the same way, one accomplished in virtue, a person of faith, outshines all the stingy people in the world with their generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud, thundering, wreathed in lightning, with a hundred peaks, fills the high ground and the low, raining down upon the earth;
translations.an5.31:12: Even so, a wise disciple of the Fully Enlightened One, accomplished in vision, surpasses the stingy person in five ways.
translations.an5.31:2: “Bhante, suppose there are two disciples of the Blessed One who are equal in faith, equal in virtue, and equal in wisdom—one is a giver and one is not a giver. With the breaking up of the body, after death, they would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But as they have become gods, bhante, would there be a distinction, would there be a difference between them?”
translations.an5.31:3: “There would be, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said. “The one who was a giver, Sumanā, having become a god, surpasses the one who was not a giver in five ways: in divine life-span, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, and divine sovereignty. The one who was a giver, Sumanā, having become a god, surpasses the one who was not a giver in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:4: “But if, bhante, they pass away from there and come to this state, as they have become humans, bhante, would there be a distinction, would there be a difference between them?” “There would be, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said. “The one who was a giver, Sumanā, having become a human, surpasses the one who was not a giver in five ways: in human life-span, human beauty, human happiness, human fame, and human sovereignty. The one who was a giver, Sumanā, having become a human, surpasses the one who was not a giver in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:5: “But if, bhante, they both go forth from the home life into homelessness, as they have gone forth, bhante, would there be a distinction, would there be a difference between them?” “There would be, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said. “The one who was a giver, Sumanā, having gone forth, surpasses the one who was not a giver in five ways: he mostly uses a robe when requested and rarely when not requested; he mostly uses almsfood when requested and rarely when not requested; he mostly uses a lodging when requested and rarely when not requested; he mostly uses medicines and provisions for the sick when requested and rarely when not requested. Furthermore, the spiritual companions with whom he lives mostly treat him with agreeable bodily actions and rarely with disagreeable ones; they mostly treat him with agreeable verbal actions and rarely with disagreeable ones; they mostly treat him with agreeable mental actions and rarely with disagreeable ones; they mostly present him with agreeable offerings and rarely with disagreeable ones. The one who was a giver, Sumanā, having gone forth, surpasses the one who was not a giver in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:6: “But if, bhante, they both attain arahantship, for those who have attained arahantship, bhante, would there be a distinction, would there be a difference between them?” “In this case, Sumanā, I say there is no difference at all, that is, between liberation and liberation.”
translations.an5.31:9: “Just as the moon, stainless, moving through the space of the sky, outshines all the clusters of stars in the world with its radiance;
translations.an5.34:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Forest in the Gabled Hall. Then General Sīha went to the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, General Sīha said to the Blessed One: “Is it possible, bhante, for the Blessed One to point out a fruit of giving visible in this life?”
translations.an5.34:2: “It is possible, Sīha,” the Blessed One said. “A giver, Sīha, a master of giving, is dear and appealing to many people. Since a giver, a master of giving, is dear and appealing to many people, this is a fruit of giving visible in this life.
translations.an5.34:8: Giving, one is dear; many people associate with them. They gain a good reputation and their fame grows. They enter an assembly without embarrassment; a person who is not stingy is confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore the wise, seeking happiness, give gifts, having removed the stain of stinginess. Established for a long time in the Triple Heaven, they rejoice, having gone to the company of the gods.
translations.an5.36:1: “Mendicants, there are these five timely gifts. Which five? One gives a gift to a guest; one gives a gift to someone departing; one gives a gift to the sick; one gives a gift during a famine; and when the new crops and new fruits come in, one first presents them to the virtuous. These, mendicants, are the five timely gifts.
translations.an5.36:2: The wise give in the right season, generous and free from stinginess; what is given in the right season to the Noble Ones, who are upright and such.
translations.an5.36:3: With a confident mind, one's offering is vast; those who rejoice in that, or provide service, their offering is not diminished by that, they too share in the merit.
translations.an5.37:1: “Mendicants, in giving food, a donor gives five things to the recipients. Which five? They give long life, beauty, happiness, strength, and eloquence. Having given long life, they become a partaker of long life, whether divine or human; having given beauty, they become a partaker of beauty, whether divine or human; having given happiness, they become a partaker of happiness, whether divine or human; having given strength, they become a partaker of strength, whether divine or human; having given eloquence, they become a partaker of eloquence, whether divine or human. Mendicants, in giving food, a donor gives these five things to the recipients.”
translations.an5.37:2: The wise person who gives life, strength, beauty, and eloquence; the giver of happiness, being intelligent, attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: “Just as, mendicants, a great banyan tree on a piece of good ground at a crossroads is a refuge for birds all around; even so, mendicants, a faithful son of a good family is a refuge for many people—for monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.”
translations.an5.38:3: Possessing branches, leaves, and fruit, like a great tree with a trunk; having roots and being full of fruit, it is a support for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: In that delightful place, the birds frequent it; those seeking shade go to its shade, those seeking fruit eat its fruit.
translations.an5.38:5: In the same way, a person of faith, accomplished in virtue; humble in conduct, not stubborn, gentle, friendly, and mild.
translations.an5.38:6: Those free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, and without defilements; the fields of merit in the world, frequent such a person.
translations.an5.41:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him: “Householder, there are these five benefits of wealth. Which five? Here, householder, with wealth earned by energetic effort, accumulated by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, a noble disciple makes himself happy and pleased, and properly maintains that happiness; he makes his parents happy and pleased, and properly maintains that happiness; he makes his children, wife, slaves, workers, and servants happy and pleased, and properly maintains that happiness. This is the first benefit of wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, with wealth earned by energetic effort... a noble disciple makes the five offerings: to relatives, to guests, to the departed, to the king, and to the deities. This is the fourth benefit of wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, with wealth earned by energetic effort... a noble disciple establishes an uplifting offering for those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from intoxication and negligence, who are settled in patience and gentleness, who each tame themselves, each calm themselves, and each extinguish themselves—an offering that is heavenly, resulting in happiness, and leading to heaven. This is the fifth benefit of wealth. These, householder, are the five benefits of wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If, householder, while a noble disciple is pursuing these five benefits of wealth, his wealth comes to an end, he thinks: ‘I have pursued the benefits of wealth, but my wealth has come to an end.’ Thus he has no regret. If, householder, while a noble disciple is pursuing these five benefits of wealth, his wealth increases, he thinks: ‘I have pursued the benefits of wealth, and my wealth has increased.’ Thus he has no regret in either case.”
translations.an5.41:7: Wealth has been enjoyed, dependents supported, and I have crossed over misfortunes; I have given an uplifting offering, and made the five offerings; I have attended to the virtuous, the self-controlled, the practitioners of the spiritual life.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever purpose a wise person living at home would desire wealth for, that purpose has been attained by me; what I have done is not a cause for regret.
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him:
translations.an5.43:4: “Householder, a noble disciple who desires long life should not pray for long life or delight in it for the sake of long life. A noble disciple who desires long life should practice the path that leads to long life. For when he practices the path that leads to long life, it leads to the attainment of long life. He becomes a gainer of long life, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: Householder, a noble disciple who desires beauty should not pray for beauty or delight in it for the sake of beauty. A noble disciple who desires beauty should practice the path that leads to beauty. For when he practices the path that leads to beauty, it leads to the attainment of beauty. He becomes a gainer of beauty, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: Householder, a noble disciple who desires happiness should not pray for happiness or delight in it for the sake of happiness. A noble disciple who desires happiness should practice the path that leads to happiness. For when he practices the path that leads to happiness, it leads to the attainment of happiness. He becomes a gainer of happiness, whether divine or human.”
translations.an5.43:7: Householder, a noble disciple who desires fame should not pray for fame or delight in it for its own sake. A noble disciple who desires fame should practice the way that leads to fame. For when they practice the way that leads to fame, it leads to the acquisition of fame. They then become a possessor of fame, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:9: Long life, beauty, fame, and reputation; heaven and birth in high families; and grand delights following one after another—for one who desires these things,
translations.an5.49:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now at that time Queen Mallikā had passed away. Then a certain man went up to King Pasenadi and whispered in his ear: “Your Majesty, Queen Mallikā has passed away.” When he heard this, King Pasenadi was miserable and unhappy, and sat with shoulders drooping and head down, brooding, at a loss for words.
translations.an5.51:3: It is impossible, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu who has not abandoned these five obstacles and hindrances, which overspread the mind and weaken wisdom, would know his own good, or the good of others, or the good of both, or realize a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones that transcends human limits, with his weak and feeble wisdom. Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a mountain river, flowing far, with a swift current, carrying everything along with it. If a man were to open channels on both sides of it, then the current in the middle of the river would be dispersed, spread out, and divided; it would no longer flow far, its current would not be swift, and it would not carry everything along. In the same way, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has not abandoned these five obstacles and hindrances... would realize a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones that transcends human limits.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain bhikkhu went to his preceptor and said: “Venerable sir, my body feels as if it were drugged, the quarters are not clear to me, and the teachings do not occur to me. Sloth and torpor persist in obsessing my mind, I live the spiritual life without interest, and I have doubt about the teachings.”
translations.an5.56:3: “So it is, bhikkhu, for one who dwells with the doors of the senses unguarded, who is immoderate in eating, not devoted to wakefulness, not discerning of wholesome qualities, and not devoted to the practice of developing the qualities that lead to awakening in the first and last watches of the night. It is then that the body feels as if it were drugged, the quarters are not clear, the teachings do not occur, sloth and torpor obsess the mind, one lives the spiritual life without interest, and has doubt about the teachings. Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train yourself like this: ‘I will be one who guards the doors of the senses, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, discerning of wholesome qualities, and devoted to the practice of developing the qualities that lead to awakening in the first and last watches of the night.’ That is how you should train, bhikkhu.”
translations.an5.56:4: Then that bhikkhu, having been exhorted with this advice by the Buddha, rose from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then that bhikkhu, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the spiritual life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness. He understood: ‘Birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.
translations.an5.57:10: ‘I am not the only one who must be parted and separated from all that is dear and appealing to me. For as long as beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings must be parted and separated from all that is dear and appealing to them.’ As they frequently reflect on this, the path is born. They pursue, develop, and cultivate that path. As they pursue, develop, and cultivate that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are uprooted.
translations.an5.57:11: ‘I am not the only one who is the owner of my kamma, the heir of my kamma, born of my kamma, related to my kamma, and has kamma as my refuge. Whatever kamma I do—whether good or evil—I will be its heir. For as long as beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings are the owners of their kamma, the heirs of their kamma, born of their kamma, related to their kamma, and have kamma as their refuge. Whatever kamma they do—whether good or evil—they will be its heirs.’ As they frequently reflect on this, the path is born. They pursue, develop, and cultivate that path. As they pursue, develop, and cultivate that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are uprooted.
translations.an5.57:15: I have overcome all intoxications, seeing renunciation as safety. Energy arose in me as I looked toward Nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: That noble disciple reflects: ‘I am not the only one who is subject to old age, not exempt from old age. For as long as beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings are subject to old age, not exempt from old age.’ As they frequently reflect on this, the path is born. They pursue, develop, and cultivate that path. As they pursue, develop, and cultivate that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are uprooted.
translations.an5.57:8: ‘I am not the only one who is subject to illness, not exempt from illness. For as long as beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings are subject to illness, not exempt from illness.’ As they frequently reflect on this, the path is born. They pursue, develop, and cultivate that path. As they pursue, develop, and cultivate that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are uprooted.
translations.an8.13:1: “Monks, a noble thoroughbred steed of a king, possessed of eight qualities, is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a factor of royalty. What eight? Here, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred steed is well-born on both sides—on the mother’s side and the father’s side. He is born in the region where other noble thoroughbred steeds are born. Whatever food they give him—whether moist or dry—he eats it carefully, without scattering it. He is disgusted by sitting or lying down in excrement or urine. He is gentle and pleasant to live with, and does not harass other horses. Whatever deceits, tricks, frauds, or crooks he has, he reveals them as they are to the trainer. The trainer then strives to correct them. He is a bearer. He thinks: ‘Let other horses carry or not, I will carry here.’ When he goes, he goes by a straight path. He is strong, showing strength until the end of his life and death. Possessed of these eight qualities, monks, a noble thoroughbred steed of a king is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a factor of royalty.”
translations.an8.14:1: “Monks, I will teach you the eight horse-stallions and the eight horse-defects, and the eight man-stallions and the eight man-defects. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.14:2: “And what, monks, are the eight horse-stallions and the eight horse-defects? Here, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, backs up and pushes the chariot backward. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the first horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:3: Furthermore, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, leaps backward, strikes the crossbar, and breaks the triple-pole. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the second horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:4: Furthermore, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, throws his thigh over the pole and tramples on the pole itself. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the third horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:5: Furthermore, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, takes the wrong path and makes the chariot go off-road. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the fourth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:6: Furthermore, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, rears up, lifting his forebody and forelegs. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the fifth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:7: Furthermore, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, disregarding the trainer and disregarding the goad-stick, takes the bit in his teeth and goes wherever he wants. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the sixth horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:8: Furthermore, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, neither advances nor retreats, but stands right there like a post. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the seventh horse-defect.
translations.an8.14:9: Furthermore, monks, a certain horse-stallion, when told ‘Go!’, being pricked and urged by the trainer, pulls in his forelegs and pulls in his hind legs and sits down right there on all four legs. Such a horse-stallion is found here. This, monks, is the eighth horse-defect. These, monks, are the eight horse-stallions and the eight horse-defects.”
translations.an8.19:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Verañjā at the foot of the Naḷeru Neem tree. Then Pahārāda, the lord of the Asuras, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. As he was standing there, the Blessed One said to Pahārāda, the lord of the Asuras:
translations.an8.22:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Vajjis at Hatthigāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, remember Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma as being possessed of eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: “If I, bhante, should pass away before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to declare of me: ‘There is no fetter bound by which Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma would return again to this world.’ This, bhante, is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These eight wonderful and marvelous qualities, bhante, are found in me. But I do not know which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities the Blessed One was referring to when he declared me to be possessed of them.”
translations.an8.22:12: Then that monk, having received almsfood in the house of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then, after the meal, when he had returned from his almsround, that monk approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, that monk reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain bhikkhu robed himself in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the house of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma; having gone there, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma went to that bhikkhu; having gone there, he bowed to that bhikkhu and sat down to one side. As Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma was sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to him: “Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. What are those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities, householder, with which you are endowed as declared by the Blessed One?”
translations.an8.22:3: “Venerable sir, I do not know what those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities are with which I am endowed as declared by the Blessed One. However, venerable sir, as for the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that are found in me, listen to that and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, householder,” that bhikkhu replied to Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma. Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma said this: “Venerable sir, when I was enjoying myself in the Elephant Forest, I first saw the Blessed One from a distance. Upon seeing him, venerable sir, my heart was inspired by the Blessed One, and my intoxication from liquor vanished. This, venerable sir, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:4: With an inspired heart, venerable sir, I attended upon the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave me a progressive talk, that is to say: talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation. When the Blessed One knew that I had a ready heart, a soft heart, a heart free from hindrances, an uplifted heart, and an inspired heart, then he explained the teaching unique to the Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth, free of dark spots, would properly take dye; even so, in that very seat, the dustless, stainless eye of the Dhamma arose in me: ‘Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.’ Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, plunged into the Dhamma, having crossed over doubt, being free from hesitation, having attained self-confidence, and being independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, I then and there went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and I undertook the training rules with celibacy as the fifth. This, venerable sir, is the second wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:5: Venerable sir, I had four young wives. Then, venerable sir, I went to those wives; having gone there, I said this to those wives: ‘Sisters, I have undertaken the training rules with celibacy as the fifth. Whoever wishes may enjoy the wealth here and do merit, or go to her own relatives’ family. Or if there is a desire for another man, to whom shall I give you?’ When this was said, my eldest wife said this to me: ‘Young master, give me to such-and-such a man.’ Then, venerable sir, having summoned that man, I took my wife with my left hand and, taking a water jar with my right hand, I poured water over his hands. While giving away my young wife, venerable sir, I do not recall any alteration in my mind. This, venerable sir, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:6: Furthermore, venerable sir, there is wealth in my family. And that is shared without reservation with those of virtuous and good character. This, venerable sir, is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:7: Furthermore, venerable sir, whichever bhikkhu I attend upon, I attend upon him only with respect, not without respect. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen only with respect, not without respect. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma. This, venerable sir, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:8: Furthermore, venerable sir, it is not unusual that when the Saṅgha is invited, deities come and announce: ‘Householder, such-and-such a bhikkhu is liberated in both ways, such-and-such is liberated by wisdom, such-and-such is a body-witness, such-and-such is attained to view, such-and-such is liberated by faith, such-and-such is a Dhamma-follower, such-and-such is a faith-follower, such-and-such is virtuous and of good character, such-and-such is immoral and of bad character.’ While serving the Saṅgha, venerable sir, I do not recall such a thought arising: ‘I will give a little to this one, or I will give much to that one.’ Rather, venerable sir, I give with an impartial mind. This, venerable sir, is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:9: Furthermore, venerable sir, it is not unusual that deities come and announce to me: ‘Householder, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One.’ When this is said, venerable sir, I say this to those deities: ‘Whether you deities say so or not, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One.’ Yet, venerable sir, I do not recall any elation of mind because of that: ‘The deities come to me, or I converse with deities.’ This, venerable sir, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
translations.an8.23:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. What seven? Bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful; bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is virtuous; bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has a sense of shame; bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has a sense of fear of wrongdoing; bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned; bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous; bhikkhus, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise. Bhikkhus, remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
