translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain bhikkhu robed himself in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the house of Hatthaka of Āḷavī; having gone there, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī went to that bhikkhu; having gone there, he bowed to that bhikkhu and sat down to one side. As Hatthaka of Āḷavī was sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to him:
translations.an8.23:3: “Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be possessed of seven amazing and wonderful qualities. What seven? ‘Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is virtuous … conscientious … prudent … learned … generous … Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise.’ Friend, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be possessed of these seven amazing and wonderful qualities.” “I hope, bhante, there was no layperson dressed in white present?” “No, friend, there was no layperson dressed in white present.” “It is good, bhante, that no layperson dressed in white was present there.”
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having taken almsfood in the house of Hatthaka of Āḷavī, rose from his seat and departed. Then, after the meal, when he had returned from his almsround, that monk went to the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava Shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, went to the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As Hatthaka of Āḷavī was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Hatthaka, your assembly is large. How then, Hatthaka, do you win over this large assembly?” “Bhante, I win over this large assembly by these four means of winning over others taught by the Blessed One. When I know, bhante: ‘This one is to be won over by giving,’ I win them over by giving; when I know: ‘This one is to be won over by kind words,’ I win them over by kind words; when I know: ‘This one is to be won over by beneficial conduct,’ I win them over by beneficial conduct; when I know: ‘This one is to be won over by impartiality,’ I win them over by impartiality. Moreover, bhante, there is wealth in my family. They do not think one should listen to a poor person in the same way.” “Good, good, Hatthaka! This is the right way for you to win over a large assembly. For whoever, Hatthaka, won over a large assembly in the past, they all did so by these same four means of winning over others. Whoever, Hatthaka, will win over a large assembly in the future, they all will do so by these same four means of winning over others. And whoever, Hatthaka, wins over a large assembly at present, they all do so by these same four means of winning over others.”
translations.an8.26:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: “To what extent, bhante, is one a lay follower?” “When, Jīvaka, one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; to that extent, Jīvaka, one is a lay follower.”
translations.an8.26:2: “But to what extent, bhante, is a lay follower virtuous?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower abstains from killing living beings … abstains from wine, liquor, and intoxicants which cause heedlessness; to that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous.”
translations.an8.26:3: “But to what extent, bhante, is a lay follower practicing for their own benefit, but not for the benefit of others?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower is themselves accomplished in faith, but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of faith … themselves, having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, practices in accordance with the Dhamma, but does not encourage others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. To that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for their own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.”
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, bhante, the four establishments of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed. Since the four establishments of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed, this too is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, by relying on which a monk whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, bhante, the four bases of psychic power have been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed … the five faculties have been developed and well-developed … the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed and well-developed … the noble eightfold path has been developed and well-developed. Since the noble eightfold path has been developed and well-developed by a monk whose taints are destroyed, this too is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, by relying on which a monk whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.2:1: “Monks, there are these eight causes and eight conditions that lead to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired. What eight? Here, monks, a monk lives in dependence on the Teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher, toward whom he has established a keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, and love and respect. This, monks, is the first cause and first condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:11: ‘Having heard that Dhamma, this venerable one achieves it by way of a twofold withdrawal—withdrawal of body and withdrawal of mind. Surely this venerable one knows knowing and sees seeing.’ This quality also leads to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the ascetic life, and to oneness.
translations.an8.2:15: ‘When gone to the Saṅgha, this venerable one does not engage in various kinds of talk or in animal talk. He either speaks Dhamma himself or invites another to do so, and he does not despise noble silence. Surely this venerable one knows knowing and sees seeing.’ This quality also leads to being loved, to being respected, to development, to the ascetic life, and to oneness.
translations.an8.2:2: Living in dependence on that teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher, toward whom he has established a keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, and love and respect, he approaches them from time to time and asks and inquires: ‘How is this, bhante? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones then reveal what was unrevealed, clarify what was not clear, and dispel doubt regarding various things that give rise to doubt. This, bhikkhus, is the second cause and second condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:4: He is virtuous, living restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth cause and fourth condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:5: He is learned, a sustainer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has heard much of, retained, practiced verbally, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated by view. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth cause and fifth condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:6: He lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, being steadfast, firm in effort, not shirking the responsibility regarding wholesome states. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth cause and sixth condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:7: When he has gone to the Sangha, he does not engage in various kinds of talk or common animal-talk. He either speaks on the Dhamma himself or invites another to do so, and he does not despise noble silence. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh cause and seventh condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:8: He lives contemplating the rise and fall of the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling, such its origin, such its passing away; such is perception … such are choices … such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.’ This, bhikkhus, is the eighth cause and eighth condition that leads to the acquisition of wisdom fundamental to the holy life when it has not been acquired, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:9: His fellow practitioners then think of him thus: ‘This venerable one lives in dependence on the teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher, toward whom he has established a keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, and love and respect. Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen.’ This quality also leads to being loved, respected, developed, to the ascetic life, and to oneness.
translations.an8.30:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Bhaggas at Suṁsumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. At that time, the venerable Anuruddha was staying among the Cetis in the Eastern Bamboo Park. Then, while the venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: “This Dhamma is for one with few wishes, not for one with many wishes; this Dhamma is for the contented, not for the discontented; this Dhamma is for the secluded, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for the energetic, not for the lazy; this Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one with muddled mindfulness; this Dhamma is for the concentrated, not for the unconcentrated; this Dhamma is for the wise, not for the unwise.”
translations.an8.30:10: “When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, and you obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, these four jhanas which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as a gabled house belonging to a householder or a householder’s son might be plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows shut; even so will your dwelling at the foot of a tree appear to you as you live contented, for your delight, without anxiety, for a comfortable dwelling, for the descent into Nibbana.”
translations.an8.30:11: “When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, and you obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, these four jhanas which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as a couch belonging to a householder or a householder’s son might be spread with a long-haired coverlet, a white woollen coverlet, a floral coverlet, a choice spread of antelope hide, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends; even so will your bed and seat of spread grass appear to you as you live contented, for your delight, without anxiety, for a comfortable dwelling, for the descent into Nibbana.”
translations.an8.30:12: “When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, and you obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, these four jhanas which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as the various medicines belonging to a householder or a householder’s son—that is, ghee, butter, oil, honey, and molasses; even so will your medicine of fermented urine appear to you as you live contented, for your delight, without anxiety, for a comfortable dwelling, for the descent into Nibbana. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should stay right here in the Eastern Bamboo Park among the Cetis for the next rainy season.” “Yes, bhante,” the venerable Anuruddha replied to the Blessed One.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Blessed One, having given this advice to the venerable Anuruddha—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm; even so—disappeared from the Eastern Bamboo Grove in the Ceti country and reappeared in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park, at Crocodile Hill in the Bhagga country. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, I will teach you the eight thoughts of a great man. Listen to them … and what, monks, are the eight thoughts of a great man? This Dhamma is for one with few wishes, not for one with many wishes; this Dhamma is for the contented, not for the discontented; this Dhamma is for the secluded, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for the energetic, not for the lazy; this Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one with muddled mindfulness; this Dhamma is for the concentrated, not for the unconcentrated; this Dhamma is for the wise, not for the unwise; this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation.”
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in the venerable Anuruddha’s mind with his own mind—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm; even so—disappeared from the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park, at Crocodile Hill in the Bhagga country and reappeared in the Eastern Bamboo Grove in the Ceti country right in front of the venerable Anuruddha. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. The venerable Anuruddha also bowed to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the venerable Anuruddha:
translations.an8.30:22: Then the venerable Anuruddha spent the next rainy season right there in the Eastern Bamboo Grove in the Ceti country. Then the venerable Anuruddha, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the spiritual life for the sake of which gentlemen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and having attained it, he dwelt in it. He understood: “Birth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to this state of being.” And the venerable Anuruddha became one of the perfected ones. Then the venerable Anuruddha, having attained arahantship, at that time spoke these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: “Knowing my thought, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, came to me by means of his psychic power with a mind-made body.
translations.an8.30:24: Just as I had thought, he taught me even further; the Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation, taught non-proliferation.
translations.an8.30:3: “Good, good, Anuruddha! It is good, Anuruddha, that you think these thoughts of a great man: ‘This Dhamma is for one with few wishes, not for one with many wishes; this Dhamma is for the contented, not for the discontented; this Dhamma is for the secluded, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for the energetic, not for the lazy; this Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one with muddled mindfulness; this Dhamma is for the concentrated, not for the unconcentrated; this Dhamma is for the wise, not for the unwise.’ Therefore, Anuruddha, you should also think this eighth thought of a great man: ‘This Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation.’
translations.an8.30:4: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, whenever you wish, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, you will enter and dwell in the first absorption, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
translations.an8.30:5: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, whenever you wish, with the subsiding of thought and examination, you will enter and dwell in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration.
translations.an8.30:6: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, whenever you wish, with the fading away of rapture, you will dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experience happiness with the body, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness,’ you will enter and dwell in the third absorption.
translations.an8.30:7: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, whenever you wish, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the previous passing away of joy and dejection, you will enter and dwell in the fourth absorption, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness and equanimity.
translations.an8.39:1: “Monks, there are these eight streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nourishments of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which lead to what is liked, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. What eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple has gone to the Buddha for refuge. This is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is liked, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an8.39:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone to the Dhamma for refuge. This is the second stream of merit … and so on … it leads to happiness.”
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, a noble disciple has gone to the Sangha for refuge. This is the third overflowing of merit, overflowing of the wholesome, a nutrient for happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is liked, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. There are these five gifts, great gifts, original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, which are not being adulterated and will not be adulterated, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. What five? Here, a noble disciple, having given up killing living beings, abstains from killing living beings. By abstaining from killing living beings, the noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from ill will. Having given immeasurable beings freedom from fear, enmity, and ill will, they share in immeasurable freedom from fear, enmity, and ill will. This is the first gift, a great gift... not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. This is the fourth overflowing of merit... which leads to what is liked, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an8.39:7: Having given up intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause heedlessness, they abstain from intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause heedlessness. By abstaining from intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause heedlessness, the noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from enmity, and freedom from ill will. Having given immeasurable beings freedom from fear, enmity, and ill will, they share in immeasurable freedom from fear, enmity, and ill will. This is the fifth gift, a great gift... not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. This is the eighth overflowing of merit, overflowing of the wholesome, a nutrient for happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, which leads to what is liked, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an8.40:1: “Killing living beings, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The slightest result of killing living beings is that, when one is born as a human, it leads to a short lifespan.
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The slightest result of taking what is not given is that, when one is born as a human, it leads to the loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Sexual misconduct, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The slightest result of sexual misconduct is that, when one is born as a human, it leads to enmity and rivals.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The slightest result of false speech is that, when one is born as a human, it leads to false accusations.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The slightest result of divisive speech is that, when one is born as a human, it leads to being divided from friends.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The slightest result of harsh speech is that, when one is born as a human, it leads to disagreeable sounds.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, monks, when cultivated, developed, and practiced frequently, leads to hell, leads to the animal realm, leads to the realm of hungry ghosts. The slightest result of idle chatter is that, when one is born as a human, it leads to speech that is not taken to heart.
translations.an8.6:2: Monks, for an unlearned ordinary person, there arises gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. For a learned noble disciple, there also arises gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. Therein, monks, what is the distinction, what is the specific feature, what is the difference between the learned noble disciple and the unlearned ordinary person?” “Bhante, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, Bhante, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”
translations.an8.6:4: Gain occupies their mind and stays there, loss occupies their mind... fame... disrepute... blame... praise... pleasure... pain occupies their mind and stays there. They favor the gain that has arisen and oppose the loss; they favor the fame and oppose the disrepute; they favor the praise and oppose the blame; they favor the pleasure and oppose the pain. Being thus involved in favoring and opposing, they are not freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. They are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, and pleasure and pain; these conditions among humans are impermanent, transient, and subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Knowing these, the mindful and wise person observes their changing nature. Desirable conditions do not churn their mind, nor do they feel repulsion toward the undesirable.
translations.an8.7:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta: “It is good, mendicants, for a mendicant from time to time to reflect on their own failure. It is good for a mendicant from time to time to reflect on another’s failure. It is good for a mendicant from time to time to reflect on their own success. It is good for a mendicant from time to time to reflect on another’s success. Overcome and with his mind obsessed by eight things that lead to the downfall, Devadatta is headed for a place of loss, headed for hell, to stay there for an eon, irredeemable.”
translations.an8.7:2: “What eight? Overcome and with his mind obsessed by gain, Devadatta is headed for a place of loss, headed for hell, to stay there for an eon, irredeemable. Overcome and with his mind obsessed by loss … fame … disgrace … honor … dishonor … evil desires … evil friendship, Devadatta is headed for a place of loss, headed for hell, to stay there for an eon, irredeemable. Overcome and with his mind obsessed by these eight things that lead to the downfall, Devadatta is headed for a place of loss, headed for hell, to stay there for an eon, irredeemable.”
translations.an8.7:3: “It is good, mendicants, if a mendicant lives having overcome arisen gain, having overcome arisen loss … fame … disgrace … honor … dishonor … evil desires … having overcome arisen evil friendship.”
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of the gods, as easily as a strong man would extend his arm or draw it back, vanished from among the gods of the Thirty-Three and appeared in front of Venerable Uttara on the Saṅkheyyaka Mountain at the Boar’s Slope. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, went up to Venerable Uttara, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: “Is it true, sir, that Venerable Uttara teaches the mendicants like this: ‘It is good, friends, for a mendicant from time to time to reflect on their own failure, another’s failure, their own success, and another’s success’?” “It is so, lord of the gods.” “But sir, is this Venerable Uttara’s own inspiration, or is it the word of the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully enlightened one?” “Well then, lord of the gods, I will give you a simile. Through a simile, some sensible people here understand the meaning of what is said.”
translations.an8.8:6: “Suppose, lord of the gods, there was a large heap of grain not far from a village or town. A large crowd of people would carry away grain—with poles, baskets, hip-pockets, or cupped hands. If someone were to go up to that large crowd and ask: ‘Where are you getting this grain from?’, how would that crowd rightly answer?” “Sir, they would rightly answer: ‘We are carrying it from that large heap of grain.’” “In the same way, lord of the gods, whatever is well-spoken is the word of the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully enlightened one. It is from that that we and others speak.”
translations.an8.8:7: “It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing! How well this was said by Venerable Uttara: ‘Whatever is well-spoken is the word of the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully enlightened one. It is from that that we and others speak.’ At one time, sir, the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta:”
translations.mn108:1: So I have heard. At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, not long after the Buddha had attained final Nibbāna.
translations.mn108:13: “Brahmin, there are ten qualities that inspire confidence which were declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully enlightened one. When we find these qualities in someone, we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them; and having honored and respected them, we live in dependence on them. What ten?”
translations.mn108:14: “Here, brahmin, a mendicant is ethical, living restrained by the Pātimokkha, acting properly and in the right place, seeing danger in the slightest faults, they keep to the training rules they have undertaken.”
translations.mn108:15: “They are very learned, remembering and storing what they have learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the entirely full and pure spiritual life—such teachings they have much learned, remembered, recited, mentally scrutinized, and well-penetrated with view.”
translations.mn108:17: “They obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four absorptions, which provide a happy dwelling in this very life and are higher states of mind.”
translations.mn108:18: “They experience many kinds of psychic power: having been one, they become many; having been many, they become one; they appear and vanish; they go unhindered through walls, ramparts, and mountains as if through space; they dive in and out of the earth as if in water; they walk on water without sinking as if on earth; they travel cross-legged through the sky like a bird; they touch and stroke with their hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; they exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahmā realm.”
translations.mn108:19: “With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, they hear both kinds of sounds, celestial and human, whether far or near.”
translations.mn108:2: At that time King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was having Rājagaha fortified, as he was suspicious of King Pajjota.
translations.mn108:20: He understands the minds of other beings and other individuals, having encompassed them with his own mind. He understands a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' and a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust.' He understands a mind with hatred as 'a mind with hatred,' and a mind without hatred as 'a mind without hatred.' He understands a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion,' and a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion.' He understands a constricted mind as 'a constricted mind,' and a scattered mind as 'a scattered mind.' He understands an expanded mind as 'an expanded mind,' and an unexpanded mind as 'an unexpanded mind.' He understands a surpassable mind as 'a surpassable mind,' and an unsurpassable mind as 'an unsurpassable mind.' He understands a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind,' and an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind.' He understands a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind,' and an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind.'
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, he enters and remains in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself with direct knowledge in this very life. These, brahmin, are the ten qualities inspiring confidence that were declared by that Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One. Since these qualities are found in us, we now honor, respect, revere, and venerate him; and having honored and respected him, we live in dependence on him.
translations.mn108:25: Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said to the venerable Ānanda: 'Where is Master Ānanda staying now?' 'I am staying in the Bamboo Grove now, brahmin.' 'Is the Bamboo Grove delightful, Master Ānanda, quiet and free from noise, secluded from people, a place for privacy, suitable for retreat?' 'Indeed, brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet and free from noise, secluded from people, a place for privacy, suitable for retreat, because of guardians and protectors like yourselves.' 'Indeed, Master Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet and free from noise, secluded from people, a place for privacy, suitable for retreat, because of masters like yourselves who are meditators and make a habit of meditation. You masters are both meditators and make a habit of meditation. Once, Master Ānanda, Master Gotama was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then I went to the Hall with the Peaked Roof in the Great Wood to see Master Gotama. There Master Gotama spoke in many ways about meditation. Master Gotama was a meditator and made a habit of meditation. And Master Gotama praised every kind of meditation.'
translations.mn108:28: 'It seems, Master Ānanda, that Master Gotama criticized the kind of meditation that should be criticized, and praised the kind that should be praised. And now, Master Ānanda, we must go; we are busy and have much to do.' 'Whenever you think it is the right time, brahmin.' Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, having rejoiced and appreciated the venerable Ānanda’s words, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then the venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the venerable Ānanda: 'It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. What if I went to the workplace of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, where the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna is?'
translations.mn108:4: Then the venerable Ānanda went to the workplace of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, where the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna was. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna saw the venerable Ānanda coming from afar. Seeing the venerable Ānanda, he said to him: 'Let Master Ānanda come. Welcome to Master Ānanda. It has been a long time since Master Ānanda made an occasion to come here. Let Master Ānanda sit down; this seat is prepared.' The venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna also took a low seat and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said to the venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: 'Is there, Master Ānanda, even one bhikkhu who is endowed in every way and in every respect with those qualities with which Master Gotama, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, was endowed?' 'There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, who is endowed in every way and in every respect with those qualities with which the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, was endowed. For the Blessed One, brahmin, was the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path, the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the expert in the path; and now the disciples live following the path, becoming endowed with it afterwards.'
translations.mn108:7: 'Is there, Master Ānanda, even one bhikkhu who was appointed by Master Gotama, saying: "This one will be your refuge after I am gone," whom you might follow now?' 'There is no single bhikkhu, brahmin, who was appointed by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, saying: "This one will be your refuge after I am gone," whom we might follow now.'
translations.mn108:9: 'But if there is no such refuge, Master Ānanda, what is the cause for your unity?' 'We are not without a refuge, brahmin; we have a refuge, brahmin; we have the Dhamma as our refuge.'
translations.mn117:10: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong intention as 'wrong intention,' and one understands right intention as 'right intention'; this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong intention? The intention of sensual desire, the intention of ill will, the intention of cruelty—this, bhikkhus, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? Right intention, I say, is twofold: there is right intention that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; and there is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-cruelty: this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:14: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The thinking, thought, intention, absorption, fixed absorption, application of mind, verbal formation in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path: this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: One makes an effort to abandon wrong intention and to enter upon right intention: this is one’s right effort. Mindfully one abandons wrong intention, mindfully one enters upon and dwells in right intention: this is one’s right mindfulness. Thus these three states run and circle around right intention, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? One understands wrong speech as wrong speech, and one understands right speech as right speech: this is one’s right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Right speech, I say, is twofold: there is right speech that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; and there is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? Abstinence from false speech, abstinence from malicious speech, abstinence from harsh speech, abstinence from idle chatter: this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:2: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you noble right concentration with its supports and its instruments. Listen and attend closely to what I shall say.” — “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The desisting, abstaining, refraining, and abstinence from the four kinds of verbal misconduct in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path: this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? One understands wrong action as wrong action, and one understands right action as right action: this is one’s right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Right action, I say, is twofold: there is right action that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; and there is right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what, bhikkhus, is right action that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? Abstinence from taking life, abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from sexual misconduct: this, bhikkhus, is right action that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:28: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? One understands wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, and one understands right livelihood as right livelihood: this is one’s right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood? Scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain: this, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Right livelihood, I say, is twofold: there is right livelihood that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; and there is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple abandons wrong livelihood and earns his living by right livelihood: this, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:34: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? In one of right view, right intention comes into being; in one of right intention, right speech comes into being; in one of right speech, right action comes into being; in one of right action, right livelihood comes into being; in one of right livelihood, right effort comes into being; in one of right effort, right mindfulness comes into being; in one of right mindfulness, right concentration comes into being; in one of right concentration
translations.mn117:35: In this, mendicants, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? For one of right view, mendicants, wrong view is worn away. And the many bad, unskillfulH{
translations.mn117:36: Thus, bhikkhus, there are twenty factors on the side of the wholesome and twenty factors on the side of the unwholesome—this Great Forty exposition of the Dhamma has been set in motion and cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or deva or Mara or Brahma or by anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong view as wrong view, and one understands right view as right view: this is one’s right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong view? ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; no fruit or result of good and bad actions; no this world, no other world; no mother, no father; no beings reborn spontaneously; no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have gone rightly and practiced rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known’—this, bhikkhus, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Right view, I say, is twofold: there is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions; and there is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions? ‘There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings reborn spontaneously; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have gone rightly and practiced rightly, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known’—this, bhikkhus, is right view that is affected by taints, partaking of merit, ripening in the acquisitions.
translations.mn117:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, the path factor of right view in one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path—this is called, bhikkhus, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: One makes an effort to abandon wrong view and to enter upon right view: this is one’s right effort. Mindfully one abandons wrong view, mindfully one enters upon and dwells in right view: this is one’s right mindfulness. Thus these three states run and circle around right view, namely: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in the Eastern Park, in the Palace of Migara’s Mother, together with many very well-known elder disciples—with the Venerable Sariputta, the Venerable Maha Moggallana, the Venerable Maha Kassapa, the Venerable Maha Kaccayana, the Venerable Maha Kotthika, the Venerable Maha Kappina, the Venerable Maha Cunda, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ananda, and other very well-known elder disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness. The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven enlightenment factors. The seven enlightenment factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.’
translations.mn118:19: He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing rapture’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing rapture.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquilizing the mental formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquilizing the mental formation.’
translations.mn118:2: At that time the elder bhikkhus were teaching and instructing the new bhikkhus. Some elder bhikkhus were teaching and instructing ten bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were teaching and instructing twenty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were teaching and instructing thirty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus were teaching and instructing forty bhikkhus. And the new bhikkhus, being taught and instructed by the elder bhikkhus, achieved high and wide successive distinction.
translations.mn118:20: He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in gladdening the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out gladdening the mind.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in concentrating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out concentrating the mind.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out liberating the mind.’
translations.mn118:21: He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating fading away’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating fading away.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating cessation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating cessation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.’
translations.mn118:23: And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu breathing in long knows: ‘I breathe in long,’ or breathing out long knows: ‘I breathe out long’; breathing in short knows: ‘I breathe in short,’ or breathing out short knows: ‘I breathe out short’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquillizing the bodily formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquillizing the bodily formation’—on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. I say, bhikkhus, that this is a certain body among the bodies, namely, in-breathing and out-breathing. Therefore, on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:25: On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing rapture’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing rapture’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in tranquillizing the mental formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out tranquillizing the mental formation’—on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. I say, bhikkhus, that this is a certain feeling among the feelings, namely, close attention to in-breathing and out-breathing. Therefore, on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:26: On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in gladdening the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out gladdening the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in concentrating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out concentrating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out liberating the mind’—on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. I do not say, bhikkhus, that there is mindfulness of breathing for one who is forgetful, who lacks clear comprehension. Therefore, on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:27: On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating fading away’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating fading away’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating cessation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating cessation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment’—on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. Having seen with wisdom the abandoning of covetousness and displeasure, he looks on with perfect equanimity. Therefore, on that occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:28: Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, developed and cultivated in this way, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: And how, bhikkhus, are the four foundations of mindfulness developed and cultivated so that they fulfill the seven enlightenment factors?
translations.mn118:3: On that occasion, the Blessed One was seated in the open air on the night of the full moon Uposatha day, the fifteenth, the day of the invitation ceremony, surrounded by the Sangha of bhikkhus. Then the Blessed One, having looked around at the Sangha of bhikkhus, which was perfectly silent, addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.mn118:30: On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world—on that occasion, his mindfulness is established and unconfused. On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s mindfulness is established and unconfused, on that occasion the mindfulness enlightenment factor is aroused in the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor; on that occasion the mindfulness enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:31: Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates, examines, and undertakes an inquiry into that phenomenon with wisdom. On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwelling thus mindful investigates, examines, and undertakes an inquiry into that phenomenon with wisdom, on that occasion the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is aroused in the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor; on that occasion the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:33: In one whose energy is aroused, unworldly rapture arises. On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, unworldly rapture arises in a bhikkhu whose energy is aroused, on that occasion the rapture enlightenment factor is aroused in the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the rapture enlightenment factor; on that occasion the rapture enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:34: For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil. On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil for a bhikkhu whose mind is rapturous, on that occasion the tranquillity enlightenment factor is aroused in the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the tranquillity enlightenment factor; on that occasion the tranquillity enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:35: For one whose body is tranquil and who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. On whatever occasion, bhikkhus, the mind of a bhikkhu whose body is tranquil and who is happy becomes concentrated, on that occasion the concentration enlightenment factor is aroused in the bhikkhu; on that occasion the bhikkhu develops the concentration enlightenment factor; on that occasion the concentration enlightenment factor goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:36: He looks on with equanimity at the mind thus concentrated. Whenever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu looks on with equanimity at the mind thus concentrated, at that time the enlightenment factor of equanimity is aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time the bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity; at that time the development of the enlightenment factor of equanimity goes to fulfillment in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:4: “Bhikkhus, I am content with this progress; Bhikkhus, I am content in my heart with this progress. Therefore, bhikkhus, stir up even more energy for the sake of attaining the unattained, for reaching the unreached, for realizing the unrealized. I will wait right here at Sāvatthī for the Komudī full moon of the fourth month.”
translations.mn118:40: Bhikkhus, the four foundations of mindfulness, developed and cultivated in this way, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
translations.mn118:41: And how, bhikkhus, are the seven factors of enlightenment developed and cultivated so that they fulfill true knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: And those senior bhikkhus were exhorting and instructing the new bhikkhus even more. Some senior bhikkhus were exhorting and instructing ten bhikkhus, some senior bhikkhus were exhorting and instructing twenty bhikkhus, some senior bhikkhus were exhorting and instructing thirty bhikkhus, some senior bhikkhus were exhorting and instructing forty bhikkhus. And the new bhikkhus, being exhorted and instructed by the senior bhikkhus, understood a grand and successive distinction.
translations.mn118:9: Bhikkhus, there are in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, arahants, those whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through right final knowledge—such bhikkhus as these, bhikkhus, are in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
translations.mn11:13: In such a Dhamma and Vinaya, bhikkhus, whatever confidence one has in the Teacher is not said to be rightly directed; whatever confidence one has in the Dhamma is not said to be rightly directed; whatever fulfillment of the precepts one has is not said to be rightly directed; whatever affection and liking one has for fellow practitioners is not said to be rightly directed. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that is how it is in a poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, poorly expounded, not leading out, not tending to peace, expounded by one who is not a Fully Enlightened One.
translations.mn11:14: But, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, claiming to have full understanding of all clinging, rightly describes the full understanding of all clinging: he describes the full understanding of clinging to sensual pleasures, he describes the full understanding of clinging to views, he describes the full understanding of clinging to rules and observances, and he describes the full understanding of clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn11:15: In such a Dhamma and Vinaya, bhikkhus, whatever confidence one has in the Teacher is said to be rightly directed; whatever confidence one has in the Dhamma is said to be rightly directed; whatever fulfillment of the precepts one has is said to be rightly directed; whatever affection and liking one has for fellow practitioners is said to be rightly directed. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that is how it is in a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, well-expounded, leading out, tending to peace, expounded by a Fully Enlightened One.
translations.mn11:2: “Bhikkhus, only here is there an ascetic, here a second ascetic, here a third ascetic, here a fourth ascetic; other doctrines are empty of ascetics. Thus, bhikkhus, roar this right lion's roar.”
translations.mn11:6: Bhikkhus, there are these two views: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Any recluses or brahmins who are attached to the view of existence, who have gone to the view of existence, who are obsessed with the view of existence, are opposed to the view of non-existence. Any recluses or brahmins who are attached to the view of non-existence, who have gone to the view of non-existence, who are obsessed with the view of non-existence, are opposed to the view of existence.
translations.mn11:7: Any recluses or brahmins who do not understand as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of these two views are with lust, with hate, with delusion, with craving, with clinging, without vision, favoring and opposing, delighting in and enjoying proliferation; they are not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.mn11:9: Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clinging. Which four? Clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the grove outside the city to the west.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. Since the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible, this is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the Brahma-wheel in motion.
translations.mn12:19: Furthermore, Sāriputta, with the destruction of the taints, the Tathāgata enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life. Since the Tathāgata enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, having realized it for himself by direct knowledge in this very life, this is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the Brahma-wheel in motion.
translations.mn12:2: At that time Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, had recently left this Dhamma and Vinaya. In an assembly in Vesālī he spoke these words: “The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following a line of inquiry as it occurs to him. And the Dhamma he teaches for someone's benefit leads to the complete destruction of suffering for one who practices it.”
translations.mn12:20: These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the Brahma-wheel in motion.
translations.mn12:22: Sāriputta, there are these four intrepidities of the Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the Brahma-wheel in motion. What are the four?
translations.mn12:23: ‘While you claim to be a fully enlightened Buddha, you have not fully understood these things.’ I see no ground, Sāriputta, for any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone else in the world to reasonably accuse me of this. Since I see no such ground, Sāriputta, I dwell attained to security, attained to fearlessness, attained to self-confidence.
translations.mn12:24: ‘While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints are not destroyed.’ I see no ground, Sāriputta, for any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone else in the world to reasonably accuse me of this. Since I see no such ground, Sāriputta, I dwell attained to security, attained to fearlessness, attained to self-confidence.
translations.mn12:25: ‘Those things you have called obstructions are not actually obstructions for one who practices them.’ I see no ground, Sāriputta, for any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone else in the world to reasonably accuse me of this. Since I see no such ground, Sāriputta, I dwell attained to security, attained to fearlessness, attained to self-confidence.
translations.mn12:26: ‘The Dhamma you have taught for a specific purpose does not lead one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering.’ I see no ground, Sāriputta, for any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone else in the world to reasonably accuse me of this. Since I see no such ground, Sāriputta, I dwell attained to security, attained to fearlessness, attained to self-confidence.
translations.mn12:32: Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of birth. Which four? Egg-born birth, womb-born birth, moisture-born birth, and spontaneous birth.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is egg-born birth? Those beings who are born by breaking out of an eggshell—this is called egg-born birth. And what is womb-born birth? Those beings who are born by breaking out of a womb-membrane—this is called womb-born birth. And what is moisture-born birth? Those beings who are born in rotting fish, in a rotting corpse, in rotting dough, in a cesspool, or in a sewer—this is called moisture-born birth. And what is spontaneous birth? Gods, hell-beings, some humans, and some beings in the lower worlds—this is called spontaneous birth. These, Sāriputta, are the four kinds of birth.
translations.mn12:35: Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. Which five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, humanity, and the gods.
translations.mn12:36: I understand hell, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to hell; and I also understand how one who has practiced accordingly, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. I understand the animal realm... I understand the realm of ghosts... I understand humanity... I understand the gods... I understand Nibbāna, Sāriputta, and the path and way leading to Nibbāna; and I also understand how one who has practiced accordingly, by the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for oneself with direct knowledge in this very life.
translations.mn12:4: “Sāriputta, Sunakkhatta is a foolish man, and he is angry. It is out of anger that he has spoken these words. While thinking, ‘I will speak dispraise,’ Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta actually speaks praise of the Tathāgata. For it is indeed praise of the Tathāgata when someone says: ‘The Dhamma he has taught for a specific purpose leads one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering.’
translations.mn12:43: Sāriputta, if anyone should say of me, who knows and sees like this: ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following a line of inquiry, the product of his own ingenuity’—unless he abandons that speech, abandons that state of mind, and relinquishes that view, he will be deposited in hell as if carried there. Just as a bhikkhu possessed of virtue, concentration, and wisdom would attain final knowledge in this very life, I say this is comparable: unless he abandons that speech, abandons that state of mind, and relinquishes that view, he will be deposited in hell as if carried there.
translations.mn12:44: Sāriputta, I recall having lived a holy life possessed of four factors: I was an ascetic, the foremost in asceticism; I was coarse, the foremost in coarseness; I was scrupulous, the foremost in scrupulousness; I was secluded, the foremost in seclusion.
translations.mn12:46: This was my coarseness, Sāriputta: the dirt and dust of many years had accumulated on my body until it formed a crust. Just as a tinduka tree-stump that has stood for many years accumulates a crust, so too the dirt and dust of many years had accumulated on my body until it formed a crust. It never occurred to me, Sāriputta: ‘Oh, let me brush off this dirt and dust with my hand, or let others brush off this dirt and dust with their hands.’ Such a thought did not occur to me. This was my coarseness.
translations.mn12:47: This was my scrupulousness, Sāriputta: I was always mindful in stepping forward and mindful in stepping back, and my compassion was established even toward a drop of water: ‘May I not bring destruction to the tiny creatures in uneven places.’ This was my scrupulousness.
translations.mn12:49: Sāriputta, when the cows had left the cow-pen and the cowherds had gone away, I would go there on all fours and eat the dung of the young nursing calves. As long as my own urine and excrement lasted, I would eat my own urine and excrement. This, Sāriputta, was my practice in great filth-eating.
translations.mn12:5: Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta will never have this kind of inference from the Dhamma regarding me: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully enlightened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to train, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’
translations.mn12:50: Sāriputta, I would live by plunging into a certain terrifying forest grove. Such was the terror of that terrifying forest grove that if anyone who was not free from lust entered it, their hair would mostly stand on end. During the cold winter nights, in the time of the mid-winter frosts, I would spend the night in the open air and the day in the forest grove. In the last month of summer, I would spend the day in the open air and the night in the forest grove. And Sāriputta, these marvelous verses never heard before occurred to me: ‘Scorched and frozen, alone in the terrifying forest; naked, not sitting near a fire, the sage is intent on his quest.’
translations.mn12:51: Sāriputta, I would make my bed in a charnel ground, leaning against a skeleton. And Sāriputta, cowherd boys would come up to me and spit on me, urinate on me, throw dirt on me, and even poke sticks into my ear holes. Yet, Sāriputta, I do not recall ever giving rise to a wicked heart toward them. This, Sāriputta, was my practice in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘Purity comes through food.’ They say: ‘We live on jujube fruits.’ They eat jujube fruits, they eat jujube powder, they drink jujube water, and they consume various kinds of jujube preparations. I recall, Sāriputta, eating only a single jujube fruit as my food. Now, Sāriputta, you might think: ‘The jujube fruit must have been large at that time.’ But Sāriputta, you should not see it like that. Even then, a jujube fruit was at most the same size as it is now. Because of eating only a single jujube fruit, my body became extremely emaciated. Like the joints of a withered creeper or a bamboo, so did my limbs become through such lack of food. Like a camel’s hoof, so did my buttocks become through such lack of food. Like a string of beads, so did my backbone become, rising and falling, through such lack of food. Just as the rafters of an old shed are collapsed and broken, so did my ribs become collapsed and broken through such lack of food. Just as in a deep well the sparkle of the water is seen sunk deep down, so in my eye-sockets the sparkle of my eyes was seen sunk deep down through such lack of food. Just as a bitter gourd cut while green becomes shriveled and withered by the wind and sun, so did the skin of my head become shriveled and withered through such lack of food. Sāriputta, when I thought, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I would seize my backbone; when I thought, ‘I will touch my backbone,’ I would seize the skin of my belly, so much did the skin of my belly cling to my backbone through such lack of food. Sāriputta, when I thought, ‘I will go to defecate or urinate,’ I would fall down face-first right there through such lack of food. Sāriputta, when I would stroke my limbs with my hand to comfort my body, the hair, rotted at its roots, would fall from my body through such lack of food.
translations.mn12:56: Yet, Sāriputta, by this conduct, by this practice, by this performance of difficulties, I did not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why was that? Because of the non-attainment of that noble wisdom which, when attained, is noble and leading out, and leads the one who acts upon it to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘Purity comes through wandering in saṃsāra.’ But Sāriputta, there is no kind of wandering in saṃsāra that I have not already wandered through in this long journey, except for the Pure Abodes. If I had wandered in the Pure Abodes, Sāriputta, I would not have come back to this world.
translations.mn12:6: Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta will never have this kind of inference from the Dhamma regarding me: ‘That Blessed One experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, ramparts, and mountains as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if in water; he walks on water without sinking as if on earth; he travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.’
translations.mn12:60: Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘Purity comes through sacrifice.’ But Sāriputta, there is no kind of sacrifice that I have not already offered in this long journey, when I was a king, a kshatriya, an anointed monarch, or a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:61: Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘Purity comes through fire-worship.’ But Sāriputta, there is no kind of fire that I have not already worshipped in this long journey, when I was a king, a kshatriya, an anointed monarch, or a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:62: But, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘As long as this good man is young, a youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, so long is he endowed with the utmost lucidity of wisdom. But when this good man is old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, being eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, then that lucidity of wisdom is lost.’ But, Sāriputta, it should not be seen like this. I am now old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life; my age is turning eighty. Suppose, Sāriputta, I had four disciples who lived for a hundred years, who were endowed with the utmost mindfulness, memory, and resolution, and with the utmost lucidity of wisdom. Just as, Sāriputta, a skilled archer, trained, practiced, and experienced, could easily shoot a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree, so were they endowed with such extreme mindfulness, memory, resolution, and the utmost lucidity of wisdom. They would ask me question after question about the four foundations of mindfulness, and I would answer each question they asked. They would remember my answers as they were given, and they would not ask me a follow-up question. Except for the time taken for eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, for answering the calls of nature, and for dispelling sleep and fatigue, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma would be inexhaustible, the Tathāgata’s phrasing of the Dhamma would be inexhaustible, and the Tathāgata’s quick-wittedness in answering questions would be inexhaustible. Then those four disciples of mine, living for a hundred years, would pass away at the end of those hundred years. Even if you have to carry me around on a litter, Sāriputta, there is no change in the Tathāgata’s lucidity of wisdom.
translations.mn12:7: Even in this, Sāriputta, that foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have confidence in me according to the Dhamma: ‘The Blessed One, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, hears both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near.’
translations.mn12:8: Even in this, Sāriputta, that foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have confidence in me according to the Dhamma: ‘The Blessed One understands the minds of other beings and other persons, having encompassed them with his own mind. He understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust, and a mind without lust as a mind without lust; he understands a mind with hate as a mind with hate, and a mind without hate as a mind without hate; he understands a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; he understands a constricted mind as a constricted mind, and a scattered mind as a scattered mind; he understands an exalted mind as an exalted mind, and an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; he understands a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, and an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; he understands a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; he understands a liberated mind as a liberated mind, and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.’
translations.mn12:9: Sāriputta, the Tathāgata has these ten powers of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets the Wheel of Brahma in motion. What are the ten?
translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.
translations.mn135:13: Here, student, some woman or man is not a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps. Because of performing and undertaking such action, at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, even hell. If, at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, or hell, but instead come to the human state, then wherever they are reborn, they are poor. This is the way, student, that leads to poverty: not being a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
translations.mn135:2: Then the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When the polite and courteous talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their actions, student, heirs of their actions, they originate from their actions, are bound to their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as inferior and superior.”
