translations.mn135:3: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason why among human beings, though they are all humans, inferiority and superiority are seen? For humans are seen to be short-lived and long-lived; sickly and healthy; ugly and beautiful; insignificant and influential; poor and wealthy; low-born and high-born; and stupid and wise. Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason why among human beings, though they are all humans, inferiority and superiority are seen?”
translations.mn135:4: “Beings are owners of their actions, student, heirs of their actions, they originate from their actions, are bound to their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as inferior and superior.” “I do not understand the detailed meaning of what Master Gotama has said in brief without explaining the details. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma so that I might understand the detailed meaning of what Master Gotama has said in brief.” “Then, student, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the student Subha, Todeyya’s son, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn135:5: “Here, student, some woman or man is a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings. Because of performing and undertaking such action, at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. But if, at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell, but instead come to the human state, then wherever they are reborn they are short-lived. This is the way, student, that leads to being short-lived, namely—to be a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings.
translations.mn135:6: But here, student, some woman or man, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, they are conscientious, merciful, and dwell compassionate for the welfare of all living beings. Because of performing and undertaking such action, at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But if, at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, but instead come to the human state, then wherever they are reborn they are long-lived. This is the way, student, that leads to being long-lived, namely—having abandoned the killing of living beings, to abstain from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, to be conscientious, merciful, and dwell compassionate for the welfare of all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: If, bhikkhus, while that clansman strives, exerts himself, and makes an effort, those riches do not materialize, he sorrows, grieves, and laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught, saying: ‘My effort is in vain, my exertion is fruitless.’ But if those riches do materialize, he experiences pain and grief in the effort to protect them: ‘How can I ensure that kings do not take my riches, thieves do not take them, fire does not burn them, water does not sweep them away, or unloved heirs do not take them?’ And as he guards and protects them, kings take them, or thieves take them, or fire burns them, or water sweeps them away, or unloved heirs take them. He sorrows, grieves, and laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught, saying: ‘What I once had, I have no longer.’ This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible here and now, having sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:11: Again, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasures as the cause... kings quarrel with kings, nobles quarrel with nobles, brahmins quarrel with brahmins, householders quarrel with householders; mother quarrels with son, son quarrels with mother, father quarrels with son, son quarrels with father; brother quarrels with brother, brother quarrels with sister, sister quarrels with brother, friend quarrels with friend. Having entered into quarrel, strife, and dispute, they attack each other with fists, with clods, with sticks, or with weapons. There they incur death or deadly suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures...
translations.mn13:12: Again, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasures as the cause... they take up sword and shield, buckle on bow and quiver, and charge into battle in double array while arrows are flying, spears are flying, and swords are flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, and their heads are cut off by swords. There they incur death or deadly suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures...
translations.mn13:13: Again, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasures as the cause... they take up sword and shield, buckle on bow and quiver, and charge against slippery bastions while arrows are flying, spears are flying, and swords are flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, splashed with boiling dung, crushed by falling weights, and their heads are cut off by swords. There they incur death or deadly suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures...
translations.mn13:15: Again, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasures as the cause... they practice misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced misconduct by body, speech, and mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures pertaining to the future life, a mass of suffering having sensual pleasures as its cause...
translations.mn13:16: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from sensual pleasures? The removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for sensual pleasures—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: That any ascetics or brahmins who do not understand as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape in the case of sensual pleasures, should either themselves fully understand sensual pleasures or instruct another so that he might fully understand sensual pleasures—that is impossible. That any ascetics or brahmins who understand as it actually is the gratification as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape in the case of sensual pleasures, should either themselves fully understand sensual pleasures or instruct another so that he might fully understand sensual pleasures—that is possible.
translations.mn13:18: And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in the case of forms? Suppose there were a girl of the noble caste, the brahmin caste, or the householder caste, fifteen or sixteen years old, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair. Is her beauty and loveliness then at its height? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on that beauty and loveliness—this is the gratification in the case of forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in material forms? Here, bhikkhus, one might see that same woman at a later time, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, as crooked as a roof-rafter, bent, leaning on a stick, going along trembling, frail, youth gone, teeth broken, hair grey, scanty or bald, wrinkled, with limbs all blotchy. What do you think, bhikkhus? Has her former beauty and radiance vanished, and the danger appeared? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then those bhikkhus thought: 'It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. What if we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?' Then those bhikkhus went to the park of the wanderers of other sects. They exchanged greetings with the wanderers of other sects and, when the polite and courteous talk was finished, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the wanderers of other sects said to them:
translations.mn13:20: Furthermore, bhikkhus, one might see that same woman afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill, lying fouled in her own urine and excrement, lifted up by others and laid down by others. What do you think, bhikkhus? Has her former beauty and radiance vanished, and the danger appeared? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Furthermore, bhikkhus, one might see that same woman's body discarded in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews; the bones disconnected and scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, here an ankle-bone, there a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a rib-bone, there a back-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth, there the skull. What do you think, bhikkhus? Has her former beauty and radiance vanished, and the danger appeared? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:29: Furthermore, bhikkhus, one might see that same woman's body discarded in a charnel ground—the bones bleached white, the color of shells; the bones piled up, more than a year old; the bones rotted and crumbled to dust. What do you think, bhikkhus? Has her former beauty and radiance vanished, and the danger appeared? 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:3: “Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of sensual pleasures, and we also teach the full understanding of sensual pleasures. The ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of material forms, and we also teach the full understanding of material forms. The ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of feelings, and we also teach the full understanding of feelings. Here, friends, what is the distinction, what is the specific intent, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us—that is, regarding teaching versus teaching, or instruction versus instruction?”
translations.mn13:30: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from material forms? The removal of desire and lust, the giving up of desire and lust for material forms—this is the escape from material forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in feelings? Here, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. At the time when a bhikkhu... abides in the first jhāna, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both; at that time he feels only unafflicted feeling. The unafflicted, I say, bhikkhus, is the highest gratification in feelings.
translations.mn13:36: And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in feelings? The fact that feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from feelings? The removal of desire and lust, the giving up of desire and lust for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those bhikkhus neither approved nor disapproved of the words of those wanderers of other sects. Without approving or disapproving, they rose from their seats and left, thinking: 'We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'
translations.mn13:6: “Bhikkhus, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be asked: 'But friends, what is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape regarding sensual pleasures? What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape regarding material forms? What is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape regarding feelings?' Being thus questioned, bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects would not be able to explain, and further, they would meet with frustration. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, it is outside their scope. I do not see anyone, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for a Tathāgata, or a disciple of a Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them."
translations.mn13:8: And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in sensual pleasures? Here, bhikkhus, a clansman earns his living by some craft—whether by sealing, or by accounting, or by calculating, or by farming, or by trading, or by cattle-breeding, or by archery, or by royal service, or by some other craft—confronting cold, confronting heat, being harmed by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, dying of hunger and thirst. This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible here and now, having sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:9: If, bhikkhus, while that clansman is thus striving, exerting himself, and struggling, those riches do not materialize, he sorrows, tires, and laments; he beats his breast and cries, falling into confusion: 'My striving is in vain, my effort is fruitless!' This too, bhikkhus, is a danger in sensual pleasures, a mass of suffering visible here and now, having sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, the cause being simply sensual pleasures.
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Magadhan country and eventually arrived at Rājagaha. He went to the potter Bhaggava and said to him:
translations.mn140:12: ‘One should not neglect wisdom, one should preserve truth, one should cultivate relinquishment, and one should train for peace’—so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or it may be external. And what is the internal earth element? Whatever is internal, within oneself, hard, solid, and clung-to, such as: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, contents of the stomach, feces, or whatever else is internal, within oneself, hard, solid, and clung-to—this is called the internal earth element. Now both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element. This should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, bhikkhu, is the water element? The water element may be internal or it may be external. And what is the internal water element? Whatever is internal, within oneself, water, watery, and clung-to, such as: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine, or whatever else is internal, within oneself, water, watery, and clung-to—this is called the internal water element. Now both the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element. This should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or it may be external. And what is the internal fire element? Whatever is internal, within oneself, fire, fiery, and clung-to, such as: that by which one is warmed, aged, and consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted gets completely digested, or whatever else is internal, within oneself, fire, fiery, and clung-to—this is called the internal fire element. Now both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element. This should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, bhikkhu, is the air element? The air element may be internal or it may be external. And what is the internal air element? Whatever is internal, within oneself, air, airy, and clung-to, such as: up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else is internal, within oneself, air, airy, and clung-to—this is called the internal air element. Now both the internal air element and the external air element are simply the air element. This should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, bhikkhu, is the space element? The space element may be internal or it may be external. And what is the internal space element? Whatever is internal, within oneself, space, spatial, and clung-to, such as: the ear-holes, the nostrils, the door of the mouth, and that through which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is swallowed, and where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted remains, and through which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted passes out below, or whatever else is internal, within oneself, space, spatial, empty, void, and a hole, not touched by flesh and blood, and clung-to—this is called the internal space element. Now both the internal space element and the external space element are simply the space element. This should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the space element.
translations.mn140:2: “If it is no trouble for you, Bhaggava, I would stay for one night in your workshop.” “It is no trouble for me, bhante. But there is a renunciant who has already taken up residence there. If he allows it, stay as long as you like, bhante.”
translations.mn140:20: Then there remains only equanimity, pure and bright, soft, wieldy, and radiant. Suppose, bhikkhu, a skilled goldsmith or his apprentice were to prepare a furnace, light the fire in the furnace mouth, take some gold with tongs and put it into the furnace mouth. From time to time he would blow on it, from time to time he would sprinkle it with water, and from time to time he would just look on. That gold would become well-refined, fully refined, brought to a state of purity, with its dross removed, soft, wieldy, and radiant. Then whatever kind of ornament he wishes to make from it—whether a headband, earrings, a necklace, or a golden chain—it serves his purpose. In the same way, bhikkhu, then there remains only equanimity, pure and bright, soft, wieldy, and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’
translations.mn140:29: ‘One should not neglect wisdom, one should preserve truth, one should cultivate relinquishment, and one should train for peace’—so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:3: Now at that time a young man of good family named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith in the Blessed One. He had already taken up residence in that potter’s workshop. Then the Blessed One approached Pukkusāti and said to him: “If it is not an inconvenience to you, bhikkhu, we might stay for one night in the workshop.” “The potter’s workshop is spacious, friend. Let the venerable one stay as he pleases.”
translations.mn140:30: ‘Wherein the tides of conceiving do not flow, and when the tides of conceiving do not flow, he is called a sage at peace’—so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:31: ‘I am,’ bhikkhu, is a conceiving; ‘I am this’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall not be’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be possessed of form’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be formless’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be percipient’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be non-percipient’ is a conceiving; ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’ is a conceiving. Conceiving is a disease, conceiving is a tumor, conceiving is a dart. By overcoming all conceivings, bhikkhu, one is called a sage at peace. And the sage at peace is not born, does not age, does not die, is not shaken, and does not yearn. For there is nothing in him by which he might be born. Not being born, how could he age? Not aging, how could he die? Not dying, how could he be shaken? Not being shaken, for what could he yearn?
translations.mn140:32: ‘Wherein the tides of conceiving do not flow, and when the tides of conceiving do not flow, he is called a sage at peace’—so it was said, and it was said with reference to this. Bhikkhu, remember this, my brief Exposition of the Six Elements.”
translations.mn140:33: Then the venerable Pukkusāti thought: “Indeed, the Teacher has come to me! The Happy One has come to me! The Fully Enlightened One has come to me!” He rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and prostrating himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, he said: “Venerable sir, a transgression overcame me, in that I was so foolish, so confused, and so unskilled as to address the Blessed One as ‘friend.’ Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my confession of my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.” “Surely, bhikkhu, a transgression overcame you, in that you were so foolish, so confused, and so unskilled as to address me as ‘friend.’ But since you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it. For it is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline when one sees one’s transgression as a transgression and makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and practices restraint in the future.”
translations.mn140:34: “Venerable sir, may I receive the full ordination in the Blessed One’s presence?” “But, bhikkhu, are your bowl and robes complete?” “Venerable sir, my bowl and robes are not complete.” “Bhikkhu, Tathāgatas do not give the full ordination to those whose bowl and robes are incomplete.”
translations.mn140:35: Then the venerable Pukkusāti, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed to search for a bowl and robes. Then, while the venerable Pukkusāti was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a stray cow killed him.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Blessed One entered the potter’s workshop, prepared a spread of grass at one side, and sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Then the Blessed One spent much of the night sitting. The venerable Pukkusāti also spent much of the night sitting. Then the Blessed One thought: “This young man of good family conducts himself in an inspiring way. Suppose I were to question him.” Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: “Under whom, bhikkhu, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?” “Friend, there is the recluse Gotama, a son of the Sakyans, who went forth from a Sakyan family. Now a good report of that Blessed One Gotama has been spread abroad thus: ‘That Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ I have gone forth under that Blessed One. That Blessed One is my teacher. I profess the Dhamma of that Blessed One.” “But, bhikkhu, where is that Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, living now?” “Friend, in the northern countries there is a city named Sāvatthī. That Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, is living there now.” “But, bhikkhu, have you ever seen that Blessed One? If you saw him, would you recognize him?” “No, friend, I have never seen that Blessed One, nor if I saw him would I recognize him.”
translations.mn140:6: Then the Blessed One thought: “This clansman has gone forth on my account. What if I were to teach him the Dhamma?” Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Pukkusāti: “I will teach you the Dhamma, bhikkhu. Listen and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” the venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn140:7: “‘A person consists of six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen examinations of mind, and four foundations. Standing upon these, the currents of conceiving do not flow; and when the currents of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace. One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should cultivate relinquishment, and should train for peace.’ This is the summary of the Exposition of the Elements.
translations.mn146:12: “Sisters, I have made this simile to convey a meaning. This is the meaning: ‘The inner mass of flesh’ is a term for the six internal bases. ‘The outer hide’ is a term for the six external bases. ‘The inner flesh, the inner sinews, the inner ligaments’ is a term for delight and greed. ‘The sharp butcher’s knife’ is a term for noble wisdom—the noble wisdom that cuts, severs, and carves away the inner defilements, the inner fetters, and the inner bonds.
translations.mn146:13: Sisters, there are these seven factors of enlightenment, which, when developed and cultivated, lead a bhikkhu to realize for himself with direct knowledge, here and now, the heart’s release and the release by wisdom that are free from defilements. What seven? Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens in release. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of states… energy… rapture… tranquility… immersion… equanimity, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens in release. These, sisters, are the seven factors of enlightenment, which, when developed and cultivated, lead a bhikkhu to realize for himself with direct knowledge, here and now, the heart’s release and the release by wisdom that are free from defilements.”
translations.mn146:14: Then, having exhorted those bhikkhunīs with this instruction, the venerable Nandaka dismissed them: “Go, sisters; it is time.” Then those bhikkhunīs, having delighted and rejoiced in the venerable Nandaka’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the venerable Nandaka, and keeping him on their right, went to the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, they paid homage to him and stood to one side. As they stood there, the Blessed One said to them: “Go, bhikkhunīs; it is time.” Then those bhikkhunīs paid homage to the Blessed One and, keeping him on their right, departed.
translations.mn146:3: Now at that time the senior bhikkhus were exhorting the bhikkhunīs in rotation. But the venerable Nandaka did not want to exhort the bhikkhunīs in his turn. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, whose turn is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?” “Everyone has taken their turn, bhante, to exhort the bhikkhunīs. But this venerable Nandaka does not want to exhort the bhikkhunīs in his turn.”
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka: “Exhort the bhikkhunīs, Nandaka; instruct the bhikkhunīs, Nandaka; give the bhikkhunīs a talk on the Dhamma, brahmin.” “Yes, bhante,” the venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One. In the morning, he dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. After walking for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from his almsround after the meal, he went with a companion to the Royal Park. The bhikkhunīs saw the venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for his feet. The venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat and washed his feet. The bhikkhunīs also paid homage to the venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side. When they were seated, the venerable Nandaka said to them:
translations.mn146:5: “Sisters, this will be a talk in the form of questions. Where you understand, you should say: ‘We understand.’ Where you do not understand, you should say: ‘We do not understand.’ Or if you have any doubt or uncertainty, you should question me about it: ‘How is this, bhante? What is the meaning of this?’” “Bhante, we are already satisfied and pleased with the venerable Nandaka for even this much, that he invites us in this way.”
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard—At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: “The qualities that ripen in liberation are mature in Rāhula. What if I were to lead Rāhula further to the destruction of the defilements?” Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. After walking for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from his almsround after the meal, he addressed the venerable Rāhula: “Take your sitting cloth, Rāhula; let us go to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, bhante,” the venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One, and taking his sitting cloth, he followed close behind the Blessed One.
translations.mn147:2: Now at that time many thousands of deities followed the Blessed One, thinking: “Today the Blessed One will further lead the venerable Rāhula to the destruction of the taints.” Then the Blessed One, having entered the Blind Men’s Grove, sat down at the foot of a certain tree on a seat made ready. The venerable Rāhula also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the venerable Rāhula: “What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, bhante.” “Is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, bhante.” “Is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, bhante.”
translations.mn148:16: And this, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the origination of identity: one regards the eye as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
translations.mn148:2: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. I will reveal a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure, namely, the six sextets. Listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn148:22: And this, bhikkhus, is the way leading to the cessation of identity: one regards the eye as ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.mn148:3: “The six internal bases should be known, the six external bases should be known, the six classes of consciousness should be known, the six classes of contact should be known, the six classes of feeling should be known, the six classes of craving should be known.
translations.mn148:34: Bhikkhus, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition there arises a feeling felt as pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When one is touched by a pleasant feeling, if one does not delight in it, welcome it, or remain attached to it, then the underlying tendency to lust does not lie within one. When one is touched by a painful feeling, if one does not sorrow, grieve, or lament, does not weep beating one's breast and become distraught, then the underlying tendency to aversion does not lie within one. When one is touched by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands as it really is the origination, the disappearance, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to that feeling; then the underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie within one. Bhikkhus, that one—having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling, having abolished the underlying tendency to aversion for painful feeling, having uprooted the underlying tendency to ignorance for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge—should here and now make an end of suffering: this is possible.
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with craving.
translations.mn149:11: And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be fully understood by direct knowledge? It should be said: the five aggregates of clinging, namely, the material form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging, the perception aggregate of clinging, the formations aggregate of clinging, the consciousness aggregate of clinging. These are the things to be fully understood by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be abandoned by direct knowledge? Ignorance and craving for existence—these are the things to be abandoned by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be developed by direct knowledge? Serenity and insight—these are the things to be developed by direct knowledge. And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be realized by direct knowledge? True knowledge and liberation—these are the things to be realized by direct knowledge.
translations.mn149:2: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Great Sixfold Base. Listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn149:3: “Bhikkhus, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and not seeing forms as they really are, not knowing and not seeing eye-consciousness as it really is, not knowing and not seeing eye-contact as it really is, and not knowing and not seeing as it really is whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one is infatuated with the eye, infatuated with forms, infatuated with eye-consciousness, infatuated with eye-contact, and infatuated with whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition. For one who dwells infatuated, fettered, and infatuated, observing gratification, the five aggregates of clinging go on to accumulation in the future. And one's craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there—increases. One's bodily disturbances increase, and one's mental disturbances increase; one's bodily distresses increase, and one's mental distresses increase; one's bodily fevers increase, and one's mental fevers increase. One experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:8: For one who dwells infatuated, fettered, and infatuated, observing gratification, the five aggregates of clinging go on to accumulation in the future. And one's craving—which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there—increases. One's bodily disturbances increase, and one's mental disturbances increase; one's bodily distresses increase, and one's mental distresses increase; one's bodily fevers increase, and one's mental fevers increase. One experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: But, bhikkhus, when a person knows and sees the eye as it really is, knows and sees forms as they really are, knows and sees eye-consciousness as it really is, knows and sees eye-contact as it really is, and knows and sees as it really is whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful—then they are not infatuated with the eye, not infatuated with forms, not infatuated with eye-consciousness, not infatuated with eye-contact, and not infatuated with whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition. For them, living uninfatuated, unattached, unconfused, contemplating the danger, the five aggregates of clinging go towards diminution in the future. Their craving—which leads to rebirth, is accompanied by delight and lust, and finds delight here and there—is abandoned. Their bodily distresses are abandoned, and their mental distresses are abandoned; their bodily fevers are abandoned, and their mental fevers are abandoned; their bodily burnings are abandoned, and their mental burnings are abandoned. They experience both bodily pleasure and mental pleasure.
translations.mn19:11: Whatever a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. If a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of renunciation, he has abandoned thoughts of sensual desire; he has made much of thoughts of renunciation, and his mind inclines to thoughts of renunciation. If a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of non-ill will... if a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of non-cruelty, he has abandoned thoughts of cruelty; he has made much of thoughts of non-cruelty, and his mind inclines to thoughts of non-cruelty.
translations.mn19:12: Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been brought into the village, a cowherd would guard his cows; while at the foot of a tree or in the open, he has only to be mindful: 'Those are the cows.' So too, bhikkhus, I had only to be mindful: 'Those are states.'
translations.mn19:13: My energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, my body was tranquil and relaxed, my mind was concentrated and one-pointed.
translations.mn19:14: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thinking and pondering, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn19:24: This was the third true knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night; ignorance was banished, true knowledge arose; darkness was banished, light arose; as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn19:25: Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great low-lying marsh in a forested woodland, and a large herd of deer lived in dependence on it. Then some man would appear who desired their harm, their misfortune, and their insecurity. He would close off the safe, secure path that leads to joy, and he would open up a false path, set out a decoy, and station a lure. Thus, bhikkhus, that large herd of deer would later come to ruin and destruction. But then some man would appear who desired their benefit, their welfare, and their security. He would open up the safe, secure path that leads to joy, and he would close off the false path, remove the decoy, and destroy the lure. Thus, bhikkhus, that large herd of deer would later come to growth, increase, and abundance.
translations.mn19:26: I have made this simile, bhikkhus, to convey a meaning. This is the meaning here: 'The great low-lying marsh' is a designation for sensual pleasures. 'The large herd of deer' is a designation for beings. 'The man who desires their harm, misfortune, and insecurity' is a designation for Māra the Evil One. 'The false path' is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, that is: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. 'The decoy' is a designation for delight and lust. 'The lure' is a designation for ignorance. 'The man who desires their benefit, welfare, and security' is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'The safe, secure path that leads to joy' is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. So, bhikkhus, the safe, secure path that leads to joy has been opened by me, the false path has been closed, the decoy removed, and the lure destroyed.
translations.mn19:3: As I abided thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, a thought of sensual desire arose in me. I understood: 'This thought of sensual desire has arisen in me. This leads to my own affliction, to others' affliction, and to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, causes distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna.' When I reflected, 'It leads to my own affliction,' it subsided in me; when I reflected, 'It leads to others' affliction,' it subsided in me; when I reflected, 'It leads to the affliction of both,' it subsided in me; when I reflected, 'It obstructs wisdom, causes distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna,' it subsided in me. Thus, bhikkhus, whenever a thought of sensual desire arose, I abandoned it, dispelled it, and did away with it.
translations.mn19:6: Whatever a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. If a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of sensual desire, he has abandoned thoughts of renunciation; he has made much of thoughts of sensual desire, and his mind inclines to thoughts of sensual desire. If a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of ill will... if a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of cruelty, he has abandoned thoughts of non-cruelty; he has made much of thoughts of cruelty, and his mind inclines to thoughts of cruelty.
translations.mn19:7: Suppose, bhikkhus, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn time when the crops are thick, a cowherd would guard his cows. He would strike them with his stick here and there, check them, restrain them, and keep them out. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that cowherd sees that he might be killed, imprisoned, fined, or blamed on that account. Even so, bhikkhus, I saw the danger, degradation, and defilement in unskillful qualities, and the benefit in skillful qualities, the side of purification in renunciation.
translations.mn19:8: As I lived thus, bhikkhus, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a thought of renunciation arose. I understood: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It does not lead to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it furthers wisdom, it is on the side of non-distress, and it leads to Nibbāna.’ If I were to think and ponder upon it even for a night, I see no fear arising from that. If I were to think and ponder upon it even for a day, I see no fear arising from that. If I were to think and ponder upon it even for a night and a day, I see no fear arising from that. But with too much thinking and pondering, my body would become tired. When the body is tired, the mind is disturbed. When the mind is disturbed, it is far from concentration. So I steadied my mind internally, quieted it, brought it to singleness, and concentrated it. Why is that? So that my mind should not be disturbed.
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a royal sal tree. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:10: He perceives Brahmā as Brahmā. Having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, he conceives Brahmā, he conceives in Brahmā, he conceives from Brahmā, he conceives ‘Brahmā is mine,’ he delights in Brahmā. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:11: He perceives the Ābhassara gods as the Ābhassara gods. Having perceived the Ābhassara gods as the Ābhassara gods, he conceives the Ābhassara gods, he conceives in the Ābhassara gods, he conceives from the Ābhassara gods, he conceives ‘The Ābhassara gods are mine,’ he delights in the Ābhassara gods. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:123: Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, he too directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive ‘earth is mine,’ he does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because of the destruction of delusion, because he is free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: He perceives the Vehapphala gods as the Vehapphala gods. Having perceived the Vehapphala gods as the Vehapphala gods, he conceives the Vehapphala gods, he conceives in the Vehapphala gods, he conceives from the Vehapphala gods, he conceives ‘The Vehapphala gods are mine,’ he delights in the Vehapphala gods. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:14: He perceives the Overlord as the Overlord. Having perceived the Overlord as the Overlord, he conceives the Overlord, he conceives in the Overlord, he conceives from the Overlord, he conceives ‘The Overlord is mine,’ he delights in the Overlord. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:147: Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, too, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive ‘earth is mine,’ he does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata has fully understood it to the end, I say.
translations.mn1:171: Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, too, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive ‘earth is mine,’ he does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because he has understood that ‘delight is the root of suffering,’ and that ‘with being there is birth, and for what has come to be there is aging and death.’ Therefore, bhikkhus, I say that through the complete destruction, fading away, cessation, giving up, and relinquishing of cravings, the Tathāgata has awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment.
translations.mn1:19: He perceives the seen as the seen. Having perceived the seen as the seen, he conceives the seen, he conceives in the seen, he conceives from the seen, he conceives ‘the seen is mine,’ he delights in the seen. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:2: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the exposition of the root of all things. Listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:20: He perceives the heard as the heard. Having perceived the heard as the heard, he conceives the heard, he conceives in the heard, he conceives from the heard, he conceives ‘the heard is mine,’ he delights in the heard. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:22: He perceives the cognized as the cognized. Having perceived the cognized as the cognized, he conceives the cognized, he conceives in the cognized, he conceives from the cognized, he conceives ‘the cognized is mine,’ he delights in the cognized. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:23: He perceives unity as unity. Having perceived unity as unity, he conceives unity, he conceives in unity, he conceives from unity, he conceives ‘unity is mine,’ he delights in unity. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:24: He perceives diversity as diversity. Having perceived diversity as diversity, he conceives diversity, he conceives in diversity, he conceives from diversity, he conceives ‘diversity is mine,’ he delights in diversity. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:25: He perceives the all as the all. Having perceived the all as the all, he conceives the all, he conceives in the all, he conceives from the all, he conceives ‘the all is mine,’ he delights in the all. Why is that? Because he has not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:27: Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is a trainee, who has not attained his heart's goal but lives aspiring to the supreme security from bondage, he too directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, let him not conceive earth, let him not conceive in earth, let him not conceive from earth, let him not conceive ‘earth is mine,’ let him not delight in earth. Why is that? Because he must fully understand it, I say.
translations.mn1:3: “Mendicants, take an uneducated ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is unskilled and untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has not seen good persons, and is unskilled and untrained in the Dhamma of good persons. They perceive earth as earth. Having perceived earth as earth, they conceive earth, they conceive in earth, they conceive from earth, they conceive ‘earth is mine’, they delight in earth. Why is that? Because they have not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:4: They perceive water as water. Having perceived water as water, they conceive water, they conceive in water, they conceive from water, they conceive ‘water is mine’, they delight in water. Why is that? Because they have not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:5: They perceive fire as fire. Having perceived fire as fire, they conceive fire, they conceive in fire, they conceive from fire, they conceive ‘fire is mine’, they delight in fire. Why is that? Because they have not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:51: Mendicants, a mendicant who is a perfected one, with defilements ended, who has completed the task, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of rebirth, and is rightly liberated through enlightenment: they too directly know earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, they do not conceive earth, they do not conceive in earth, they do not conceive from earth, they do not conceive ‘earth is mine’, they do not delight in earth. Why is that? Because they have fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:7: They perceive beings as beings. Having perceived beings as beings, they conceive beings, they conceive in beings, they conceive from beings, they conceive ‘beings are mine’, they delight in beings. Why is that? Because they have not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:8: They perceive gods as gods. Having perceived gods as gods, they conceive gods, they conceive in gods, they conceive from gods, they conceive ‘gods are mine’, they delight in gods. Why is that? Because they have not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:9: They perceive Pajāpati as Pajāpati. Having perceived Pajāpati as Pajāpati, they conceive Pajāpati, they conceive in Pajāpati, they conceive from Pajāpati, they conceive ‘Pajāpati is mine’, they delight in Pajāpati. Why is that? Because they have not fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn20:2: “Mendicants, a mendicant who is pursuing the higher mind should from time to time give attention to five signs. What five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, mendicants, when you understand the meaning of what I’ve said, you should remember it accordingly. But if you don’t understand the meaning of what I’ve said, you should ask me about it, or else ask those mendicants who are experienced.
translations.mn22:14: I have taught you the Dhamma compared to a raft; for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding onto. Understanding the simile of the raft, you should even give up the teachings, let alone what is not the teaching.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain mendicant said to the Buddha: “Sir, can there be anxiety about what does not exist externally?” “There can, mendicant,” said the Buddha. “It’s when someone thinks: ‘Oh, what I had is no more! Oh, what I had I don’t have! Oh, may I have it! Oh, I don’t get it!’ They sorrow and pine and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion. That’s how there is anxiety about what does not exist externally.”
translations.mn22:19: “But sir, can there be no anxiety about what does not exist externally?” “There can, mendicant,” said the Buddha. “It’s when someone doesn’t think: ‘Oh, what I had is no more! Oh, what I had I don’t have! Oh, may I have it! Oh, I don’t get it!’ They don’t sorrow and pine and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion. That’s how there is no anxiety about what does not exist externally.”
translations.mn22:20: “Sir, can there be anxiety about what does not exist internally?” “There can, mendicant,” said the Buddha. “It’s when someone has the view: ‘The universe is the self. After death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever.’ They hear the Realized One or his disciple teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all grounds, fixations, obsessions, dogmas, and underlying tendencies regarding views; for the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, and extinguishment. They think: ‘Oh no! I’m going to be annihilated! I’m going to perish! I shall be no more!’ They sorrow and pine and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion. That’s how there is anxiety about what does not exist internally.”
translations.mn22:23: “Mendicants, you might grasp a possession that’s permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever. But do you see any such possession?” “No, sir.” “Good, mendicants. I too don’t see any such possession. Mendicants, you might grasp a doctrine of self that doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. But do you see any such doctrine of self?” “No, sir.” “Good, mendicants. I too don’t see any such doctrine of self.
translations.mn22:24: Mendicants, you might rely on a view that doesn’t give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. But do you see any such view to rely on?” “No, sir.” “Good, mendicants. I too don’t see any such view to rely on.
translations.mn22:25: Mendicants, if there were a self, would there be what belongs to a self?” “Yes, sir.” “And if there were what belongs to a self, would there be a self?” “Yes, sir.” “But since a self and what belongs to a self are not acknowledged as a genuine fact, this view—‘The universe is the self. After death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever’—isn’t it utterly and completely foolish?” “What else could it be, sir? It’s utterly and completely foolish.”
translations.mn22:27: “Therefore, bhikkhus, any kind of form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Any kind of feeling … any kind of perception … any kind of volitional formations … any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all consciousness should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, disenchanted with consciousness.
translations.mn22:29: Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.mn22:30: This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has lifted the cross-bar, who has filled in the trench, who has pulled up the pillar, who has withdrawn the bolts, a noble one who has lowered the banner, dropped the burden, and is unfettered.
translations.mn22:31: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has lifted the cross-bar? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s ignorance is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. That is how a bhikkhu is one who has lifted the cross-bar.
translations.mn22:32: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has filled in the trench? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s wandering in the round of births that leads to renewed existence is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. That is how a bhikkhu is one who has filled in the trench.
translations.mn22:33: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has pulled up the pillar? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s craving is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. That is how a bhikkhu is one who has pulled up the pillar.
translations.mn22:34: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has withdrawn the bolts? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s five lower fetters are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. That is how a bhikkhu is one who has withdrawn the bolts.
translations.mn22:35: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a noble one who has lowered the banner, dropped the burden, and is unfettered? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. That is how a bhikkhu is a noble one who has lowered the banner, dropped the burden, and is unfettered.
translations.mn22:38: In this regard, bhikkhus, if others honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata does not feel joy, gladness, or elation of mind because of that. In this regard, if others honor, revere, esteem, and worship the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata thinks: ‘It is towards this which was formerly fully understood that such services are performed.’
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, bhikkhus, if others should abuse, revile, scold, and harass you, you should not harbor any resentment, displeasure, or aversion of mind because of that. And therefore, bhikkhus, if others should honor, revere, esteem, and worship you, you should not feel joy, gladness, or elation of mind because of that. Therefore, bhikkhus, if others should honor, revere, esteem, and worship you, you should think: ‘It is towards this which was formerly fully understood that such services are performed.’
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever is not yours, abandon it; when you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
translations.mn22:42: The Dhamma has been thus well-proclaimed by me, made clear, open, evident, and free of patchwork. In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me… those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—for them there is no cycle to be described.
translations.mn22:43: The Dhamma has been thus well-proclaimed by me… In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me… those bhikkhus who have abandoned the five lower fetters are all due to be reborn spontaneously, to attain final Nibbāna there, without ever returning from that world.
translations.mn22:44: The Dhamma has been thus well-proclaimed by me… In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me… those bhikkhus who have abandoned three fetters and weakened greed, hatred, and delusion are all once-returners, who will come back to this world only once more to make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: The Dhamma has been thus well-proclaimed by me… In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me… those bhikkhus who have abandoned three fetters are all stream-enterers, no longer subject to perdition, assured of enlightenment.
translations.mn22:46: The Dhamma has been thus well-proclaimed by me… In the Dhamma thus well-proclaimed by me… those bhikkhus who are Dhamma-followers or faith-followers are all headed for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:6: “Misguided man, to whom have you ever known me to teach the Dhamma in such a way? Misguided man, haven't I stated in many ways that obstructive things are truly obstructions, and that they are sufficient to obstruct one who indulges in them? I have said that sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair, and the danger in them is even greater. I have said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton... like a piece of meat... like a grass torch... like a pit of glowing coals... like a dream... like borrowed goods... like a fruit tree... like a butcher's knife and block... like a sword stake... like a snake's head; they provide much suffering and much despair, and the danger in them is even greater. But you, misguided man, by your own wrong grasp, misrepresent us, injure yourself, and store up much demerit. For that will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.”
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus? Has this bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, sparked even a glimmer of understanding in this Dhamma and Training?” “How could he, sir? No, sir.” When this was said, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly of the vulture killers, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, brooding, speechless. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha was silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, brooding, speechless, said to him: “Misguided man, you will be known by this own evil view of yours. I will question the bhikkhus here.”
translations.mn22:9: “That one could indulge in sensual pleasures apart from sensual desires, apart from the perception of sensual desire, apart from thoughts of sensual desire—that is impossible.”
translations.mn26:10: “And what, bhikkhus, do you say is subject to sorrow? Wife and children, bhikkhus, are subject to sorrow; male and female slaves are subject to sorrow; goats and sheep are subject to sorrow; fowl and pigs are subject to sorrow; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sorrow. These acquisitions, bhikkhus, are subject to sorrow. Tied to them, infatuated with them, and utterly cleared by them, being himself subject to sorrow, one seeks only what is subject to sorrow.”
translations.mn26:11: “And what, bhikkhus, do you say is subject to defilement? Wife and children, bhikkhus, are subject to defilement; male and female slaves... goats and sheep... fowl and pigs... elephants, cattle, horses, and mares... gold and silver are subject to defilement. These acquisitions, bhikkhus, are subject to defilement. Tied to them, infatuated with them, and utterly cleared by them, being himself subject to defilement, one seeks only what is subject to defilement. This, bhikkhus, is the ignoble quest.”
translations.mn26:13: “I too, bhikkhus, before my awakening, while I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth, sought what was subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, I sought what was subject to aging; being myself subject to illness... subject to death... subject to sorrow... being myself subject to defilement, I sought what was subject to defilement. Then it occurred to me: ‘Why do I, being myself subject to birth, seek what is subject to birth? Being myself subject to aging... illness... death... sorrow... being myself subject to defilement, why do I seek what is subject to defilement? Suppose that, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, I were to seek the unborn, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being myself subject to aging... I were to seek the unaging... being myself subject to illness... I were to seek the illness-free... being myself subject to death... I were to seek the deathless... being myself subject to sorrow... I were to seek the sorrowless... being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, I were to seek the undefiled, the supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna.’”
translations.mn26:14: “Later, bhikkhus, while still young, a black-haired young man endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, though my mother and father wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.”
translations.mn26:17: “Then, bhikkhus, being a seeker of what is wholesome, searching for the supreme state of sublime peace, I wandered by stages through the Magadhan country and eventually arrived at Senānigama near Uruvelā. There I saw an agreeable piece of ground, a delightful grove with a clear-flowing river with pleasant fords, and a village nearby for alms resort. Then it occurred to me: ‘This is an agreeable piece of ground, this is a delightful grove, the river is clear-flowing with pleasant fords, and there is a village nearby for alms resort. This is enough for the striving of a clansman intent on striving.’ So, bhikkhus, I sat down right there, thinking: ‘This is enough for striving.’”
translations.mn26:21: Then, monks, having understood the Brahma’s request, out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha. Surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, and some who lived seeing fear in fault and the next world, and some who lived not seeing fear in fault and the next world. Just as in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain immersed in the water, nourished by it; some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand at the surface of the water; and some lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand rising out of the water, unsullied by the water; even so, monks, surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, and some who lived seeing fear in fault and the next world, and some who lived not seeing fear in fault and the next world. Then, monks, I replied to Brahma Sahampati in verse: ‘Open for them are the doors to the Deathless, let those who have ears release their faith; perceiving trouble, O Brahma, I did not speak the refined Dhamma among humans.’ Then Brahma Sahampati, thinking, ‘I have created the opportunity for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma,’ paid homage to me, kept me on his right, and vanished right there.
translations.mn26:25: Monks, Upaka the Ajivaka saw me on the highway between Gaya and the Bodhi tree. Having seen me, he said: ‘Friend, your faculties are serene, your complexion is pure and bright. Under whom have you gone forth, friend? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?’ When this was said, I addressed Upaka the Ajivaka in verses: ‘I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all, unsullied among all things; having given up everything, liberated in the destruction of craving, having realized it myself, whom should I point to as teacher? I have no teacher, no one like me exists; in the world with its gods, I have no equal. For I am the Arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed teacher; I alone am the Rightly Self-Awakened One, I have become cooled and extinguished. To set the wheel of Dhamma in motion, I go to the city of the Kasis; in the world become blind, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.’ ‘According to what you claim, friend, you ought to be the Infinite Conqueror.’ ‘Conquerors like me are those who have reached the destruction of the taints; I have conquered evil states, therefore, Upaka, I am a conqueror.’ When this was said, monks, Upaka the Ajivaka said, ‘It may be so, friend,’ shook his head, took a side path, and departed.
translations.mn26:26: Then, monks, wandering by stages, I approached the Deer Park at Isipatana near Varanasi where the group of five monks were. The group of five monks saw me coming from afar. Seeing me, they agreed among themselves: ‘Friends, here comes the ascetic Gotama, who lives in luxury, who gave up the struggle and reverted to luxury. He should not be greeted, nor should we stand up for him; his bowl and robe should not be received. However, a seat should be set out; if he wishes, he may sit down.’ But as I approached, the group of five monks were unable to keep their agreement. Some came out to meet me and took my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, and some set out water for washing my feet. However, they addressed me by name and as “friend.”
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, I told the group of five monks: ‘Monks, do you recall me ever speaking like this before?’ ‘No, bhante.’ ‘Monks, the Tathagata is an Arahant, a Rightly Self-Awakened One. Give ear, monks, the Deathless has been attained; I instruct you, I teach the Dhamma. Practicing as instructed, you will soon—by realizing for yourselves with direct knowledge here and now—enter and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.’
translations.mn26:29: I was able to convince the group of five monks. I would instruct two monks while three went for alms. What the three monks brought back from their almsround, the six of us would live on. Then I would instruct three monks while two went for alms. What the two monks brought back from their almsround, the six of us would live on.
translations.mn26:30: Then, monks, being thus instructed and exhorted by me, the group of five monks—being themselves subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbana—attained the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbana. Being themselves subject to aging... seeking the unaging... attained the unaging... Being themselves subject to illness... Being themselves subject to death... Being themselves subject to sorrow... Being themselves subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbana—they attained the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbana. And the knowledge and vision arose in them: ‘Unshakeable is our liberation, this is the last birth, now there is no more rebirth.’
translations.mn26:31: “Mendicants, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—agreeable, pleasing, charming, lovely, bound up with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. Sounds cognizable by the ear … Smells cognizable by the nose … Tastes cognizable by the tongue … Tangibles cognizable by the body—agreeable, pleasing, charming, lovely, bound up with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, mendicants, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.”
translations.mn26:34: “Suppose, mendicants, a wild deer roaming in the forest and jungle walks confidently, stands confidently, sits confidently, and lies down confidently. Why is that? Because it is out of range of the hunter. In the same way, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has directed thought and evaluation, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. This is called a bhikkhu who has blinded Māra, who has tracklessly destroyed Māra’s vision and gone beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:35: “Furthermore, mendicants, with the stilling of directed thought and evaluation, a bhikkhu enters and remains in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without directed thought and evaluation, and has rapture and happiness born of immersion. This is called a bhikkhu … beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:36: “Furthermore, mendicants, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu remains equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and remains in the third absorption, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.’ This is called a bhikkhu … beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:37: “Furthermore, mendicants, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and remains in the fourth absorption, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is called a bhikkhu … beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:38: “Furthermore, mendicants, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space. This is called a bhikkhu … beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:39: “Furthermore, mendicants, with the complete surmounting of the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This is called a bhikkhu … beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:4: Then the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. At that time, many bhikkhus were sitting together in the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka engaged in a Dhamma discussion. Then the Blessed One stood outside the porch waiting for the discussion to end. When the Blessed One knew the discussion had ended, he coughed and knocked on the bolt. The bhikkhus opened the door for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka and sat down on the seat prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Mendicants, what was the subject of your discussion just now? What was the discussion that was interrupted?” “Bhante, our Dhamma discussion was about the Blessed One himself when the Blessed One arrived.” “Good, mendicants. It is fitting for you, young men of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, to sit together for Dhamma discussion. When you gather together, mendicants, you should do one of two things: Dhamma discussion or noble silence.”
translations.mn26:40: “Furthermore, mendicants, with the complete surmounting of the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ a bhikkhu enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness. This is called a bhikkhu … beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:41: “Furthermore, mendicants, with the complete surmounting of the dimension of nothingness, a bhikkhu enters and remains in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called a bhikkhu … beyond the sight of the Evil One.”
translations.mn26:5: “Mendicants, there are these two searches: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, mendicants, is the ignoble search? Here, mendicants, someone being themselves subject to birth, seeks what is also subject to birth; being themselves subject to aging, seeks what is also subject to aging; being themselves subject to illness, seeks what is also subject to illness; being themselves subject to death, seeks what is also subject to death; being themselves subject to sorrow, seeks what is also subject to sorrow; being themselves subject to defilement, seeks what is also subject to defilement.”
translations.mn26:6: “And what, mendicants, would you say is subject to birth? Children and wives are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; fowl and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. These acquisitions are subject to birth. Tied to them, infatuated with them, and utterly cleared by them, being themselves subject to birth, they seek what is also subject to birth.”
translations.mn27:12: “A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Possessed of that faith he has gained, he reflects: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect, utterly pure, and polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’ Later, giving up a small amount of wealth or a large amount of wealthH{
translations.mn27:13: Having gone forth in this way, possessing the training and way of life of the monks, abandoning the destruction of life, he abstains from the destruction of life; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious and kindly, he dwells compassionate toward all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a self that is pure and honest. Abandoning unchastity, he is celibate, living apart, abstaining from the sexual act, the village practice.
