Abandoning false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is bound to the truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and no deceiver of the world. Abandoning malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to cause division among these people, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere in order to cause division among those people. Thus he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of unity, delighting in harmony, rejoicing in harmony, loving harmony, a speaker of words that create harmony. Abandoning harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks words that are blameless, pleasing to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, liked by many, and agreeable to many. Abandoning idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; at the right time he speaks words worth treasuring, reasonable, moderate, and beneficial. He abstains from damaging seeds and plants. He eats in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and outside the proper time. He abstains from watching dancing, singing, music, and shows. He abstains from wearing garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics, and from finery and adornments. He abstains from high and large beds. He abstains from accepting gold and silver. He abstains from accepting raw grain. He abstains from accepting raw meat. He abstains from accepting women and girls. He abstains from accepting female and male slaves. He abstains from accepting goats and sheep. He abstains from accepting fowl and pigs. He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He abstains from accepting fields and land. He abstains from running errands and going on missions. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from false weights, false metals, and false measures. He abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud. He abstains from wounding, killing, binding, highway robbery, plundering, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to protect his stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden; so too, a monk is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to protect his stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only these with him. Possessing this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself a blameless happiness.
translations.mn27:15: On seeing a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might invade him, he practices the way of its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear... On smelling an odor with the nose... On tasting a flavor with the tongue... On feeling a tactile object with the body... On cognizing a mind-object with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might invade him, he practices the way of its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. Possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself an unalloyed happiness.
translations.mn27:16: He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking away; he acts with clear comprehension when flexing and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his robes and carrying his outer robe and bowl; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, consuming food, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent.
translations.mn27:17: Possessing this noble aggregate of virtue, and possessing this noble contentment, and possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, and possessing this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded resting place: the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, the open air, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: On returning from his almsround, after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind from covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate toward all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Abandoning dullness and drowsiness, he dwells free from dullness and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from dullness and drowsiness. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he dwells undisturbed, with a mind stilled within; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he dwells having gone beyond doubt, unperplexed about wholesome states; he purifies his mind from doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This too, brahmin, is called a footprint of the Tathāgata, something used by the Tathāgata, something enjoyed by the Tathāgata. But a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way.'
translations.mn27:2: At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was driving out of Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares. He saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the wanderer Pilotika: 'Now then, where is Master Vacchāyana coming from in the middle of the day?' 'Sir, I am coming from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.' 'What do you think of the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom? Do you think he is a wise man?' 'Sir, who am I to know the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom? One would surely have to be his equal to know the ascetic Gotama’s lucidity of wisdom.' 'Master Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with high praise indeed.' 'Sir, who am I to praise the ascetic Gotama? Master Gotama is praised by the praised, the best among gods and humans.' 'But what reasons does Master Vacchāyana see that he is so devoted to the ascetic Gotama?'
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, a mendicant, with the stilling of directed thought and evaluation, enters and remains in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without directed thought and evaluation, and has happiness and pleasure born of immersion. This too is called, brahmin... 'the community of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, a mendicant, with the fading away of happiness, remains equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and remains in the third absorption, of which the noble ones declare: 'Equanimous and mindful, he has a pleasant abiding.' This too is called, brahmin... 'the community of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, a mendicant, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the previous disappearance of joy and sadness, enters and remains in the fourth absorption, which is without-pleasure-or-pain and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This too is called, brahmin, a footprint of the Realized One, something used by the Realized One, something enjoyed by the Realized One. But a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is a fully enlightened Buddha, the teaching is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the community of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:3: 'Sir, suppose an elephant hunter were to enter an elephant woods. He would see in the elephant woods a large footprint, long and wide. He would come to the conclusion: "Indeed, this is a large elephant." In the same way, sir, when I saw four footprints in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: "The Blessed One is a fully enlightened Buddha, the teaching is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the community of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well."'
translations.mn27:4: 'What are the four? Here, sir, I see some kshatriya pundits who are clever, skilled in the arguments of others, like hair-splitters; they go about, as it were, shattering the views of others with their wisdom. They hear: "The ascetic Gotama will visit such and such a village or town." They prepare a question: "We will go to the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If he answers like this, we will refute him like this; and if he answers like that, we will refute him like that." They hear: "The ascetic Gotama has arrived at such and such a village or town." They go to the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, encourages, fires up, and inspires them with a talk on the Dhamma. Having been instructed, encouraged, fired up, and inspired by the ascetic Gotama with a talk on the Dhamma, they do not even ask him the question, so how could they refute him? On the contrary, they actually become disciples of the ascetic Gotama. When, sir, I saw this first footprint in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: "The Blessed One is a fully enlightened Buddha, the teaching is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the community of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well."'
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with the wanderer Pilotika. When this was said, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: "Brahmin, the simile of the elephant's footprint is not yet complete in detail. As to how the simile of the elephant's footprint is completed in detail, listen and pay close attention, I will speak." "Yes, sir," the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn28:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the venerable Sāriputta addressed the mendicants: "Friends, mendicants!" "Friend," those mendicants replied to the venerable Sāriputta. The venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn28:10: If, friends, while a bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in him, he is troubled by that and becomes stirred: ‘It is a loss for me, it is no gain for me; it is ill-gotten for me, it is not well-gotten for me, that while I am thus recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in me.’ Just as, friends, a daughter-in-law is troubled and stirred on seeing her father-in-law; so too, if while a bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established in him, he is troubled by that and becomes stirred... But if, while a bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established in him, he is satisfied with that. To that extent, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friends, when the external water element is disturbed. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean goes down to a depth of a hundred leagues, two hundred leagues, three hundred leagues, four hundred leagues, five hundred leagues, six hundred leagues, seven hundred leagues. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands only seven palm-trees deep, six palm-trees, five palm-trees, four palm-trees, three palm-trees, two palm-trees, one palm-tree deep. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands only seven fathoms deep, six fathoms, five fathoms, four fathoms, three fathoms, two fathoms, one fathom deep. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands only half a fathom deep, waist-deep, knee-deep, ankle-deep. There comes a time, friends, when there is not even enough water in the great ocean to wet a finger-joint. So, friends, in the case of even that great external water element, impermanence will be discerned, its nature to be exhausted will be discerned, its nature to pass away will be discerned, its nature to change will be discerned.
translations.mn28:13: What then of this transient body, clung to by craving, that it should be considered as ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? Instead, there should be no such thing for him...
translations.mn28:14: If, friends, while a bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established in him, he is satisfied with that.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friends, when the external fire element is disturbed. It burns up villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. Having come to green grass, or a road, or a rock, or water, or a pleasant stretch of ground, it goes out for lack of fuel. There comes a time, friends, when they seek to produce fire even with a chicken feather or a scrap of sinew. So, friends, in the case of even that great external fire element, impermanence will be discerned, its nature to be exhausted will be discerned, its nature to pass away will be discerned, its nature to change will be discerned. What then of this transient body, clung to by craving, that it should be considered as ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’?
translations.mn28:18-20: Instead, there should be no such thing for him... if, friends, while a bhikkhu is thus recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established in him, he is satisfied with that. To that extent, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu.
translations.mn28:2: “Just as, friends, the footprints of all living beings that walk the earth are encompassed by the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant’s footprint is reckoned the foremost of them in terms of size; even so, friends, all wholesome states are included in the four noble truths. In which four? In the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friends, when the external air element is disturbed. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There comes a time, friends, in the last month of the hot season, when they seek wind with a palm-leaf fan or a bellows, and even the grasses in the thatch do not stir. So, friends, in the case of even that great external air element, impermanence will be discerned, its nature to be exhausted will be discerned, its nature to pass away will be discerned, its nature to change will be discerned. What then of this transient body, clung to by craving, that it should be considered as ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? Instead, there should be no such thing for him.
translations.mn28:23: If others abuse, revile, scold, and harass that bhikkhu, he understands: ‘This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me. And that is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact.’ He sees that contact is impermanent, he sees that feeling is impermanent, he sees that perception is impermanent, he sees that formations are impermanent, he sees that consciousness is impermanent. His mind, making the elements its object, enters into them, acquires confidence, settles, and becomes resolute.
translations.mn28:24: “Friends, if others abuse, revile, scold, and harass a bhikkhu with unwelcome, disagreeable, unpleasant contact—by contact with the hand, with a clod, with a stick, or with a knife—he understands thus: ‘This body is of such a nature that contact with the hand, with a clod, with a stick, and with a knife impinges upon it. But this has been said by the Blessed One in the Simile of the Saw: “Bhikkhus, even if bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, if anyone gave way to a mind of hate, he would not be carrying out my teaching on that account.” My energy shall be aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body calm and untroubled, my mind concentrated and one-pointed. Now let contact with the hand, with a clod, with a stick, and with a knife impinge upon this body; for this is how the Buddhas’ teaching is practiced.’"
translations.mn28:26: “Just as, friends, when a space is enclosed by timber, creepers, grass, and clay, it comes to be termed a ‘house,’ so too, when a space is enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, it comes to be termed a ‘form.’"
translations.mn28:27: “Friends, if the internal eye is intact but external forms do not come into range and there is no corresponding conscious engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness. If the internal eye is intact and external forms come into range, but there is no corresponding conscious engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness. But when the internal eye is intact, external forms come into range, and there is a corresponding conscious engagement, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness."
translations.mn28:28: “The form in what has thus come to be is included in the aggregate of affected form. The feeling in what has thus come to be is included in the aggregate of affected feeling. The perception in what has thus come to be is included in the aggregate of affected perception. The volitional formations in what has thus come to be are included in the aggregate of affected volitional formations. The consciousness in what has thus come to be is included in the aggregate of affected consciousness. He understands thus: ‘This, it seems, is how there comes to be the inclusion, gathering, and assembly of these five aggregates affected by clinging. Now this has been said by the Blessed One: “One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.” And these five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently arisen. Any desire, attachment, attraction, and clinging for these five aggregates affected by clinging is the origin of suffering. Any removal of desire and lust, any abandoning of desire and lust for these five aggregates affected by clinging is the cessation of suffering.’ To that extent, friends, much has been done by the bhikkhu."
translations.mn28:3: “And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates affected by clinging are suffering. And what, friends, are the five aggregates affected by clinging? They are: the aggregate of affected form, the aggregate of affected feeling, the aggregate of affected perception, the aggregate of affected volitional formations, and the aggregate of affected consciousness."
translations.mn28:37: “the mind is intact but external mind-objects do not come into range and there is no corresponding conscious engagement, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness."
translations.mn28:7: “There comes a time, friends, when the external water element is disturbed. At that time the external earth element disappears. When even in that external earth element, great as it is, impermanence will be discerned, a nature of dwindling will be discerned, a nature of vanishing will be discerned, a nature of change will be discerned, what of this body, which is clung to by craving and lasts but a little while? There is no considering it as ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am.’ Instead, there is only a ‘no’ to that."
translations.mn29:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rajagaha on the Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta:
translations.mn29:3: “Here, bhikkhus, some son of a good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking: ‘I am a victim of birth, aging, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I am a victim of suffering, a prey to suffering. Surely an end to this entire mass of suffering can be known.’ When he has gone forth thus, he acquires gain, honor, and renown. He is not pleased with that gain, honor, and renown, and his intention is not fulfilled. He does not, on account of that gain, honor, and renown, exalt himself and disparage others. He does not become intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown, he does not become negligent, and he does not fall into negligence. Being diligent, he achieves the attainment of virtue. He is pleased with that attainment of virtue, and his intention is fulfilled. On account of that attainment of virtue, he exalts himself and disparages others: ‘I am virtuous, of good character, but these other bhikkhus are immoral, of evil character.’ He becomes intoxicated by that attainment of virtue, becomes negligent, and falls into negligence. Being negligent, he lives in suffering. Suppose, bhikkhus, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, he would cut off the outer bark and take it away, thinking it was heartwood. Then a man with good sight, seeing him, might say: ‘This good man did not know the heartwood, he did not know the sapwood, he did not know the inner bark, he did not know the outer bark, he did not know the twigs and leaves. Thus, while needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, he came to a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and passing over the heartwood, passing over the sapwood, passing over the inner bark, he cut off the outer bark and took it away, thinking it was heartwood; and whatever it was he had to do with heartwood, his purpose will not be served.’"
translations.mn2:10: And what, bhikkhus, are the things unfit for attention that he attends to? Whatever things he attends to such that the unarisen ferment of sensual desire arises, or the arisen ferment of sensual desire increases; the unarisen ferment of existence arises, or the arisen ferment of existence increases; the unarisen ferment of ignorance arises, or the arisen ferment of ignorance increases—these are the things unfit for attention that he attends to. And what, bhikkhus, are the things fit for attention that he does not attend to? Whatever things he attends to such that the unarisen ferment of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen ferment of sensual desire is abandoned; the unarisen ferment of existence does not arise, and the arisen ferment of existence is abandoned; the unarisen ferment of ignorance does not arise, and the arisen ferment of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things fit for attention that he does not attend to. By his attending to things fit for attention and his not attending to things unfit for attention, unarisen ferments do not arise and arisen ferments are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: He attends wisely: ‘This is suffering’; he attends wisely: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he attends wisely: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he attends wisely: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ When he attends wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned in him: self-identity view, doubt, and attachment to precepts and observances. These are called, bhikkhus, the ferments that should be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Ferments to be abandoned by restraint. And what, bhikkhus, are the ferments that should be abandoned by restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, lives restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty. Whereas ferments, vexation, and fever might arise in one who lives unrestrained in the eye faculty, those ferments, vexation, and fever do not exist in one who lives restrained in the eye faculty. Reflecting wisely, he lives restrained with the restraint of the ear faculty … the nose faculty … the tongue faculty … the body faculty … the mind faculty. Whereas ferments, vexation, and fever might arise in one who lives unrestrained in the mind faculty, those ferments, vexation, and fever do not exist in one who lives restrained in the mind faculty. Whereas ferments, vexation, and fever might arise in one who lives unrestrained, those ferments, vexation, and fever do not exist in one who lives restrained. These are called, bhikkhus, the ferments that should be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: Reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood: ‘Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for adornment, but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the spiritual life, thinking: “Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not create new feelings, and I shall have livelihood, blamelessness, and living in comfort.”’
translations.mn2:16: Reflecting wisely, he uses medicinal requisites for the sick: ‘Only for the sake of warding off arisen painful feelings and for the sake of maximum well-being.’
translations.mn2:17: Whereas ferments, vexation, and fever might arise in one who does not use these things, those ferments, vexation, and fever do not exist in one who uses them. These are called, bhikkhus, the ferments that should be abandoned by using.
translations.mn2:3: “Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the ferments is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. For one who knows what and sees what, bhikkhus, is there the destruction of the ferments? Wise attention and unwise attention. When one attends unwisely, bhikkhus, unarisen ferments arise and arisen ferments increase. When one attends wisely, bhikkhus, unarisen ferments do not arise and arisen ferments are abandoned.
translations.mn2:6: And what, bhikkhus, are the things unfit for attention that he attends to? Whatever things he attends to such that the unarisen ferment of sensual desire arises, or the arisen ferment of sensual desire increases; the unarisen ferment of existence arises, or the arisen ferment of existence increases; the unarisen ferment of ignorance arises, or the arisen ferment of ignorance increases—these are the things unfit for attention that he attends to. And what, bhikkhus, are the things fit for attention that he does not attend to? Whatever things he attends to such that the unarisen ferment of sensual desire does not arise, and the arisen ferment of sensual desire is abandoned; the unarisen ferment of existence does not arise, and the arisen ferment of existence is abandoned; the unarisen ferment of ignorance does not arise, and the arisen ferment of ignorance is abandoned—these are the things fit for attention that he does not attend to.
translations.mn2:7: Through his attention to things unfit for attention and his non-attention to things fit for attention, unarisen ferments arise and arisen ferments increase. He attends unwisely in this way: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?’ Or else he is inwardly perplexed about the present: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?’
translations.mn2:8: When he attends unwisely in this way, one of six views arises in him. The view ‘self exists for me’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘no self exists for me’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘I perceive self with self’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘I perceive not-self with self’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘I perceive self with not-self’ arises in him as true and established; or else he has some such view as this: ‘This self of mine that speaks and feels and experiences here and there the result of good and bad actions—this self of mine is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and it will endure as long as eternity.’ This is called a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views. Fettered by the fetter of views, the uninstructed worldling is not freed from birth, ageing, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.mn2:9: But, bhikkhus, a well-taught noble disciple—who has regard for noble ones, is skilled in their Dhamma, and disciplined in their Dhamma, who has regard for true men, is skilled in their Dhamma, and disciplined in their Dhamma—understands what things are fit for attention and what things are unfit for attention. Since he knows what things are fit for attention and what things are unfit for attention, he does not attend to those things unfit for attention and he attends to those things fit for attention.
translations.mn31:10: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But while you are living thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter upon and abide in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, venerable sir, is a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding that we have attained while living diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.mn31:11-13: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there any other superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, which you have attained by surmounting this abiding, by making this abiding subside?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, we enter upon and abide in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This, venerable sir, is another superhuman state... which we have attained by surmounting that abiding, by making that abiding subside.”
translations.mn31:14: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there any other superhuman state...?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the fading away as well of rapture, we abide in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, we enter upon and abide in the third jhāna, on account of which the noble ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’ This, venerable sir, is another superhuman state... which we have attained by surmounting that abiding, by making that abiding subside.”
translations.mn31:15: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there any other superhuman state...?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, we enter upon and abide in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, venerable sir, is another superhuman state... which we have attained by surmounting that abiding, by making that abiding subside.”
translations.mn31:16: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there any other superhuman state...?” “Why not, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we want, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ we enter upon and abide in the base of infinite space. This, venerable sir, is another superhuman state... which we have attained by surmounting that abiding, by making that abiding subside.”
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimila with a talk on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: At that time the venerable Anuruddha, the venerable Nandiya, and the venerable Kimila were living in the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood.
translations.mn31:3: Then, when it was evening, the Blessed One rose from meditation and went to the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree Wood. The park-keeper saw the Blessed One coming from a distance and said to him: “Do not enter this wood, recluse. There are three clansmen living here seeking their own good. Do not disturb them.”
translations.mn31:4: The venerable Anuruddha heard the park-keeper speaking with the Blessed One. Having heard him, he said to the park-keeper: “Friend park-keeper, do not keep the Blessed One out. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.” Then the venerable Anuruddha went to the venerable Nandiya and the venerable Kimila and said to them: “Come out, venerable ones! Come out, venerable ones! Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”
translations.mn31:5: Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila went out to meet the Blessed One. One took the Blessed One's bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing the feet. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Those venerables also bowed to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Anuruddha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him: “I hope you are all keeping well, Anuruddha, I hope you are getting by, I hope you are not weary with the quest for alms?” “We are keeping well, Blessed One, we are getting by, Blessed One; and we are not weary with the quest for alms, sir.”
translations.mn31:6: “But I hope, Anuruddha, that you are living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?” “Surely, sir, we are living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes.” “But how, Anuruddha, do you live in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with kindly eyes?”
translations.mn31:9: “Surely, sir, we live diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “But how, Anuruddha, do you live diligent, ardent, and resolute?” “Here, sir, whoever of us returns first from the village for alms prepares the seats, sets out the water for drinking and for washing, and sets out the refuse bucket. Whoever returns last from the village for alms, if there are leftovers and he wishes to, he eats them; if he does not wish to, he throws them out where there is little grass or drops them into water where there are no living beings. He puts away the seats, puts away the water for drinking and for washing, puts away the refuse bucket, and sweeps the refectory. Whoever sees a pot for drinking water, a pot for washing water, or a pot for the toilet that is empty and hollow, he sets it out. If it is beyond his strength, he beckons a companion with a hand signal and they set it out by joining hands; but we do not, sir, break into speech for that reason. And every five days, sir, we sit together for the whole night for a talk on the Dhamma. In this way, sir, we live diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn36:10: “I have confidence in Master Gotama in this way. For Master Gotama is one whose body is developed and whose mind is developed.” “Certainly, Aggivessana, your words are offensive and presumptive, yet I will answer you. Ever since I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, it is impossible that an arisen pleasant feeling should remain obsessing my mind, or that an arisen painful feeling should remain obsessing my mind.”
translations.mn36:12: “And why should it not be so, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, I thought: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect, utterly pure, and polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’”
translations.mn36:2: Now at that time, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, was intending to enter Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: Then, Aggivessana, I thought: ‘What if I were to clench my teeth, press my tongue against my palate, and with my mind, restrain, crush, and burn out my thought?’ So, Aggivessana, I clenched my teeth, pressed my tongue against my palate, and with my mind, restrained, crushed, and burned out my thought. As I did so, sweat poured from my armpits. Just as if a strong man were to seize a weaker man by the head or shoulders and restrain, crush, and burn him out; even so, Aggivessana, as I clenched my teeth... sweat poured from my armpits. My energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, but my body was overwrought and uncalm because I was exhausted by that painful striving. Yet, Aggivessana, such painful feeling that arose did not remain obsessing my mind.
translations.mn36:26: Then, Aggivessana, some deities seeing me said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is dead.’ Other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’ Other deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, nor is he dying; the ascetic Gotama is an Arahant, for such is the way an Arahant dwells.’
translations.mn36:27: Then, Aggivessana, I thought: ‘What if I were to practice the total cutting off of food?’ Then, Aggivessana, deities approached me and said: ‘Good sir, do not practice the total cutting off of food. If you do, we will infuse divine nourishment into your pores, and you will survive on that.’ Then, Aggivessana, I thought: ‘If I were to claim to be fasting completely, and these deities were to infuse divine nourishment into my pores and I were to survive on that, it would be a lie on my part.’ So, Aggivessana, I dismissed those deities, saying: ‘Enough.’”
translations.mn36:28: Then, Aggivessana, I thought: ‘What if I were to take food only in very small amounts, as much as would fit in my hollowed palm, whether it be bean soup, lentil soup, vetch soup, or pea soup?’ So I took food only in very small amounts, as much as would fit in my hollowed palm, whether it be bean soup, lentil soup, vetch soup, or pea soup. While I was taking food only in very small amounts, my body became extremely emaciated. Because of eating so little, my limbs became like the jointed segments of vine stems or bamboo stems. Because of eating so little, my backside became like a camel’s hoof. Because of eating so little, my spine stood out like a string of beads. Because of eating so little, my ribs were as gaunt as the rafters of an old, tumbledown barn. Because of eating so little, the gleam of my eyes appeared sunk deep in their sockets like the gleam of water seen at the bottom of a deep well. Because of eating so little, my scalp shriveled and withered like a green bitter gourd shrivels and withers in the wind and sun. Aggivessana, when I thought, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I seized my spine; and when I thought, ‘I will touch my spine,’ I seized the skin of my belly, so much did the skin of my belly cling to my spine because of eating so little. Aggivessana, when I thought, ‘I will go to relieve myself,’ I fell down right there on my face because of eating so little. Aggivessana, when I tried to comfort my body by rubbing my limbs with my hand, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell away from my body because of eating so little.
translations.mn36:29: And when people saw me, Aggivessana, they said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black, he is brown.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown, he is golden-skinned.’ So much had the pure, bright color of my skin been ruined because of eating so little.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son, while walking and wandering for exercise, went to the Great Wood, to the Hall with the Peaked Roof. The venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka the Nigantha’s son coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, here comes Saccaka the Nigantha’s son, a debater, a clever speaker, held in high esteem by many. He wishes to disparage the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would sit down for a moment out of compassion.' The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared. Then Saccaka the Nigantha’s son went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When this courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Saccaka the Nigantha’s son said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:30: Then, Aggivessana, I thought: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have experienced painful, racking, piercing, bitter feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, racking, piercing, bitter feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present experience painful, racking, piercing, bitter feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. But by this racking practice of austerities I have not attained any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to enlightenment?’
translations.mn36:32: Then, Aggivessana, I thought: ‘Why am I afraid of that pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual pleasures and unwholesome states?’ Then, Aggivessana, I thought: ‘I am not afraid of that pleasure that has nothing to do with sensual pleasures and unwholesome states.’
translations.mn36:34: Aggivessana, after I had taken solid food and regained my strength, then quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered upon and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Yet such pleasant feeling that arose in me did not obsess my mind.
translations.mn36:38: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of recollecting past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth... thus with their aspects and particulars I recollected my manifold past lives.
translations.mn36:39: This was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night; ignorance was banished and true knowledge arose, darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who abides diligent, ardent, and resolute. Yet such pleasant feeling that arose in me did not obsess my mind.
translations.mn36:4: “Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who live devoted to the development of the body, but not the development of the mind. They experience painful physical feelings. In the past, Master Gotama, it has happened that when one was touched by painful physical feelings, his thighs would become stiff, his heart would burst, hot blood would gush from his mouth, and he would go mad, out of his mind. In that case, the mind follows the body and is under the control of the body. Why is that? Because the mind has not been developed. But there are some ascetics and brahmins who live devoted to the development of the mind, but not the development of the body. They experience painful mental feelings. In the past, Master Gotama, it has happened that when one was touched by painful mental feelings, his thighs would become stiff, his heart would burst, hot blood would gush from his mouth, and he would go mad, out of his mind. In that case, the body follows the mind and is under the control of the mind. Why is that? Because the body has not been developed. It occurred to me, Master Gotama: ‘Surely Master Gotama’s disciples live devoted to the development of the mind, but not the development of the body.’”
translations.mn36:40: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understood how beings pass on according to their kamma...
translations.mn36:42: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
translations.mn36:43: When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.mn36:45: “Aggivessana, I recall teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. And it may be that each person there thinks: ‘The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma especially for me.’ But it should not be seen like that; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others merely for the purpose of giving knowledge. When the talk is finished, Aggivessana, then I steady my mind internally, quiet it, bring it to singleness, and concentrate it on that same basis of concentration as before, in which I constantly abide.” “That is believable of Master Gotama, as he is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One. But does Master Gotama recall sleeping during the day?”
translations.mn36:46: “I recall, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after returning from my almsround and having eaten my meal, spreading out my outer robe folded in four, and lying down on my right side to fall asleep, mindful and clearly comprehending.” “Some ascetics and brahmins, Master Gotama, call that living in delusion.” “Aggivessana, one is not deluded or undeluded merely by that. But as to how one is deluded or undeluded, listen and attend closely to what I shall say.” “Yes, sir,” Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn36:47: “Aggivessana, anyone whose taints—which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death—are not abandoned, him I call ‘deluded.’ For it is because taints are not abandoned that one is deluded. Anyone whose taints—which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death—are abandoned, him I call ‘undeluded.’ For it is because taints are abandoned that one is undeluded. In the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, the taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death, have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Just as a palm tree whose crown is cut off is incapable of further growth, so too, in the Tathāgata, those taints... have been abandoned... and are no longer subject to future arising.”
translations.mn36:5: “But Aggivessana, how have you heard that the body is developed?” “There are, Master Gotama, Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, Makkhali Gosāla. These are naked ascetics, rejecting conventions, licking their hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked. They do not accept food brought to them, or food specially prepared for them, or an invitation to a meal. They receive nothing from the mouth of a pot or a pan, nor across a threshold, nor across a stick, nor across a pestle, nor from two eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman giving suck, nor from a woman lying with a man, nor from where food is advertised, nor from where a dog is waiting, nor from where flies are swarming. They eat no fish or meat, and drink no liquor, wine, or fermented rice-scum. They are one-house-men, taking one mouthful; or two-house-men, taking two mouthfuls... or seven-house-men, taking seven mouthfuls. They subsist on one small saucer of food a day, or two saucers... or seven saucers. They take food once a day, once every two days... or once every seven days. Thus they live devoted to the practice of taking food at intervals up to half a month.”
translations.mn36:6: “But, Aggivessana, do they survive on only that much?” “No, Master Gotama. Sometimes, Master Gotama, they eat choice solid foods, they eat choice soft foods, they taste choice savories, they drink choice drinks. They give this body strength, they nourish it, they make it fat.” “What they first gave up and later accumulated, in this way there is the growth and decay of this body. But, Aggivessana, what have you heard about the development of the mind?” When Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son was asked by the Blessed One about the development of the mind, he was unable to answer.
translations.mn36:8: “And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind? Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in an unlearned ordinary person. Being touched by that pleasant feeling, he becomes lustful for pleasure and falls into lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of his ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by that painful feeling, he sorrows, pines, and laments, beats his breast and falls into confusion. That arisen pleasant feeling remains obsessing his mind because the body is undeveloped, and that arisen painful feeling remains obsessing his mind because the mind is undeveloped. For anyone, Aggivessana, in whom on both sides the arisen pleasant feeling remains obsessing the mind because the body is undeveloped, and the arisen painful feeling remains obsessing the mind because the mind is undeveloped, in this way one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
translations.mn36:9: And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind? Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in a learned noble disciple. Being touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not become lustful for pleasure and does not fall into lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling of his ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by that painful feeling, he does not sorrow, does not pine, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion. That arisen pleasant feeling does not remain obsessing his mind because the body is developed, and that arisen painful feeling does not remain obsessing his mind because the mind is developed. For anyone, Aggivessana, in whom on both sides the arisen pleasant feeling does not remain obsessing the mind because the body is developed, and the arisen painful feeling does not remain obsessing the mind because the mind is developed, in this way one is developed in body and developed in mind.”
translations.mn38:10: “Bhikkhus, does doubt arise in one who is uncertain, thinking: ‘Is this a being?’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, does doubt arise in one who is uncertain, thinking: ‘Does it come into being through that nutriment?’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, does doubt arise in one who is uncertain, thinking: ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come into being is subject to cessation?’?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:11: “Bhikkhus, for one who sees it as it actually is with right wisdom: ‘This is a being,’ is the doubt abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, for one who sees it as it actually is with right wisdom: ‘It comes into being through that nutriment,’ is the doubt abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, for one who sees it as it actually is with right wisdom: ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come into being is subject to cessation,’ is the doubt abandoned?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:12: “Bhikkhus, are you free from doubt about this: ‘This is a being’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, are you free from doubt about this: ‘It comes into being through that nutriment’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, are you free from doubt about this: ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come into being is subject to cessation’?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:13: “Bhikkhus, has it been well seen by you as it actually is with right wisdom: ‘This is a being’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, has it been well seen by you as it actually is with right wisdom: ‘It comes into being through that nutriment’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, has it been well seen by you as it actually is with right wisdom: ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come into being is subject to cessation’?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:14: “Bhikkhus, if you were to adhere to this view, so purified and so bright, if you were to cherish it, treasure it, and treat it as a possession, would you then understand the Dhamma taught by me as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?” “No, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, if you do not adhere to this view, so purified and so bright, if you do not cherish it, treasure it, and treat it as a possession, would you then understand the Dhamma taught by me as similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:15: “Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come into being or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth. Which four? Physical food, gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental volition the third; and consciousness the fourth.
translations.mn38:17: So, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:19: “Good, bhikkhus. So, bhikkhus, you say thus, and I also say thus: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.’ That is: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.mn38:2: Now at that time, a harmful misconception had arisen in a bhikkhu named Sāti, the fisherman's son, like this: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, not another.'
translations.mn38:20: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of choices; with the cessation of choices, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name and form; with the cessation of name and form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of grasping; with the cessation of grasping, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, then old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: “Good, bhikkhus. So, bhikkhus, you say this, and I also say this: when this is not, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of choices; with the cessation of choices, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name and form; with the cessation of name and form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of grasping; with the cessation of grasping, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, then old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
translations.mn38:23: “Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing like this, would you run back to the past: ‘Did we exist in the past? Did we not exist in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? Having been what, what did we become in the past?’” “No, bhante.” “Bhikkhus, knowing and seeing like this, would you run forward to the future: ‘Will we exist in the future? Will we not exist in the future? What will we be in the future? How will we be in the future? Having been what, what will we become in the future?’” “No, bhante.”
translations.mn38:25: “Good, bhikkhus. You have been guided by me with this Dhamma that is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. It is for this reason it was said: ‘This Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.’”
translations.mn38:26: “Bhikkhus, the descent of the embryo occurs through the union of three things. Here, there is the union of the mother and father, but the mother is not in her season, and the gandhabba is not present—then there is no descent of the embryo. Here, there is the union of the mother and father, and the mother is in her season, but the gandhabba is not present—then there is no descent of the embryo. But when, bhikkhus, there is the union of the mother and father, and the mother is in her season, and the gandhabba is present—then through the union of these three things, the descent of the embryo occurs.”
translations.mn38:27: “Then, bhikkhus, the mother carries the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months with great anxiety, as a heavy burden. Then, at the end of nine or ten months, the mother gives birth with great anxiety, as a heavy burden. When it is born, she nourishes it with her own blood. For in the Noble One’s discipline, mother’s milk is considered blood.”
translations.mn38:28: “As that boy grows up and his faculties mature, he plays with the playthings of children, such as: a toy plow, tip-cat, somersaults, toy windmills, toy measures, toy carts, and toy bows.”
translations.mn38:39: “Having abandoned these five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and remains in the first jhāna, which has initial and sustained application, and the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Furthermore, bhikkhus, with the stilling of initial and sustained application, a bhikkhu enters and remains in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained application, and has the rapture and happiness born of immersion... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna.”
translations.mn38:6: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus? Is this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, even warmed up in this Dhamma and Discipline?” “How could he be, bhante? No, bhante.” When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, brooding, speechless. Then the Blessed One, knowing that the bhikkhu Sāti was silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, brooding, and speechless, said to him: “You will be known, misguided man, by this harmful misconception of yours. I will question the bhikkhus here.”
translations.mn38:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, do you also understand the Dhamma as taught by me in the same way that this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, does, when he misrepresents us by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and stores up much demerit?” “No, bhante. For in many ways, bhante, dependently arisen consciousness has been described to us by the Blessed One; without a cause, there is no origination of consciousness.” “Good, good, bhikkhus. It is good that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way. For in many ways, bhikkhus, dependently arisen consciousness has been described by me to you; without a cause, there is no origination of consciousness. But this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman's son, misrepresents us by his wrong grasp, harms himself, and stores up much demerit. That will lead to that misguided man's harm and suffering for a long time.”
translations.mn38:9: “Mendicants, do you see: ‘This has come to be’?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see: ‘Its origination is due to that nutriment’?” “Yes, sir.” “Do you see: ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation’?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.mn41:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous conduct, unharmonious conduct by way of mind? Here, householders, someone is covetous; they covet the wealth and property of others: ‘Oh, if only what belongs to others were mine!’ They have a mind of ill will and intentions of hate: ‘May these sentient beings be killed, slaughtered, annihilated, destroyed, or may they not exist!’ And they have wrong view and distorted vision: ‘There is no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There is no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously reborn beings. There are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the highest point and practiced rightly, and who describe this world and the other world after realizing them for themselves with direct knowledge.’ That is how there is threefold unrighteous conduct, unharmonious conduct by way of mind. It is because of such unrighteous and unharmonious conduct that some sentient beings here, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous conduct, harmonious conduct by way of body? Here, householders, someone, having given up killing living beings, abstains from killing living beings. They have laid down the rod and the weapon; they are conscientious and kind, living full of compassion for all living beings. Having given up taking what is not given, they abstain from taking what is not given. They do not take the wealth and property of others in a village or a forest with the intention to steal. Having given up sexual misconduct, they abstain from sexual misconduct. They do not have sexual relations with those protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan; nor with those protected by the Dhamma, those who have a husband, those whose violation entails a penalty, or even those garlanded with a token of betrothal. That is how there is threefold righteous conduct, harmonious conduct by way of body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is there fourfold righteous conduct, harmonious conduct by way of speech? Here, householders, someone, having given up lying, abstains from lying. When summoned to a council, an assembly, a family gathering, a guild, or a royal court, and asked as a witness: ‘Come, good man, tell us what you know,’ if they do not know, they say ‘I don’t know’; if they do know, they say ‘I know’; if they haven’t seen, they say ‘I haven’t seen’; and if they have seen, they say ‘I’ve seen.’ They do not consciously tell a lie for their own sake, or for the sake of another, or for some small material gain. Having given up divisive speech, they abstain from divisive speech. They don’t repeat elsewhere what they’ve heard here in order to divide these people from those, nor do they repeat here what they’ve heard elsewhere in order to divide those people from these. Thus they are reconcilers of those who are divided, and supporters of those who are united. They love concord, delight in concord, enjoy concord, and speak words that create concord. Having given up harsh speech, they abstain from harsh speech. They speak words that are flawless, pleasant to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, pleasing to many, and agreeable to many. Having given up idle chatter, they abstain from idle chatter. They speak at the right time, speak what is true, speak what is beneficial, speak on the Dhamma and the Vinaya. They say things worth treasuring, spoken at the right time, with reasons, defined, and beneficial. That is how there is fourfold righteous conduct, harmonious conduct by way of speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous conduct, harmonious conduct by way of mind? Here, householders, someone is not covetous; they do not covet the wealth and property of others: ‘Oh, if only what belongs to others were mine!’ They do not have a mind of ill will and have intentions free of hate: ‘May these sentient beings live free from enmity, free from affliction, free from anxiety, and may they look after themselves happily.’ And they have right view and undistorted vision: ‘There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is this world, there is the other world, there is mother, there is father, there are spontaneously reborn beings. There are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the highest point and practiced rightly, and who describe this world and the other world after realizing them for themselves with direct knowledge.’ That is how there is threefold righteous conduct, harmonious conduct by way of mind. It is because of such righteous and harmonious conduct that some sentient beings here, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If a person who lives righteously and harmoniously should wish: ‘Oh, if only, when my body breaks up, after death, I were to be reborn in the company of well-to-do aristocrats!’ it is possible that this would happen. Why is that? Because they live righteously and harmoniously.
translations.mn41:3: Then the brahmin householders of Sālā went to the Buddha. Some bowed to him and sat down to one side. Some exchanged greetings with him and, when the greetings and polite conversation were over, sat down to one side. Some held up their joined palms toward the Buddha and sat down to one side. Some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side. Some sat down to one side in silence. When they were seated, the brahmin householders of Sālā said to the Buddha:
translations.mn41:4: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason why some sentient beings here, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell? And what is the cause, what is the reason why some sentient beings here, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world?”
translations.mn41:43: “Householders, if one who lives righteously and harmoniously should wish: ‘Oh, that by the destruction of the taints, I might here and now enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for myself with direct knowledge!’—it is possible that, by the destruction of the taints, they might here and now enter and dwell in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for themselves with direct knowledge. Why is that? Because they have lived righteously and harmoniously.”
translations.mn41:5: “Householders, it is by reason of unrighteous living and unharmonious living that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower world, even in hell. It is by reason of righteous living and harmonious living that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
translations.mn41:6: “We do not understand the detailed meaning of what Master Gotama has said in brief without explaining the details. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach us the Dhamma in such a way that we might understand the detailed meaning of what Master Gotama has said in brief.” “Then, householders, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmin householders of Sālā replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn41:8: “And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous and unharmonious conduct by body? Here, someone kills living beings; they are murderous, bloody-handed, given to blows and violence, merciless to living beings. They take what is not given; they take by way of theft the wealth and property of others in the village or in the forest. They conduct themselves wrongly in sensual pleasures; they have sexual relations with those protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan, or those protected by Dhamma, those who have a husband, those whose violation entails a penalty, or even those garlanded with a token of betrothal. That is how there is threefold unrighteous and unharmonious conduct by body.”
translations.mn41:9: “And how, householders, is there fourfold unrighteous and unharmonious conduct by speech? Here, someone is a liar. When summoned to a council, an assembly, a gathering of relatives, a guild, or a royal court, and questioned as a witness: ‘Come, good man, tell what you know,’ not knowing, they say, ‘I know,’ or knowing, they say, ‘I do not know’; not seeing, they say, ‘I see,’ or seeing, they say, ‘I do not see.’ Thus they consciously speak lies for their own sake, for the sake of another, or for some small material gain. They are a slanderer; repeating elsewhere what they have heard here in order to divide these people from those, or repeating here what they have heard elsewhere in order to divide those people from these. Thus they divide those who are united, a creator of divisions, enjoying factionalism, delighting in factionalism, rejoicing in factionalism, speaking words that create factionalism. They are harsh in speech; they speak words that are rough, hard, severe on others, abusive of others, bordering on anger, not conducive to concentration. They are a gossip; they speak at the wrong time, speak what is not a fact, speak what is useless, speak what is contrary to the Dhamma and the Discipline. They speak words that are not worth treasuring, at the wrong time, without reason, without limits, and unbeneficial. That is how there is fourfold unrighteous and unharmonious conduct by speech.”
translations.mn4:20: “The thought occurred to me, brahmin: ‘What if, on those nights that are well-known and marked—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—I were to dwell in such frightening and hair-raising resting places as park shrines, forest shrines, and tree shrines? Perhaps I might see that fear and dread.’ And later, brahmin, on those nights that are well-known and marked... I dwelt in such frightening and hair-raising resting places... While I was dwelling there, a wild animal would come, or a peacock would knock down a branch, or the wind would rustle the fallen leaves. The thought occurred to me: ‘Is this that fear and dread coming?’ Then the thought occurred to me: ‘Why do I dwell constantly expecting fear? What if, in whatever posture I am when that fear and dread come, I should subdue that fear and dread while remaining in that very posture?’ While I was walking, that fear and dread came. I did not stand or sit or lie down until I had subdued that fear and dread while walking. While I was standing, that fear and dread came. I did not walk or sit or lie down until I had subdued that fear and dread while standing. While I was sitting, that fear and dread came. I did not lie down or stand or walk until I had subdued that fear and dread while sitting. While I was lying down, that fear and dread came. I did not sit or stand or walk until I had subdued that fear and dread while lying down.”
translations.mn4:22-26: Brahmin, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, my body was tranquil and relaxed, and my mind was concentrated and one-pointed. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and remained in the first absorption, which has rapture and happiness born of seclusion, accompanied by placing the mind and keeping it connected. As the placing of the mind and keeping it connected were stilled, I entered and remained in the second absorption, which has rapture and happiness born of concentration, with internal clarity and confidence, and unified mind, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. And with the fading away of rapture, I remained equanimous, mindful and aware, and experienced happiness with the body; I entered and remained in the third absorption, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in happiness.’ With the giving up of pleasure and pain, and the previous disappearance of joy and sadness, I entered and remained in the fourth absorption, which is purified by equanimity and mindfulness, neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
translations.mn4:27: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfections, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of recollecting past lives. I recollected many kinds of past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘There I was named such, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; and there too I was named such, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn here.’ Thus I recollected many kinds of past lives with their features and details.
translations.mn4:28: This was the first knowledge I attained in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:29: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfections, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understood how beings pass on according to their deeds: ‘These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views—at the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. But these worthy beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views—at the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate. I understood how beings pass on according to their deeds.
translations.mn4:3: Brahmin, before my awakening, while I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta, I thought: ‘Remote jungle thickets in the forest are difficult to endure; seclusion is hard to practice, and it is difficult to enjoy solitude.
