I think the forests steal away the mind of a bhikkhu who has not attained concentration.’
translations.mn4:30: This was the second knowledge I attained in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:34: Brahmin, you might think: ‘Even today the ascetic Gotama is not free from greed, hate, and delusion, and that is why he frequents remote jungle thickets in the forest.’ But you should not see it like that. It is because I see two benefits that I frequent remote jungle thickets in the forest: seeing a pleasant dwelling for myself in this very life, and having compassion for future generations.
translations.mn4:4: I thought: ‘Whenever ascetics or brahmins who have unpurified bodily conduct frequent remote jungle thickets in the forest, then because of the defect of their unpurified bodily conduct, these worthy ascetics and brahmins evoke unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not have unpurified bodily conduct when I frequent remote jungle thickets in the forest; I have purified bodily conduct. I am one of those noble ones who frequent remote jungle thickets in the forest with purified bodily conduct.’ Seeing this purification of bodily conduct in myself, I felt even more confident about staying in the forest.
translations.mn4:5: I thought: ‘Whenever ascetics or brahmins who have unpurified verbal conduct … unpurified mental conduct … unpurified livelihood frequent remote jungle thickets in the forest, then because of the defect of their unpurified livelihood, these worthy ascetics and brahmins evoke unwholesome fear and dread.
translations.mn4:6: But I do not have an unpurified livelihood when I frequent remote jungle thickets in the forest; I have a purified livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: I am one of those noble ones who frequent remote jungle thickets in the forest with a purified livelihood.’ Seeing this purification of livelihood in myself, I felt even more confident about staying in the forest.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the venerable Ānanda was staying at Vesālī in Beluva village. Now at that time the householder Dasama from Aṭṭhakanāgara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, thinking 'space is infinite.' He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of infinite space is also conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Standing on that, ... he attains the supreme security from bondage.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, thinking 'there is nothing.' He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of nothingness is also conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.' Standing on that, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that desire for the Dhamma, through that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, due to attain final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, whereby if a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his undestroyed taints come to destruction, and he attains the unexcelled security from bondage.
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to the venerable Ānanda: “Venerable Ānanda, just as if a man seeking a single opening to a treasure were to come upon eleven openings to a treasure all at once; even so, venerable sir, seeking a single door to the Deathless, I have all at once gained eleven doors to the Deathless for the sake of cultivation. Just as if a man had a house with eleven doors, and if that house were on fire, he could save himself by any one of those doors; even so, venerable sir, I will be able to save myself by any one of these eleven doors to the Deathless. Venerable sir, those of other sects will seek a teacher's fee for their teacher, so why should I not perform a puja for the venerable Ānanda?”
translations.mn52:2: Then Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara went to the Kukkuṭa Monastery to see a certain bhikkhu; having approached, he paid homage to that bhikkhu and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to that bhikkhu: “Where, venerable sir, is the venerable Ānanda staying now? For we wish to see the venerable Ānanda.” “Householder, the venerable Ānanda is staying at Vesālī, in Beluvagāmaka.”
translations.mn52:3: Then Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara, having finished his business in Pāṭaliputta, went to Vesālī, to Beluvagāmaka, to see the venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to the venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to the venerable Ānanda: “Venerable Ānanda, is there a single thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, whereby if a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his undestroyed taints come to destruction, and he attains the unexcelled security from bondage?” “There is, householder, a single thing declared by the Blessed One... whereby if a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute... he attains the unexcelled security from bondage.” “But what, venerable Ānanda, is that single thing declared by the Blessed One...?”
translations.mn52:4: “Here, householder, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He reflects thus: ‘This first jhāna is also conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.’ Standing on that, he attains the destruction of the taints. If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that desire for the Dhamma, through that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, due to attain final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world. This too, householder, is a single thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, whereby if a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his undestroyed taints come to destruction, and he attains the unexcelled security from bondage.
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere and to everyone as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility and without ill will. He reflects thus: ‘This liberation of mind by loving-kindness is also conditioned and volitionally produced. Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation.’ Standing on that, ... he attains the supreme security from bondage.
translations.mn54:18: “Suppose, householder, there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals without flame or smoke. Then a man would come along, wanting to live, not wanting to die, desiring pleasure and recoiling from pain. Two strong men would grab him by both arms and drag him toward the charcoal pit. What do you think, householder? Would that man twist his body this way and that?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Why is that?” “Because, venerable sir, that man knows: ‘I will fall into this charcoal pit, and because of that I will meet death or deadly suffering.’” “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘Sensual pleasures have been compared to a charcoal pit by the Blessed One; they are full of suffering and despair, and the danger in them is great.’ Having seen this as it really is with right wisdom … he develops equanimity alone.”
translations.mn54:23: “Relying on this very same supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, that noble disciple, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … he understands how beings pass on according to their karma.”
translations.mn54:24: “Relying on this very same supreme purity of mindfulness and equanimity, with the destruction of the taints, that noble disciple realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells in it.”
translations.mn60:10: “In this case, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: ‘There is what is given … there are those who, having realized for themselves with direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known’—it is to be expected of them that, having avoided these three unskillful qualities—namely, bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—they will undertake and practice these three skillful qualities—namely, good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct. Why is that? Because those venerable ascetics and brahmins see the danger, degradation, and defilement in unskillful qualities, and the benefit in renunciation and the side of purification in skillful qualities.”
translations.mn60:12: “In this case, householders, a wise person reflects: ‘If there is another world, then this venerable person, at the breaking up of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Even if we assume there is no other world, and the word of those venerable ascetics and brahmins is true, still this venerable person is praised by the wise in this very life as a person of integrity, one of right view who holds the doctrine of existence.’ If there is indeed another world, then this venerable person has won on both counts: in that he is praised by the wise in this very life, and in that at the breaking up of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus he has correctly undertaken this ‘infallible teaching’ in such a way that it extends to both sides and leaves behind the unskillful position.”
translations.mn60:13: “There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: ‘When one acts or gets others to act, mutilates or gets others to mutilate, cooks or gets others to cook, sorrows or gets others to sorrow, fatigues or gets others to fatigue, trembles or gets others to tremble, kills, steals, breaks into houses, plunders, commits burglary, ambushes, commits adultery, or lies—no evil is done by the doer. If one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, a single heap of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, there would be no evil because of that, no arrival of evil. If one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and slaughtering, mutilating and getting others to mutilate, cooking and getting others to cook, there would be no evil because of that, no arrival of evil. If one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and getting others to give, sacrificing and getting others to sacrifice, there would be no merit because of that, no arrival of merit. Through giving, self-control, restraint, and truthful speech, there is no merit, no arrival of merit.’”
translations.mn60:14: “There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold a doctrine directly opposed to those ascetics and brahmins, and they say: ‘When one acts or gets others to act … no evil is done’—that is not so; evil is done. ‘If one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh … there would be no evil’—that is not so; there is evil. ‘If one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges … there would be no evil’—that is not so; there is evil. ‘If one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges … there would be no merit’—that is not so; there is merit. ‘Through giving, self-control, restraint, and truthful speech, there is no merit’—that is not so; there is merit. What do you think, householders? Do not these ascetics and brahmins hold doctrines directly opposed to each other?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn60:16: “When there is indeed efficacy of action, his view is ‘there is no efficacy of action’; that is his wrong view. When there is indeed efficacy of action, he intends ‘there is no efficacy of action’; that is his wrong intention. When there is indeed efficacy of action, he says ‘there is no efficacy of action’; that is his wrong speech. When there is indeed efficacy of action, he says ‘there is no efficacy of action,’ thus opposing those arahants who hold the doctrine of the efficacy of action. When there is indeed efficacy of action, he convinces another ‘there is no efficacy of action’; that is his convincing others of a false Dhamma. And because of that convincing others of a false Dhamma, he exalts himself and disparages others. Thus his former good character is abandoned and bad character is established—this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, convincing others of a false Dhamma, self-exaltation, and disparagement of others. Thus these many evil unskillful qualities arise with wrong view as their condition.”
translations.mn60:17: In this case, householders, a wise person reflects: ‘If there is no efficacy of action, then this good person, at the breaking up of the body, will make themselves safe. But if there is efficacy of action, then this good person, at the breaking up of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. Even if we assume that there is no efficacy of action, and the word of those ascetics and brahmins is true, still this good person is censured by the wise in the present life as an immoral person, one of wrong view, a teacher of non-action. But if there is indeed efficacy of action, then this good person has a losing throw on both counts: because they are censured by the wise in the present life, and because at the breaking up of the body, after death, they will be reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. Thus they have wrongly undertaken this incontrovertible teaching in such a way that it extends only to one side, and they neglect the wholesome possibility.’
translations.mn60:19: Since there is indeed efficacy of action, the view that ‘there is efficacy of action’ is their right view. Since there is indeed efficacy of action, the thought that ‘there is efficacy of action’ is their right intention. Since there is indeed efficacy of action, the speech that ‘there is efficacy of action’ is their right speech. Since there is indeed efficacy of action, they say ‘there is efficacy of action’; thus they do not oppose those perfected ones who teach the efficacy of action. Since there is indeed efficacy of action, they convince another that ‘there is efficacy of action’; that is their convincing another of the true teaching. And through that convincing another of the true teaching, they do not exalt themselves or disparage others. Thus their former immorality is abandoned and good conduct is established—this right view, right intention, right speech, non-opposition to the noble ones, convincing another of the true teaching, not exalting oneself, and not disparaging others. Thus these many wholesome qualities arise with right view as their condition.
translations.mn60:21: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘There is no cause or condition for the corruption of beings; beings are corrupted without cause or condition. There is no cause or condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition. There is no power, no energy, no human strength, no human effort. All beings, all breathing things, all creatures, all souls are without mastery, power, or energy; molded by destiny, coincidence, and nature, they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.’
translations.mn60:22: Regarding this, householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine is directly opposite to those ascetics and brahmins. They say: ‘There is a cause and condition for the corruption of beings; beings are corrupted with cause and condition. There is a cause and condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause and condition. There is power, energy, human strength, and human effort. It is not the case that all beings, all breathing things, all creatures, all souls are without mastery, power, or energy, molded by destiny, coincidence, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.’ What do you think, householders, don’t these ascetics and brahmins hold doctrines directly opposite to each other?” “Yes, bhante.”
translations.mn60:29: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘There are no formless states at all.’
translations.mn60:30: Regarding this, householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine is directly opposite to those ascetics and brahmins. They say: ‘There are formless states.’ What do you think, householders, don’t these ascetics and brahmins hold doctrines directly opposite to each other?” “Yes, bhante.”
translations.mn60:32: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘There is no total cessation of existence.’
translations.mn60:35: Householders, these four types of persons are found existing in the world. Which four? Here, householders, some person is a self-tormentor, intent on the practice of self-mortification. Here, householders, some person is a private-tormentor, intent on the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, some person is both a self-tormentor, intent on the practice of self-mortification, and a private-tormentor, intent on the practice of tormenting others. Here, householders, some person is neither a self-tormentor, not intent on the practice of self-mortification, nor a private-tormentor, not intent on the practice of tormenting others; being neither a self-tormentor nor a private-tormentor, in this very life they are hungerless, extinguished, cooled, experiencing happiness, dwelling with a self become divine.
translations.mn60:36: And what, householders, is the person who is a self-tormentor, intent on the practice of self-mortification? Here, householders, some person goes naked, is of loose habits, licks their hands … and so on … thus they dwell intent on the practice of many kinds of bodily heat and torment. This is called, householders, the person who is a self-tormentor, intent on the practice of self-mortification.
translations.mn60:37: And what, householders, is the person who is a private-tormentor, intent on the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, some person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs … and so on … or whoever else follows any other such cruel occupations. This is called, householders, the person who is a private-tormentor, intent on the practice of tormenting others.
translations.mn60:38: And what, householders, is the person who is both a self-tormentor, intent on the practice of self-mortification, and a private-tormentor, intent on the practice of tormenting others? Here, householders, some person is a king, a kshatriya duly anointed … and so on … and their employees, driven by punishment and fear, perform their tasks with tearful faces and weeping. This is called, householders, the person who is both a self-tormentor and a private-tormentor.
translations.mn60:39: And what, householders, is the person who is neither a self-tormentor, not intent on the practice of self-mortification, nor a private-tormentor, not intent on the practice of tormenting others; who, being neither a self-tormentor nor a private-tormentor, in this very life is hungerless, extinguished, cooled, experiencing happiness, dwelling with a self become divine?
translations.mn60:4: “But householders, is there any teacher you find pleasing, in whom you have gained a grounded faith?” “No, bhante, there is no teacher we find pleasing in whom we have gained a grounded faith.” “Householders, since you do not have a pleasing teacher, you should undertake and practice this incontrovertible teaching. For when the incontrovertible teaching is fully undertaken, it will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what, householders, is the incontrovertible teaching?
translations.mn60:5: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously reborn beings; there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path and are practicing rightly, who having realized for themselves by direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known.’
translations.mn60:6: Regarding those ascetics and brahmins, householders, there are other ascetics and brahmins who directly oppose them. They say: ‘There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is the fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously reborn beings; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have reached the right path and are practicing rightly, who having realized for themselves by direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known.’ What do you think, householders: ‘Do these ascetics and brahmins directly oppose each other?’ ‘Yes, bhante.’
translations.mn63:8: And why, Mālukyaputta, has this not been declared by me? Because it is not beneficial, it does not belong to the fundamentals of the holy life, it does not lead to disillusionment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. That is why it has not been declared by me.
translations.mn64:13: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite space. Whatever is there of feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness... he is of a nature not to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the dimension of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness. Whatever is there of feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness... he is of a nature not to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: “Bhikkhus, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?” When this was said, the venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One.” “And how, Mālukyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters as taught by me?” “Bhante, I remember identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember attachment to precepts and observances as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I remember ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. That is how, bhante, I remember the five lower fetters as taught by the Blessed One.”
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is the time, Blessed One, it is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.” “Then, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn64:7: Ānanda, that there is a path, a way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters, and that by following that path, that way, one will know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters—this is possible.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, through seclusion from acquisitions, through the abandoning of unwholesome states, through the complete tranquilizing of bodily discomfort, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Whatever is there of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness, he regards those states as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as non-self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the deathless element: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Standing there, he reaches the destruction of the taints; if he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then by that very lust for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous rebirth, attaining Nibbāna there, not of a nature to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the way to the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I experience the various kinds of psychic power—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; appear and disappear; go unhindered through walls, enclosures, and mountains as though through space; dive in and out of the earth as though through water; walk on water without sinking as though on earth; travel through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird; touch and stroke with my hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; and exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts... a frequenter of empty huts.
translations.mn6:15: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘With the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, may I hear both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts … and nurtures the practice of empty huts.
translations.mn6:16: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and other persons, having encompassed them with my own mind. May I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust, and a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hate as a mind with hate, and a mind without hate as a mind without hate; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind, and a scattered mind as a scattered mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind, and an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, and an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, and an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind, and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts … and nurtures the practice of empty huts.
translations.mn6:2: “Bhikkhus, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest faults; having undertaken them, train in the training rules.
translations.mn6:3: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be dear and agreeable to my companions in the holy life, respected and esteemed by them,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts, who is devoted to internal serenity of mind, who does not neglect meditation, who is possessed of insight, and who nurtures the practice of empty huts.
translations.mn6:6: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May it be of great fruit and great benefit for those departed relatives and kinsmen who remember me with a confident heart,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts, who is devoted to internal serenity of mind, who does not neglect meditation, who is possessed of insight, and who nurtures the practice of empty huts.
translations.mn6:7: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be a conqueror of discontent and delight, and may discontent not conquer me; may I dwell having overcome discontent whenever it arises,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts … and nurtures the practice of empty huts.
translations.mn6:8: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be a conqueror of fear and dread, and may fear and dread not conquer me; may I dwell having overcome fear and dread whenever it arises,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts … and nurtures the practice of empty huts.
translations.mn6:9: If a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be one who obtains at will, without difficulty, without trouble, the four jhānas, which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts … and nurtures the practice of empty huts.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kāsī country together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.mn70:11: “And because this has been known, seen, understood, realized, and experienced by me through wisdom: ‘When someone feels such a neutral feeling, unskillful qualities decline and skillful qualities increase,’ therefore I say: ‘Enter upon and dwell in such a neutral feeling.’
translations.mn70:12: Bhikkhus, I do not say of all bhikkhus that they have work to do with diligence; nor do I say of all bhikkhus that they do not have work to do with diligence. Those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through right final knowledge—of such bhikkhus I say that they do not have work to do with diligence. Why is that? They have done it with diligence. They are incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:13: But those bhikkhus who are trainees, who have not yet attained their heart's goal, but dwell aspiring for the supreme security from bondage—of such bhikkhus I say that they have work to do with diligence. Why is that? It is because these venerable ones, while using suitable resting places, associating with good friends, and balancing their spiritual faculties, might—for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—realize for themselves with direct knowledge, enter upon, and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life in this very life. Seeing this fruit of diligence for these bhikkhus, I say that they have work to do with diligence.
translations.mn70:14: Bhikkhus, these seven persons are found existing in the world. Which seven? One liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a follower by Dhamma, and a follower by faith.
translations.mn70:15: And what kind of person is one liberated in both ways? Here, some person dwells having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, the formless attainments, and having seen with wisdom, his taints are destroyed. This is called a person liberated in both ways. I do not say of this bhikkhu that he has work to do with diligence. Why is that? He has done it with diligence. He is incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:17: And what kind of person is a body-witness? Here, some person dwells having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend form, the formless attainments, and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed. This is called a person who is a body-witness. I say of this bhikkhu that he has work to do with diligence. Why is that? It is because this venerable one, while using suitable resting places, associating with good friends, and balancing his spiritual faculties, might—for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—realize for himself with direct knowledge, enter upon, and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life in this very life. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this bhikkhu, I say that he has work to do with diligence.
translations.mn70:2: “Monks, I do not eat at night. By refraining from eating at night, I experience good health, lack of illness, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, monks, you too should refrain from eating at night. By refraining from eating at night, you too will experience good health, lack of illness, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.mn70:20: And what kind of person, monks, is a follower by Dhamma? Here, some person does not dwell having touched with the body those peaceful deliverances that transcend forms, the formless states; but having seen with wisdom, some of their taints are destroyed. And the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are accepted by them after being pondered to a sufficient degree with wisdom. Furthermore, they have these qualities: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. This is called a person who is a follower by Dhamma. I say of such a monk, monks, that ‘there is work to be done with diligence.’ Why is that? Because while this venerable one is using suitable resting places, associating with good friends, and balancing his faculties, he might—for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—realize for himself with direct knowledge, here and now, that supreme goal of the holy life and dwell having entered upon it. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk, I say that ‘there is work to be done with diligence.’
translations.mn70:22: Monks, I do not say that the attainment of final knowledge happens at the very beginning; rather, monks, the attainment of final knowledge comes through gradual training, gradual action, and gradual practice.
translations.mn70:23: And how, monks, does the attainment of final knowledge come through gradual training, gradual action, and gradual practice? Here, monks, one who has faith visits; visiting, he pays respect; paying respect, he lends an ear; lending an ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he remembers it; he examines the meaning of the teachings he has remembered; while examining the meaning, the teachings are accepted after being pondered; when there is acceptance of the teachings through pondering, desire arises; when desire has arisen, he applies effort; having applied effort, he scrutinizes; having scrutinized, he strives; being resolute, he realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom.
translations.mn70:24: But, monks, there was not that faith; there was not that visiting; there was not that paying respect; there was not that lending an ear; there was not that hearing of the Dhamma; there was not that remembering of the Dhamma; there was not that examination of the meaning; there was not that acceptance of the teachings through pondering; there was not that desire; there was not that effort; there was not that scrutiny; there was not that striving. You have practiced wrongly, monks; you have practiced incorrectly, monks. How far these misguided men have strayed from this Dhamma and Discipline!
translations.mn70:25: Monks, there is a four-phrase statement which, when recited, a wise person would soon understand the meaning of. I shall recite it for you, monks; will you understand it from me?” “Who are we, venerable sir, and who are those who understand the Dhamma?”
translations.mn70:26: “Monks, even with a teacher who is concerned with material things, an heir to material things, who lives entangled with material things, such haggling by his disciples would not be appropriate: ‘If it is like this for us, we will do it; if it is not like this for us, we will not do it.’ How much more so, monks, when the Tathāgata lives altogether detached from material things?
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages in the Kāsī country, arrived at a town of the Kāsīs named Kīṭāgiri. There the Blessed One stayed at Kīṭāgiri, the town of the Kāsīs.
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time the monks named Assaji and Punabbasu were residing at Kīṭāgiri. Then a number of monks went to the monks Assaji and Punabbasu and said to them: “Friends, the Blessed One refrains from eating at night, and so does the community of monks. By refraining from eating at night, friends, they experience good health, lack of illness, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Come, friends, you too should refrain from eating at night. By refraining from eating at night, you too will experience good health, lack of illness, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding.” When this was said, the monks Assaji and Punabbasu said to those monks: “Friends, we eat in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the wrong time. Eating in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the wrong time, we experience good health, lack of illness, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding. Why should we abandon what is visible here and now to pursue what is subject to time? We shall eat in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the wrong time.”
translations.mn70:7: “Monks, do you not understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way: that for someone feeling a certain kind of pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish; but for someone else feeling such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase? That for someone feeling a certain kind of painful feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish; but for someone else feeling such a painful feeling, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase? That for someone feeling a certain kind of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish; but for someone else feeling such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn75:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was living among the Kurus, where there is a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma, in the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, on a spread of grass.
translations.mn75:10: “Māgaṇḍiya, in the past, when I was a householder, I was provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, and I enjoyed myself with forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; with sounds cognizable by the ear … with smells cognizable by the nose … with tastes cognizable by the tongue … with touches cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. I had three palaces: one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer. In the rainy-season palace, during the four months of the rains, I was entertained by musicians, none of whom were men, and I did not descend from the palace. On a later occasion, having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the satisfaction, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, I dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, and I dwell without thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace. I see other beings who are not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not envy them, nor do I delight therein. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, which surpasses even divine bliss. Since I delight in that, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight therein.”
translations.mn75:12: “In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past, when I was a householder, I was provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, and I enjoyed myself with forms cognizable by the eye … with sounds cognizable by the ear … with smells cognizable by the nose … with tastes cognizable by the tongue … with touches cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. On a later occasion, having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the satisfaction, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, I dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, and I dwell without thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace. I see other beings who are not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures; I do not envy them, nor do I delight therein. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, which surpasses even divine bliss. Since I delight in that, I do not envy what is inferior, nor do I delight therein.”
translations.mn75:13: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing coals. Then his friends and colleagues, kinsmen and relatives, would summon a physician and surgeon. The physician and surgeon would make a medicine for him. By means of that medicine he would be cured of his leprosy and would become well, happy, free, his own master, able to go where he likes. Then he might see another leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing coals. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that man envy the leper for his pit of glowing coals or for his use of the medicine?” “No, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because when there is a disease, there is a need for medicine; when there is no disease, there is no need for medicine.”
translations.mn75:16: “In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past sensual pleasures were painful to the touch, very hot, and very burning; in the future sensual pleasures will be painful to the touch, very hot, and very burning; and now in the present sensual pleasures are painful to the touch, very hot, and very burning. But these beings, not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, with their faculties impaired, have acquired the distorted perception of pleasure in what is actually painful to the touch.”
translations.mn75:17: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing coals. The more that leper scratches the openings of his wounds and cauterizes his body, the more those openings of his wounds become even more foul-smelling, putrid, and infected; yet he finds a certain measure of satisfaction and enjoyment in scratching the openings of his wounds. In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from passion for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures. The more such beings indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures increases and the more they burn with the fever of sensual pleasures; yet they find a certain measure of satisfaction and enjoyment in dependence on the five cords of sensual pleasure.”
translations.mn75:18: “What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Have you ever seen or heard of a king or a royal minister, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoying them, who—without abandoning craving for sensual pleasures, without removing the fever of sensual pleasures—dwelt, dwells, or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace?” “No, Master Gotama.” “Good, Māgaṇḍiya. I too have never seen or heard of a king or a royal minister... who dwelt, dwells, or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace. But rather, Māgaṇḍiya, those ascetics or brahmins who dwelt, dwell, or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace—all of them, having understood as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, and having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures and removed the fever of sensual pleasures, dwelt, dwell, or will dwell free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace.”
translations.mn75:2: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having walked for alms in Kammāsadhamma and returned from his almsround after his meal, he went to a certain grove for the day's abiding. Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn75:22: “I have confidence in Master Gotama in this way. Master Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might know health and see Nibbāna.” “Māgaṇḍiya, suppose there were a man born blind; he could not see dark and light forms, he could not see blue, yellow, red, or crimson forms, he could not see what is level and uneven, he could not see the forms of the stars, he could not see the moon and sun. His friends and colleagues, kinsmen and relatives, might engage a physician and surgeon. That physician and surgeon might prepare a medicine for him. But despite that medicine, he might not produce vision or purify his vision. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that doctor not have a share of weariness and vexation?” “Yes, Master Gotama.” “Even so, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: ‘This is that health, this is that Nibbāna,’ you would not know health, you would not see Nibbāna. That would be wearisome for me, that would be troublesome for me.”
translations.mn75:24: “Even so, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: ‘This is that health, this is that Nibbāna,’ you would know health, you would see Nibbāna. With the arising of vision in you, the desire and lust for the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned. Furthermore, it would occur to you: ‘For a long time indeed I have been cheated, deceived, and deluded by this mind. For in clinging, I clung only to form, I clung only to feeling, I clung only to perception, I clung only to choices, I clung only to consciousness. With my clinging as condition, there is existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.’”
translations.mn75:25: “I have confidence in Master Gotama in this way. Master Gotama is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat no longer blind.” “In that case, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with true persons. When you associate with true persons, you will hear the True Dhamma. When you hear the True Dhamma, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma. When you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, you will know for yourself and see for yourself: ‘These are diseases, boils, and arrows; here diseases, boils, and arrows cease without remainder. With the cessation of my clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as if one were to set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or point out the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms; even so has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I receive the going forth in the presence of Master Gotama, may I receive the full admission.”
translations.mn75:27: “Māgaṇḍiya, one who was formerly a follower of another sect and desires the going forth and the full admission in this Dhamma and Discipline lives on probation for four months. At the end of four months, the monks who are satisfied in mind give him the going forth and the full admission to the state of a monk. But I recognize a difference in persons in this regard.” “If, bhante, those who were formerly followers of another sect... live on probation for four months... then I will live on probation for four years. At the end of four years, let the monks who are satisfied in mind give me the going forth and the full admission to the state of a monk.”
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, went to the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. The wanderer Māgaṇḍiya saw a grass mat spread out in the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Seeing it, he said to the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan: “For whom is this grass mat spread out in Master Bhāradvāja’s fire-hall? It looks like the bed of a contemplative.”
translations.mn75:6: The Blessed One, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, heard this conversation between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya. Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan; having gone there, he sat down on the prepared grass mat. Then the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan went to the Blessed One; having gone there, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had finished the polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. As the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Bhāradvāja, was there some conversation between you and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya concerning this very grass mat?” When this was said, the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, shocked and with his hair standing on end, said to the Blessed One: “This is exactly what we wanted to tell Master Gotama. But Master Gotama has stated it even before it was told!”
translations.mn75:7: This was the conversation between the Blessed One and the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan that was interrupted. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering for exercise, went to the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan where the Blessed One was; having gone there, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had finished the polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. As the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him:
translations.mn77:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
translations.mn77:10: “There are, Udāyi, five other things for which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and worship me, and having honored and respected me, live in dependence on me. What are the five? Here, Udāyi, my disciples esteem me for higher virtue: ‘The contemplative Gotama is virtuous, possessed of the highest aggregate of virtue.’
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way, practicing which my disciples develop the four establishments of mindfulness. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … he dwells contemplating mind in mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way, practicing which my disciples develop the four right efforts. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way, practicing which my disciples develop the four bases of psychic power. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the basis of psychic power possessed of concentration due to desire and the fabrications of effort; he develops the basis of psychic power possessed of concentration due to energy and the fabrications of effort; he develops the basis of psychic power possessed of concentration due to mind and the fabrications of effort; he develops the basis of psychic power possessed of concentration due to investigation and the fabrications of effort. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way, practicing which my disciples develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the faculty of faith leading to peace, leading to enlightenment; he develops the faculty of energy … the faculty of mindfulness … the faculty of concentration … the faculty of wisdom leading to peace, leading to enlightenment. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:2: Now at that time many well-known wanderers were staying in the Wanderers’ Park at the Peacocks’ Feeding Place, namely, Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way, practicing which my disciples develop the seven factors of enlightenment. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment; he develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena … the enlightenment factor of energy … the enlightenment factor of rapture … the enlightenment factor of tranquility … the enlightenment factor of concentration … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that they develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that they develop the eight liberations. Possessing form, one sees forms: this is the first liberation. Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally: this is the second liberation. One is resolved only on the beautiful: this is the third liberation. With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite space: this is the fourth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness: this is the fifth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ one enters and dwells in the dimension of nothingness: this is the sixth liberation. With the complete surmounting of the dimension of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: this is the seventh liberation. With the complete surmounting of the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling: this is the eighth liberation. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that they develop the ten universal bases. One perceives the earth-universal—above, below, across, undivided, measureless. One perceives the water-universal … the fire-universal … the air-universal … the blue-universal … the yellow-universal … the red-universal … the white-universal … the space-universal … One perceives the consciousness-universal—above, below, across, undivided, measureless. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that they develop the four absorptions. Here, Udāyi, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first absorption, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Just as, Udāyi, a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice might strew bathing powder in a bronze basin and, sprinkling it again and again with water, knead it together so that the ball of bathing powder is saturated with moisture, encompassed by moisture, permeated by moisture inside and out, yet does not trickle; even so, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second absorption … He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of immersion, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of immersion. Just as, Udāyi, there might be a deep lake whose waters well up from below. It has no inflow from the east, the west, the north, or the south, and the heavens do not provide it with regular rainfall; yet the cool fount of water welling up from within the lake would drench, steep, fill, and pervade that lake with cool water, so there would be no part of that whole lake unpervaded by cool water; even so, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of immersion, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of immersion.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the fading away of rapture … a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the third absorption. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the happiness divested of rapture, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the happiness divested of rapture. Just as, Udāyi, in a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses, some lotuses born and growing in the water might thrive submerged in the water without rising out of it, and they would be drenched, steeped, filled, and pervaded with cool water from their tips to their roots, so there would be no part of those whole blue, red, or white lotuses unpervaded by cool water; even so, Udāyi, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the happiness divested of rapture, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the happiness divested of rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the giving up of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth absorption, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. He sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the pure, bright mind. Just as, Udāyi, a man might be sitting covered from the head down with a white cloth, so there would be no part of his whole body uncovered by the white cloth; even so, Udāyi, a bhikkhu sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind, so there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the pure, bright mind. And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:3: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. What if I were to go to the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground, the park of the wanderers, to see the wanderer Sakuludāyī?”
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that they hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near—with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human. Just as a powerful conch-blower might make himself heard in the four directions without much difficulty; even so, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice... And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that they recollect their manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... many eons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; there too I was so named... passing away from there, I reappeared here.’ Thus they recollect their manifold past lives with their aspects and details. Just as if a man were to go from his own village to another village, and from that village to another village, and then return to his own village; he would think: ‘I went from my own village to that village, there I stood in such a way, sat in such a way, spoke in such a way, was silent in such a way... and now I have returned to my own village.’ Even so, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice... And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, they see beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and they understand how beings pass on according to their kamma: ‘These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of noble ones, wrong in their views... have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the underworld, even hell; but these worthy beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind... have reappeared in a happy destination, the heavenly world.’ Just as if there were two houses with doors, and a man with good sight standing between them were to see people entering the houses, leaving them, and walking back and forth; even so, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice... And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice so that by the destruction of the taints, they realize for themselves with direct knowledge, here and now, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, they dwell in it. Just as if in a mountain glen there were a pool of water, clear, bright, and unclouded, where a man with good sight standing on the bank could see shells, gravel, and pebbles, and shoals of fish moving about or staying still. He would think: ‘This pool of water is clear, bright, and unclouded; here are shells, gravel, and pebbles, and shoals of fish moving about or staying still.’ Even so, Udāyi, I have explained to my disciples the way to practice... And therein many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One went to the wanderer Sakuludāyī. The wanderer Sakuludāyī said to the Blessed One: “Let the Blessed One come, venerable sir. Welcome to the Blessed One. It has been a long time since the Blessed One made an occasion to come here. Let the Blessed One sit down; this seat is prepared.” The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Sakuludāyī the wanderer also took a low seat and sat to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “For what discussion are you sitting gathered here now, Udāyi, and what was your discussion that was interrupted?”
translations.mn77:7: “But Udāyi, how many qualities do you see in me because of which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me?”
translations.mn77:9: “Udāyi, if my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and worship me, and live in dependence on me, thinking: ‘The ascetic Gotama eats little, and he speaks in praise of eating little,’ there are disciples of mine who eat as little as a cupful, or half a cupful, or a bael fruit, or half a bael fruit. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat a full bowl or even more. If my disciples were to honor me thinking I eat little, then those disciples of mine who eat a cupful or half a cupful would not honor, respect, revere, and worship me for this quality. If they were to honor me thinking: ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe,’ there are disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wearing coarse robes; they pick up rags from cemeteries, rubbish heaps, or shops, make them into outer robes, and wear them. But I, Udāyi, sometimes wear robes given by householders, which are strong, fine, and soft. If my disciples were to honor me thinking I am content with any kind of robe, then those disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers would not honor me for this quality. If they were to honor me thinking: ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of almsfood,’ there are disciples of mine who are alms-gatherers, who go on an uninterrupted almsround, delighting in the practice of gathering scraps; when they have entered a house, they do not accept even an invitation to a seat. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat on invitation, eating fine rice with the black grains removed, with many soups and many curries. If my disciples were to honor me thinking I am content with any kind of almsfood, then those disciples of mine who are alms-gatherers would not honor me for this quality. If they were to honor me thinking: ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging,’ there are disciples of mine who live at the foot of trees or in the open air, and for eight months they do not go under a roof. But I, Udāyi, sometimes live in gabled houses, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows shut. If my disciples were to honor me thinking I am content with any kind of lodging, then those disciples of mine who live at the foot of trees or in the open air would not honor me for this quality. If they were to honor me thinking: ‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he speaks in praise of seclusion,’ there are disciples of mine who are forest-dwellers, living in remote lodgings, having plunged into remote jungle-thicket lodgings; they come into the midst of the Sangha once every fortnight for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But I, Udāyi, sometimes live crowded with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, other sectarians, and their disciples. If my disciples were to honor me thinking I am secluded, then those disciples of mine who are forest-dwellers would not honor me for this quality. Thus, Udāyi, it is not because of these five qualities that my disciples honor, respect, revere, and worship me, and live in dependence on me.”
translations.mn7:11: When he knows: ‘In such a way, this has been given up, vomited, released, abandoned, and relinquished by me,’ he gains inspiration in the meaning, inspiration in the Dhamma, and joy connected with the Dhamma. When he is joyful, rapture is born; for one who is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil feels happiness; the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility and without ill will.
translations.mn7:17: He understands: ‘There is this, there is the inferior, there is the superior, and beyond this field of perception there is an escape.’
translations.mn7:18: When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the stain of sensual desire, from the stain of becoming, and from the stain of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’ This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is bathed with the inner bathing.
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja said to the Blessed One: “But does Master Gotama go to the Bāhukā River to bathe?” “What, brahmin, is the Bāhukā River? What can the Bāhukā River do?” “Master Gotama, the Bāhukā River is considered by many people to be a means of purification; the Bāhukā River is considered by many people to be a means of merit; many people wash away their past evil deeds in the Bāhukā River.”
translations.mn7:2: “Bhikkhus, suppose a cloth were stained and dirty, and a dyer were to dip it into whatever dye he chose—whether blue, yellow, red, or crimson—it would look poorly dyed and impure in color. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth, bhikkhus. So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is defiled, an unhappy destination is to be expected. Bhikkhus, suppose a cloth were pure and bright, and a dyer were to dip it into whatever dye he chose—whether blue, yellow, red, or crimson—it would look well dyed and pure in color. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth, bhikkhus. So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is undefiled, a happy destination is to be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja in verses: ‘The Bāhukā and the Adhikakkā, the Gayā and the Sundarikā too, the Sarassatī and the Payāga, and then the river Bāhumatī; a fool may constantly plunge into them, yet his dark deeds are not cleansed. What can the Sundarikā do? What the Payāga? What the Bāhukā River? They cannot cleanse the person of hateful and evil deeds, the perpetrator of wicked crimes. For the pure person, it is always the spring festival; for the pure person, it is always the holy day; for the pure person of clean deeds, his vows always succeed. Bathe here, brahmin, create safety for all beings. If you do not speak lies, if you do not harm living beings, if you do not take what is not given, being faithful and not stingy; what will you gain by going to Gayā? Even a well is your Gayā.’
translations.mn7:3: And what, bhikkhus, are the imperfections of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed is an imperfection of the mind; ill will... anger... resentment... contempt... insolence... envy... stinginess... deceit... fraud... obstinacy... rivalry... conceit... arrogance... vanity... negligence is an imperfection of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: He possesses experiential confidence in the Teaching: ‘The Teaching is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, onward-leading, to be experienced by the wise for themselves.’
translations.mn7:7: He possesses experiential confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kuru country together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and he eventually arrived at a Kuru town named Thullakoṭṭhika.
translations.mn82:11: Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to his parents and said: “Mother and father, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla is lying there on the bare ground, saying: ‘Right here I will either die or receive the going forth.’ If you do not give the clansman Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness, he will die right there. But if you give him permission, you will see him even after he has gone forth. And if the clansman Raṭṭhapāla does not enjoy the life of homelessness, what other course will he have? He will return right here. Give the clansman Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness.” “We give our permission, dear ones, for the clansman Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness. But once he has gone forth, he must show himself to his parents.” Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to him and said: “Get up, friend Raṭṭhapāla, you have been given permission by your parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness. But once you have gone forth, you must show yourself to your parents.”
translations.mn82:12: Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla got up, and having regained his strength, he went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side and said: “Venerable sir, I have been given permission by my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness. Let the Blessed One give me the going forth.”
translations.mn82:13: The clansman Raṭṭhapāla received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he received the full ordination. Then the Blessed One, when the venerable Raṭṭhapāla had been ordained for half a month, having stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika as long as he liked, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī. Walking by stages, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One stayed at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.
translations.mn82:14: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon—by realizing for himself with direct knowledge in this very life—attained and dwelt in that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness. He directly knew: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' And the venerable Raṭṭhapāla became one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla rose from his seat, bowed to the Blessed One, and after performing a right-hand circumambulation, set his lodgings in order, took his bowl and robe, and set out on a wandering tour toward Thullakoṭṭhika. Walking by stages, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There the venerable Raṭṭhapāla stayed at Thullakoṭṭhika in King Koravya's Migacīra garden. Then, in the morning, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. As he was walking for alms from house to house in Thullakoṭṭhika, he approached his own father's house.
translations.mn82:17: At that time, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father was having his hair combed in the hall of the middle gate. The venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father saw the venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar. Seeing him, he said: 'Our only son, dear and beloved, was made to go forth by these shaveling recluses.' Then, at his own father's house, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla received neither a gift nor a refusal; instead, he received only abuse.
translations.mn82:18: At that time, a slave-woman of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's family wanted to throw away some stale porridge from the previous evening. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to that slave-woman: 'Sister, if that is to be thrown away, pour it here into my bowl.'
