Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's slave-woman, while pouring that stale porridge into the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's bowl, recognized the features of his hands, his feet, and his voice. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's slave-woman went to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother and said: 'My lady, you should know: the young master Raṭṭhapāla has arrived!' 'If you speak the truth, girl, I will make you a free woman.' Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother went to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father and said: 'Householder, you should know: they say the clansman Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.'
translations.mn82:19: At that time, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla was eating that stale porridge leaning against a certain wall. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father went to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla and said: 'Is it possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you are eating stale porridge? Should you not, dear Raṭṭhapāla, go to your own home?' 'Where, householder, is there a home for us who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We did go to your home, householder, but there we received neither a gift nor a refusal; instead, we received only abuse.' 'Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go to the house.' 'Enough, householder, my meal for today is finished.' 'Then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, accept an invitation for tomorrow's meal.' The venerable Raṭṭhapāla accepted by remaining silent.
translations.mn82:20: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, knowing that the venerable Raṭṭhapāla had accepted, went to his own house. Having gone there, he had a great heap of gold and bullion made and covered it with mats. Then he addressed the former wives of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'Come, daughters-in-law, dress yourselves in the ornaments in which you used to be dear and beloved to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla.'
translations.mn82:21: Then, at the end of that night, the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, having had fine food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own house, announced the time to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.'
translations.mn82:22: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, went to his father's house and sat down on the prepared seat. Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father had that heap of gold and bullion uncovered and said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your mother's wealth, this other is your father's, and this other is your grandfather's. It is possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, both to enjoy wealth and to do meritorious deeds. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth and do meritorious deeds.' 'Householder, if you would follow my word, you would have this heap of gold and bullion loaded onto carts, hauled away, and sunk in the middle of the river Ganges. Why is that? Because, householder, it will be for you a source of sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.'
translations.mn82:23: Then the former wives of the venerable Raṭṭhapāla each took him by the feet and said to him: 'What are they like, young master, those celestial nymphs for whose sake you lead the spiritual life?' 'Sisters, we do not lead the spiritual life for the sake of celestial nymphs.' Thinking, 'The young master Raṭṭhapāla addresses us as "sisters"!', they fainted and fell right there.
translations.mn82:24: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his father: 'Householder, if there is food to be given, give it; do not harass us.' 'Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.' Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father served and satisfied the venerable Raṭṭhapāla with his own hands with fine hard and soft food. When the venerable Raṭṭhapāla had finished eating and had removed his hand from the bowl, he stood and recited these verses:
translations.mn82:26: Then the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having recited these verses while standing, went to King Koravya’s Migacīra park; having arrived, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Koravya addressed his gamekeeper: 'My friend gamekeeper, tidy up the Migacīra park; we are going to see the beautiful grounds.' 'Yes, your majesty,' the gamekeeper replied to King Koravya. While tidying the Migacīra park, he saw the venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Seeing him, he went to King Koravya and said: 'Your majesty, the Migacīra park is tidied. But the clansman named Raṭṭhapāla is there—the son of the leading family in this very Thullakoṭṭhika, whom you have often praised—he is sitting at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding.' 'In that case, my friend gamekeeper, enough of the park for today. We shall now go to pay respects to that Master Raṭṭhapāla.'
translations.mn82:28: Then King Koravya, saying, 'Distribute all the hard and soft food that was prepared there,' had the finest carriages harnessed. He mounted a fine carriage and, accompanied by other fine carriages, drove out from Thullakoṭṭhika in great royal state to see the venerable Raṭṭhapāla. He went by carriage as far as the ground allowed, then dismounted and approached the venerable Raṭṭhapāla on foot with a great following. He exchanged greetings with the venerable Raṭṭhapāla, and after the exchange of friendly and courteous talk, he stood to one side. Standing there, King Koravya said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'Let Master Raṭṭhapāla sit here on the elephant rug.' 'Enough, great king, you sit; I am sitting on my own seat.' King Koravya sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, King Koravya said to the venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: 'Master Raṭṭhapāla, there are these four kinds of loss, because of which some people here shave off their hair and beard, put on yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. What four? Loss through old age, loss through sickness, loss of wealth, and loss of relatives.'
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika went to the Blessed One. On arrival, some bowed to the Blessed One and sat to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, after the exchange of friendly and courteous talk, sat to one side; some held up their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat to one side; some announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One and sat to one side; some sat to one side in silence. When they were seated, the Blessed One instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: 'These, Master Raṭṭhapāla, are the four kinds of loss because of which some people here shave off their hair and beard, put on yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. But Master Raṭṭhapāla has none of these. What has Master Raṭṭhapāla known or seen or heard that he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness?'
translations.mn82:35: 'Great king, there are four Dhamma summaries taught by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, which I, having known and seen and heard, went forth from the home life into homelessness. What four?'
translations.mn82:4: Now at that time a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the leading family in that same Thullakoṭṭhika, was sitting in that assembly. Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla thought: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the spiritual life that is entirely complete, entirely pure, and polished like a conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on yellow robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?'
translations.mn82:6: Then, after the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita had left, the young nobleman Raṭṭhapāla went to the Blessed One, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life that is entirely complete, entirely pure, and polished like a conch shell. I wish, venerable sir, to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. May I receive the going forth in the Blessed One's presence, may I receive the higher ordination. May the Blessed One let me go forth.' 'But Raṭṭhapāla, have you been permitted by your parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness?' 'No, venerable sir, I have not been permitted by my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness.' 'Raṭṭhapāla, Tathāgatas do not let a son go forth without the permission of his parents.' 'Venerable sir, I will act in such a way that my parents will permit me to go forth from the home life into homelessness.'
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Opāsāda. There the Blessed One stayed at Opāsāda in the Gods' Grove, the Sal-tree Grove to the north of Opāsāda.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When the polite and courteous talk was finished, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: Now at that time the Blessed One was sitting and exchanging some polite talk with some very old brahmins. Also at that time, a young brahmin student named Kāpaṭika was sitting in that assembly—young, shaven-headed, sixteen years old, a master of the three Vedas with their vocabularies, rituals, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; a philologist, a grammarian, and fully proficient in natural philosophy and the marks of a Great Man. He kept breaking into the conversation while the very old brahmins were talking with the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One rebuked the student Kāpaṭika: 'Let not the venerable Bhāradvāja break into the conversation while the very old brahmins are talking. Let the venerable Bhāradvāja wait until the end of the talk.' When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to the Blessed One: 'Let not Master Gotama rebuke the student Kāpaṭika. The student Kāpaṭika is a gentleman, he is very learned, he is wise, he is a good speaker; he is capable of taking part in this discussion with Master Gotama.'
translations.mn95:2: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī was living in Opāsāda, a place teeming with life, with much grass, wood, and water, and with much grain, a royal property given to him by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal grant, a divine gift.
translations.mn95:20: When, on examining him, he sees that he is pure of states based on delusion, then he places faith in him. Born of faith, he visits him; visiting him, he pays respect; paying respect, he lends an ear; lending an ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he remembers it; he examines the meaning of the teachings he has remembered; while examining the meaning, he comes to an agreement through pondering the teachings; when there is agreement through pondering the teachings, desire arises; when desire has arisen, he applies effort; having applied effort, he scrutinizes; having scrutinized, he strives; being resolute, he realizes the ultimate truth with the body and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom. To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is the discovery of truth; to this extent one discovers truth, and to this extent we describe the discovery of truth. But it is not yet the arrival at truth."
translations.mn95:33: “But Master Gotama, what state is most helpful for visiting?” “We ask Master Gotama about the state most helpful for visiting.” “Faith, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for visiting. If faith did not arise, one would not visit. But because faith arises, one visits. Therefore, faith is most helpful for visiting.”
translations.mn95:5: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī had gone to his upper terrace for his siesta. The brahmin Caṅkī saw the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in large groups and heading north toward the Gods' Grove, the Sal-tree Grove. Seeing this, he addressed his steward: 'My good steward, why are the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in large groups and heading north toward the Gods' Grove, the Sal-tree Grove?'
translations.mn9:11: “And what, friends, is nutriment, what is the origin of nutriment, what is the cessation of nutriment, what is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? There are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth. Which four? Physical food, whether coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; and consciousness is the fourth. With the arising of craving, there is the arising of nutriment. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of nutriment. This very noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.”
translations.mn9:12: “When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands nutriment, thus understands the origin of nutriment, thus understands the cessation of nutriment, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, he entirely abandons the underlying tendency to greed, he removes the underlying tendency to aversion, he uproots the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am,’ he abandons ignorance and gives rise to true knowledge, and makes an end of suffering in this very life. To this extent too, friends, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
translations.mn9:15: And what, friends, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair are suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wishes for is suffering—in brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering. This, friends, is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friends, is the origin of suffering? It is this craving that leads to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, friends, is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friends, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation, the giving up, relinquishing, letting go, and rejecting of that same craving. This, friends, is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friends, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view ...pe... right immersion. This, friends, is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: “‘Right view, right view,’ it is said, friends. To what extent, friends, is a noble disciple one of right view, whose view is upright, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to this true Dhamma?” “Friends, we would come from far away to the presence of the venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the venerable Sāriputta himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the venerable Sāriputta, the mendicants will remember it.” “Then, friends, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those mendicants replied to the venerable Sāriputta. The venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn9:20: “Good, friend.” Then those mendicants, having delighted and rejoiced in the venerable Sāriputta’s words, asked the venerable Sāriputta a further question: “But, friends, might there be another way in which a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to this true Dhamma?”
translations.mn9:3: “When, friends, a noble disciple understands the unskillful and understands the root of the unskillful, understands the skillful and understands the root of the skillful—to that extent, friends, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:4: And what, friends, is the unskillful, what is the root of the unskillful, what is the skillful, what is the root of the skillful? Killing living beings is unskillful, taking what is not given is unskillful, sexual misconduct is unskillful, lying is unskillful, divisive speech is unskillful, harsh speech is unskillful, idle chatter is unskillful, covetousness is unskillful, ill will is unskillful, wrong view is unskillful—this, friends, is called the unskillful.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friends, is the root of the unskillful? Greed is a root of the unskillful, hate is a root of the unskillful, delusion is a root of the unskillful—this, friends, is called the root of the unskillful.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friends, is the root of the skillful? Non-greed is a root of the skillful, non-hate is a root of the skillful, non-delusion is a root of the skillful—this, friends, is called the root of the skillful.
translations.mn9:70: And what, friends, is a defilement, what is the origin of defilement, what is the cessation of defilement, what is the way leading to the cessation of defilement? There are these three defilements: the defilement of sensual pleasure, the defilement of existence, and the defilement of ignorance. With the origin of ignorance comes the origin of defilement; with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of defilement. This Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of defilement, that is: right view ...pe... right immersion.
translations.mn9:8: When, friends, a noble disciple has thus understood the unskillful, thus understood the root of the unskillful, thus understood the skillful, and thus understood the root of the skillful, having entirely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, having removed the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am,’ having abandoned ignorance and given rise to knowledge, they make an end of suffering in this very life—to that extent too, friends, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is upright, who has experiential confidence in the teaching, and has come to this true Dhamma.”
translations.sn1.10:2: “For those living in the forest, peaceful, living the spiritual life; eating only one meal a day, why is their complexion so clear?”
translations.sn1.10:3: “They do not sorrow over the past, nor do they long for the future; they sustain themselves with the present, therefore their complexion is clear.
translations.sn1.17:1: “The spiritual life is difficult to do and difficult to endure, especially for the unskilled; many are the obstacles there, where the fool founders.”
translations.sn1.17:2: “How many days could one live the spiritual life if one does not restrain the mind? At every step one would founder, under the sway of one's intentions.
translations.sn1.17:3: Like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs into its own shell, a mendicant should withdraw the mind's thoughts; independent, not harming others, fully extinguished, one should not find fault with anyone.”
translations.sn1.18:1: “Is there any person in the world restrained by shame, who avoids reproach as a fine horse avoids the whip?”
translations.sn1.18:2: “Those restrained by shame are few, who live always mindful; having reached the end of suffering, they walk evenly over the uneven.”
translations.sn1.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, when the night was fading, a certain deity, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Buddha; having approached and paid homage to the Buddha, she stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Buddha: “How, dear sir, did you cross the flood?” “By not halting, friend, and by not straining, I crossed the flood.” “But how exactly, dear sir, did you cross the flood by not halting and not straining?” “When I halted, friend, then I sank; when I strained, friend, then I was swept away. That is how, friend, by not halting and not straining, I crossed the flood.”
translations.sn1.1:2: “After a long time I see a brahmin who is fully extinguished; who, neither halting nor straining, has crossed the attachment to the world.”
translations.sn1.1:3: This is what that deity said. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, thinking “The Teacher has approved of me,” paid homage to the Buddha, circled him right-wise, and vanished right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Tapoda Park. Then the venerable Samiddhi, having risen at the crack of dawn, went to the Tapoda River to bathe his limbs. Having bathed his limbs and come out of the water, he stood in a single robe drying his limbs. Then a certain deity, in the far extreme of the night, with a magnificent radiance that lit up the entire Tapoda, approached the venerable Samiddhi. Standing in the air, she addressed the venerable Samiddhi in verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: “You beg without having eaten, monk; you do not beg after having eaten. Having eaten, monk, then beg; don't let the time pass you by.”
translations.sn1.20:20: “Beings who perceive what can be expressed, established upon the expressible; not fully understanding the expressible, they come under the yoke of Death.
translations.sn1.20:21: But having fully understood the expressible, one does not conceive an expresser; for that does not exist for him, by which one might describe him. If you understand, spirit, then speak.”
translations.sn1.20:22: “I do not, sir, understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha has said in brief. It would be good, sir, if the Buddha would speak so that I might understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha has said in brief.”
translations.sn1.20:23: “One who thinks ‘I am equal, better, or worse’ would for that reason engage in disputes. But one who is unshaken in the three modes of conceit does not have the thought ‘I am equal or better.’ If you understand, spirit, then speak.”
translations.sn1.20:25: “He has abandoned calculations and reached no measurement; he has cut off craving here for name and form. Him, with knots cut, free from distress and desire, they cannot find though they search—gods and humans, here or beyond, in the heavens or in any dwelling place.”
translations.sn1.20:3: “I do not know the time; the time is hidden and not seen. Therefore I beg without having eaten, lest the time pass me by.”
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity, standing on the ground, said to the venerable Samiddhi: “You are young, monk, a recently gone-forth youth with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not having played with sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures, monk; do not abandon what is visible here and now to chase after what is subject to time.”
translations.sn1.20:5: “I am not, friend, abandoning what is visible here and now to chase after what is subject to time. I am abandoning what is subject to time to chase after what is visible here and now. For sensual pleasures, friend, are said by the Buddha to be subject to time, with much suffering and much despair; the danger in them is great. But this Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally known by the wise.”
translations.sn1.20:6: “And how, monk, are sensual pleasures said by the Buddha to be subject to time, with much suffering and much despair, with great danger? And how is this Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally known by the wise?”
translations.sn1.20:7: “I am new, friend, not long gone forth, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline. I am not able to explain it in detail. But the Buddha, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is staying near Rājagaha in the Tapoda Park. Go to the Buddha and ask him about this matter. As the Buddha explains it to you, so you should remember it.”
translations.sn1.20:8: “It is not easy for us, monk, to approach the Buddha, as he is surrounded by other powerful deities. If you, monk, would approach the Buddha and ask him about this matter, we too would come to hear the Dhamma.” “Yes, friend,” the venerable Samiddhi replied to the deity. He went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Samiddhi said to the Buddha:
translations.sn1.21:2: “As if struck by a sword, or as if his head were on fire; a monk should wander mindful for the abandoning of sensual desire.”
translations.sn1.21:3: “As if struck by a sword, or as if his head were on fire; a monk should wander mindful for the abandoning of identity view.”
translations.sn1.25:1: “A monk who is an Arahant, who has finished the task, with taints destroyed and wearing his last body; might he say, ‘I speak,’ or might he say, ‘They speak to me’?”
translations.sn1.25:2: “A monk who is an Arahant, who has finished the task, with taints destroyed and wearing his last body; he might say ‘I speak,’ and he might say ‘They speak to me.’ Skillful, knowing the world’s parlance, he would use it merely as a common expression.”
translations.sn1.25:3: “A monk who is an Arahant, who has finished the task, with taints destroyed and wearing his last body; would such a monk say ‘I speak’ or ‘They speak to me’ because he has succumbed to conceit?”
translations.sn1.25:4: “For one who has abandoned conceit, there are no ties; all his ties of conceit are vanished. That wise one, having transcended what is conceived, might still say ‘I speak.’
translations.sn1.25:5: He might also say ‘They speak to me.’ Skillful, knowing the world’s parlance, he would use it merely as a common expression.”
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain deity, in the far extreme of the night, with a magnificent radiance that lit up the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Buddha. Having approached and bowed, she stood to one side. Standing there, she said to the Buddha:
translations.sn1.2:5: “By the total ending of delight and existence, by the destruction of perception and consciousness, by the cessation and stilling of feelings; thus, friend, do I know the release, the liberation, the seclusion for beings.”
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then many deities of the Satullapa host, in the far extreme of the night, with a magnificent radiance that lit up the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Buddha. Having approached and bowed, they stood to one side. Standing there, one deity recited this verse in the presence of the Buddha:
translations.sn1.36:2: “Faith is a person’s partner, if lack of faith does not remain; then fame and reputation come to them, and they go to heaven when they leave the body behind.”
translations.sn1.36:4: “One should give up anger, one should abandon conceit, one should transcend every fetter. Suffering does not befall one who does not cling to name and form, who is possessionless.”
translations.sn1.36:5: “Fools, people of little intelligence, indulge in negligence; but the wise person guards diligence as their best treasure.
translations.sn1.36:6: Do not indulge in negligence, nor in intimacy with sensual delight; for the diligent one, meditating, attains supreme happiness.”
translations.sn1.38:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi Deer Park. Now at that time the Blessed One’s foot had been cut by a stone splinter. Severe pains affected the Blessed One—bodily feelings that were painful, sharp, harsh, piercing, disagreeable, and unpleasant; but the Blessed One endured them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending.
translations.sn1.38:10: Overcome by craving, bound by vows and ascetic habits, practicing harsh austerities for a hundred years; their minds are not rightly liberated, they are of inferior nature and do not reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.38:11: There is no taming here for one who loves conceit, nor is there sagehood for one who is not concentrated; living alone in the forest while negligent, one would not cross to the far shore of Death’s realm.
translations.sn1.38:12: Having abandoned conceit, with a well-concentrated self, with a good mind, everywhere completely released; living alone in the forest, diligent, one would cross to the far shore of Death’s realm.
translations.sn1.38:2: Then seven hundred deities of the Satullapa host, when the night was far spent, with magnificent beauty illuminating the whole of Maddakucchi, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity uttered this inspired exclamation in the presence of the Blessed One: “A bull of a man indeed, sir, is the ascetic Gotama! And like a bull, when painful bodily feelings have arisen—sharp, harsh, piercing, disagreeable, and unpleasant—he endures them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed.”
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity uttered this inspired exclamation in the presence of the Blessed One: “A lion indeed, sir, is the ascetic Gotama! And like a lion, when painful bodily feelings have arisen—sharp, harsh, piercing, disagreeable, and unpleasant—he endures them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed.”
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity uttered this inspired exclamation in the presence of the Blessed One: “See the well-developed concentration and the well-liberated mind, neither leaning forward nor leaning back, and not restrained by forceful suppression. If anyone should think they could surpass such a bull of a man, a lion of a man, a thoroughbred of a man, a leader of men, a burden-bearer of a man, a tamed man—what is that but lack of vision?”
translations.sn1.38:9: “Though practicing for a hundred years with the five Vedas, as a brahmin ascetic; if their mind is not rightly liberated, they are of inferior nature and do not reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.41:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then a certain deity, when the night was far spent, with magnificent beauty illuminating the whole of Jeta's Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity spoke these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.41:4: What is given brings happiness as its fruit, but what is not given is not like that; thieves take it away, kings seize it, fire burns it and it is lost.
translations.sn1.41:5: In the end, one leaves behind the body along with one's possessions; knowing this, the wise person should enjoy and should give; having given and enjoyed according to their means, blameless, they go to a heavenly place.”
translations.sn1.42:1: “Giving what does one give strength? Giving what does one give beauty? Giving what does one give happiness? Giving what does one give sight? And who is the giver of everything? Tell me this when asked.”
translations.sn1.42:2: “Giving food one gives strength; giving clothing one gives beauty; giving a vehicle one gives happiness; giving a lamp one gives sight.
translations.sn1.42:3: And the one who gives a dwelling is the giver of everything; but the one who teaches the Dhamma is the giver of the Deathless.”
translations.sn1.51:1: “What is good until old age? What is good when well-established? What is the treasure of humans? What is hard for thieves to take away?”
translations.sn1.51:2: “Virtue is good until old age; faith is good when well-established; wisdom is the treasure of humans; merit is hard for thieves to take away.”
translations.sn1.55:1: “What gives birth to a person? What of theirs runs about? What enters into wandering? What is their great fear?”
translations.sn1.55:2: “Craving gives birth to a person; their mind runs about; a being enters into wandering; suffering is their great fear.”
translations.sn1.56:1: “What gives birth to a person? What of theirs runs about? What enters into wandering? From what is one not released?”
translations.sn1.56:2: “Craving gives birth to a person; their mind runs about; a being enters into wandering; from suffering one is not released.”
translations.sn1.57:1: “What gives birth to a person? What of theirs runs about? What enters into wandering? What is their destination?”
translations.sn1.57:2: “Craving gives birth to a person; their mind runs about; a being enters into wandering; kamma is their destination.”
translations.sn1.59:1: “What is a person’s companion? What is it that instructs them? In what being delighted is a mortal released from all suffering?”
translations.sn1.59:2: “Faith is a person’s companion; wisdom is what instructs them; being delighted in Nibbāna, a mortal is released from all suffering.”
translations.sn1.62:1: “By what is the world led? By what is it dragged around? Under the power of what one thing have all gone?”
translations.sn1.62:2: “By the mind the world is led; by the mind it is dragged around; under the power of the mind as one thing have all gone.”
translations.sn1.63:2: “By craving the world is led; by craving it is dragged around; under the power of craving as one thing have all gone.”
translations.sn1.64:1: “By what is the world fettered? What is its wandering? By the abandoning of what is it called Nibbāna?”
translations.sn1.64:2: “By delight the world is fettered; thought is its wandering; by the abandoning of craving it is called Nibbāna.”
translations.sn1.65:1: “By what is the world bound? What is its wandering? By the abandoning of what does one cut all bonds?”
translations.sn1.65:2: “By delight the world is bound; thought is its wandering; by the abandoning of craving one cuts all bonds.”
translations.sn1.69:1: “By what is the world bound? By the removal of what is it freed? By the abandoning of what does one cut all bonds?”
translations.sn1.69:2: “By desire the world is bound; by the removal of desire it is freed; by the abandoning of desire one cuts all bonds.”
translations.sn1.71:2: “Having cut what does one sleep soundly? Having cut what does one not sorrow? Of what one thing do you approve the killing, Gotama?”
translations.sn1.71:3: “Having cut anger one sleeps soundly; having cut anger one does not sorrow; of anger with its poisoned root and honeyed tip, O deity, the Noble Ones praise the killing, for having cut it one does not sorrow.”
translations.sn1.73:1: “What is a person’s best wealth here? What, when well-practiced, brings happiness? What is indeed the sweetest of tastes? Living in what way do they say one's life is best?”
translations.sn1.73:2: “Faith is a person’s best treasure here; the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness; truth is indeed the sweetest of tastes; the life of one living by wisdom is called the best.”
translations.sn1.7:2: “Those for whom the teachings are not understood are led away by the arguments of others; they are asleep and do not wake up; it is time for them to awaken.”
translations.sn1.7:3: “Those for whom the teachings are well understood are not led away by the arguments of others; they are fully awakened, with right knowledge, they walk evenly in an uneven world.”
translations.sn1.8:2: “Those for whom the teachings are completely forgotten are led away by the arguments of others; they are asleep and do not wake up; it is time for them to awaken.”
translations.sn1.8:3: “Those for whom the teachings are not forgotten are not led away by the arguments of others; they are fully awakened, with right knowledge, they walk evenly in an uneven world.”
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: “Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the gods, addressed the Tāvatiṁsa gods: ‘Friends, do not be annoyed with this son of the gods. Friends, this son of the gods, when he was previously a human being, undertook faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata. Having undertaken faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata, with the breaking up of the body, after death, he has been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the Tāvatiṁsa gods. He outshines the other gods in both beauty and glory.’ Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the gods, persuading the Tāvatiṁsa gods, at that time recited these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6: ‘Therefore, the wise person should pursue faith and virtue, confidence and vision of the Dhamma, remembering the Buddhas’ teaching.’”
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is a delightful place?”
translations.sn11.15:2: “Park-shrines and forest-shrines, well-constructed lotus ponds; these are not worth a sixteenth part of a delightful human being.”
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove. There… he said this: “Bhikkhus, once in the past, a certain ugly, stunted yakkha sat down on the throne of Sakka, lord of the gods. Thereupon, bhikkhus, the Tāvatiṁsa gods were annoyed, complained, and became indignant: ‘It is wonderful, indeed! It is amazing, indeed! This ugly, stunted yakkha is sitting on the throne of Sakka, lord of the gods!’ But, bhikkhus, the more the Tāvatiṁsa gods were annoyed, complained, and became indignant, the more handsome, more beautiful, and more pleasing that yakkha became.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the gods, approached that anger-eating yakkha; having approached, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and extending his hands in reverential salutation toward that anger-eating yakkha, he announced his name three times: ‘I am Sakka, friend, the lord of the gods! I am Sakka, friend, the lord of the gods!’ But, bhikkhus, the more Sakka, lord of the gods, announced his name, the more ugly and stunted that yakkha became. Having become more ugly and stunted, he vanished right there. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the gods, sat down on his own throne and, persuading the Tāvatiṁsa gods, at that time recited these verses:
translations.sn11.22:4: ‘I am not one whose mind is easily struck, nor am I easily led away by a whirlpool; I do not get angry for long, anger does not persist in me.
translations.sn11.22:5: When angry I do not speak harsh words, nor do I proclaim things that are not Dhamma; I restrain myself, seeing my own benefit.’”
translations.sn11.24:2: “Bhikkhus, there are these two fools. One who does not see a mistake as a mistake, and one who does not rightfully accept the confession of one who is disclosing a mistake—these, bhikkhus, are the two fools. There are these two wise people. One who sees a mistake as a mistake, and one who rightfully accepts the confession of one who is disclosing a mistake—these, bhikkhus, are the two wise people.
translations.sn11.24:3: Once in the past, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the gods, persuading the Tāvatiṁsa gods in the Sudhamma assembly hall, at that time recited this verse:
translations.sn11.24:4: ‘Let your anger come under your control, and do not let your friendship decay; do not blame what is not blameworthy, and do not speak malicious words; for anger crushes the evil person like a mountain.’”
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you should not remember me, then you should remember the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.’ For, bhikkhus, when you remember the Dhamma, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation there may be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you should not remember the Dhamma, then you should remember the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing properly; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ For, bhikkhus, when you remember the Saṅgha, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation there may be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion; he is fearless, not subject to trepidation, not terrified, not one who flees.’ This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:
translations.sn11.3:13: “In the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, O bhikkhus, remember the Fully Enlightened One; no fear will come to you.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you do not remember the Buddha, the eldest in the world, the bull among men, then remember the Dhamma, the well-expounded leading out.
translations.sn11.3:15: If you do not remember the Dhamma, the well-expounded leading out, then remember the Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: For those thus remembering the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, O bhikkhus, fear, trepidation, or horripilation will not occur.”
translations.sn11.3:2: “In the past, bhikkhus, there was a battle between the gods and the asuras. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, addressed the Tāvatiṁsa gods:
translations.sn11.3:3: ‘If, dear sirs, fear, trepidation, or hair-standing-on-end should arise in the gods who have gone to battle, at that time you should look up at the crest of my banner. For when you look up at the crest of my banner, whatever fear, trepidation, or hair-standing-on-end there may be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you do not look up at the crest of my banner, then you should look up at the crest of the banner of Pajāpati, the king of gods. For when you look up at the crest of the banner of Pajāpati, the king of gods, whatever fear, trepidation, or hair-standing-on-end there may be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:8: Why is that? Because Sakka, lord of the gods, is not free from lust, not free from hatred, not free from delusion; he is fearful, trembling, terrified, and flees.
translations.sn11.3:9: But I say this to you, bhikkhus: ‘If, bhikkhus, fear, trepidation, or hair-standing-on-end should arise in you when you have gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, at that time you should recollect me: “The Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.” For when you recollect me, bhikkhus, whatever fear, trepidation, or hair-standing-on-end there may be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:12: He practices for the welfare of both, his own and the other’s; when he knows the other is angry, he is mindful and becomes calm.
translations.sn11.5:14: When these verses were spoken by Sakka, lord of the gods, the gods were pleased, but the asuras were silent. Then the assemblies of the gods and the asuras said this: ‘The verses spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, involve the rod and the sword; thus there is quarreling, strife, and conflict. The verses spoken by Sakka, lord of the gods, do not involve the rod or the sword; thus there is no quarreling, no strife, and no conflict. Victory belongs to Sakka, lord of the gods, because of his well-spoken words.’ Thus, bhikkhus, victory belonged to Sakka, lord of the gods, because of his well-spoken words.”
translations.sn11.5:2: ‘Fools would break out even more if there were no one to restrain them; therefore, the wise should restrain the fool with a heavy rod.’
translations.sn11.5:3: When this verse was spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, the asuras were pleased, but the gods were silent. Then Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, said to Sakka, lord of the gods: ‘Speak a verse, lord of the gods.’ When this was said, Sakka, lord of the gods, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: ‘I think that this alone is the restraint of the fool: when one knows the other is angry, one is mindful and becomes calm.’
translations.sn11.5:5: When this verse was spoken by Sakka, lord of the gods, the gods were pleased, but the asuras were silent. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, said to Vepacitti, lord of the asuras: ‘Speak a verse, Vepacitti.’ When this was said, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: ‘I see this very fault in patience, Vāsava: when the fool thinks of it, “He endures me out of fear”; the dull-witted one climbs all over you, like a cow over one who flees.’
translations.sn11.5:8: ‘Let him think what he likes, or not, that “He endures me out of fear”; of goals that culminate in one's own good, none is found better than patience.
translations.sn12.11:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park … “Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come into being or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth. Which four? Edible food, whether coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; and consciousness is the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come into being or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth.
translations.sn12.12:1: Staying at Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come into being or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth. Which four? Edible food, whether coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; and consciousness is the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings that have come into being or for the assistance of those seeking a new birth.”
translations.sn12.15:1: Staying at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Kaccānagotta said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘right view, right view.’ To what extent, venerable sir, is there right view?”
translations.sn12.15:2: “Kaccāna, this world mostly relies on a duality—on existence and non-existence. But for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no ‘non-existence’ in regard to the world. And for one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, there is no ‘existence’ in regard to the world. Kaccāna, this world is mostly bound by engagement, clinging, and inclination. But this one does not follow, cling to, or settle on that engagement and clinging, that mental standpoint, inclination, and underlying tendency: ‘my self.’ He has no doubt or perplexity that ‘it is only suffering that arises when arising, and suffering that ceases when ceasing’; his knowledge about this is independent of others. It is to this extent, Kaccāna, that there is right view.
translations.sn12.17:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: “We would like to ask Master Gotama about a certain point, if Master Gotama would grant us the opportunity for an answer to a question.” “It is not the right time for a question, Kassapa; we have entered among the houses.”
translations.sn12.17:5: “Kassapa, if one thinks, ‘The one who acts is the same one who experiences the result,’ then for one who has existed from the beginning, this amounts to the view that ‘suffering is self-created,’ which borders on eternalism. Kassapa, if one thinks, ‘One acts and another experiences the result,’ then for one stricken by feeling, this amounts to the view that ‘suffering is created by another,’ which borders on annihilationism. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as condition, choices; with choices as condition, consciousness … and so on. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of choices; with the cessation of choices, the cessation of consciousness … and so on. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, sir! Magnificent, sir! Just as if, sir, one were to upright what had been overturned … and so on … ‘those with eyes will see forms’; even so has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I receive the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, may I receive the full ordination.”
translations.sn12.17:7: “Kassapa, one who was formerly a member of another sect and desires the going forth and full ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline must reside on probation for four months. At the end of four months, the monks who are satisfied in heart give the going forth and the full ordination for the status of a monk. However, I have recognized a difference in individuals in this regard.”
translations.sn12.18:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: “Timbaruka, if one thinks, ‘The feeling is the same as the one who feels it,’ then for one who has existed from the beginning, I do not say that ‘pleasure and pain are self-created.’ Timbaruka, if one thinks, ‘The feeling is one thing, the one who feels it is another,’ then for one stricken by feeling, I do not say that ‘pleasure and pain are created by another.’ Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as condition, choices; with choices as condition, consciousness … and so on. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of choices; with the cessation of choices, the cessation of consciousness … and so on. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.19:1: At Sāvatthī. “Monks, for the fool who is hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has been produced. Thus there is this body and external name-and-form: so this is a dyad. Dependent on this dyad there is contact and the six sense bases, touched by which the fool experiences pleasure and pain through one or another of these.
translations.sn12.19:2: Monks, for the wise person who is hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has been produced. Thus there is this body and external name-and-form: so this is a dyad. Dependent on this dyad there is contact and the six sense bases, touched by which the wise person experiences pleasure and pain through one or another of these.
translations.sn12.19:3: Therein, monks, what is the distinction, what is the specific feature, what is the difference between the wise person and the fool?” “Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”
translations.sn12.19:5: “Monks, that ignorance by which the fool is obstructed and that craving by which they are fettered, through which this body has been produced—that ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, and that craving is not exhausted. Why is that? Because, monks, the fool has not lived the spiritual life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool goes to another body. Being one who goes to another body, they are not released from birth, aging and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. They are not released from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.23:5: And what, monks, is the proximate cause for craving? ‘Feeling,’ it should be said … and so on … ‘Contact,’ it should be said … ‘The six sense bases,’ it should be said … ‘Name-and-form,’ it should be said … ‘Consciousness,’ it should be said … ‘Choices,’ it should be said. Monks, I say that choices have a proximate cause, they do not lack a proximate cause. And what, monks, is the proximate cause for choices? ‘Ignorance,’ it should be said.
translations.sn12.23:6: Thus, monks, ignorance is the proximate cause for choices; choices are the proximate cause for consciousness; consciousness is the proximate cause for name-and-form; name-and-form is the proximate cause for the six sense bases; the six sense bases are the proximate cause for contact; contact is the proximate cause for feeling; feeling is the proximate cause for craving; craving is the proximate cause for grasping; grasping is the proximate cause for existence; existence is the proximate cause for birth; birth is the proximate cause for suffering; suffering is the proximate cause for faith; faith is the proximate cause for joy; joy is the proximate cause for rapture; rapture is the proximate cause for tranquility; tranquility is the proximate cause for happiness; happiness is the proximate cause for immersion; immersion is the proximate cause for knowledge and vision of things as they really are; knowledge and vision of things as they really are is the proximate cause for disillusionment; disillusionment is the proximate cause for dispassion; dispassion is the proximate cause for liberation; liberation is the proximate cause for the knowledge of destruction.
translations.sn12.23:7: Just as, monks, when rain falls in thick drops on a mountain top, the water flowing down according to the slope fills the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, rifts, and gullies are full, they fill the small ponds. When the small ponds are full, they fill the large lakes. When the large lakes are full, they fill the small rivers. When the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers. When the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the venerable Bhūmija, having emerged from seclusion in the late afternoon, approached the venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Sāriputta. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Bhūmija said to the venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: Ānanda, when there is the body, pleasure and pain arise internally due to bodily intention. When there is speech, pleasure and pain arise internally due to verbal intention. When there is the mind, pleasure and pain arise internally due to mental intention, with ignorance as a condition.
translations.sn12.25:11: Either by oneself, Ānanda, one instigates that bodily formation conditioned by which that internal pleasure and pain arises. Or others, Ānanda, instigate that bodily formation conditioned by which that internal pleasure and pain arises. Either deliberately, Ānanda, one instigates that bodily formation conditioned by which that internal pleasure and pain arises. Or undeliberately, Ānanda, one instigates that bodily formation conditioned by which that internal pleasure and pain arises.
translations.sn12.25:2: “Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as self-made. There are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as made by another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as both self-made and made by another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as neither self-made nor made by another, but as arising by chance. Here, friend Sāriputta, what does the Blessed One say, what does he teach? And how should we explain so that we speak what the Blessed One says, do not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false, explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no fellow practitioner would have cause to legitimately criticize our statement?”
translations.sn12.25:3: “Friend, the Blessed One has said that pleasure and pain are dependently originated. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One speaking thus would be speaking what the Blessed One says, would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false, would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no fellow practitioner would have cause to legitimately criticize their statement.
translations.sn12.25:4: There, friend, regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as self-made, that too is conditioned by contact. Regarding those who ... regarding those who ... regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as neither self-made nor made by another, but as arising by chance, that too is conditioned by contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: There, friend, regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as self-made, it is impossible that they will experience it apart from contact. Regarding those who ... regarding those who ... regarding those ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who describe pleasure and pain as neither self-made nor made by another, but as arising by chance, it is impossible that they will experience it apart from contact.”
translations.sn12.25:6: The venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the venerable Sāriputta and the venerable Bhūmija. Then the venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the venerable Sāriputta and the venerable Bhūmija.
translations.sn12.25:7: “Good, good, Ānanda! Sāriputta has explained it just as a Sāriputta should rightly explain. Ānanda, I have said that pleasure and pain are dependently originated. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One speaking thus would be speaking what I say, would not misrepresent me with what is false, would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no fellow practitioner would have cause to legitimately criticize their statement.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, bhikkhus, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, intention, contact, attention—this is called name. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—this is called form. Thus this is name and this is form. This, bhikkhus, is called name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness, bhikkhus: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This, bhikkhus, is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, bhikkhus, are formations? There are these three formations, bhikkhus: bodily formation, verbal formation, mental formation. These, bhikkhus, are called formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, bhikkhus, is ignorance? That which is non-knowledge regarding suffering, non-knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, non-knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, non-knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, bhikkhus, is existence? There are these three existences, bhikkhus: sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence. This, bhikkhus, is called existence.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, bhikkhus, is clinging? There are these four kinds of clinging, bhikkhus: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, clinging to a doctrine of self. This, bhikkhus, is called clinging.
translations.sn12.31:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, this was said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.31:2: ‘Those who have fully understood the Dhamma, and the many here who are in training; when asked, dear sir, tell me their way of life, for you are wise.’
translations.sn12.31:3: Sāriputta, how should the meaning of this brief statement be understood in detail?” When this was said, the venerable Sāriputta remained silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: “Sāriputta, do you see that ‘this has come to be’?” “Venerable sir, one sees that ‘this has come to be’ as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen that ‘this has come to be’ as it really is with correct wisdom, one is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be. One sees that ‘it has originated from that nutriment’ as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen that ‘it has originated from that nutriment’ as it really is with correct wisdom, one is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding its origination from nutriment. One sees that ‘with the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation’ as it really is with correct wisdom. Having seen that ‘with the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation’ as it really is with correct wisdom, one is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation. In this way, venerable sir, one is a trainee.”
translations.sn12.31:8: “And how, bhante, is one a person who has understood the Dhamma? Here, bhante, one sees with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This has come to be.’ Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This has come to be,’ one is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, fading away, and cessation regarding what has come to be, and is liberated through non-clinging. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: ‘It has originated from that nutriment.’ Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘It has originated from that nutriment,’ one is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, fading away, and cessation regarding the origination from nutriment, and is liberated through non-clinging. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation.’ Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation,’ one is practicing for the sake of disenchantment, fading away, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation, and is liberated through non-clinging. It is in this way, bhante, that one is a person who has understood the Dhamma. This, bhante, is what was said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Ajita:”
translations.sn12.35:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, choices; with choices as condition, consciousness … and so there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.” When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But bhante, what is old age and death, and for whom is this old age and death?” “The question is not valid,” the Blessed One said. “Bhikkhu, if one should say, ‘What is old age and death, and for whom is this old age and death?’ or if one should say, ‘Old age and death is one thing, and this old age and death belongs to another,’ both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. Bhikkhu, if there is the view ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life. Bhikkhu, if there is the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body is another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With birth as condition, old age and death.’”
translations.sn12.35:2: “But bhante, what is birth, and for whom is this birth?” “The question is not valid,” the Blessed One said. “Bhikkhu, if one should say, ‘What is birth, and for whom is this birth?’ or if one should say, ‘Birth is one thing, and this birth belongs to another,’ both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. Bhikkhu, if there is the view ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life. Bhikkhu, if there is the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body is another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With existence as condition, birth.’”
translations.sn12.35:3: “But bhante, what is existence, and for whom is this existence?” “The question is not valid,” the Blessed One said. “Bhikkhu, if one should say, ‘What is existence, and for whom is this existence?’ or if one should say, ‘Existence is one thing, and this existence belongs to another,’ both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. Bhikkhu, if there is the view ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life; if there is the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body is another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With clinging as condition, existence’ … ‘with craving as condition, clinging’ … ‘with feeling as condition, craving’ … ‘with contact as condition, feeling’ … ‘with the six sense bases as condition, contact’ … ‘with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases’ … ‘with consciousness as condition, name-and-form’ … ‘with choices as condition, consciousness.’”
translations.sn12.35:4: “But bhante, what are choices, and for whom are these choices?” “The question is not valid,” the Blessed One said. “Bhikkhu, if one should say, ‘What are choices, and for whom are these choices?’ or if one should say, ‘Choices are one thing, and these choices belong to another,’ both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. Bhikkhu, if there is the view ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life; if there is the view ‘the soul is one thing and the body is another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, choices.’”
translations.sn12.35:5: “But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, bhikkhu, whatever distortions, maneuvers, and agitations there are—such as ‘What is old age and death, and for whom is this old age and death?’ or ‘Old age and death is one thing, and this old age and death belongs to another,’ or ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body is another’—all these are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and are no longer subject to future arising.
translations.sn12.35:7: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, bhikkhu, whatever distortions, maneuvers, and agitations there are… ‘What is existence’ … ‘What is clinging’ … ‘What is craving’ … ‘What is feeling’ … ‘What is contact’ … ‘What are the six sense bases’ … ‘What is name-and-form’ … ‘What is consciousness’ …
translations.sn12.38:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, what one intends, and what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards: this becomes an object for the standing of consciousness. When there is an object, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is supported and grows, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, future birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come to be. Such is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.38:2: If, bhikkhus, one does not intend and does not plan, but one still has a tendency towards something: this becomes an object for the standing of consciousness. When there is an object, there is a support for consciousness. When consciousness is supported and grows, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, future birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come to be. Such is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.44:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the origination and the passing away of the world. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: “And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:3: Dependent on the ear and sounds … dependent on the nose and odors … dependent on the tongue and tastes … dependent on the body and tactile objects … dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling … with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the passing away of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving comes cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence … such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the passing away of the world.”
translations.sn12.46:1: Staying at Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging friendly and polite greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that brahmin said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.46:2: “How is it, Master Gotama: is it the case that the one who acts is the same one who experiences the result?” “‘The one who acts is the same one who experiences,’ brahmin, this is one extreme.”
translations.sn12.46:3: “Then, Master Gotama, is it the case that one acts and another experiences the result?” “‘One acts and another experiences,’ brahmin, this is the second extreme. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations … such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.51:10: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached.
translations.sn12.51:11: When feeling a feeling limited to the body, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to the body.’ When feeling a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, after the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; only the bodily remains will be left.’
translations.sn12.51:12: Just as, bhikkhus, a man might remove a hot jar from a potter’s kiln and set it on level ground; the heat would subside right there and the shards would be left. Even so, bhikkhus, when feeling a feeling limited to the body, a bhikkhu understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to the body.’ When feeling a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, after the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; only the bodily remains will be left.’
translations.sn12.51:13: “What do you think, bhikkhus, would a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed generate a meritorious volitional formation, or a demeritorious volitional formation, or an imperturbable volitional formation?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.51:14: “When there are no volitional formations at all, with the cessation of volitional formations, would consciousness be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.51:2: “Bhikkhus, to what extent should a bhikkhu be investigating so that he would be investigating for the complete destruction of suffering?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.” “Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.51:3: “Here, bhikkhus, an investigating bhikkhu investigates: ‘This manifold, various kinds of suffering that arise in the world as aging and death; what is the source of this suffering, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its cause? When what exists does aging and death come to be? When what does not exist does aging and death not come to be?’ Investigating, he understands: ‘This manifold, various kinds of suffering that arise in the world as aging and death; this suffering has birth as its source, birth as its origin, birth as its birth, birth as its cause. When there is birth, aging and death come to be; when there is no birth, aging and death do not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:4: He understands aging and death, he understands the origin of aging and death, he understands the cessation of aging and death, and he understands the practice that is fit for the cessation of aging and death, and he is practicing accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma. This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is practicing for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of aging and death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Then, investigating further, he investigates: ‘And this birth, what is its source, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its cause? When what exists does birth come to be? When what does not exist does birth not come to be?’ Investigating, he understands: ‘Birth has existence as its source, existence as its origin, existence as its birth, existence as its cause. When there is existence, birth comes to be; when there is no existence, birth does not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:6: He understands birth, he understands the origin of birth, he understands the cessation of birth, and he understands the practice that is suitable for leading to the cessation of birth, and he is one who practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma. This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is practicing for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, investigating further, he investigates: 'Now what is the source of this existence? ... What is the source of this clinging? ... What is the source of this craving? ... feeling ... contact ... What is the source of these six sense bases? ... name-and-form ... consciousness ... What is the source of these choices, what is their origin, what is their birth, what is their cause? When what exists do choices come to be? When what does not exist do choices not come to be?' Investigating, he understands: 'Choices have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, ignorance as their cause. When ignorance exists, choices come to be; when ignorance does not exist, choices do not come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:8: He understands choices, he understands the origin of choices, he understands the cessation of choices, and he understands the practice that is suitable for leading to the cessation of choices, and he is one who practices accordingly, living in accordance with the Dhamma. This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is practicing for the complete destruction of suffering, for the cessation of choices.
translations.sn12.51:9: Bhikkhus, if a person immersed in ignorance constructs a meritorious choice, consciousness leads to merit. If he constructs a demeritorious choice, consciousness leads to demerit. If he constructs an imperturbable choice, consciousness leads to the imperturbable.
