But when a bhikkhu has abandoned ignorance and produced true knowledge, then, with the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, he does not construct a meritorious choice, he does not construct a demeritorious choice, he does not construct an imperturbable choice. Not constructing, not intending, he does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, he is not agitated; not being agitated, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'
translations.sn12.52:2: Suppose, bhikkhus, a great bonfire were burning with ten, twenty, thirty, or forty loads of wood. And a person would from time to time throw dry grass into it, throw dry cow dung into it, throw dry wood into it. Thus, bhikkhus, that great bonfire, with that as its fuel and that as its sustenance, would burn for a long, long time. In the same way, bhikkhus, for one who lives contemplating gratification in things that are prone to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging... such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.52:3: Bhikkhus, for one who lives contemplating the danger in things that are prone to clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for one who lives contemplating gratification in things that are prone to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence... such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:2: Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a great tree. All its roots going downwards and those going across bring up the sap. Thus, bhikkhus, that great tree, with that as its fuel and that as its sustenance, would stand for a long, long time. In the same way, bhikkhus, for one who lives contemplating gratification in things that are prone to clinging, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging... such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:3: Bhikkhus, for one who lives contemplating the danger in things that are prone to clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence... such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.61:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery... “Bhikkhus, an unlearned ordinary person might become disillusioned with this body made of the four great elements, might become dispassionate toward it, might be liberated from it. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the growth and decline of this body made of the four great elements is seen, its being taken up and laid down is seen. Therefore, an unlearned ordinary person might become disillusioned with it, might become dispassionate toward it, might be liberated from it.
translations.sn12.61:2: But that which is called 'mind,' 'mentality,' or 'consciousness,' the unlearned ordinary person is unable to become disillusioned with, unable to become dispassionate toward, unable to be liberated from. Why is that? Because for a long time, bhikkhus, that has been for the unlearned ordinary person something clung to, something possessed, something misapprehended as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' Therefore, an unlearned ordinary person is unable to become disillusioned with it, unable to become dispassionate toward it, unable to be liberated from it.
translations.sn12.61:3: It would be better, bhikkhus, for an unlearned ordinary person to take this body made of the four great elements as self, rather than the mind. Why is that? Because this body made of the four great elements is seen to stand for one year, for two years, for three years, for four years, for five years, for ten years, for twenty years, for thirty years, for forty years, for fifty years, for a hundred years, or even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: In this case, bhikkhus, a well-taught noble disciple attends carefully and properly to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases—that is, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness ... and so on ... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness ... and so on ... such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.62:3: In this case, bhikkhus, a well-taught noble disciple attends carefully and properly to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.' Dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, bhikkhus, a pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and subsides. Dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful, bhikkhus, a painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as painful, the corresponding feeling—the painful feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as painful—ceases and subsides. Dependent on a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, bhikkhus, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, bhikkhus, from the friction and collision of two fire-sticks heat is generated and fire is produced, but with the separation and detachment of those same two fire-sticks, the corresponding heat ceases and subsides; so too, bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and subsides ... and so on ... dependent on a contact to be experienced as painful ... dependent on a contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose dependent on that contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, bhikkhus? Would they eat that food for fun, or for intoxication, or for fattening, or for beautification?" "No, venerable sir." "Would they not eat that food, bhikkhus, only for the sake of crossing the desert?" "Yes, venerable sir." "In the same way, I say, should edible food be seen. When edible food is fully understood, lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood. When lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood, there is no fetter bound by which a noble disciple would come back again to this world.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, bhikkhus, should the food of contact be seen? Suppose, bhikkhus, a flayed cow were to stand leaning against a wall. The creatures living in the wall would bite her. If she stood leaning against a tree, the creatures living in the tree would bite her. If she stood in the water, the creatures living in the water would bite her. If she stood in the open air, the creatures living in the air would bite her. Whatever that flayed cow stood leaning against, the creatures living there would bite her. In the same way, I say, should the food of contact be seen. When the food of contact is fully understood, the three kinds of feeling are fully understood. When the three kinds of feeling are fully understood, I say that there is nothing further for the noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, bhikkhus, should the food of mental volition be seen? Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man's height, full of coals without flame or smoke. Then a man would come along, wanting to live, not wanting to die, desiring happiness and recoiling from pain. Two strong men would grab him by both arms and drag him toward the pit of glowing coals. Then, bhikkhus, the man's volition would be far away, his wish would be far away, his aspiration would be far away. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the man would think: 'I will fall into this pit of glowing coals, and because of that I will meet death or deadly suffering.' In the same way, I say, should the food of mental volition be seen. When the food of mental volition is fully understood, the three kinds of craving are fully understood. When the three kinds of craving are fully understood, I say that there is nothing further for the noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.64:2: If, bhikkhus, there is lust, delight, and craving for edible food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that is accompanied by sorrow, by anguish, and by despair.
translations.sn12.64:4: Suppose, bhikkhus, a dyer or a painter, with dye, lac, turmeric, indigo, or crimson, would create the figure of a woman or a man, complete in all its parts, on a well-polished board, a wall, or a strip of cloth. In the same way, bhikkhus, if there is lust, delight, and craving for solid food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of choices. Where there is the growth of choices, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that is accompanied by sorrow, anguish, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: If, bhikkhus, there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for solid food, consciousness is not established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of choices. Where there is no growth of choices, there is no production of renewed existence in the future. Where there is no production of renewed existence in the future, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, I say that is without sorrow, without anguish, and without despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a peaked house or a peaked hall with windows on the north, south, or east. When the sun rises and a ray enters through the window, where would it land? 'On the western wall, bhante.' If there were no western wall, where would it land? 'On the ground, bhante.' If there were no ground, where would it land? 'On the water, bhante.' If there were no water, where would it land? 'It would not land, bhante.' In the same way, bhikkhus, if there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for solid food...
translations.sn12.65:1: Staying at Sāvatthī. 'Bhikkhus, before my awakening, while I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta, the thought occurred to me: "Alas, this world has fallen into trouble! It is born, it ages, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn. Yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death. When will an escape be found from this suffering, from aging and death?" Then, bhikkhus, the thought occurred to me: "When what exists does aging and death come to be? What is the condition for aging and death?" Then, bhikkhus, through rational application of mind, there came a breakthrough of wisdom: "When there is birth, aging and death come to be; birth is the condition for aging and death."'
translations.sn12.65:3: Then, bhikkhus, the thought occurred to me: 'This consciousness turns back from name-and-form, it goes no further. To this extent one may be born, age, die, pass away, or be reborn; that is: consciousness with name-and-form as condition; name-and-form with consciousness as condition; the six sense bases with name-and-form as condition; contact with the six sense bases as condition... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.' 'Origin, origin'—thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then, bhikkhus, the thought occurred to me: 'When what is absent does consciousness not come to be? From the cessation of what does consciousness cease?' Then, bhikkhus, through rational application of mind, there came a breakthrough of wisdom: 'When name-and-form is absent, consciousness does not come to be; from the cessation of name-and-form, consciousness ceases.'
translations.sn12.65:6: Then, bhikkhus, the thought occurred to me: 'I have discovered this path to awakening, namely: from the cessation of name-and-form, consciousness ceases; from the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; from the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; from the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases... such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.' 'Cessation, cessation'—thus, bhikkhus, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
translations.sn12.65:7: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wandering through a forest, a jungle, were to see an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of former times. He would follow it. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient capital inhabited by people of former times, complete with parks, groves, lotus ponds, and high walls—a delightful place. Then that man would inform the king or a royal minister: 'Sire, you should know that while wandering through a forest, a jungle, I saw an ancient path... I followed it and saw an ancient city... Sire, rebuild that city!' Then the king or royal minister would rebuild that city. In time, that city would become successful, prosperous, populous, crowded with people, and attained to growth and expansion. In the same way, bhikkhus, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by the Rightly Self-Awakened Ones of former times.
translations.sn12.66:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Kurus at a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus!" "Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said: "Do you practice the internal exploration, bhikkhus?" When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: "I, bhante, practice the internal exploration." "But in what way, bhikkhu, do you practice the internal exploration?" Then that bhikkhu explained. However, the way that bhikkhu explained did not satisfy the Blessed One's mind.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Now is the time, Blessed One; now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to speak on the internal exploration. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.” “Then listen, Ānanda, and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.66:5: “Then, exploring further, he explores the internal exploration: ‘When this craving arises, where does it arise? When it settles, where does it settle?’ Exploring, he knows this: ‘Whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable, there this craving arises when it arises, there it settles when it settles.’ And what in the world is pleasant and agreeable? The eye in the world is pleasant and agreeable, there this craving arises when it arises, there it settles when it settles. The ear in the world is pleasant and agreeable … the nose … the tongue … the body … the mind in the world is pleasant and agreeable, there this craving arises when it arises, there it settles when it settles.
translations.sn12.66:6: Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past saw whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure—they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased acquisitions. Those who increased acquisitions increased suffering. Those who increased suffering were not freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. They were not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.66:7: Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will see whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure—they will increase craving. Those who increase craving will increase acquisitions. Those who increase acquisitions will increase suffering. Those who increase suffering will not be freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. They will not be freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.66:8: Whatever ascetics or brahmins now see whatever in the world is pleasant and agreeable as permanent, as happiness, as self, as healthy, as secure—they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase acquisitions. Those who increase acquisitions increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. They are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.67:1: At one time the venerable Sāriputta and the venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were staying at Benares in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the venerable Mahākoṭṭhika emerged from seclusion and went to the venerable Sāriputta. He exchanged greetings with the venerable Sāriputta and, after exchanging polite and friendly remarks, sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to the venerable Sāriputta: “How is it, friend Sāriputta: is aging-and-death self-made, or made by another, or both self-made and made by another, or is it neither self-made nor made by another, having arisen by chance?” “No, friend Koṭṭhika, aging-and-death is not self-made, nor made by another, nor both self-made and made by another, nor is it neither self-made nor made by another, having arisen by chance. Rather, with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death.”
translations.sn12.67:2: “How is it, friend Sāriputta: is birth self-made, or made by another, or both self-made and made by another, or is it neither self-made nor made by another, having arisen by chance?” “No, friend Koṭṭhika, birth is not self-made, nor made by another, nor both self-made and made by another, nor is it neither self-made nor made by another, having arisen by chance. Rather, with existence as condition, there is birth.”
translations.sn12.67:4: “How is it, friend Sāriputta: is consciousness self-made, or made by another, or both self-made and made by another, or is it neither self-made nor made by another, having arisen by chance?” “No, friend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is not self-made, nor made by another, nor both self-made and made by another, nor is it neither self-made nor made by another, having arisen by chance. Rather, with name-and-form as condition, there is consciousness.”
translations.sn12.67:5: “Just now we understood the venerable Sāriputta’s statement thus: ‘No, friend Koṭṭhika, name-and-form is not self-made, nor made by another, nor both self-made and made by another, nor is it neither self-made nor made by another, having arisen by chance. Rather, with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.’
translations.sn12.67:7: “But how, Reverend Sāriputta, should the meaning of this statement be seen?” “Then, reverend, I will give you a simile. For it is by a simile that some sensible people understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, reverend, there were two bundles of reeds leaning against each other. In the same way, name-and-form is a condition for consciousness; consciousness is a condition for name-and-form; name-and-form is a condition for the six sense fields; the six sense fields are a condition for contact … and so there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. If one were to pull away one of those bundles of reeds, the other would fall; if one were to pull away the other, the first would fall. In the same way, with the cessation of name-and-form, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense fields cease; with the cessation of the six sense fields, contact ceases … and so there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”
translations.sn12.67:8: “It’s incredible, Reverend Sāriputta; it’s amazing, Reverend Sāriputta. How well-spoken this was by the venerable Sāriputta. And we rejoice in this statement of the venerable Sāriputta with these thirty-six grounds:”
translations.sn12.68:13: “Then is the venerable Nārada an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?” “‘Cessation of existence is nibbāna’—this has been clearly seen by me as it really is with right wisdom, but I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. Suppose, reverend, there was a well on a desert road, and it had neither a rope nor a bucket. Then a person would come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, weary, parched, and thirsty, and they would look down into that well. They would have the knowledge ‘there is water,’ but they would not dwell having touched it with the body. In the same way, reverend, ‘cessation of existence is nibbāna’ has been clearly seen by me as it really is with right wisdom, but I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.”
translations.sn12.68:6: “Then is the venerable Musila an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?” When this was said, the venerable Musila was silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There … “Mendicants, when the great ocean swells, it makes the great rivers swell; when the great rivers swell, they make the small rivers swell; when the small rivers swell, they make the great lakes swell; when the great lakes swell, they make the small lakes swell. In the same way, mendicants, when ignorance swells, it makes choices swell; when choices swell, they make consciousness swell; when consciousness swells, it makes name-and-form swell; when name-and-form swells, it makes the six sense fields swell; when the six sense fields swell, they make contact swell; when contact swells, it makes feeling swell; when feeling swells, it makes craving swell; when craving swells, it makes grasping swell; when grasping swells, it makes existence swell; when existence swells, it makes rebirth swell; when rebirth swells, it makes old age and death swell.”
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Now at that time the Buddha was honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and he received robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. The Sangha of monks was also honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated, and they received robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, respected, esteemed, worshipped, or venerated, and they did not receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.
translations.sn12.70:10: “But do you venerables, knowing thus and seeing thus, dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms?” “No, reverend.”
translations.sn12.70:11: “Here now, venerables, is this answer and the non-attainment of these states; how is this, reverend?” “We are liberated by wisdom, Reverend Susima.”
translations.sn12.70:12: “I do not understand the detailed meaning of what the venerables have said in brief. It would be good if the venerables would speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of what the venerables have said in brief.” “Whether you understand, Reverend Susima, or whether you do not understand, we are liberated by wisdom.”
translations.sn12.70:13: Then the venerable Susima rose from his seat and went to the Buddha; having approached the Buddha and paid homage to him, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Susima reported to the Buddha the entire conversation he had with those monks. “First, Susima, comes knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma, afterwards knowledge of nibbāna.”
translations.sn12.70:14: “I do not understand, bhante, the detailed meaning of what the Buddha has said in brief. It would be good if the Buddha would speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of what the Buddha has said in brief.” “Whether you understand, Susima, or whether you do not understand, first comes knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma, afterwards knowledge of nibbāna.
translations.sn12.70:16: “Therefore, Susima, any kind of form whatsoever—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Any kind of feeling whatsoever … Any kind of perception whatsoever … Any kind of choices whatsoever … Any kind of consciousness whatsoever—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing thus, Susima, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' They understand: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.'
translations.sn12.70:18: “Susima, do you see that: ‘With birth as condition, aging and death come to be’?” “Yes, bhante.” “Susima, do you see that: ‘With existence as condition, birth comes to be’?” “Yes, bhante.” “Susima, do you see that: ‘With grasping as condition, existence comes to be’?” “Yes, bhante.” “Susima, do you see that: ‘With craving as condition, grasping comes to be’?” “Yes, bhante.” “With feeling as condition, craving... with contact as condition, feeling... with the six sense bases as condition, contact... with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases... with consciousness as condition, name-and-form... with volitional formations as condition, consciousness... Susima, do you see that: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be’?” “Yes, bhante.”
translations.sn12.70:2: At that time, the wanderer Susima was staying at Rajagaha with a large following of wanderers. Then the following of the wanderer Susima said to him: “Come, friend Susima, live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. When you have mastered the Dhamma, you can teach it to us. When we have mastered that Dhamma, we will preach it to the laity. In this way, we too will be honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed, and we will be recipients of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.” “Yes, friends,” the wanderer Susima replied to his following, and he went to the Venerable Ananda. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ananda. When they had finished their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Susima said to the Venerable Ananda: “Friend Ananda, I wish to live the holy life in this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
translations.sn12.70:21: “But Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you hear with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near?” “No, bhante.”
translations.sn12.70:25: “But Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend forms, the formless states?” “No, bhante.”
translations.sn12.70:27: Then the Venerable Susima prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One's feet and said to the Blessed One: “A transgression has overcome me, bhante, in my folly, my delusion, and my unskillfulness, in that I went forth as a thief of the Dhamma in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya. Bhante, may the Blessed One accept my confession of this transgression as a transgression, for the sake of future restraint.”
translations.sn12.70:3: Then the Venerable Ananda took the wanderer Susima and went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, this wanderer Susima said this: ‘Friend Ananda, I wish to live the holy life in this Dhamma and Vinaya.’” “Then, Ananda, give Susima the going forth.” The wanderer Susima received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he received the full ordination.
translations.sn12.70:5: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, exercise the various kinds of psychic power—having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one; you appear and vanish; you go unhindered through walls, enclosures, and mountains as if through space; you dive in and out of the earth as if in water; you walk on water without sinking as if on earth; you travel through the sky cross-legged like a winged bird; you touch and stroke with your hand these sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; you exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:6: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, hear with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:7: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, understand the minds of other beings and other persons, having encompassed them with your own mind? Do you understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust; a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind; a scattered mind as a scattered mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind; an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind; an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:8: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, recollect your manifold past abodes, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here.’ Thus do you recollect your manifold past abodes with their aspects and details?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:9: “But venerable ones, knowing and seeing thus, do you see with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and understand how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of noble ones, wrong in their views, undertaking kammic actions based on wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower world, even in hell; but these worthy beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, not revilers of noble ones, right in their views, undertaking kammic actions based on right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world’? Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, do you see beings passing away and being reborn... and understand how beings fare according to their kamma?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn16.11:1: At one time the venerable Mahākassapa was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Now at that time the venerable Ānanda was wandering in the Southern Hills together with a large community of monks.
translations.sn16.11:10: ‘Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: “A keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing shall be established in me toward the elders, the new monks, and those of middle standing.” Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: “Whatever Dhamma I shall hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will listen to all of it with an eager ear, attending to it as a matter of vital importance, applying my whole mind to it, and concentrating with undivided attention.” Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: “Mindfulness directed to the body accompanied by joy shall not desert me.” Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself.’
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friends, after the Blessed One had given me this exhortation, he rose from his seat and departed. For only seven days, friends, did I eat the country’s almsfood as a debtor; on the eighth day final knowledge arose.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friends, the Blessed One stepped off the road and went to the foot of a certain tree. I then folded my double-robe of patched cloth into four and said to the Blessed One: ‘Let the Blessed One sit here, venerable sir; that would be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.’ The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to me: ‘Soft is this double-robe of patched cloth of yours, Kassapa.’ ‘Venerable sir, let the Blessed One accept this double-robe of patched cloth out of compassion.’ ‘But will you, Kassapa, wear my worn-out hempen rag robes?’ ‘I will, venerable sir, wear the Blessed One’s worn-out hempen rag robes.’ So, friends, I gave my double-robe of patched cloth to the Blessed One, and I received from the Blessed One his worn-out hempen rag robes.
translations.sn16.11:17: Friends, by the destruction of the taints, I have realized for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, I dwell in it. One would think that a tusker seven or seven and a half cubits high could be hidden by a palm leaf, just as one might think that my six direct knowledges could be hidden.”
translations.sn16.11:2: Now at that time about thirty of the venerable Ānanda’s resident pupils had given up the training and returned to the lower life, most of them being mere youths. Then the venerable Ānanda, having wandered in the Southern Hills as long as he liked, went to the venerable Mahākassapa at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagaha. He paid homage to the venerable Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the venerable Mahākassapa said to him: “Friend Ānanda, for how many reasons did the Blessed One proscribe eating in groups of three among families?”
translations.sn16.11:3: “Venerable Kassapa, for three reasons the Blessed One proscribed eating in groups of three among families: for the restraint of ill-behaved persons and the comfort of well-behaved monks; so that those of evil wishes might not split the Saṅgha by relying on a faction; and out of compassion for families. These are the three reasons, venerable Kassapa.”
translations.sn16.11:4: “Then why, friend Ānanda, do you go wandering with these new monks who are unguarded in their sense faculties, immoderate in eating, and not devoted to wakefulness? You are wandering as if trampling the crops, as if destroying the families. Your assembly is falling apart, friend Ānanda; your young recruits are breaking away. This boy does not know his measure!”
translations.sn16.11:6: The nun Thullanandā heard: “It is said that the master Mahākassapa has rebuked the master Ānanda, the Videhan sage, by calling him a boy.”
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the nun Thullanandā, being displeased, uttered these words of displeasure: “How can the master Mahākassapa, who was formerly a member of another sect, think that he can rebuke the master Ānanda, the Videhan sage, by calling him a boy?” The venerable Mahākassapa heard the nun Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then the venerable Mahākassapa said to the venerable Ānanda: “Indeed, friend Ānanda, the nun Thullanandā spoke words impulsively and without reflection. Since I, friend, shaved off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, I have not known any other teacher to be pointed out, except for that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Formerly, friend, when I was still a householder, it occurred to me: ‘Household life is crowded, a path of dust; going forth is the open air. It is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life entirely complete, entirely pure, like a polished shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’ Then, friend, at a later time, having made a double-layered robe out of rags, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, dedicating myself to those who are Arahants in the world.”
translations.sn16.13:2: “Just as, Kassapa, gold does not disappear as long as counterfeit gold has not appeared in the world; but when counterfeit gold appears in the world, then gold disappears. In the same way, Kassapa, the true Dhamma does not disappear as long as a counterfeit of the true Dhamma has not appeared in the world; but when a counterfeit of the true Dhamma appears in the world, then the true Dhamma disappears.”
translations.sn16.13:4: “These five detrimental things, Kassapa, lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma. Which five? Here, Kassapa, the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen dwell without respect and without deference toward the Teacher; they dwell without respect and without deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell without respect and without deference toward the Saṅgha; they dwell without respect and without deference toward the training; they dwell without respect and without deference toward immersion. These five detrimental things, Kassapa, lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.”
translations.sn16.2:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the venerable Mahākassapa and the venerable Sāriputta were staying at Benares in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then the venerable Sāriputta, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to the venerable Mahākassapa and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Sāriputta said to the venerable Mahākassapa: “It is said, friend Kassapa, that one who is unenergetic and reckless is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme security from bondage; but one who is energetic and prudent is capable of enlightenment, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the supreme security from bondage.”
translations.sn16.2:3: “And how, friend, is one reckless? Here, friend, a monk is not prudent, thinking: ‘If unarisen evil unwholesome states arise in me, they would lead to my harm’; he is not prudent, thinking: ‘If arisen evil unwholesome states are not abandoned in me, they would lead to my harm’; he is not prudent, thinking: ‘If unarisen wholesome states do not arise in me, they would lead to my harm’; he is not prudent, thinking: ‘If arisen wholesome states cease in me, they would lead to my harm.’ That is how one is reckless. In this way, friend, one who is unenergetic and reckless is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the supreme security from bondage.”
translations.sn16.2:4: “And how, friend, is one energetic? Here, friend, a monk applies energy, thinking: ‘If unarisen evil unwholesome states arise in me, they would lead to my harm’; he applies energy, thinking: ‘If arisen evil unwholesome states are not abandoned in me, they would lead to my harm’; he applies energy, thinking: ‘If unarisen wholesome states...’ [and so on]. That is how one is energetic.”
translations.sn16.5:1: Thus have I heard... at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then the venerable Mahākassapa went to the Blessed One, bowed, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “You are old now, Kassapa, and those worn-out hempen rag robes are heavy for you. Therefore, Kassapa, you should wear robes offered by householders, accept invitations for meals, and dwell near me.”
translations.sn21.10:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Now at that time a certain monk named Thera lived alone and spoke in praise of living alone. He entered the village for alms alone, returned alone, sat in private alone, and resolved on walking meditation alone. Then a number of monks went to the Blessed One, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, there is a certain monk named Thera who lives alone and speaks in praise of living alone.”
translations.sn21.10:3: “There is such a way of living alone, Thera, I do not say there is not. But, Thera, as to how living alone is fulfilled in detail, listen and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied... “And how, Thera, is living alone fulfilled in detail? Here, Thera, what is past is abandoned, what is future is relinquished, and desire and lust for present forms of existence are thoroughly discarded. That, Thera, is how living alone is fulfilled in detail.”
translations.sn21.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the monks: “Friends, monks!” “Friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: “Just now, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind: ‘It is said, “noble silence, noble silence.” What is noble silence?’ Then, friends, it occurred to me: ‘Here, a bhikkhu, with the stilling of directed thought and evaluation, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind, is without directed thought and evaluation, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This is called noble silence.’ So, friends, with the stilling of directed thought and evaluation, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna... While I was dwelling in this state, perceptions and mental attention accompanied by directed thought assailed me.
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus!” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.2:2: “Just now, friends, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind: ‘Is there anything in the world whose change and alteration would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair in me?’ Then, friends, it occurred to me: ‘There is nothing in the world whose change and alteration would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair in me.’”
translations.sn21.3:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. At that time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place, in the same dwelling. Then, in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.3:2: “Friend Moggallāna, your faculties are serene; your facial complexion is pure and bright. Has Venerable Mahāmoggallāna perhaps spent the day in a peaceful dwelling?” “Friend, I have spent the day in a sublime dwelling. And I had a Dhamma talk.” “With whom did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma talk?” “I had a Dhamma talk with the Blessed One, friend.” “Friend, the Blessed One is far away; he is currently staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approach the Blessed One by psychic power, or did the Blessed One approach Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by psychic power?” “Friend, I did not approach the Blessed One by psychic power, nor did the Blessed One approach me by psychic power. Rather, as far as the Blessed One was, my divine eye and divine ear element were purified; and as far as I was, the Blessed One's divine eye and divine ear element were purified.” “And what kind of Dhamma talk did Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have with the Blessed One?”
translations.sn21.3:3: “Here, friend, I said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, it is said, “one of aroused energy, one of aroused energy.” To what extent, venerable sir, is one of aroused energy?’ When this was said, friend, the Blessed One said to me: ‘Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused: “Gladly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up; but there shall be no relaxation of energy until I have attained what can be reached by manly strength, manly energy, and manly persistence.” It is in this way, Moggallāna, that one is of aroused energy.’ Such was the Dhamma talk I had with the Blessed One, friend.”
translations.sn21.3:6: ‘Sāriputta is like this in wisdom, in virtue, and in peace; even a bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore could at most be his equal.’
translations.sn21.6:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya coming from afar. Seeing him, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, do you see that bhikkhu coming—ugly, unsightly, dwarfish, and looked down upon by the bhikkhus?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu is of great psychic power and great majesty. There is no attainment that has not been previously attained by that bhikkhu. And for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, that supreme goal of the holy life he has realized for himself in this very life with direct knowledge, and having attained it, he dwells in it.” The Blessed One said this... the Teacher:
translations.sn21.6:2: “Swans, cranes, and peacocks, elephants and spotted deer; they all fear the lion, for there is no equality in bodies.
translations.sn21.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Nanda, the Blessed One's cousin, having put on well-pressed and ironed robes, having anointed his eyes, and carrying a clear bowl, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Venerable Nanda as he sat there: “Nanda, it is not proper for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness to wear well-pressed and ironed robes, to anoint his eyes, and to carry a clear bowl. This, Nanda, is proper for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness: that you should be a forest dweller, an alms-food eater, a rag-robe wearer, and that you should dwell indifferent to sensual pleasures.” The Blessed One said this... the Teacher:
translations.sn21.8:2: “When shall I see Nanda as a forest dweller, a rag-robe wearer, living on scraps gathered in search of alms, indifferent to sensual pleasures?”
translations.sn21.9:1: He was staying at Savatthi. Then the venerable Tissa, the Buddha's paternal cousin, went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side, miserable and sad, shedding tears. Then the Buddha said to the venerable Tissa: “Tissa, why are you sitting to one side, miserable and sad, shedding tears?” “Because, bhante, the monks have been badgering me on all sides with stinging words.” “That is because, Tissa, you are a talker but not patient with words. It is not fitting for you, Tissa, a son of a good family who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, to be a talker but not patient with words. This is what is fitting for you, Tissa, a son of a good family who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith: that you should be a talker and also patient with words.”
translations.sn22.100:2: “Bhikkhus, have you seen the picture called ‘The Wandering’?” “Yes, bhante.” “Bhikkhus, even that picture called ‘The Wandering’ was designed by the mind. But the mind is even more diverse than that picture called ‘The Wandering.’ Therefore, bhikkhus, one should frequently reflect upon one's own mind: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion.’ By the defilement of the mind, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; by the purification of the mind, beings are purified.”
translations.sn22.100:3: “Bhikkhus, I do not see any other single group of beings as diverse as the animals. Even those animals, bhikkhus, are diverse because of the mind, but the mind is even more diverse than those animals. Therefore, bhikkhus, one should frequently reflect upon one's own mind: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion.’ By the defilement of the mind, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; by the purification of the mind, beings are purified.”
translations.sn22.101:1: At Savatthi. “Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And for one knowing what, seeing what, bhikkhus, does the destruction of the taints occur? ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling… such is perception… such are volitional formations… such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness’—it is for one knowing thus, seeing thus, bhikkhus, that the destruction of the taints occurs.”
translations.sn22.101:2: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is not committed to the practice of mental development, even though such a wish might arise in him: ‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints through non-clinging!’, yet his mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Why is that? It should be said: ‘Because of lack of development.’ Lack of development of what? Lack of development of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.”
translations.sn22.101:3: “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were eight, ten, or twelve hen's eggs. But the hen had not properly sat on them, properly warmed them, or properly incubated them. Even though such a wish might arise in that hen: ‘Oh, that my chicks might pierce the eggshells with their claws and beaks and hatch safely!’, yet those chicks are unable to pierce the eggshells with their claws and beaks and hatch safely. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the hen had not properly sat on those eight, ten, or twelve eggs, properly warmed them, or properly incubated them. In the same way, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is not committed to the practice of mental development, even though such a wish might arise in him: ‘Oh, that my mind might be liberated from the taints through non-clinging!’, yet his mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Why is that? It should be said: ‘Because of lack of development.’ Lack of development of what? Lack of development of the four foundations of mindfulness… and the noble eightfold path.”
translations.sn22.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Buddha was staying among the Bhaggas at Sumsumaragira in the Bhesakala Grove, the Deer Park. Then the householder Nakulapita went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Nakulapita said to the Buddha:
translations.sn22.1:10: They regard feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. They are obsessed with the idea: ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine.’ As they are obsessed with the idea ‘I am feeling, feeling is mine,’ that feeling changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of feeling, there arise in them sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.
translations.sn22.1:11: They regard perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. They are obsessed with the idea: ‘I am perception, perception is mine.’ As they are obsessed with the idea ‘I am perception, perception is mine,’ that perception changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of perception, there arise in them sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.
translations.sn22.1:12: They regard volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations. They are obsessed with the idea: ‘I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine.’ As they are obsessed with the idea ‘I am volitional formations, volitional formations are mine,’ those volitional formations change and become otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of volitional formations, there arise in them sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress.
translations.sn22.1:13: They regard consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. They are obsessed with the idea: ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.’ As they are obsessed with these ideas, that consciousness changes and alters. With the change and alteration of consciousness, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. This is how, householder, one is afflicted in body and afflicted in mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind? Here, householder, a well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the teaching of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the teaching of the noble ones; who has seen true persons, is skilled in the teaching of true persons, and is well-trained in the teaching of true persons—does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They are not obsessed with the idea: ‘I am form, form is mine.’ As they are not obsessed with these ideas, that form changes and alters. With the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair do not arise.
translations.sn22.1:2: “Bhante, I am old, elderly, burdened with years, advanced in life, come to the last stage; my body is afflicted and I am constantly ailing. I am one who rarely gets to see the Blessed One and the esteemed bhikkhus. Let the Blessed One exhort me, bhante; let the Blessed One instruct me, bhante, for my long-term welfare and happiness.”
translations.sn22.1:3: “So it is, householder, so it is! For this body, householder, is afflicted, fragile, and encumbered. For one carrying this body around to claim even a moment of health—what is that but foolishness? Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: ‘Even though I am afflicted in body, my mind shall not be afflicted.’ Thus should you train yourself.”
translations.sn22.1:4: Then Nakulapitā the householder, having rejoiced and appreciated the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, went to the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said to him: “Householder, your faculties are very bright; your facial complexion is pure and clear. Did you have the opportunity today to hear a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One?”
translations.sn22.1:7: “But did it not occur to you, householder, to further question the Blessed One: ‘To what extent, bhante, is one afflicted in body and afflicted in mind, and to what extent is one afflicted in body but not afflicted in mind?’” “Bhante, we would travel from far away to learn the meaning of this statement from the Venerable Sāriputta. It would be good if the Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement.”
translations.sn22.1:8: “Then listen, householder, and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” Nakulapitā the householder replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.1:9: “And how, householder, is one afflicted in body and afflicted in mind? Here, householder, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for noble ones, is unskilled in their teaching, and untrained in their teaching; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in their teaching, and untrained in their teaching—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They are obsessed with the idea: ‘I am form, form is mine.’ As they are obsessed with these ideas, that form changes and alters. With the change and alteration of form, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
translations.sn22.22:2: And who, bhikkhus, is the carrier of the burden? The person, it should be said. This venerable one of such a name and such a clan; this, bhikkhus, is called the carrier of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the taking up of the burden? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the taking up of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the laying down of the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, its giving up, relinquishment, letting go, and rejection. This, bhikkhus, is called the laying down of the burden.”
translations.sn22.22:6: “The five aggregates are truly the burden, and the person is the carrier of the burden. Taking up the burden is suffering in the world, laying the burden down is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at a Sakyan town named Devadaha. Then a number of bhikkhus who were going to the Western District approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, we wish to go to the Western District and take up residence there.”
translations.sn22.2:10: Friends, if for one dwelling having undertaken unwholesome states there were a happy dwelling in this very life, without distress, without despair, without fever, and with the breakup of the body, after death, a good destination could be expected, then the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome states. But because for one dwelling having undertaken unwholesome states there is a painful dwelling in this very life, with distress, with despair, with fever, and with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.
translations.sn22.2:2: “But have you, bhikkhus, asked leave of Sāriputta?” “Bhante, we have not asked leave of the Venerable Sāriputta.” “Bhikkhus, ask leave of Sāriputta. Sāriputta is wise, bhikkhus, a helper to his fellow monks in the holy life.” “Yes, bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.2:3: At that time the venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One in a certain clump of eḷagalā bushes. Then those bhikkhus, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on their right, went to the venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the venerable Sāriputta. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said to the venerable Sāriputta: “Friend Sāriputta, we wish to go to the Western Districts and take up residence there. We have already asked the Teacher’s permission.”
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One … sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “It would be good, bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “Bhikkhu, what one underlies, by that one is measured; what one is measured by, by that one is reckoned. What one does not underlie, by that one is not measured; what one is not measured by, by that one is not reckoned.” “Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Fortunate One!”
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the venerable Mahākaccāna was staying among the Avantians on Mount Papāta at Kuraraghara. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached the venerable Mahākaccāna, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the householder Hāliddikāni said to the venerable Mahākaccāna: “Bhante, this was said by the Blessed One in ‘The Questions of Māgaṇḍiya’ in the Aṭṭhakavagga:
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one not empty of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has not rid themselves of greed for sensual pleasures, has not rid themselves of desire, affection, thirst, passion, and craving. That is how one is not empty of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one empty of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has rid themselves of greed for sensual pleasures, has rid themselves of desire, affection, thirst, passion, and craving. That is how one is empty of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, is one a 'preoccupier'? Here, householder, someone thinks: ‘May I have such a form in the future, may I have such a feeling in the future, may I have such a perception in the future, may I have such choices in the future, may I have such a consciousness in the future.’ That is how one is a preoccupier.
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, does one engage in verbal disputes with people? Here, householder, someone engages in this kind of talk: ‘You don’t understand this Dhamma and Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma and Vinaya. How could you understand this Dhamma and Vinaya? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. You said last what should have been said first; you said first what should have been said last. What I say is consistent; what you say is inconsistent. What you have practiced so long is overturned. Your argument is refuted; go and try to save your argument. You are defeated; extricate yourself if you can!’ That is how one engages in verbal disputes with people.
translations.sn22.3:17: ‘Having left the home, wandering without a fixed abode, / In the village the sage does not form intimate ties; / Empty of sensual pleasures, not preoccupied, / He would not engage in verbal disputes with people.’
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, is one a 'home-wanderer'? One is called a 'home-wanderer' because of being bound by the shackles of the home of the sign of forms. One is called a 'home-wanderer' because of being bound by the shackles of the home of the sign of sounds … smells … tastes … touches … ideas. That is how one is a home-wanderer.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, does one form intimate ties in the village? Here, householder, someone lives in association with laypeople, sharing their joys and sorrows, happy when they are happy and sad when they are sad; when duties arise, they involve themselves in them. That is how one forms intimate ties in the village.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, does one not form intimate ties in the village? Here, householder, a bhikkhu lives without associating with laypeople, not sharing their joys and sorrows, not happy when they are happy nor sad when they are sad; when duties arise, he does not involve himself in them. That is how one does not form intimate ties in the village.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard the self in various ways, they all regard the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one of them. Which five? Here, bhikkhus, an unlearned ordinary person who has no regard for the noble ones, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has no regard for true men, who is unskilled in the Dhamma of true men, undisciplined in the Dhamma of true men, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They regard feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: Thus there is this regarding, and the notion ‘I am’ has not disappeared for them. As long as the notion ‘I am’ has not disappeared, there is the descent of the five faculties—the faculty of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. There is, bhikkhus, the mind, there are ideas, there is the element of ignorance. When an unlearned ordinary person is touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance, the thought ‘I am’ occurs to them; ‘I am this’ occurs to them; ‘I will be’ occurs to them; ‘I will not be’ occurs to them; ‘I will be possessed of form’ occurs to them; ‘I will be formless’ occurs to them; ‘I will be percipient’ occurs to them; ‘I will be non-percipient’ occurs to them; ‘I will be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’ occurs to them.”
translations.sn22.2:5: “Friends, we would come from afar to the presence of the venerable Sāriputta to learn the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the meaning of this statement would occur to the venerable Sāriputta himself.” “Then, friends, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Sāriputta. The venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.48:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five aggregates affected by clinging. Listen to that. And what, mendicants, are the five aggregates? Whatever kind of form there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, far or near: this is called the aggregate of form. Whatever kind of feeling … whatever kind of perception … whatever kind of choices, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine … this is called the aggregate of choices. Whatever kind of consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, far or near: this is called the aggregate of consciousness. These, mendicants, are called the five aggregates."
translations.sn22.53:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, one who is involved is unfree; one who is uninvolved is free. Consciousness, mendicants, while standing, might stand involved with form; with form as its object, grounded on form, sprinkled with delight, it would come to growth, increase, and abundance. Or consciousness, while standing, might stand involved with feeling … or involved with perception … or involved with choices; with choices as its object, grounded on choices, sprinkled with delight, it would come to growth, increase, and abundance."
translations.sn22.53:2: Mendicants, if someone were to say: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from choices, I will describe the coming, going, passing away, rebirth, growth, increase, or abundance of consciousness,’ that is not possible."
translations.sn22.54:2: Consciousness, mendicants, while standing, might stand involved with form; with form as its object, grounded on form, sprinkled with delight, it would come to growth, increase, and abundance. Or consciousness, while standing, might stand involved with feeling … or involved with perception … or involved with choices; with choices as its object, grounded on choices, sprinkled with delight, it would come to growth, increase, and abundance."
translations.sn22.55:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One uttered this inspired exclamation: “‘It might not be, and it might not be mine; it will not be, and it will not be mine’—resolving thus, a bhikkhu could cut off the lower fetters.” When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, by resolving thus: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine; it will not be, and it will not be mine,’ could a bhikkhu cut off the lower fetters?”
translations.sn22.55:10: “But, venerable sir, for one who knows and sees in what way does the immediate destruction of the taints occur?” “Here, bhikkhu, an unlearned worldling falls into terror over a groundless matter. For this is a terror to an unlearned worldling: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine; it will not be, and it will not be mine.’”
translations.sn22.55:4: They do not understand as it really is suffering form as ‘suffering form’ … suffering feeling … suffering perception … suffering choices … suffering consciousness as ‘suffering consciousness.’
translations.sn22.55:5: They do not understand as it really is not-self form as ‘not-self form’ … not-self feeling as ‘not-self feeling’ … not-self perception as ‘not-self perception’ … not-self choices as ‘not-self choices’ … not-self consciousness as ‘not-self consciousness.’
translations.sn22.55:6: They do not understand as it really is conditioned form as ‘conditioned form’ … conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned choices … conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness.’ They do not understand as it really is that form will be annihilated … feeling will be annihilated … perception will be annihilated … choices will be annihilated … consciousness will be annihilated.
translations.sn22.55:8: They understand as it really is impermanent form as ‘impermanent form’ … impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent choices … impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness.’ Suffering form … suffering consciousness … not-self form … not-self consciousness … conditioned form … conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness.’ They understand as it really is that form will be annihilated … feeling … perception … choices … consciousness will be annihilated.
translations.sn22.55:9: With the annihilation of form, the annihilation of feeling, the annihilation of perception, the annihilation of choices, the annihilation of consciousness—it is in this way, bhikkhu, that by resolving thus: ‘It might not be, and it might not be mine; it will not be, and it will not be mine,’ a bhikkhu could cut off the lower fetters.” “Venerable sir, ‘resolving thus, a bhikkhu could cut off the lower fetters.’"
translations.sn22.56:13: And what, mendicants, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called consciousness. With the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of consciousness; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness. This very noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness, namely: right view … right immersion.
translations.sn22.56:14: Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known consciousness thus, its origin thus, its cessation thus, and the way leading to its cessation thus, are practicing for the sake of disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness—they are practicing rightly. Those who practice rightly are grounded in this Dhamma and Training.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it fourfold? I directly knew form, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; I directly knew feeling … perception … choices … consciousness, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation.
translations.sn22.56:5: Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known form thus …pe… the way leading to its cessation thus, through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, are liberated without grasping—they are well-liberated. Those who are well-liberated are consummate ones. For those consummate ones, there is no cycle of rebirth to be described.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Savatthi. “Monks, a bhikkhu who is skilled in seven points and an investigator in three ways is called a consummate one, one who has lived the life, a supreme person in this Dhamma and Training. And how, monks, is a bhikkhu skilled in seven points? Here, monks, a bhikkhu understands form, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; he understands the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding form; he understands feeling … perception … choices … consciousness, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; he understands the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, monks, are choices? There are these six classes of volition: volition regarding forms …pe… volition regarding mental phenomena. These are called choices. With the origin of contact, there is the origin of choices; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of choices. This very noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of choices, namely—right view …pe… right immersion.
translations.sn22.57:15: The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal and giving up of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known consciousness thus, its origin thus, its cessation thus, the way leading to its cessation thus; its gratification thus, its danger thus, and its escape thus, through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, are liberated without grasping—they are well-liberated. Those who are well-liberated are consummate ones. For those consummate ones, there is no cycle of rebirth to be described. It is in this way, monks, that a bhikkhu is skilled in seven points.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, monks, is form? The four great elements and form derived from the four great elements. This is called form. With the origin of nutriment, there is the origin of form; with the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of form. This very noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of form, namely—right view …pe… right immersion.
translations.sn22.57:5: Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who, having directly known form thus, its origin thus, its cessation thus, the way leading to its cessation thus; its gratification thus, its danger thus, and its escape thus, through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, are liberated without grasping—they are well-liberated. Those who are well-liberated are consummate ones. For those consummate ones, there is no cycle of rebirth to be described.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what, monks, is feeling? There are these six classes of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact …pe… feeling born of mind-contact. This is called feeling. With the origin of contact, there is the origin of feeling; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling. This very noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, namely—right view …pe… right immersion.
translations.sn22.57:7: The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on feeling—this is the gratification in feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feeling. The removal and giving up of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: At Savatthi. “Monks, the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, being liberated without grasping, is called a Perfectly Enlightened One. A bhikkhu, too, monks, who is liberated by wisdom, through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, being liberated without grasping, is called one liberated by wisdom.
translations.sn22.58:3: Monks, the Tathagata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding perception … choices … consciousness, being liberated without grasping, is called a Perfectly Enlightened One.
