A bhikkhu, too, monks, who is liberated by wisdom, through disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, being liberated without grasping, is called one liberated by wisdom.
translations.sn22.59:10: Any kind of consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, far or near, all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.59:7: “Therefore, bhikkhus, any kind of form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near, all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.5:11: He does not delight in consciousness, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it. As he does not delight in it, welcome it, or remain clinging to it, delight in consciousness ceases. With the cessation of delight comes cessation of grasping ... such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of form, the origin of feeling, the origin of perception, the origin of choices, the origin of consciousness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu delights in, welcomes, and remains clinging to it.
translations.sn22.5:3: And what does he delight in, welcome, and remain clinging to? He delights in form, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it. As he delights in form, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, delight arises. Any delight in form is grasping. With grasping as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:4: He delights in feeling ... perception ... choices ... consciousness, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it. As he delights in consciousness, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, delight arises. Any delight in consciousness is grasping. With grasping as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition ... such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:8: And what does he not delight in, not welcome, and not remain clinging to? He does not delight in form, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it. As he does not delight in form, welcome it, or remain clinging to it, delight in form ceases. With the cessation of delight comes cessation of grasping; with the cessation of grasping, the cessation of existence ... such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.60:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One ... seated to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.60:2: “Venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa says this: ‘There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition. There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition.’ What does the Blessed One say about this?”
translations.sn22.60:3: “Mahāli, there is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause and condition. Mahāli, there is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause and condition.”
translations.sn22.60:4: “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the defilement of beings? How is it that beings are defiled with cause and condition?”
translations.sn22.60:5: “Mahāli, if this form were exclusively suffering, steeped in suffering, overwhelmed by suffering, and not steeped in pleasure, beings would not become enamored with form. But because form is pleasant, steeped in pleasure, overwhelmed by pleasure, and not steeped in suffering, beings become enamored with form. Through infatuation they are fettered; through the fetter they are defiled. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings; thus beings are defiled with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.60:8: Mahāli, if this consciousness were exclusively suffering, steeped in suffering, overwhelmed by suffering, and not steeped in pleasure, beings would not become enamored with consciousness. But because consciousness is pleasant, steeped in pleasure, overwhelmed by pleasure, and not steeped in suffering, beings become enamored with consciousness. Through infatuation they are fettered; through the fetter they are defiled. This too, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings. Thus beings are defiled with cause and condition.”
translations.sn22.60:9: “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings? How is it that beings are purified with cause and condition?” “Mahāli, if this form were exclusively pleasant, steeped in pleasure, overwhelmed by pleasure, and not steeped in suffering, beings would not become disillusioned with form. But because form is suffering, steeped in suffering, overwhelmed by suffering, and not steeped in pleasure, beings become disillusioned with form. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate; through dispassion they are purified. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings. Thus beings are purified with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disillusioned with form, disillusioned with feeling ... perception ... choices ... disillusioned with consciousness. Being disillusioned, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion he is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ As far, bhikkhus, as there are abodes of beings, as far as the peak of existence, these are the foremost, these are the best in the world, namely the Arahants.”
translations.sn22.76:4:
“Happy indeed are the Arahants, 
In them no craving is found; 
The conceit ‘I am’ is cut off, 
The net of delusion is burst asunder.
translations.sn22.76:6:
Having fully understood the five aggregates, 
Those seven who range in the true Dhamma; 
Those true men are praiseworthy, 
The Buddha’s own breast-born sons.
translations.sn22.76:7:
Endowed with the seven treasures, 
Trained in the three trainings; 
Those great heroes wander about, 
With fear and dread abandoned.
translations.sn22.76:8:
Endowed with the ten factors, 
Great Nagas, concentrated; 
These are the best in the world, 
In them no craving is found.
translations.sn22.76:9:
The knowledge of an adept has arisen, 
This is the last body; 
In that which is the core of the holy life, 
They are no longer dependent on others.”
translations.sn22.79:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins recollect their manifold past lives, they all recollect the five aggregates affected by clinging, or one of them. Which five? ‘I had such form in the past’—thus, bhikkhus, in recollecting, one recollects form itself. ‘I had such feeling in the past’—thus, bhikkhus, in recollecting, one recollects feeling itself. ‘I had such perception in the past’ … ‘I had such choices in the past’ … ‘I had such consciousness in the past’—thus, bhikkhus, in recollecting, one recollects consciousness itself.
translations.sn22.79:10: ‘I am now being devoured by consciousness. In the past, I was also devoured by consciousness in just the same way as I am being devoured by present consciousness now. And if I were to delight in future consciousness, then in the future I would also be devoured by consciousness in just the same way as I am being devoured by present consciousness now.’ Reflecting thus, he is indifferent toward past consciousness; he does not delight in future consciousness; and he is practicing for the sake of revulsion, fading away, and cessation regarding present consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:7: There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I am now being devoured by form. In the past, I was also devoured by form in just the same way as I am being devoured by present form now. And if I were to delight in future form, then in the future I would also be devoured by form in just the same way as I am being devoured by present form now.’ Reflecting thus, he is indifferent toward past form; he does not delight in future form; and he is practicing for the sake of revulsion, fading away, and cessation regarding present form.
translations.sn22.80:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery. Then the Blessed One, having dismissed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus for a certain reason, dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu and returned from his alms round after his meal, he went to the Great Forest for the day's abiding. Having plunged into the Great Forest, he sat down at the foot of a young beluva tree for the day's abiding.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Blessed One consented by silence. Then Brahmā Sahampati, having understood the Blessed One's consent, paid homage to the Blessed One and, keeping him on his right, disappeared right there.
translations.sn22.80:5: Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to the Banyan Tree Monastery; having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that those bhikkhus, looking embarrassed, approached him one or two at a time. Those bhikkhus, looking embarrassed, approached the Blessed One one or two at a time; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said to them:
translations.sn22.80:6: “Bhikkhus, this is the lowest of livelihoods, this scavenging for alms. It is a curse in the world: ‘You go about as a scavenger with a bowl in your hand.’ Yet, bhikkhus, sons of good family take this up for a reason, for a purpose; not because they are driven by kings, nor driven by thieves, nor because of debt, nor because of fear, nor because they are deprived of a livelihood; but with the thought: ‘We are victims of birth, aging, and death, of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; we are victims of suffering, overwhelmed by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.’
translations.sn22.80:7: Such is the way this son of good family has gone forth, bhikkhus. Yet he is covetous, with strong passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill will, with corrupt intentions, muddled in mindfulness, lacking situational awareness, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind and unrestrained faculties. Just as, bhikkhus, a brand from a funeral pyre, burning at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle, serves no purpose as timber in the village nor as timber in the forest. I say this person is just like that, bhikkhus: he has fallen away from the enjoyments of a householder and does not fulfill the purpose of asceticism.
translations.sn22.80:9: Bhikkhus, there are these two views: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. There, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Is there anything in the world that I could cling to without being at fault?’ He understands thus: ‘There is nothing in the world that I could cling to without being at fault. For if I were to cling, I would be clinging to form, to feeling, to perception, to choices, or to consciousness. With my clinging as condition, there would be existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would come to be. Such would be the origin of this entire mass of suffering.’
translations.sn22.81:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kosambī and returned from his alms round after his meal, he set his own lodging in order, took his bowl and robe, and without addressing his attendants or notifying the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, set out on tour alone, without a companion.
translations.sn22.81:10: He does not indeed regard form as self, nor feeling as self, nor perception … nor choices … nor consciousness as self; but he has such a view: ‘The self is the same as the world; after death I shall be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.’ That eternalist view, bhikkhus, is a construction. And what is the source of that construction? … In this way, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there is the immediate destruction of the taints.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages, arrived at Pālileyyaka. There the Blessed One stayed at Pālileyyaka at the foot of the auspicious Sal tree. Then many bhikkhus went to the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we heard a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One’s own lips; we wish, friend Ānanda, to hear a Dhamma talk from the Blessed One’s own lips.”
translations.sn22.82:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother, together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Now at that time, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, on the night of the full moon, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
translations.sn22.82:10: “But, bhante, what is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape in the case of form? What is the gratification, what is the danger, what is the escape in the case of feeling … perception … choices … consciousness?” “Bhikkhu, the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on form—this is the gratification in form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in form. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form. The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on feeling … perception … choices … consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.” “Good, bhante,” that bhikkhu said, and having rejoiced and appreciated the Blessed One’s words, he asked the Blessed One a further question:
translations.sn22.82:11: “But, bhante, how does one know, how does one see, so that in regard to this conscious body and all external signs, there are no notions of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and the underlying tendency to conceit?” “Bhikkhu, any kind of form whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, far or near—one sees all form as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Any kind of feeling … perception … choices … consciousness whatsoever, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or fine, inferior or superior, far or near—one sees all consciousness as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ It is in this way, bhikkhu, that for one knowing and seeing, in regard to this conscious body and all external signs, there are no notions of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and the underlying tendency to conceit.”
translations.sn22.82:12: Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu had this thought in his mind: “So it seems that form is nonself, feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is nonself. Then what self will the deeds done by the nonself touch?” Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in that bhikkhu’s mind with his own mind, addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.sn22.82:13: “Bhikkhus, it is possible that some foolish person here, ignorant and fallen into nescience, with a mind dominated by craving, might think he can outrun the Teacher’s instruction thus: ‘So it seems that form is nonself, feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is nonself. Then what self will the deeds done by the nonself touch?’ Now, bhikkhus, you have been trained by me through interrogation here and there in these various teachings.
translations.sn22.82:4: “But, bhante, what is the root of these five aggregates subject to clinging?” “Bhikkhu, these five aggregates subject to clinging have desire as their root.” … “Bhante, is that clinging the same as the five aggregates subject to clinging, or is clinging something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging?” “Bhikkhu, clinging is neither the same as the five aggregates subject to clinging, nor is it something apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging. But rather, the desire and lust for them is the clinging there.” “Good, bhante,” that bhikkhu said … and asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:5: “But, bhante, can there be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging?” “There can, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said. “Here, bhikkhu, someone thinks: ‘May I have such a form in the future, may I have such a feeling … such a perception … such choices … such a consciousness in the future.’ In this way, bhikkhu, there can be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging.” “Good, bhante,” that bhikkhu said … and asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:7: “But, bhante, what is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of form? What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of feeling … perception … choices … consciousness?” “Bhikkhu, the four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of form. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of feeling. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of perception. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of choices. Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of consciousness.” “Good, bhante,” that bhikkhu said … and asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: “But sir, how does identity view come about?” “Bhikkhu, here an unlearned ordinary person who has no regard for noble ones and is unskilled and untrained in their Dhamma, who has no regard for true persons and is unskilled and untrained in their Dhamma, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They regard feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. That is how identity view comes about.” “Good, sir,” said that bhikkhu … and asked another question:
translations.sn22.82:9: “But sir, how does identity view not come about?” “Bhikkhu, here a learned noble disciple who has regard for noble ones and is skilled and trained in their Dhamma, who has regard for true persons and is skilled and trained in their Dhamma, does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They do not regard feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. That is how identity view does not come about.” “Good, sir,” said that bhikkhu … and asked another question:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus!” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn22.83:3: “Just as, friend Ānanda, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of ornaments, would examine their own facial reflection in a mirror that is clean and bright or in a bowl of clear water, and would see it by clinging, not without clinging; even so, friend Ānanda, by clinging to form the notion ‘I am’ occurs, not without clinging. By clinging to feeling … perception … choices … consciousness the notion ‘I am’ occurs, not without clinging.”
translations.sn22.84:10: “I have made this simile, Tissa, to make the meaning clear. And this is the meaning: ‘The man unskilled in the way’ is a term for the ordinary person. ‘The man skilled in the way’ is a term for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘The fork in the road’ is a term for doubt. ‘The left-hand road’ is a term for the eightfold wrong path, that is: wrong view … wrong immersion. ‘The right-hand road’ is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion. ‘The thick jungle’ is a term for ignorance. ‘The great low-lying marsh’ is a term for sensual pleasures. ‘The steep precipice’ is a term for anger and despair. ‘The level ground, the delightful place’ is a term for Nibbāna. Rejoice, Tissa! Rejoice, Tissa! I am here to advise, I am here to help, I am here to instruct.”
translations.sn22.84:5: “Good, good, Tissa! So it is, Tissa. Just as it is for one who is not free from greed for choices, not free from greed for consciousness, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from passion, not free from craving; with the change and alteration of that consciousness, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn22.84:6: “Good, good, Tissa! So it is, Tissa. Just as it is for one who is not free from greed for consciousness. What do you think, Tissa, for one who is free from greed for form, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from passion, free from craving; with the change and alteration of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arise?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.85:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Now at that time a bhikkhu named Yamaka had fallen into such a harmful misconception: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes when the body breaks up, and does not exist after death.”
translations.sn22.85:10: “What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata as form … feeling … perception … choices … consciousness?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn22.85:11: “What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata as this one who is without form … without feeling … without perception … without choices … without consciousness?” “No, friend.” “Then, friend Yamaka, since the Tathāgata is not to be found as a real and true entity even in this very life, is it fit for you to declare: ‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes when the body breaks up, and does not exist after death’?”
translations.sn22.85:12: “Friend Sāriputta, I used to have that harmful misconception when I was ignorant. But now that I have heard this Dhamma teaching from Venerable Sāriputta, I have given up that harmful misconception and have realized the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.85:16: They do not understand as it really is impermanent form as ‘impermanent form.’ They do not understand as it really is impermanent feeling as ‘impermanent feeling.’ They do not understand as it really is impermanent perception as ‘impermanent perception.’ They do not understand as it really is impermanent choices as ‘impermanent choices.’ They do not understand as it really is impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness.’
translations.sn22.85:19: They do not understand as it really is conditioned form as ‘conditioned form.’ They do not understand as it really is conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned choices … conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness.’
translations.sn22.85:20: They do not truly understand murderous form as ‘murderous form.’ They do not truly understand murderous feeling as ‘murderous feeling’ … murderous perception as ‘murderous perception’ … murderous choices as ‘murderous choices’ … murderous consciousness as ‘murderous consciousness.’
translations.sn22.85:21: They approach, grasp, and insist on form as ‘my self.’ They approach, grasp, and insist on feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as ‘my self.’ These five grasping aggregates, being approached and grasped, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
translations.sn22.85:23: They truly understand impermanent form as ‘impermanent form.’ They truly understand impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent choices … impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness.’
translations.sn22.85:25: They truly understand not-self form as ‘not-self form.’ They truly understand not-self feeling … not-self perception … not-self choices … not-self consciousness as ‘not-self consciousness.’
translations.sn22.85:5: When those monks were unable to dissuade the venerable Yamaka from that harmful misconception, they rose from their seats and went to the venerable Sāriputta. They said to him: ‘Friend Sāriputta, a harmful misconception has arisen in a monk named Yamaka: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes when the body breaks up, and does not exist after death.” It would be good if the venerable Sāriputta would go to the monk Yamaka out of compassion.’ The venerable Sāriputta consented by silence. Then, in the evening, the venerable Sāriputta emerged from retreat and went to the venerable Yamaka. He exchanged greetings with him … and sitting to one side, the venerable Sāriputta said to the venerable Yamaka:
translations.sn22.85:6: ‘Is it true, friend Yamaka, that such a harmful misconception has arisen in you: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, a monk whose taints are destroyed is annihilated and perishes when the body breaks up, and does not exist after death”?’ ‘Indeed, friend, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in that way.’
translations.sn22.85:9: ‘What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard the Realized One as form?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘Do you regard the Realized One as apart from form?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘Do you regard the Realized One as feeling … apart from feeling … perception … apart from perception … choices … apart from choices … consciousness?’ ‘No, friend.’ ‘Do you regard the Realized One as apart from consciousness?’ ‘No, friend.’
translations.sn22.86:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. At that time the venerable Anurādha was staying not far from the Blessed One in a forest hut. Then several wanderers of other sects went to the venerable Anurādha and exchanged greetings with him. When the polite and friendly talk was over, they sat down to one side and said to him: ‘Friend Anurādha, when a Realized One is being described—the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has reached the highest attainment—in which of these four ways is he described: “A Realized One exists after death,” “A Realized One does not exist after death,” “A Realized One both exists and does not exist after death,” or “A Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death”?’
translations.sn22.86:10: ‘What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form … feeling … perception … choices … consciousness as the Realized One?’ ‘No, sir.’
translations.sn22.86:11: ‘What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Realized One as this one who is without form … without feeling … without perception … without choices … without consciousness?’ ‘No, sir.’
translations.sn22.86:12: ‘Since, Anurādha, the Realized One is not found by you in truth and reality even in this very life, is it fitting for you to declare: “Friend, when a Realized One is being described—the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has reached the highest attainment—he is described other than these four ways: ‘A Realized One exists after death’ … ‘does not exist’ … ‘both exists and does not exist’ … ‘neither exists nor does not exist’?”’ ‘No, sir.’
translations.sn22.86:2: When this was said, the venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers of other sects: ‘Friends, when a Realized One is being described—the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has reached the highest attainment—he is described other than these four ways: “A Realized One exists after death,” “A Realized One does not exist after death,” “A Realized One both exists and does not exist after death,” or “A Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death.”’ When this was said, the wanderers of other sects said of the venerable Anurādha: ‘This monk must be new, recently ordained, or if he is an elder, he is a foolish incompetent.’ Then the wanderers of other sects, having dismissed the venerable Anurādha by calling him new and foolish, rose from their seats and left.
translations.sn22.86:3: Soon after those wanderers of other sects had left, the venerable Anurādha thought: ‘If those wanderers of other sects were to ask me further questions, how should I answer so that I speak what the Blessed One says, do not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false, explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no legitimate follow-up question would give grounds for criticism?’
translations.sn22.86:8: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Realized One as form?” “No, sir.” “Do you regard the Realized One as feeling … perception … choices … consciousness?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.86:9: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Realized One as in form?” “No, sir.” “Do you regard the Realized One as distinct from form?” “No, sir.” “Do you regard the Realized One as in feeling … distinct from feeling … in perception … distinct from perception … in choices … distinct from choices … in consciousness … distinct from consciousness?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn22.89:10: “Suppose, friends, there was the fragrance of a blue, red, or white lotus. If someone were to say: ‘The fragrance is in the petals,’ or ‘The fragrance is in the color,’ or ‘The fragrance is in the filaments,’ would they be speaking rightly?” “No, friend.” “Then how should they rightly answer?” “‘The fragrance is in the flower,’ friend, is how they should rightly answer.” “In the same way, friends, I do not say form is ‘I am,’ nor do I say ‘I am’ is distinct from form. I do not say feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is ‘I am,’ nor do I say ‘I am’ is distinct from consciousness. Yet, friends, in these five grasping aggregates I have found ‘I am,’ but I do not regard that ‘I am this.’”
translations.sn22.89:11: “Even though, friends, a noble disciple has given up the five lower fetters, they still have a residual conceit ‘I am,’ a desire ‘I am,’ an underlying tendency ‘I am’ that has not been eradicated. At a later time they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling … such is perception … such are choices … such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.’ As they meditate observing rise and fall in these five grasping aggregates, that residual conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ and underlying tendency ‘I am’ that was not eradicated is eventually pulled up.”
translations.sn22.89:12: “Suppose, friends, there was a cloth that was soiled and stained. The owners would give it to a laundryman. The laundryman would scrub it with salt, lye, or cow dung, and rinse it in clear water. Even though that cloth would be clean and bright, it would still have a residual smell of salt, lye, or cow dung that was not eradicated. The laundryman gives it back to the owners. The owners put it in a chest scented with perfume. Then that residual smell of salt, lye, or cow dung that was not eradicated is eventually pulled up. In the same way, friends, even though a noble disciple has given up the five lower fetters, they still have a residual conceit ‘I am,’ a desire ‘I am,’ an underlying tendency ‘I am’ that has not been eradicated. At a later time they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling … such is perception … such are choices … such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.’ As they meditate observing rise and fall in these five grasping aggregates, that residual conceit ‘I am,’ desire ‘I am,’ and underlying tendency ‘I am’ that was not eradicated is eventually pulled up.”
translations.sn22.89:13: When this was said, the senior mendicants said to the venerable Khemaka: “We did not ask the venerable Khemaka with the intent to trouble him. But the venerable Khemaka was capable of explaining, teaching, asserting, establishing, clarifying, analyzing, and revealing the teaching of the Blessed One in detail. And the venerable Khemaka has explained, taught, asserted, established, clarified, analyzed, and revealed the teaching of the Blessed One in detail.”
translations.sn22.90:1: At one time several senior mendicants were staying near Benares, in the Isipatana Deer Park. Then the venerable Channa, having emerged from retreat in the late afternoon, took a key and went from dwelling to dwelling, saying to the senior mendicants: “May the senior venerable ones advise me, may the senior venerable ones instruct me, may the senior venerable ones give me a Dhamma talk so that I might see the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.90:2: When this was said, the senior mendicants said to the venerable Channa: “Friend Channa, form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; choices are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is not-self. All conditions are impermanent; all things are not-self.”
translations.sn22.90:3: Then the venerable Channa thought: “I too have the thought: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is not-self. All conditions are impermanent, all things are not-self.’ But my mind does not launch into, find confidence in, settle on, or resolve on the stilling of all conditions, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, and Nibbāna. Anxiety and grasping arise; the mind turns back: ‘Then who exactly is my self?’ But this does not happen to one who sees the Dhamma. Who can teach me the Dhamma so that I might see the Dhamma?”
translations.sn22.90:4: Then the venerable Channa thought: “The venerable Ānanda is staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. He is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow practitioners. The venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma; and I have such trust in the venerable Ānanda. Why don't I go to see the venerable Ānanda?” Then the venerable Channa set his lodgings in order, took his bowl and robe, and went to Ghosita’s Park in Kosambī to see the venerable Ānanda. He exchanged greetings with the venerable Ānanda … sat down to one side, and said to the venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn22.90:8: “Even by this much we are satisfied with the venerable Channa. We hope that the venerable Channa has opened himself up and broken his barrenness. Listen, friend Channa, pay attention; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma.” Then, right then and there, a great joy and rapture arose in the venerable Channa: “It seems I am capable of understanding the Dhamma!”
translations.sn22.94:1: At Sāvatthī. “Monks, I do not dispute with the world; rather, the world disputes with me. A speaker of Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world. What is not agreed upon by the wise in the world, I also say ‘it is not.’ What is agreed upon by the wise in the world, I also say ‘it is.’
translations.sn22.94:3: And what, monks, is agreed upon by the wise in the world that I also say ‘it is’? Form, monks, is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is agreed upon by the wise in the world, and I also say ‘it is.’ Feeling is impermanent … perception … choices … consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is agreed upon by the wise in the world, and I also say ‘it is.’ This, monks, is what is agreed upon by the wise in the world that I also say ‘it is.’
translations.sn22.94:4: Monks, there is a worldly nature in the world that a Realized One has awakened to and understood. Having awakened to it and understood it, he announces it, teaches it, describes it, establishes it, reveals it, analyzes it, and makes it clear.
translations.sn22.94:7: When a Realized One is thus announcing, teaching, describing, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and making it clear, if someone does not know and does not see, what can I do for that blind, unseeing, foolish ordinary person who does not know and does not see?
translations.sn22.95:1: At one time the Buddha was staying at Ayojjhā on the bank of the Ganges River. There the Buddha addressed the monks:
translations.sn22.95:10: However it is meditated upon, and carefully examined; it is just empty and void, to one who sees it carefully.
translations.sn22.95:11: Regarding this body, taught by the one of broad wisdom; with the giving up of three things, see the form discarded.
translations.sn22.95:12: Vitality, heat, and consciousness, when they leave this body; then it lies rejected, food for others, without intention.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuity, this illusion, a deceiver of fools; it is said to be a killer, no core is found here.
translations.sn22.95:2: “Suppose, monks, that this river Ganges was carrying along a large lump of foam. A person with good eyesight would see it, meditate on it, and carefully examine it. To them, seeing it, meditating on it, and carefully examining it, it would appear to be completely empty, completely void, completely coreless. For what core could there be in a lump of foam? In the same way, monks, whatever kind of form there is—past, future, or present … far or near—a monk sees it, meditates on it, and carefully examines it. To him, seeing it, meditating on it, and carefully examining it, it appears to be completely empty, completely void, completely coreless. For what core could there be in form?
translations.sn22.95:3: Suppose, monks, that in the autumn, when the rain falls in heavy drops, a water bubble arises and bursts on the water. A person with good eyesight would see it, meditate on it, and carefully examine it. To them, seeing it, meditating on it, and carefully examining it, it would appear to be completely empty, completely void, completely coreless. For what core could there be in a water bubble? In the same way, monks, whatever kind of feeling there is—past, future, or present … far or near—a monk sees it, meditates on it, and carefully examines it. To him, seeing it, meditating on it, and carefully examining it, it appears to be completely empty, completely void, completely coreless. For what core could there be in feeling?
translations.sn22.95:4: Suppose, monks, that in the last month of summer, at high noon, a mirage flickers. A person with good eyesight would see it, meditate on it, and carefully examine it. To them, seeing it, meditating on it, and carefully examining it, it would appear to be completely empty, completely void … for what core could there be in a mirage? In the same way, monks, whatever kind of perception …
translations.sn22.95:5: Suppose, monks, that a person needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would enter a forest taking a sharp axe. There he would see a large banana tree, straight, young, and without a flower-bud. He would cut it at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut off the top; having cut off the top, he would unroll the leaf-sheaths. As he was unrolling the leaf-sheaths, he would not even find softwood, let alone heartwood. A person with good eyesight would see it, meditate on it, and carefully examine it. To them, seeing it, meditating on it, and carefully examining it, it would appear to be completely empty, completely void, completely coreless. For what core could there be in the trunk of a banana tree? In the same way, monks, whatever kind of choices there are—past, future, or present … far or near—a monk sees them, meditates on them, and carefully examines them. To him, seeing them, meditating on them, and carefully examining them, they appear to be completely empty, completely void, completely coreless. For what core could there be in choices?
translations.sn22.95:6: Suppose, bhikkhus, a magician or a magician’s apprentice would display a magic trick at a crossroads. A man with good sight would see it, contemplate it, and examine it carefully. As he sees it, contemplates it, and examines it carefully, it would appear to him as empty, appear as hollow, appear as coreless. For what core could there be in a magic trick? So too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present … far or near, a bhikkhu sees it, contemplates it, and examines it carefully. As he sees it, contemplates it, and examines it carefully, it appears to him as empty, appears as hollow, appears as coreless. For what core could there be in consciousness?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with choices … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion he is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated’ … he understands: ‘… there is no more for this state of being.’
translations.sn22.95:9: “Form is like a lump of foam, feeling like a bubble; perception is like a mirage, choices like a banana tree; and consciousness is like a magic trick, so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.”
translations.sn22.96:1: At Savatthi. Then a certain bhikkhu sat to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, is there any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same as eternity? Is there any feeling … any perception … are there any choices … is there any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same as eternity?” “Bhikkhu, there is no form … no feeling … no perception … no choices … no consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same as eternity.”
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Blessed One, picking up a small piece of cow dung in his hand, said to that bhikkhu: “Bhikkhu, there is not even this much of an acquisition of self that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same as eternity. If there were even this much of an acquisition of self that was permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because there is not even this much of an acquisition of self that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.
translations.sn22.96:3: In the past, bhikkhu, I was a kshatriya king, a head-anointed monarch. At that time, as a kshatriya king, a head-anointed monarch, I had eighty-four thousand cities, with the royal capital of Kusavati at their head. I had eighty-four thousand palaces, with the Dhamma Palace at their head. I had eighty-four thousand gabled halls, with the Great Complex gabled hall at their head. I had eighty-four thousand couches made of ivory, heartwood, and gold, spread with rugs of long fleece, white woolen rugs, embroidered rugs, rugs of choice antelope hide, with canopies above and red cushions at both ends. I had eighty-four thousand elephants with gold ornaments, gold banners, and covered with gold nets, with the state elephant Uposatha at their head. I had eighty-four thousand horses with gold ornaments, gold banners, and covered with gold nets, with the horse-king Valahaka at their head. I had eighty-four thousand chariots with gold ornaments, gold banners, and covered with gold nets, with the Vejayanta chariot at their head. I had eighty-four thousand gems, with the jewel-gem at their head. I had eighty-four thousand women, with Queen Subhadda at their head. I had eighty-four thousand kshatriya retainers, with the wheel-turning monarch's counselor at their head. I had eighty-four thousand cows with silken tethers and bronze milk-pails. I had eighty-four thousand crores of garments of fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, and fine cotton. I had eighty-four thousand servings of food brought to me evening and morning.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Blessed One, placing a small amount of soil on the tip of his fingernail, said to that bhikkhu: “Bhikkhu, there is not even this much form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same as eternity. If there were even this much form that was permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, then this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be discerned. But because there is not even this much form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is discerned.”
translations.sn35.101:4: “Suppose, bhikkhus, people were to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta Grove, or burn them, or do with them as they wish. Would you think: ‘People are carrying us off, or burning us, or doing with us as they wish’?”
translations.sn35.116:2: Then those monks thought: “This venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise spiritual companions. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, which he has not explained in detail. What if we were to approach the venerable Ānanda and ask him about this matter?”
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those monks approached the venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those monks said to the venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn35.116:5: “Friends, it is as if a man seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to pass over the root and the trunk of a great standing tree possessing heartwood, and think that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and foliage. So it is with the venerable ones: though you were face to face with the Teacher, you passed over the Blessed One and think that we should be asked about this matter. For, friends, the Blessed One is the one who knows, he knows; the one who sees, he sees—he is vision, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata. That was the time when you should have asked the Blessed One himself about this matter. As the Blessed One explained it to you, so you should have remembered it.”
translations.sn35.116:6: “Surely, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One is the one who knows, he knows; the one who sees, he sees—he is vision, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata. That was indeed the time when we should have asked the Blessed One himself about this matter. As the Blessed One explained it to us, so we would have remembered it. However, the venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise spiritual companions. Venerable Ānanda is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, which he has not explained in detail. Let the venerable Ānanda explain it, if it is not a trouble.”
translations.sn35.116:7: “Then, friends, listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda. The venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn35.116:9: “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda. Then they rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn35.117:1: “Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta, it occurred to me: ‘Those five cords of sensual pleasure which I previously experienced with my mind, which have passed, ceased, and changed—toward them my mind might frequently go, or slightly toward those in the present, or toward those in the future.’ Then, bhikkhus, it occurred to me: ‘Those five cords of sensual pleasure which I previously experienced with my mind, which have passed, ceased, and changed—there I must practice diligence, mindfulness, and protection of the mind for my own sake.’ Therefore, bhikkhus, for you too, those five cords of sensual pleasure which you previously experienced with your minds, which have passed, ceased, and changed—toward them your minds might frequently go, or slightly toward those in the present, or toward those in the future. Therefore, bhikkhus, for you too, those five cords of sensual pleasure which you previously experienced with your minds, which have passed, ceased, and changed—there you must practice diligence, mindfulness, and protection of the mind for your own sakes. Therefore, bhikkhus, that dimension should be known where the eye ceases and the perception of forms ceases; that dimension should be known ... where the tongue ceases and the perception of tastes ceases; that dimension should be known ... where the mind ceases and the perception of mental phenomena ceases; that dimension should be known.” Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.sn35.118:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain. Then Sakka, the lord of devas, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing there, Sakka, the lord of devas, said to the Blessed One: “What is the cause, bhante, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? And what is the cause, bhante, what is the reason why some beings here do attain final Nibbāna in this very life?”
translations.sn35.118:2: “There are, Lord of Devas, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains fastened to them, his consciousness becomes dependent on them and clings to them. A bhikkhu with clinging, Lord of Devas, does not attain final Nibbāna ...
translations.sn35.118:3: There are, Lord of Devas, tastes cognizable by the tongue ... there are, Lord of Devas, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains fastened to them, his consciousness becomes dependent on them and clings to them. A bhikkhu with clinging, Lord of Devas, does not attain final Nibbāna. This is the cause, Lord of Devas, this is the reason why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life.
translations.sn35.118:4: But there are, Lord of Devas, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain fastened to them, his consciousness does not become dependent on them and does not cling to them. A bhikkhu without clinging, Lord of Devas, attains final Nibbāna ...”
translations.sn35.127:1: At one time the venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja was staying at Kosambi in Ghosita’s Park. Then King Udena went to the venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, King Udena said to the venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja: “What is the cause, Master Bhāradvāja, what is the reason why these young monks—youthful, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, without having indulged in sensual pleasures—practice the complete and pure spiritual life for as long as they live, and carry it through to the end?” “Great king, this was said by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One: ‘Come, monks, toward women of an age to be your mother, establish the thought of a mother; toward women of an age to be your sister, establish the thought of a sister; toward women of an age to be your daughter, establish the thought of a daughter.’ This is the cause, great king, this is the reason why these young monks... practice the complete and pure spiritual life for as long as they live, and carry it through to the end.”
translations.sn35.127:2: “The mind is fickle, Master Bhāradvāja. Sometimes states of greed arise even toward those of an age to be one’s mother, or sister, or daughter. Is there another cause, Master Bhāradvāja, another reason why these young monks... carry it through to the end?”
translations.sn35.127:3: “Great king, this was said by the Blessed One... ‘Come, monks, review this very body upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the top of the hair, enclosed by skin, full of many kinds of impurities: there are in this body hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, contents of the stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, and urine.’ This too, great king, is the cause... why these young monks... carry it through to the end.” “Master Bhāradvāja, for those monks who are developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, and developed in wisdom, that is easy to do. But for those monks who are undeveloped in body, virtue, mind, and wisdom, that is difficult to do. Sometimes, Master Bhāradvāja, when one thinks, ‘I will attend to it as unattractive,’ it actually comes to be seen as attractive. Is there another cause, Master Bhāradvāja, another reason why these young monks... carry it through to the end?”
translations.sn35.127:4: “Great king, this was said by the Blessed One... ‘Come, monks, live with the doors of your sense faculties guarded. Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if you leave the eye faculty unguarded, evil unskillful states of covetousness and displeasure might invade you, practice for its restraint. Guard the eye faculty; undertake the restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... Having smelled an odor with the nose... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having felt a touch with the body... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if you leave the mind faculty unguarded, evil unskillful states of covetousness and displeasure might invade you, practice for its restraint. Guard the mind faculty; undertake the restraint of the mind faculty.’ This too, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young monks—youthful, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, without having indulged in sensual pleasures—practice the complete and pure spiritual life for as long as they live, and carry it through to the end.”
translations.sn35.136:2: “Forms, sounds, tastes, and smells, touches and mental phenomena—the whole lot; desirable, lovely, and agreeable, as long as it is said ‘they exist.’
translations.sn35.136:3: For the world with its gods, these are considered a source of happiness; but where these cease, that is considered suffering by them.
translations.sn35.136:4: The cessation of the existing body is seen as happiness by the noble ones; this is the opposite of how it is seen by the whole world.
translations.sn35.136:5: What others call happiness, the noble ones call suffering; what others call suffering, the noble ones know as happiness.
translations.sn35.136:6: See the Dhamma so hard to understand! The ignorant are confused herein; for those who are hindered, it is darkness, a blackness for those who do not see.
translations.sn35.136:7: But for the good it is revealed, like light for those who see; though it is near, they do not understand it—fools unskilled in the Dhamma.
translations.sn35.136:8: By those overcome by lust for existence, who follow the stream of existence, who have entered the realm of Mara, this Dhamma is not easily awakened to.”
translations.sn35.63:1: At Savatthi. Then the venerable Migajala went to the Blessed One... Sitting to one side, the venerable Migajala said to the Blessed One: “‘One who dwells alone, one who dwells alone,’ it is said, bhante. How far, bhante, is one a ‘dweller alone,’ and how far is one a ‘dweller with a companion’?”
translations.sn35.69:1: At one time the venerable Sariputta and the venerable Upasena were staying at Rajagaha in the Cool Grove at the Snake’s Hood Grotto. Now at that time a venomous snake had fallen on the venerable Upasena’s body. Then the venerable Upasena addressed the monks: “Come, friends, lift this body onto a bed and carry it outside. Before this body is scattered right here like a handful of chaff.”
translations.sn35.74:1: At Savatthi. Then a certain monk went to the Blessed One... Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, in such and such a dwelling there is a certain monk, new and unknown, who is sick, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, bhante, if the Blessed One would go to that monk out of compassion.”
translations.sn35.74:12: “Good, good, monk! It is good, monk, that you understand the Dhamma taught by me for the purpose of the fading away of lust. For the Dhamma is taught by me, monk, for the purpose of the fading away of lust. What do you think, monk, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”
translations.sn35.74:18: “But is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
translations.sn35.74:2: Then the Blessed One, having heard that he was a new monk and sick, and knowing that he was an undistinguished monk, went to that monk. That monk saw the Blessed One coming from afar and tried to stir on his bed. Then the Blessed One said to that monk: 'Enough, monk, do not stir on your bed. There are these seats prepared, I will sit there.' The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to that monk: 'I hope you are keeping well, monk, I hope you are getting by, I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is evident, not their increase?'
translations.sn35.74:3: 'I am not keeping well, Bhante, I am not getting by. My painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is evident, not their subsiding.'
translations.sn35.75:7: 'Bhante, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging.'
translations.sn35.75:8: 'Good, good, monk! It is good, monk, that you understand the Dhamma taught by me to be for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging. For indeed, monk, the Dhamma is taught by me for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging.'
translations.sn35.88:1: Then the venerable Puṇṇa went to the Blessed One; having approached ... sitting to one side, the venerable Puṇṇa said to the Blessed One: 'Bhante, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.'
translations.sn35.88:12: 'If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a stick, then I will think: "These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, these people of Sunāparanta are truly very kind, in that they do not give me a blow with a weapon." In this way, Blessed One, it will be; in this way, Sugata, it will be.'
translations.sn35.88:14: 'If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a weapon, then I will think: "These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, these people of Sunāparanta are truly very kind, in that they do not take my life with a sharp weapon." In this way, Blessed One, it will be; in this way, Sugata, it will be.'
translations.sn35.88:16: 'If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta take my life with a sharp weapon, then I will think: "There are disciples of the Blessed One who, being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted by the body and by life, seek an executioner; but I have found an executioner without even having to seek one." In this way, Blessed One, it will be; in this way, Sugata, it will be.'
translations.sn35.88:17: 'Good, good, Puṇṇa! Possessing such self-control and peace, you will be able to live in the Sunāparanta country. Now, Puṇṇa, you may go when you think it is the right time.'
translations.sn35.88:18: Then the venerable Puṇṇa, having rejoiced and appreciated the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, set his lodgings in order, took his bowl and robes, and set out on a journey toward the Sunāparanta country. Wandering by stages, he arrived at the Sunāparanta country. There the venerable Puṇṇa lived in the Sunāparanta country. Then, within that same rainy season, the venerable Puṇṇa established about five hundred male lay followers. Within that same rainy season, he established about five hundred female lay followers. Within that same rainy season, he realized the three knowledges. Within that same rainy season, he attained final Nibbāna.
translations.sn35.88:19: Then many monks went to the Blessed One ... sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: 'Bhante, that clansman named Puṇṇa, who was exhorted by the Blessed One with a brief exhortation, has died. What is his destination? What is his future state?'
translations.sn35.88:4: 'Now that you have been exhorted by me with this brief exhortation, Puṇṇa, in which country will you live?' 'Bhante, there is a country named Sunāparanta; I will live there.'
translations.sn35.88:5: 'Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta are fierce; Puṇṇa, the people of Sunāparanta are rough. If the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile you, Puṇṇa, what will you think then?'
translations.sn35.88:6: 'If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, then I will think: "These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, these people of Sunāparanta are truly very kind, in that they do not give me a blow with the hand." In this way, Blessed One, it will be; in this way, Sugata, it will be.'
translations.sn35.88:8: 'If, Bhante, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with the hand, then I will think: "These people of Sunāparanta are truly kind, these people of Sunāparanta are truly very kind, in that they do not give me a blow with a clod of earth." In this way, Blessed One, it will be; in this way, Sugata, it will be.'
translations.sn35.95:1: Then the venerable Mālukyaputta went to the Blessed One ... sitting to one side, the venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: 'Bhante, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.'
translations.sn35.95:10: 'In that case, Mālukyaputta, regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will be merely the seen, in the heard there will be merely the heard, in the sensed there will be merely the sensed, in the cognized there will be merely the cognized. When, Mālukyaputta, for you, in the seen there will be merely the seen, in the heard merely the heard, in the sensed merely the sensed, and in the cognized merely the cognized, then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be "by that." When, Mālukyaputta, you are not "by that," then you will not be "in that." When, Mālukyaputta, you are not "in that," then, Mālukyaputta, you will be neither here nor beyond nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering.'
translations.sn35.95:12: Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost, as one attends to the pleasing sign; one experiences it with a lustful mind, and remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:13: Their feelings grow, many born of the form; greed and annoyance, their mind is harmed; for one who thus accumulates suffering, Nibbāna is said to be far away.
translations.sn35.95:14: Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost, as one attends to the pleasing sign; one experiences it with a lustful mind, and remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:16: Having smelled an odor, mindfulness is lost, as one attends to the pleasing sign; one experiences it with a lustful mind, and remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted a flavor, mindfulness is lost, as one gives attention to a pleasing sign; one experiences it with an infatuated mind, and remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:2: “Now, Mālukyaputta, what should I say to the young bhikkhus? For you, bhikkhu, are old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, and have reached the final stage of life, yet you ask for an exhortation in brief.”
translations.sn35.95:20: Having felt a touch, mindfulness is lost, as one gives attention to a pleasing sign; one experiences it with an infatuated mind, and remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:22: Having known an idea, mindfulness is lost, as one gives attention to a pleasing sign; one experiences it with an infatuated mind, and remains clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:24: He is not lustful for forms, having seen a form with mindfulness established; he experiences it with a mind free from lust, and does not remain clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:25: As he sees a form, and even as he experiences the feeling, it is exhausted and not accumulated; thus he lives mindful. For one thus diminishing suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:26: He is not lustful for sounds, having heard a sound with mindfulness established; he experiences it with a mind free from lust, and does not remain clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:27: As he hears a sound, and even as he experiences the feeling, it is exhausted and not accumulated; thus he lives mindful. For one thus diminishing suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:28: He is not lustful for odors, having smelled an odor with mindfulness established; he experiences it with a mind free from lust, and does not remain clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:3: “Even though, bhante, I am old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, and have reached the final stage of life, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, let the Sugata teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that I might understand the meaning of the Blessed One's words. Perhaps I might become an heir to the Blessed One's words.”
translations.sn35.95:30: He is not lustful for flavors, having tasted a flavor with mindfulness established; he experiences it with a mind free from lust, and does not remain clinging to it.
translations.sn35.95:35: As he knows an idea, and even as he experiences the feeling, it is exhausted and not accumulated; thus he lives mindful. For one thus diminishing suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:36: “Bhante, I understand the detailed meaning of what the Blessed One has said in brief in this way.” “Excellent, excellent, Mālukyaputta! It is good, Mālukyaputta, that you understand the detailed meaning of what I have said in brief.”
translations.sn35.95:4: “What do you think, Mālukyaputta, regarding those forms cognizable by the eye that you have not seen, have never seen before, do not see now, and do not think you might see: do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “No, bhante.”
translations.sn35.95:9: “Regarding those ideas cognizable by the mind that you have not known, have never known before, do not know now, and do not think you might know: do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “No, bhante.”
translations.sn36.19:12: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the dimension of infinite space, enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness, thinking 'consciousness is infinite.' This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the supreme peace, pleasure, and joy that can be experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:15: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:7: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the supreme peace, pleasure, and joy that can be experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:8: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the supreme peace, pleasure, and joy that can be experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:9: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: 'He dwells happily, with equanimity and mindfulness,' as he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the supreme peace, pleasure, and joy that can be experienced'—I do not grant them that. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and sublime than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.21:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'Whatever a person experiences, whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past.' What does Master Gotama say about this?”
translations.sn36.21:2: “Sīvaka, some feelings arise here originating from bile. You can know for yourself that some feelings arise originating from bile. It is also accepted as true by the world that some feelings arise originating from bile. In this matter, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who have such a doctrine and view: ‘Whatever a person experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—all that is caused by what was done in the past,’ they overreach what is known by themselves and they overreach what is accepted as true by the world. Therefore, I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.”
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! … Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.”
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain bhikkhu went to the Blessed One, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the practice leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feeling?”
translations.sn36.31:2: “And what, bhikkhus, is spiritual joy? Here, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. This is called spiritual joy.”
translations.sn36.31:3: “And what, bhikkhus, is joy more spiritual than the spiritual? The joy that arises in a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed as he reviews his mind liberated from greed, reviews his mind liberated from hatred, and reviews his mind liberated from delusion: this is called joy more spiritual than the spiritual.”
translations.sn36.31:5: “And what, bhikkhus, is spiritual happiness? Here, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna … With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna … With the fading away as well of rapture, he dwells equanimous, and mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells happily.’ This is called spiritual happiness.”
translations.sn36.31:6: “And what, bhikkhus, is happiness more spiritual than the spiritual? The happiness and gladness that arises in a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed as he reviews his mind liberated from greed, reviews his mind liberated from hatred, and reviews his mind liberated from delusion: this is called happiness more spiritual than the spiritual.”
translations.sn36.31:8: “And what, bhikkhus, is spiritual equanimity? Here, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and dejection, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness and equanimity. This is called spiritual equanimity.”
translations.sn36.31:9: “And what, bhikkhus, is equanimity more spiritual than the spiritual? The equanimity that arises in a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed as he reviews his mind liberated from greed, reviews his mind liberated from hatred, and reviews his mind liberated from delusion: this is called equanimity more spiritual than the spiritual.”
translations.sn36.4:2: “One who does not endure them, when painful feelings have arisen; bodily feelings that take away life, touched by which one trembles.”
translations.sn36.4:3: “He wails and weeps, weak and lacking strength; he does not stand up against the abyss, nor does he find a foothold.”
translations.sn36.6:2: “But, bhikkhus, when the instructed noble disciple is touched by a painful feeling, he does not sorrow, grieve, or lament; he does not weep beating his breast and become distraught. He feels one feeling—a bodily one, not a mental one.”
translations.sn36.6:4: “The wise one does not feel the feeling, whether pleasant or painful, though he is learned; this is the great difference between the wise one and the ordinary person, for the one who is skilled.”
translations.sn36.6:5: “For the learned one who has understood the Dhamma, seeing clearly this world and the next; desirable things do not churn his mind, nor does he feel aversion toward the undesirable.”
translations.sn36.7:3: “And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and dejection concerning the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … he dwells contemplating mind in mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and dejection concerning the world. This is how a bhikkhu is mindful.”
translations.sn36.7:4: “And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu clearly comprehending? Here, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; when looking ahead and looking aside; when bending and stretching his limbs; when wearing his robes and carrying his outer robe and bowl; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when defecating and urinating; when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent. This is how a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension. A bhikkhu should await his time mindful and clearly comprehending. This is our instruction to you.”
translations.sn36.7:5: If, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is dwelling mindful, clearly comprehending, diligent, ardent, and resolute, a pleasant feeling arises in him, he understands: ‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. It is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is inconstant, conditioned, dependently arisen. Now, when the pleasant feeling has arisen dependent on a body that is inconstant, conditioned, and dependently arisen, how could it be constant?’ He dwells contemplating inconstancy in the body and in pleasant feeling, contemplating vanishing, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. As he dwells contemplating inconstancy, vanishing, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment in the body and in pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to lust for the body and for pleasant feeling is abandoned.
