translations.sn36.7:8: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is inconstant,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling … If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is inconstant,’ he understands: ‘It is not held to,’ he understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached; if he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached; if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. When feeling a feeling limited to the body, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to the body.’ When feeling a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘With the breaking up of the body, after the end of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’
translations.sn4.13:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi Deer Park. Now at that time the Blessed One’s foot had been cut by a splinter. Severe painful bodily feelings arose in the Blessed One—sharp, piercing, racking, unpleasant, and disagreeable. The Blessed One endured them, mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded in four, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.13:2: “Do you lie there in a stupor, or are you drunk on poetry? Are your goals so few? Alone in a secluded lodging, why this sleepy face, why do you sleep?”
translations.sn4.13:3: “I do not lie in a stupor, nor am I drunk on poetry. Having reached my goal, I am free from sorrow. Alone in a secluded lodging, I lie down full of compassion for all beings.
translations.sn4.13:4: Even those with a thorn stuck in their chest, piercing the heart again and again, even they can find sleep; therefore I, with the thorn removed, can sleep.
translations.sn4.13:5: I do not worry while awake, nor do I fear to sleep. The nights and days do not burn me. I see no loss anywhere in the world; therefore I sleep full of compassion for all beings.”
translations.sn4.18:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Magadhans at the brahmin village of Pañcasālā. Now at that time a festival for young girls was being held in the brahmin village of Pañcasālā. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms. Now at that time the brahmin householders of Pañcasālā were possessed by Māra the Evil One: “Don't let the ascetic Gotama get any alms.”
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Blessed One entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms with his bowl as clean as it was when he entered, and he left with his bowl just as clean. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One and said to him: “Did you get any alms, ascetic?” “Did you, Evil One, see to it that I didn't get any alms?” “Then, bhante, let the Blessed One enter the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms a second time. I will see to it that the Blessed One gets alms.”
translations.sn4.19:4: “Those who say ‘this is mine,’ and those who say ‘it is me’; if your mind is there, ascetic, you won't escape me.”
translations.sn4.19:5: “What they speak of is not mine; those who speak are not me. Know this, Evil One: you won't even see my path.”
translations.sn4.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan Tree, having just attained supreme enlightenment. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: “I am indeed free from that difficult practice. I am well freed from that useless difficult practice. I am well freed and have reached enlightenment.”
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Evil One, knowing the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind, approached the Blessed One and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: “Having turned away from the practice of austerities by which young men are purified, you, impure, think you are pure; you have missed the path to purity.”
translations.sn4.1:6: “Developing virtue, concentration, and wisdom, the path to enlightenment, I have reached supreme purity. You are defeated, Ender!”
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The Blessed One knows me, the Fortunate One knows me,” sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.
translations.sn4.20:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Kosalans in a forest hut in the Himalayan region. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: “Is it possible to exercise kingship righteously, without killing or causing to kill, without conquering or causing to conquer, without sorrowing or causing sorrow?”
translations.sn4.20:3: “Even a whole mountain of gold, of solid bullion, would not be enough for one person; knowing this, one should live accordingly.
translations.sn4.20:4: He who has seen suffering and its source, how could that person incline toward sensual pleasures? Having understood acquisition as a bond in the world, a person should train for its removal.”
translations.sn4.21:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying among the Sakyans at Silāvatī. Now at that time several mendicants were staying not far from the Buddha, diligent, keen, and resolute. Then Māra the Wicked, having disguised himself as a brahmin with a large matted topknot, wearing an antelope skin, old, crooked like a roof-rafter, breathing heavily, and holding a staff of cluster-fig wood, approached those mendicants and said to them: “You are young, sirs, gone forth, youthful, black-haired, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, without having played with sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures, sirs. Do not abandon what is visible here and now to chase after what is subject to time.” “Brahmin, we do not abandon what is visible here and now to chase after what is subject to time. We abandon what is subject to time to chase after what is visible here and now. For the Buddha has said that sensual pleasures are subject to time, full of suffering and despair, and their danger is great. But this Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.” When this was said, Māra the Wicked shook his head, lolled his tongue, knitted his brow into three furrows, and leaning on his staff, departed.
translations.sn4.24:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Uruvelā on the bank of the Neranjara River at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree. Now at that time Māra the Wicked had been following the Buddha for seven years, looking for a lapse but not finding one. Then Māra the Wicked approached the Buddha and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: “Having found no satisfaction there, the crow departed from the stone. Like the crow attacking the rock, we leave Gotama disappointed.”
translations.sn4.24:2: “Are you overwhelmed by sorrow that you meditate in the forest? Have you lost your wealth, or do you pine for it? Have you committed some crime in the village? Why don't you make friends with people? Can you not find a friend in anyone?”
translations.sn4.24:3: “Having dug up the root of sorrow entirely, I meditate sorrowless and guiltless. Having cut off all longing and greed for existence, I meditate, O kinsman of the negligent, free from defilements.”
translations.sn4.24:6: “If you have discovered the path, the secure way to the Deathless, then go and walk it alone. Why do you instruct others?”
translations.sn4.24:7: “When people who are crossing to the far shore ask about the realm of Death, being asked, I explain to them the truth that is free from acquisitions.”
translations.sn4.24:8: “Sir, suppose there was a lotus pond not far from a village or town. Therein lived a crab. Then several boys or girls would come out from that village or town and go to that pond. They would pull the crab out of the water and place it on dry land. And whenever that crab extended a claw, those boys or girls would cut it off, break it, and smash it with a stick or a stone. Thus that crab, with all its claws cut off, broken, and smashed, would be unable to descend into that pond again. In the same way, sir, whatever distortions, deceptions, and writhings I had, all of them have been cut off, broken, and smashed by the Buddha. Now I am unable to approach the Buddha again looking for a lapse.” Then Māra the Wicked recited these verses of disillusionment in the presence of the Buddha:
translations.sn4.24:9: “A crow circled a stone that looked like a piece of fat, thinking: ‘Perhaps I’ll find something tender here, perhaps there is something tasty.’
translations.sn4.25:10: ‘The Arahant, the Sugata in the world, is not easily led by passion. He has transcended the realm of Māra; therefore I grieve so much.’
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, approached the Buddha and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Taṇhā, the daughter of Māra, addressed the Buddha in verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: “Having attained the goal, the peace of heart, and having conquered the army of pleasant forms, meditating alone, I realized happiness. Therefore I do not make friends with people; I have no need for friends.”
translations.sn4.25:16: “How does a mendicant usually live here, who has crossed the five floods and now crosses the sixth? How does one meditate so that sensual perceptions are kept at bay and do not get a hold?”
translations.sn4.25:17: “With body tranquil and mind well-released, not constructing anything, mindful, homeless; knowing the Dhamma, meditating without thought-conception, he does not get angry, he does not remember, he is not sluggish.”
translations.sn4.25:2: “Why are you downcast, father? For what man do you grieve? We will catch him with the snare of passion, like an elephant in the wild. We will bind him and bring him back; he will be under your control.”
translations.sn4.25:20: “Having cut off craving, many who are faithful will surely walk as a group. Many people, leaving their homes, will cut through and go to the far shore of the King of Death.”
translations.sn4.25:23: “Fools! You try to crush a mountain with lily stalks! You dig up a hill with your fingernails! You chew iron with your teeth!
translations.sn4.25:24: As if trying to move a rock with your head, or seeking a footing in the abyss, or striking a pillar with your chest—you leave Gotama disappointed.”
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, approached the Buddha and said to him: “We would serve at your feet, ascetic.” But the Buddha paid no attention, as he was released in the supreme ending of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, withdrew to one side and thought: “Men’s tastes are diverse. What if we each manifest as a hundred young girls?” Then Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, the daughters of Māra, each manifested as a hundred young girls and approached the Buddha, saying: “We would serve at your feet, ascetic.” But the Buddha paid no attention to that either, as he was released in the supreme ending of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.8:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then Māra the Wicked approached the Buddha and recited this verse in his presence:
translations.sn4.8:2: “One with children rejoices in children. One with cattle rejoices in cattle. Acquisitions are a person’s joy. One without acquisitions does not rejoice.”
translations.sn4.8:3: “One with children grieves because of children, and likewise a cattle-owner because of cattle. For acquisitions are a man's grief; one without acquisitions does not grieve.”
translations.sn44.1:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's monastery. Now at that time the nun Khema, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans, had taken up residence at Toranavatthu between Savatthi and Saketa. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, traveling from Saketa to Savatthi, took up a one-night residence at Toranavatthu between Saketa and Savatthi. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man: “Come, my good man, find out if there is any such ascetic or brahmin in Toranavatthu whom I might visit today.”
translations.sn44.1:2: “Yes, sire,” that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala, and after wandering through the whole of Toranavatthu, he did not see any such ascetic or brahmin whom King Pasenadi of Kosala might visit. But that man saw the nun Khema residing in Toranavatthu. Seeing her, he went to King Pasenadi of Kosala and said to him:
translations.sn44.1:3: “Sire, there is no such ascetic or brahmin in Toranavatthu whom your majesty might visit. But, sire, there is a nun named Khema, a disciple of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Now, a good reputation has spread concerning that lady: ‘She is wise, experienced, intelligent, learned, a fluent speaker, and of fine ready wit.’ Let your majesty visit her.”
translations.sn44.1:6: “In that case, Great King, I will ask you back about this same matter. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, Great King? Do you have any accountant, or calculator, or mathematician who is able to count the sand in the Ganges—saying there are so many grains of sand, or so many hundreds of grains of sand, or so many thousands of grains of sand, or so many hundreds of thousands of grains of sand?” “No, lady.” “Do you have any accountant, or calculator, or mathematician who is able to count the water in the great ocean—saying there are so many measures of water, or so many hundreds of measures of water, or so many thousands of measures of water, or so many hundreds of thousands of measures of water?” “No, lady.” “Why is that?” “Lady, the ocean is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom.” “Even so, Great King, that form by which one describing the Tathagata might describe him has been abandoned by the Tathagata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. The Tathagata, Great King, is released from the designation of form; he is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom—just like the great ocean. ‘The Tathagata exists after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathagata does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathagata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathagata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.
translations.sn44.1:9: That consciousness by which one describing the Tathagata might describe him has been abandoned by the Tathagata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. The Tathagata, Great King, is released from the designation of consciousness; he is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom—just like the great ocean. ‘The Tathagata exists after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathagata does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathagata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘The Tathagata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having rejoiced and appreciated the words of the nun Khema, rose from his seat, bowed to the nun Khema, and keeping her on his right, departed.
translations.sn45.1:2: “Ignorance, bhikkhus, is the forerunner in the entry into unwholesome states, followed by lack of shame and lack of moral dread. For an unwise person immersed in ignorance, wrong view arises; for one of wrong view, wrong intention arises; for one of wrong intention, wrong speech arises; for one of wrong speech, wrong action arises; for one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises; for one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; for one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises; for one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.”
translations.sn45.2:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka. Then the Venerable Ananda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ananda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, this is half of the holy life, that is, good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.”
translations.sn45.2:2: “Not so, Ananda! Not so, Ananda! This is the entire holy life, Ananda, that is, good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship. When a bhikkhu has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, it is to be expected that he will develop the Noble Eightfold Path, that he will cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
translations.sn45.2:3: And how, Ananda, does a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, develop the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path? Here, Ananda, a bhikkhu develops right view, which is based upon seclusion, based upon dispassion, based upon cessation, maturing in release; he develops right intention... right speech... right action... right livelihood... right effort... right mindfulness... he develops right concentration, which is based upon seclusion, based upon dispassion, based upon cessation, maturing in release. It is in this way, Ananda, that a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, develops the Noble Eightfold Path and cultivates the Noble Eightfold Path.”
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, in the morning, the venerable Ānanda dressed, and taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. The venerable Ānanda saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi leaving Sāvatthī in a chariot drawn by all-white mares. The horses yoked to it were white, with white ornaments; the chariot was white, with white fittings; the reins were white, the goad-stick was white, the parasol was white, the turban was white, the clothes were white, the sandals were white, and he was being fanned with a white yak-tail fan. When people saw this, they said: “What a divine vehicle, sir! What a divine-looking vehicle, sir!”
translations.sn45.4:10: Non-ill will and non-harming, and seclusion are his weapons; patience is his armor: he proceeds toward security from bondage.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then the venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, returned from his alms round after his meal and went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: “It is possible, Ānanda,” the Blessed One said. “This is a designation for this very Noble Eightfold Path: ‘the divine vehicle,’ and also ‘the Dhamma vehicle,’ and also ‘the unsurpassed victory in battle.’
translations.sn45.4:8: “For whom faith and wisdom are always yoked together as the pole; shame is the shaft, mind is the yoke-tie, and mindfulness is the watchful charioteer.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot is equipped with virtue, the axle is jhāna, energy is the wheels; equanimity is the pole-balance, and desirelessness is the upholstery.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Noble Eightfold Path and I will analyze it. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this, bhikkhus, is called right view.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-harming—this, bhikkhus, is called right intention.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this, bhikkhus, is called right speech.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from unchastity—this, bhikkhus, is called right action.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having given up wrong livelihood, earns his living by right livelihood—this, bhikkhus, is called right livelihood.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right effort? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire ... for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire ... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states—this, bhikkhus, is called right effort.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what, bhikkhus, is right mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world—this, bhikkhus, is called right mindfulness.
translations.sn46.11:1: “Just as, bhikkhus, whatever living beings perform the four postures—walking at times, standing at times, sitting at times, lying down at times—all of them do so by depending on the earth, by standing on the earth; even so, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, depending on virtue, standing on virtue, develops the seven factors of enlightenment, cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment.
translations.sn46.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. At that time the venerable Mahākassapa was staying at the Pipphali Cave, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, went to the venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to the venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: “I hope you are bearing up, Kassapa, I hope you are getting by. I hope your painful feelings are receding and not increasing; that their receding is evident and not their increasing?” “Bhante, I am not bearing up, I am not getting by. My painful feelings are increasing and not receding; their increasing is evident and not their receding.”
translations.sn46.29:2: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness based on seclusion ... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity based on seclusion, based on fading away, based on cessation, ripening in relinquishment. When the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and cultivated in this way, they lead to the abandoning of things that fetter.
translations.sn46.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhans at a town of the Sumbhans named Setaka. Then the venerable Udāyī went to the Blessed One ... sitting to one side, the venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: “It’s incredible, sir, it’s amazing! How much love, respect, conscience, and prudence I have for the Blessed One. For in the past, sir, when I was a householder, I did not have much regard for the Dhamma or the Saṅgha. But seeing that love, respect, conscience, and prudence for the Blessed One, I went forth from the home life into homelessness. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling … such is perception … such are choices … such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away.’
translations.sn46.30:3: Then, sir, while I was in an empty hut, turning over these five grasping aggregates inside and out, I truly understood: ‘This is suffering’; I truly understood: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I truly understood: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I truly understood: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ I have comprehended the Dhamma and attained the path. When I develop and cultivate it, it will lead me to the state where I will live knowing: ‘Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to this state of existence.’
translations.sn46.38:1: “Mendicants, at a time when a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma, paying attention, applying their whole mind, and lending an ear, at that time the five hindrances are not present in them. At that time the seven awakening factors go to the fulfillment of their development.”
translations.sn46.3:1: “Mendicants, those monks who are accomplished in ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom—I say that even the sight of those monks is very helpful. I say that even the hearing of those monks is very helpful. I say that even the approaching of those monks is very helpful. I say that even the attending on those monks is very helpful. I say that even the recollection of those monks is very helpful. I say that even the following in their going forth is very helpful. Why is that? Because, mendicants, having heard the Dhamma from such monks, one lives withdrawn in two ways: by withdrawal of the body and withdrawal of the mind. Living thus withdrawn, one recollects and thinks about that Dhamma.
translations.sn46.3:2: At a time when a monk, living thus withdrawn, recollects and thinks about that Dhamma, the awakening factor of mindfulness is aroused in that monk; at that time the monk develops the awakening factor of mindfulness; at that time the awakening factor of mindfulness goes to the fulfillment of its development. Living thus mindfully, he investigates, examines, and applies scrutiny to that Dhamma with wisdom.
translations.sn46.51:20: And what, mendicants, is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of energy, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of energy once it has arisen? There are, mendicants, the element of initiative, the element of persistence, and the element of exertion. Frequent lack of attention there—this is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of energy, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of energy once it has arisen.
translations.sn46.51:21: And what, mendicants, is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of rapture, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of rapture once it has arisen? There are, mendicants, things that are the basis for the awakening factor of rapture. Frequent lack of attention there—this is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of rapture, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of rapture once it has arisen.
translations.sn46.51:22: And what, mendicants, is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of tranquility, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of tranquility once it has arisen? There are, mendicants, tranquility of the body and tranquility of the mind. Frequent lack of attention there—this is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of tranquility, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of tranquility once it has arisen.
translations.sn46.51:23: And what, mendicants, is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of immersion, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of immersion once it has arisen? There are, mendicants, the sign of serenity and the sign of non-distraction. Frequent lack of attention there—this is the lack of food for the arising of the awakening factor of immersion, or for the fulfillment of the development of the awakening factor of immersion once it has arisen.
translations.sn46.52:1: Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then those mendicants thought: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. Why don’t we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.52:10: And what, mendicants, is the method by which the seven awakening factors become fourteen? When there is mindfulness of internal qualities, that is the awakening factor of mindfulness. When there is mindfulness of external qualities, that too is the awakening factor of mindfulness. Thus, what is designated as ‘the awakening factor of mindfulness’ becomes two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:11: When one investigates, examines, and applies scrutiny to internal qualities with wisdom, that is the awakening factor of investigation of qualities. When one investigates, examines, and applies scrutiny to external qualities with wisdom, that too is the awakening factor of investigation of qualities. Thus, what is designated as ‘the awakening factor of investigation of qualities’ becomes two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:12: When there is physical energy, that is the awakening factor of energy. When there is mental energy, that too is the awakening factor of energy. Thus, what is designated as ‘the awakening factor of energy’ becomes two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:13: When there is rapture with placed and sustained thought, that is the awakening factor of rapture. When there is rapture without placed and sustained thought, that too is the awakening factor of rapture. Thus, what is designated as ‘the awakening factor of rapture’ becomes two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:14: When there is tranquility of the body, that is the awakening factor of tranquility. When there is tranquility of the mind, that too is the awakening factor of tranquility. Thus, what is designated as ‘the awakening factor of tranquility’ becomes two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:15: Whether it is immersion with directed thought and evaluation, it is the awakening factor of immersion; whether it is immersion without directed thought and evaluation, it is also the awakening factor of immersion. Thus it comes under the heading of ‘awakening factor of immersion.’ In this way, they are two by way of exposition.
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those mendicants went to the park of the wanderers of other sects. They exchanged greetings with those wanderers and, when the polite and courteous talk was finished, sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the wanderers of other sects said to them:
translations.sn46.52:3: “Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples like this: ‘Come, mendicants, give up the five hindrances, those corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, and develop the seven awakening factors as they really are.’ We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples like this: ‘Come, friends, give up the five hindrances, those corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, and develop the seven awakening factors as they really are.’ Here, friends, what is the distinction, what is the specific purpose, what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is to say, between his Dhamma teaching and our Dhamma teaching, or between his instruction and our instruction?”
translations.sn46.52:4: Then those mendicants neither approved nor dismissed the words of those wanderers of other sects. Without approving or dismissing, they rose from their seats and left, thinking: “We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.” Then those mendicants, after wandering for alms in Sāvatthī and returning from their almsround after the meal, went to the Blessed One. They bowed to the Blessed One, sat down to one side, and told him what had happened.
translations.sn46.52:8: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other sects speak like this, they should be told: ‘But friends, is there a method by which the five hindrances become ten, and the seven awakening factors become fourteen?’ Questioned like this, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer, and furthermore, they will meet with frustration. Why is that? Because, mendicants, it is outside their domain. I do not see anyone, mendicants, in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for a Tathāgata, or a disciple of a Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what, mendicants, is the method by which the five hindrances become ten? Whether it is sensual desire internally, it is a hindrance; whether it is sensual desire externally, it is also a hindrance. Thus it comes under the heading of ‘hindrance of sensual desire.’ In this way, they are two by way of exposition. Whether it is ill will internally, it is a hindrance; whether it is ill will externally, it is also a hindrance. Thus it comes under the heading of ‘hindrance of ill will.’ In this way, they are two by way of exposition. Whether it is dullness, it is a hindrance; whether it is drowsiness, it is also a hindrance. Thus it comes under the heading of ‘hindrance of dullness and drowsiness.’ In this way, they are two by way of exposition. Whether it is restlessness, it is a hindrance; whether it is remorse, it is also a hindrance. Thus it comes under the heading of ‘hindrance of restlessness and remorse.’ In this way, they are two by way of exposition. Whether it is doubt regarding internal things, it is a hindrance; whether it is doubt regarding external things, it is also a hindrance. Thus it comes under the heading of ‘hindrance of doubt.’ In this way, they are two by way of exposition. This is the method by which the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:10: Mendicants, at a time when the mind is restless, it is the wrong time to develop the awakening factor of investigation of states, the wrong time to develop the awakening factor of energy, and the wrong time to develop the awakening factor of rapture. Why is that? Because, mendicants, a restless mind is difficult to calm down with those states.
translations.sn46.53:11: Suppose, mendicants, a man wanted to extinguish a large bonfire. If he were to throw dry grass into it, throw dry cow-dung into it, throw dry wood into it, blow on it with his mouth, and not scatter dust over it; would that man be able to extinguish that large bonfire?” “No, bhante.”
translations.sn46.53:13: But, mendicants, at a time when the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop the awakening factor of tranquility, the right time to develop the awakening factor of immersion, and the right time to develop the awakening factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because, mendicants, a restless mind is easy to calm down with those states.
translations.sn46.53:14: Suppose, mendicants, a man wanted to extinguish a large bonfire. If he were to throw wet grass into it, throw wet cow-dung into it, throw wet wood into it, spray it with water, and scatter dust over it; would that man be able to extinguish that large bonfire?” “Yes, bhante.”
translations.sn46.53:2: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other sects speak like this, they should be told: ‘Friends, at a time when the mind is sluggish, which awakening factors is it the wrong time to develop, and which awakening factors is it the right time to develop? And friends, at a time when the mind is restless, which awakening factors is it the wrong time to develop, and which awakening factors is it the right time to develop?’ Questioned like this, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer, and furthermore, they will meet with frustration. Why is that? Because, mendicants, it is outside their domain.
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see anyone, mendicants, in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for a Tathāgata, or a disciple of a Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.53:4: Mendicants, at a time when the mind is sluggish, it is the wrong time to develop the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of immersion, and the awakening factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is hard to rouse with those qualities.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. If they threw wet grass, wet cow dung, and wet wood onto it, blew on it with a spray of water, and scattered dust over it, could they make that small fire flare up?” “No, sir.”
translations.sn46.53:7: But mendicants, at a time when the mind is sluggish, it is the right time to develop the awakening factor of investigation of qualities, the awakening factor of energy, and the awakening factor of rapture. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is easy to rouse with those qualities.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. If they threw dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry wood onto it, blew on it with their mouth, and did not scatter dust over it, could they make that small fire flare up?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.sn46.54:1: At one time the Buddha was staying among the Koliyans, where they have a town named Haliddavasana. Then, in the morning, several mendicants robed up and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then those mendicants thought: “It’s too early to wander for alms in Haliddavasana. Why don’t we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.54:11: “Mendicants, when wanderers of other sects speak like this, you should say to them: ‘But friends, how is the heart’s release by loving-kindness developed? What is its destination, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, and what is its end? How is the heart’s release by compassion developed? What is its destination, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, and what is its end? How is the heart’s release by empathetic joy developed? What is its destination, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, and what is its end? How is the heart’s release by equanimity developed? What is its destination, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, and what is its end?’ When questioned like this, the wanderers of other sects will be unable to answer, and furthermore, they will be frustrated. Why is that? Because it is outside their domain. Mendicants, I do not see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, in this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions, except for a Realized One or a disciple of a Realized One, or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.54:12: And how, mendicants, is the heart’s release by loving-kindness developed? What is its destination, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, and what is its end? Here, a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness … they develop the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by loving-kindness, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, ripening as letting go. If they wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ they dwell perceiving the repulsive. If they wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ they dwell perceiving the unrepulsive. If they wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,’ they dwell perceiving the repulsive. If they wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ they dwell perceiving the unrepulsive. If they wish: ‘Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell in equanimity, mindful and aware,’ they dwell in equanimity, mindful and aware. Or else, they dwell having attained the liberation of the beautiful. I say that the heart’s release by loving-kindness has the beautiful as its culmination, for a mendicant here who has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: And how, mendicants, is the heart’s release by compassion developed? What is its destination, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, and what is its end? Here, a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by compassion … they develop the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by compassion, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, ripening as letting go. If they wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ they dwell perceiving the repulsive … If they wish: ‘Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell in equanimity, mindful and aware,’ they dwell in equanimity, mindful and aware. Or else, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ they enter and dwell in the dimension of infinite space. I say that the heart’s release by compassion has the dimension of infinite space as its culmination, for a mendicant here who has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: And how, mendicants, is the heart’s release by empathetic joy developed? What is its destination, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, and what is its end? Here, a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by empathetic joy … they develop the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by empathetic joy, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, ripening as letting go. If they wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ they dwell perceiving the repulsive … If they wish: ‘Avoiding both the unrepulsive and the repulsive, may I dwell in equanimity, mindful and aware,’ they dwell in equanimity, mindful and aware. Or else, by completely transcending the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ they enter and dwell in the dimension of infinite consciousness. I say that the heart’s release by empathetic joy has the dimension of infinite consciousness as its culmination, for a mendicant here who has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:3: “Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples in this way: ‘Come, bhikkhus, having abandoned the five hindrances, the corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to oneself, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will. Dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion... with a mind imbued with empathetic joy... with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to oneself, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, without ill will.’”
translations.sn46.8:1: On one occasion the Venerable Upavāna and the Venerable Sāriputta were staying at Kosambi in Ghosita’s Park. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to the Venerable Upavāna. He exchanged greetings with him, and when they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Upavāna:
translations.sn46.8:2: “Friend Upavāna, could a bhikkhu know for himself: ‘Through rational attention, these seven factors of enlightenment are well-undertaken by me and lead to a comfortable dwelling’?” “A bhikkhu could know for himself, friend Sāriputta: ‘Through rational attention, these seven factors of enlightenment are well-undertaken by me and lead to a comfortable dwelling.’”
translations.sn47.10:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, went to a certain dwelling of bhikkhunīs. Having arrived, he sat down on the seat prepared. Then many bhikkhunīs went to the Venerable Ānanda, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhunīs said to the Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn47.10:2: “Here, Bhante Ānanda, many bhikkhunīs, dwelling with minds well-established in the four establishments of mindfulness, perceive a grand distinction between what went before and what comes after.” “So it is, sisters, so it is, sisters. For anyone, sisters, whether a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī, who dwells with a mind well-established in the four establishments of mindfulness, this is to be expected: that they will perceive a grand distinction between what went before and what comes after.”
translations.sn47.10:7: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings... mind... principles, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. As he dwells contemplating principles, there arises in him a fever in the body based on a principle as an object, or sluggishness of mind, or the mind is distracted outwardly. Then, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should direct his mind toward some inspiring sign. As he directs his mind toward some inspiring sign, gladness is born. In one who is glad, rapture is born. In one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. He reflects thus: ‘The purpose for which I directed my mind has been achieved. Now let me withdraw it.’ He withdraws the mind and does not think or examine. He understands: ‘I am without thought and examination; internally mindful, I am happy.’ This, Ānanda, is development by direction.
translations.sn47.10:9: Thus, Ānanda, I have taught development by direction and development without direction. What should be done by a teacher seeking the welfare of his disciples, out of compassion, has been done by me for you. These, Ānanda, are the roots of trees; these are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda, do not be negligent; do not be regretful later. This is our instruction to you.”
translations.sn47.13:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time the Venerable Sāriputta was staying among the Magadhans at the village of Nālaka, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. The novice Cunda was the Venerable Sāriputta’s attendant.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then the Venerable Sāriputta attained final Nibbāna through that very illness. Then the novice Cunda, taking the Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and robes, went to the Venerable Ānanda at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Sāvatthī. Having arrived, he bowed to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the novice Cunda said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Bhante, the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna. These are his bowl and robes.”
translations.sn47.13:3: “Friend Cunda, this is a topic for conversation to see the Blessed One. Let us go, friend Cunda, to the Blessed One and report this matter to him.” “Yes, Bhante,” the novice Cunda replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda went to the Blessed One, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Bhante, this novice Cunda says: ‘The Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna; these are his bowl and robes.’ Indeed, Bhante, my body feels as if it were drugged, the quarters are not clear to me, and things do not appear to me, since hearing that the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna.”
translations.sn47.19:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhans at a town of the Sumbhans named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, once upon a time, an acrobat set up his bamboo pole and addressed his apprentice, Medakathālikā: ‘Come, dear Medakathālikā, climb the bamboo pole and stand on my shoulders.’ ‘Yes, teacher,’ the apprentice Medakathālikā replied to the acrobat, climbed the bamboo pole, and stood on the teacher’s shoulders. Then the acrobat said to the apprentice Medakathālikā: ‘You look after me, dear Medakathālikā, and I will look after you. Thus, guarding each other and protecting each other, we will show our skills, make a profit, and safely descend from the bamboo pole.’ When this was said, the apprentice Medakathālikā said to the acrobat: ‘That is not the way it will be, teacher. You, teacher, look after yourself, and I will look after myself. Thus, self-guarded and self-protected, we will show our skills, make a profit, and safely descend from the bamboo pole.’”
translations.sn47.19:2: “That was the right way there,” the Blessed One said, “just as the apprentice Medakathālikā said to the teacher. Bhikkhus, the establishment of mindfulness should be practiced with the thought, ‘I will protect myself’; the establishment of mindfulness should be practiced with the thought, ‘I will protect others.’ Protecting oneself, one protects others; protecting others, one protects oneself.
translations.sn47.20:1: Thus have I heard— At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhans at a town of the Sumbhans named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn47.20:2: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a large crowd of people were to gather, crying, ‘The most beautiful girl in the land! The most beautiful girl in the land!’ And that most beautiful girl in the land were to dance and sing with the utmost skill. Then a even larger crowd of people would gather, crying, ‘The most beautiful girl in the land is dancing and singing!’ Then a man would come along, wishing to live, not wishing to die, wishing for happiness, and recoiling from pain. They would say to him: ‘Here, mister, is a bowl of oil filled to the brim. You must carry it between the large crowd and the most beautiful girl in the land. A man with a drawn sword will follow right behind you. Wherever you spill even a little bit, right there he will cut off your head.’ What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that man, neglecting that bowl of oil, turn his attention to external things?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn47.25:1: Thus have I heard— At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging friendly and polite greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: “What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the True Dhamma does not last long? And what is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the True Dhamma lasts long?”
translations.sn47.25:2: “Brahmin, it is because the four establishments of mindfulness are not developed and not cultivated that, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the True Dhamma does not last long. And it is because the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and cultivated that, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the True Dhamma lasts long.”
translations.sn47.29:2: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, went to the house of the householder Sirivaḍḍha; having gone there, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Sirivaḍḍha: “I hope you are bearing up, householder, I hope you are getting by. I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is evident, not their increase.” “Venerable sir, I am not bearing up, I am not getting by. Strong painful feelings are increasing in me, not subsiding; their increase is evident, not their subsiding.”
translations.sn47.29:3: “Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world; I will dwell contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… mind in mind …pe… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world.’ Thus, householder, you should train yourself.”
translations.sn47.33:1: “Bhikkhus, for whomever the four establishments of mindfulness are missed, the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering is missed. For whomever the four establishments of mindfulness are undertaken, the noble path leading to the complete destruction of suffering is undertaken.”
translations.sn47.37:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, whatever desire he has for the body is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. As he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, whatever desire he has for feelings is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. As he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, whatever desire he has for the mind is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. Because the body is fully understood, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. As he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. Because feelings are fully understood, the Deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: They meditate observing the mind as a mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure for the world. For one meditating observing the mind as a mind, the mind becomes fully understood. Because the mind is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the establishment of mindfulness, the development of the establishment of mindfulness, and the practice leading to the development of the establishment of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the establishment of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu meditates observing the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure for the world; he meditates observing feelings as feelings …pe… he meditates observing the mind as a mind …pe… he meditates observing qualities as qualities, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called, bhikkhus, the establishment of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.40:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the development of the establishment of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu meditates observing the nature of arising in the body, he meditates observing the nature of vanishing in the body, he meditates observing the nature of both arising and vanishing in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure for the world. He meditates observing the nature of arising in feelings …pe… he meditates observing the nature of arising in the mind …pe… he meditates observing the nature of arising in qualities, he meditates observing the nature of vanishing in qualities, he meditates observing the nature of both arising and vanishing in qualities, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called, bhikkhus, the development of the establishment of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.4:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was staying among the Kosalans at the brahmin village of Sala. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus …pe… and said this:
translations.sn47.4:2: “Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are new, recently ordained, recently come to this Dhamma and Discipline, should be encouraged, settled, and established by you in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. In which four? ‘Come, friends, meditate observing the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the sake of knowing the body as it really is; meditate observing feelings as feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the sake of knowing feelings as they really are; meditate observing the mind as a mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the sake of knowing the mind as it really is; meditate observing qualities as qualities, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the sake of knowing qualities as they really are.’
translations.sn47.4:3: Even those bhikkhus who are trainees, who have not yet attained their heart's goal, but live aspiring for the supreme security from bondage, they too meditate observing the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the full understanding of the body; they meditate observing feelings as feelings … for the full understanding of feelings; they meditate observing the mind as a mind … for the full understanding of the mind; they meditate observing qualities as qualities, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the full understanding of qualities.
translations.sn47.4:4: Even those bhikkhus who are perfected ones, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated by right final knowledge, they too meditate observing the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, being detached from the body; they meditate observing feelings as feelings … being detached from feelings; they meditate observing the mind as a mind … being detached from the mind; they meditate observing qualities as qualities, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, and one-pointed, being detached from qualities.
translations.sn47.6:1: “Bhikkhus, once upon a time, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, bhikkhus, while being carried off by the hawk, the quail lamented: ‘We are so unlucky, we have so little merit, that we wandered out of our own range into the territory of others. If today we had wandered within our own range, in our ancestral territory, this hawk would have been no match for me, that is, in a fight.’ ‘But what, quail, is your own range, your ancestral territory?’ ‘It is a field turned up by the plow, a place of clods.’ Then the hawk, confident in her own strength, not boasting of her own strength, released the quail, saying: ‘Go then, quail, but even there you will not escape me.’
translations.sn47.6:2: Then, bhikkhus, the quail went to a field turned up by the plow, a place of clods, climbed onto a large clod, and stood challenging the hawk: ‘Come now, hawk! Come now, hawk!’ Then the hawk, confident in her own strength, not boasting of her own strength, tucked in both wings and suddenly swooped down on the quail. When the quail knew, ‘The hawk has come close,’ he slipped into the space between that very clod. Then, bhikkhus, the hawk shattered her breast right there. So it is, bhikkhus, for one who wanders out of their range into the territory of others.
translations.sn47.6:3: Therefore, bhikkhus, do not wander out of your range into the territory of others. For those who wander out of their range into the territory of others, Mara will find an opening, Mara will find an object. And what, bhikkhus, is not a bhikkhu’s range, but the territory of others? It is the five cords of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear …pe… odors cognizable by the nose …pe… tastes cognizable by the tongue …pe… tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—this, bhikkhus, is not a bhikkhu’s range, but the territory of others.
translations.sn47.7:1: “Bhikkhus, there are in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, rugged and uneven regions where neither monkeys nor humans travel. There are in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, rugged and uneven regions where monkeys travel, but not humans. There are in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, level and delightful stretches of ground where both monkeys and humans travel. There, bhikkhus, hunters set traps of pitch on the monkey-trails to catch the monkeys.”
translations.sn47.8:2: Mendicants, that foolish, incompetent, unskillful cook does not pick up on his own master’s signs: ‘Today this soup pleased my master,’ or ‘he reached for this one,’ or ‘he took a lot of this one,’ or ‘he spoke in praise of this one.’ Or ‘Today my master pleased the sour soup,’ or ‘he reached for the sour,’ or ‘he took a lot of the sour,’ or ‘he spoke in praise of the sour.’ Or ‘Today my master pleased the bitter soup … the pungent … the sweet … the alkaline … the non-alkaline … the salty … or the unsalted soup,’ or ‘he reached for the unsalted,’ or ‘he took a lot of the unsalted,’ or ‘he spoke in praise of the unsalted.’
translations.sn47.8:4: Mendicants, that foolish, incompetent, unskillful monk does not gain pleasant dwellings in this very life, nor does he gain mindfulness and situational awareness. Why is that? Because, mendicants, that foolish, incompetent, unskillful monk does not pick up on the signs of his own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Suppose, mendicants, a wise, competent, skillful cook were to serve a king or a royal minister with various kinds of soups—sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, alkaline, non-alkaline, salty, and unsalted.
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Vajirā robed up in the morning and, taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, she returned from her almsround after the meal and went to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding. Entering the Blind Men’s Grove, she sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day’s abiding. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to cause fear, trepidation, and terror in the nun Vajirā, and wanting to make her fall away from immersion, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: “By whom was this being created? Where is the creator of the being? Where has the being arisen? Where does the being cease?”
translations.sn5.10:3: Then the nun Vajirā thought: “Who is this, human or non-human, who speaks this verse?” Then she thought: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to cause me fear, trepidation, and terror, and wanting to make me fall away from immersion.” Then the nun Vajirā, knowing that this was Māra the Wicked, replied to him in verses:
translations.sn5.10:4: “Why do you believe there is a ‘being’? Māra, is this your view? This is just a heap of conditioned processes; no ‘being’ is found here.
translations.sn5.10:5: Just as, with an assembly of parts, the word ‘chariot’ is used; so, when the aggregates exist, there is the convention ‘a being’.
translations.sn5.10:6: It is only suffering that comes to be, suffering that stands and passes away. Nothing but suffering comes to be, nothing but suffering ceases.”
translations.sn5.1:1: So I have heard—at one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then the nun Āḷavikā robed up in the morning and, taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, she returned from her almsround after the meal and went to the Blind Men’s Grove seeking seclusion. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to cause fear, trepidation, and terror in the nun Āḷavikā, and wanting to make her fall away from seclusion, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: “There is no escape in the world, what will you do with seclusion? Enjoy the delights of sensual pleasure; do not be one who regrets it later.”
translations.sn5.1:3: Then the nun Āḷavikā thought: “Who is this, human or non-human, who speaks this verse?” Then she thought: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to cause me fear, trepidation, and terror, and wanting to make me fall away from seclusion.” Then the nun Āḷavikā, knowing that this was Māra the Wicked, replied to him in verses:
translations.sn5.1:4: “There is an escape in the world, well-touched by me with wisdom; O Wicked One, kinsman of the negligent, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sensual pleasures are like swords and stakes; the aggregates are their chopping block. What you call ‘delight in sensual pleasure’ has become ‘non-delight’ for me.”
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Āḷavikā knows me,” miserable and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: “That state which is to be attained by seers, so difficult to reach; that cannot be attained by a woman with her two-fingered wisdom.”
translations.sn5.2:4: “What does womanhood matter when the mind is well-concentrated, when knowledge is occurring, for one seeing the Dhamma rightly?
translations.sn5.2:5: For one who might think: ‘I am a woman’ or ‘I am a man’ or ‘I am anything at all’—to such a person Māra is fit to speak.”
translations.sn5.3:2: “Why are you like one whose son has died, sitting alone with a tearful face? Having entered the middle of the woods alone, are you looking for a man?”
translations.sn5.3:3: Then the nun Kisāgotamī thought: “Who is this, human or non-human, who speaks this verse?” Then she thought: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to cause me fear, trepidation, and terror, and wanting to make me fall away from immersion.”
translations.sn5.3:5: “I am one whose sons have died forever; men have come to an end for me. I do not sorrow, I do not weep, and I am not afraid of you, friend.
translations.sn5.3:6: Delight is destroyed everywhere, the mass of darkness is shattered; having conquered the army of Death, I live without taints.”
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Kisāgotamī knows me,” miserable and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Vijayā robed up in the morning … she sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day’s abiding. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to cause fear, trepidation, and terror in the nun Vijayā, and wanting to make her fall away from immersion, approached her and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: “You are young and beautiful, and I am a young youth; come, let us enjoy ourselves with the music of a five-piece ensemble.”
translations.sn5.4:4: “Sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches that are delightful; I hand them back to you, Māra, I have no need for them.”
translations.sn5.4:5: With this foul body, fragile and crumbling, I am disgusted and ashamed; craving for sensual pleasures has been rooted out.
translations.sn5.4:6: Those beings who have reached the form realm, and those who stay in the formless, and that peaceful attainment—darkness is destroyed everywhere.
translations.sn5.5:1: At Savatthi. Then the bhikkhuni Uppalavanna, having dressed in the morning... stood at the foot of a certain sal tree in full flower. Then Mara the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in the bhikkhuni Uppalavanna, desiring to make her fall away from concentration, approached the bhikkhuni Uppalavanna and addressed her in verse:
translations.sn5.5:2: “Having come to the sal tree with its flowering top, you stand alone at its foot, bhikkhuni. You have no companion of such beauty; foolish girl, do you not fear the rogues?”
translations.sn5.5:4: “Even if a hundred thousand rogues like you were to come here, I would not stir a hair, I would not tremble; even alone, Mara, I do not fear you.
translations.sn5.5:6: I am a master of my own mind, the bases of power are well-developed; I am released from all bonds, I do not fear you, friend.”
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Mara the Evil One, realizing 'The bhikkhuni Uppalavanna knows me,' miserable and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: “Why do you not approve of birth? One who is born enjoys sensual pleasures. Who on earth persuaded you of this: ‘Bhikkhuni, do not approve of birth’?”
translations.sn5.6:3: “For one who is born there is death; one who is born encounters sufferings—binding, slaughter, and affliction; therefore one should not approve of birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha taught the Dhamma, the transcending of birth; for the abandoning of all suffering, he established me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: Those beings who have reached the form realm, and those who stay in the formless, not fully understanding cessation, return to renewed existence.”
translations.sn5.7:1: At Savatthi. Then the bhikkhuni Upacala, having dressed in the morning... sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Then Mara the Evil One approached the bhikkhuni Upacala and said to her: “Where do you wish to be reborn, bhikkhuni?” “I do not wish to be reborn anywhere, friend.”
translations.sn5.7:2: “There are the Tavatimsa gods, the Yama gods, and the Tusita gods; the gods who delight in creation, and the gods who wield power over others' creations. Direct your mind there, and you will experience delight.”
translations.sn5.7:3: “The Tavatimsa gods, the Yama gods, and the Tusita gods; the gods who delight in creation, and the gods who wield power over others' creations—they are bound by the bond of sensual pleasure, they come again under the power of Mara.
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is on fire, the whole world is smoking; the whole world is ablaze, the whole world is trembling.
translations.sn5.7:5: That which does not tremble, which is not ablaze, which is not frequented by worldlings, where there is no access for Mara—there my mind delights.”
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Mara the Evil One, realizing 'The bhikkhuni Upacala knows me,' miserable and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Savatthi. Then the bhikkhuni Sisupacala, having dressed in the morning... sat down at the foot of a certain tree for the day's abiding. Then Mara the Evil One approached the bhikkhuni Sisupacala and said to her: “Whose creed do you approve of, bhikkhuni?” “I do not approve of anyone's creed, friend.”
translations.sn5.8:2: “On whose account have you shaved your head? You look like an ascetic, yet you do not approve of a creed. Why do you wander like one who is confused?”
translations.sn5.8:3: “Outside of here, there are creeds; they place confidence in views. I do not approve of their teaching; they are not skilled in the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: Everywhere free, unattached, the one with vision sees everything; he has reached the end of all karma, liberated in the destruction of acquisitions. He is the Blessed One, my teacher; I approve of his instruction.”
translations.sn5.9:2: “By whom was this puppet created? Where is the maker of the puppet? Where has the puppet arisen? Where does the puppet cease?”
translations.sn5.9:4: “This puppet is not self-made, nor is this misery made by another; it has come into being dependent on a cause, and with the breaking of the cause it ceases.
translations.sn5.9:6: So too these aggregates, elements, and these six sense bases; they have come into being dependent on a cause, and with the breaking of the cause they cease.”
translations.sn56.11:1: On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Varanasi in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the group of five bhikkhus:
translations.sn56.11:10: “As long as, bhikkhus, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are, with their three phases and twelve aspects, was not thoroughly purified, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in the world with its devas, Maras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths... was thoroughly purified, then I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment... Knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Unshakeable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’” This is what the Blessed One said. The group of five bhikkhus were delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words.
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this discourse was being spoken, there arose in the Venerable Kondañña the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye: “Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.”
translations.sn56.11:13: And so in that moment, in that instant, in that second, the cry reached as far as the Brahma world. And this ten-thousandfold world system shook, quaked, and trembled, and an immeasurable, magnificent radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the divine majesty of the devas.
translations.sn56.11:2: “Bhikkhus, these two extremes should not be followed by one who has gone forth. Which two? That which is devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure in sensual objects, which is low, vulgar, common, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and that which is devotion to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Middle Way has been awakened to by the Tathagata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbana.
translations.sn56.11:3: And what, bhikkhus, is that Middle Way awakened to by the Tathagata... which leads to Nibbana? It is just this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is that Middle Way awakened to by the Tathagata... which leads to Nibbana.”
translations.sn56.11:4: Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; union with what is displeasing is suffering; separation from what is pleasing is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: it is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for extermination. Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: it is this noble eightfold path; that is, right view ...pe... right concentration.
translations.sn56.11:5: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before. ‘This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood’: such was the vision ...pe... that arose in me. ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before.
translations.sn56.11:6: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned’: such was the vision ...pe... that arose in me. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before.
translations.sn56.11:7: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized’: such was the vision ...pe... that arose in me. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before.
translations.sn56.11:8: ‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before. ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed’: such was the vision ...pe... that arose in me. ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed’: such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light that arose in me, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard before.
translations.sn56.11:9: As long, bhikkhus, as my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are, with their three phases and twelve aspects, was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Maras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
translations.sn56.20:1: “Bhikkhus, these four things are real, not unreal, not otherwise.
