What four? ‘This is suffering,’ bhikkhus, is real, not unreal, not otherwise. ‘This is the origin of suffering’ is real, not unreal, not otherwise. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’ is real, not unreal, not otherwise. ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’ is real, not unreal, not otherwise. These, bhikkhus, are the four things that are real, not unreal, not otherwise.”
translations.sn56.26:1: “Bhikkhus, those for whom you have compassion and who think you should be listened to—whether friends or colleagues or relatives or kinsmen—these you should encourage, settle, and establish in the breakthrough to the four noble truths as they really are.”
translations.sn56.26:2: “To which four? To the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Those for whom you have compassion and who think you should be listened to—whether friends or colleagues or relatives or kinsmen—these you should encourage, settle, and establish in the breakthrough to these four noble truths as they really are.”
translations.sn56.27:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. These four noble truths, bhikkhus, are real, not unreal, not otherwise; therefore they are called ‘noble truths.’”
translations.sn56.28:1: “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. In this world with its devas, Maras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathagata is the Noble One; therefore they are called ‘noble truths.’”
translations.sn56.30:1: On one occasion a number of senior bhikkhus were dwelling among the Cetis at Sahancanika. Then, in the afternoon, when the senior bhikkhus had returned from their alms round and had assembled in the circular hall, this intermediate discussion arose: “Friends, does one who sees suffering also see the origin of suffering, also see the cessation of suffering, and also see the way leading to the cessation of suffering?”
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambi in a Simsapa forest. Then the Buddha, picking up a few Simsapa leaves in his hand, addressed the mendicants: “What do you think, mendicants? Which is more: the few Simsapa leaves in my hand, or those in the forest above?” “Sir, the few Simsapa leaves in your hand are tiny; those in the forest above are far more.” “In the same way, mendicants, there is much more that I have known but not told you. And why haven't I told you? Because it is not beneficial, it does not belong to the fundamentals of the spiritual life, and it does not lead to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, enlightenment, and Nibbana. That is why I have not told you.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what have I told you? I have told you: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.sn56.31:3: And why have I told you this? Because it is beneficial, it belongs to the fundamentals of the spiritual life, and it leads to disillusionment, dispassion, cessation, peace, insight, enlightenment, and Nibbana. That is why I have told you.
translations.sn56.35:1: “Suppose, mendicants, there was a man who lived for a hundred years. Someone might say to him: ‘Come now, my good man, they will strike you with a hundred spears in the morning, a hundred spears at noon, and a hundred spears in the evening. And you, my good man, being struck every day by three hundred spears, living for a hundred years, at the end of those hundred years you will realize the four noble truths which you had not realized before.’
translations.sn56.35:2: It would be worth it for a gentleman to accept this, for his own benefit. Why is that? Because this transmigration is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not discerned of the blows from spears, swords, arrows, and axes. Even if it were so, mendicants, I do not say that the realization of the four noble truths is accompanied by pain and sorrow; rather, I say that the realization of the four noble truths is accompanied by pleasure and happiness. Which four? The noble truth of suffering … the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.”
translations.sn56.36:1: “Suppose, mendicants, a man were to cut up all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Rose-apple Continent and collect them into a single pile; having collected them, he would make them into skewers. Having made them into skewers, he would impale the large creatures in the great ocean on the large skewers, the middle-sized creatures on the middle-sized skewers, and the tiny creatures on the tiny skewers. The large creatures in the great ocean would not be exhausted, mendicants.
translations.sn56.36:2: Then the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Rose-apple Continent would be used up and exhausted. But there are far more tiny creatures in the great ocean, mendicants, which would not be easy to impale on skewers. Why is that? Because of the smallness of their bodies. So great, mendicants, is the state of loss. A person accomplished in view, being freed from such a great state of loss, understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.sn56.42:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rajagaha on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain. Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: “Come, mendicants, let’s go to the Peak of the Echo for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, sir,” those mendicants replied. Then the Buddha, together with many mendicants, went to the Peak of the Echo. One of the mendicants saw a great abyss at the Peak of the Echo. Seeing it, he said to the Buddha: “Sir, this abyss is indeed great; it is indeed terrifying. Is there, sir, any other abyss greater and more terrifying than this one?” “There is, monk, another abyss greater and more terrifying than this one.”
translations.sn56.42:2: “But what, sir, is that other abyss greater and more terrifying than this one?” “Mendicants, those ascetics or brahmins who do not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering,’ they delight in choices that lead to birth, they delight in choices that lead to old age, they delight in choices that lead to death, they delight in choices that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Delighting in these choices, they continue to construct choices that lead to birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Having constructed these choices, they fall into the abyss of birth, they fall into the abyss of old age, they fall into the abyss of death, they fall into the abyss of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from suffering, I say.”
translations.sn56.45:1: At one time the Buddha was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then the venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms. The venerable Ānanda saw many Licchavi youths practicing archery in the assembly hall, shooting arrows through a tiny keyhole from a distance, shot after shot without missing. Seeing this, he thought: “These Licchavi youths are indeed trained, these Licchavi youths are indeed well-trained; in that they can shoot arrows through a tiny keyhole from a distance, shot after shot without missing.”
translations.sn56.45:3: “What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult and harder to achieve—to shoot arrows through a tiny keyhole from a distance, shot after shot without missing, or to pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with another tip?” “This is more difficult, bhante, and harder to achieve—to pierce the tip of a hair split seven times with another tip.” “But, Ānanda, they pierce something even more difficult to pierce who pierce as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’”
translations.sn56.46:1: “Monks, there are world-interstices, abysmal, open, of blinding darkness and gloom, where the light of the moon and sun, so powerful and mighty, does not reach.”
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Buddha: “That is indeed a great darkness, bhante, a very great darkness. Is there, bhante, another darkness greater and more terrifying than that one?” “There is, monk, another darkness greater and more terrifying than that one.”
translations.sn56.48:1: “Monks, suppose this great earth were covered with one mass of water. A man would throw a yoke with a single hole into it. The east wind would carry it west, the west wind would carry it east, the north wind would carry it south, and the south wind would carry it north. There was a blind turtle there. It would surface once every hundred years. What do you think, monks, would that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, put its neck into that yoke with a single hole?” “It would be a matter of chance, bhante, that the blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, would put its neck into that yoke with a single hole.”
translations.sn56.48:2: “So too, monks, it is a matter of chance that one obtains the human state. So too, it is a matter of chance that a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One arises in the world. So too, it is a matter of chance that the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata shines in the world. But now, monks, this human state has been obtained, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by a Tathāgata shines in the world.”
